en: Preface to the Commentary on the Essential Points of the Ritual Procedures for Dissolving and Explaining the *Vajra* [Sūtra].

As for taking the Dharma-body as the Way: it is vast enough to encompass all sand-grained worlds and subtle enough to enter a single mote of dust. It is neither empty nor existent, and has no interior or exterior.
To awaken to it is to become one of the Four Holy Ones; to be deluded by it is to become one of the Six Worlds of Ordinary Beings. Therefore...
Śākyamuni beheld the truth upon seeing the morning star. Then, at places such as the Deer Park, Śrāvastī, and Jetavana, he intended to awaken sentient beings through this Way;
thus, he first expounded the Hinayana teachings and subsequently developed the school of Emptiness, proclaiming the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in successive order.
This present sutra is included within the section of the Great *Prajñāpāramitā*, beginning from...

Subhūti extended his request, and the Great Awakened One ultimately answered his questions. By abiding in cessation and subduing [the afflictions], they together severed twenty-seven doubts, gradually eliminated the two attachments, and entered suddenly into the One Vehicle.
Now, there was the Chan Master Zongjing of the Song dynasty, who was among the ranks of those who have attained the truth (*arhat*).

His compassion was profound and his wisdom vast; his learning was as expansive as the ocean. His realization of the Way penetrated the subtle and the manifest; his diction was powerful and his principles...
He grasps the profound essence within the palm of his hand and brings forth wondrous meanings before a single word is spoken. Within his speech, jade turns; within his phrases, pearls emerge.
He surveys heaven and mirrors the earth, attaining the *samādhi* of playful mastery and possessing unimpeded eloquence.

He melts together gold refined a hundred times and carves the beautiful jade of the Threefold Array. Thus, he shall take the thirty-two divisions as categorized by Xiao Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty...

Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, based on the text to elaborate upon its meaning and analyze its subtle nuances, a formal structure (*kō-i*) has been established to elucidate the intent of the scripture.

This comprises seven general frameworks: first, the summary of the outline; second, the essential points; third, the prose sections; fourth, the classification of themes; fifth, the verses of the sūtra text;

sixth, the exhortations to the world; and seventh, the conclusion by returning to the Pure Land. Alternatively, one may extensively gather materials from various sūtras and śāstras to provide direct annotations to the root text, or...
Citing the tenets of other schools to clarify its essential purpose, it sweeps away intellectual understanding and cuts through entanglements.
It serves as the correct path for gods and humans, and acts as a vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering. From the Song dynasty until the present, it has flourished throughout the four seas;

those who have seen, heard, read, or recited it are numerous, and those who have benefited in the unseen realms are many. It is like a sick person encountering a skilled King of Physicians, or a pauper...
One who attains this obtains the true jewel that fulfills all wishes. Now, this essential commentary on the assembly is due to Master Wujinding’s pilgrimage to Putuo Shan.

While passing through Suzhou, he was respectfully invited by the scholar Xu Gongjingyu and others to produce the *Ke-yi Zhu-song* (Commentary and Verses on Ritual Procedures) originally explained by his teacher, Dading.
They intended to carve it into printing blocks for wide circulation, but Master Deng declined, saying: "No."
It is well. Regarding this ritual manual (*vidhi*), the Dharma Master Shanguo Da of the capital previously compiled a commentary.

Its prose was vast and extensive, spanning ten fascicles, such that later students could not fathom its depths. Subsequently, the Dharma Master Puen Gui followed in his footsteps, compiling a *Shuoji* (Explanatory Record) in two fascicles, all of which have been carved for publication.
Nevertheless, the principles and phrasing are profound and subtle; there are occasionally points where the primary intent must be discerned.

[The previous] traces were incomplete in their selection and investigation. Your Excellency wishes to provide a golden rampart for the internal teaching; you must request a wise person to collate and revise it before it can be circulated.
For this reason, you have specially commissioned Mr. Zhang Dànzhāi to travel a thousand li with silks to request that I recompile it.

I consider this scripture to be a Mahāyāna teaching intended for those of bodhisattva capacity; as for the *Zhōngjìng* (Mirror of the Holy State), it is not— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

Only those who have fathomed the depths of the human condition are fit to provide a critical commentary (*keju*). How could people of our station, with their mundane sentiments and shallow knowledge, dare to undertake such a task?
Nevertheless, as we are disciples of the Buddha, we ought to repay his grace. If we do not propagate the Dharma and save sentient beings, we would betray the legacy left by the former sages.

Therefore, I have extracted the most essential commentaries from various schools and appended them beneath the original text of the ritual procedures (*koyi*), so that they may be preserved for posterity.
The meanings of this Illustrated Scripture have been thoroughly understood; I have not dared to impose my own arbitrary views, but have merely recorded them as they were.
Furthermore, the recluse Wu Gongqi, styled Bishan, was commissioned to transcribe the text with incense-scented brushes.

Once the work was fully completed, the lay devotee Meng Zhun of Jietuo in Baodi County and others provided the funds for carving the printing blocks, thereby fulfilling the late master’s遗志 (bequeathed will) from Daining and broadening its dissemination.

This transmission embodies the intention for an eternal plan that shall never decay. I pray that all who see, hear, or peruse it shall raise the sun of wisdom high in the mid-heavens and shatter the path of darkness within the chamber of gloom.
May all beings throughout the nine realms receive its saving grace, and may those in the three miserable paths all attain Bodhi.
By this merit, I pray for the longevity of the sovereign and to repay the auspicious kindness of the fourfold debt of gratitude; thus, I look toward the Buddha-sun with increasing reverence.
May the Dharma wheel thus be perpetually turned.
Written in the fortieth year of the Jiajing era of the Great Ming, the year of Xinhai, in the fourth month.
On the Anniversary of the Buddha’s Birth, at Shaoshi Mountain, the Dharma-heir Śramaṇa Juelian bathed his hands, burned incense,
and composed this preface for the *Annotated Ten-Volume General Catalogue of the Essential Ritual Procedures for Expounding the Diamond Sūtra*, Volume One.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
compiled by Chan Master Zongjing of Baifu Monastery in Longxing Prefecture;
and recompiled by the Śramaṇa Juelian, a successor to the ancestral lineage of the Cao-Dong orthodox school.
"Explaining and Resolving the *Vajra*" means using a metaphor to explain the title of the metaphor. "Vajra" is the metaphor for the title of the sutra;

"explaining and resolving" is the metaphor for the heading of the topical analysis (*kośa*). "Vajra" is a metaphor for the hardness and sharpness of *prajñā*, which is capable of shattering afflictions (*kleśa*).

"Xiaoshie" (Exhausting and Explaining) refers to the analytical interpretation of the structural divisions of the text, capable of distinguishing between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). "Xiao" means to smelt away; "Shi" means to explain.
It is like gold within ore: it must rely upon the red furnace, tongs, and hammer for refinement. Once the ore is removed, the gold remains.
Only then does it become a true treasure, usable with mastery. It is likewise with the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings.
Gold is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature of sentient beings; ore is a metaphor for ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*).

The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is hidden within the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), shrouded layer upon layer by the ore of afflictions. Foolish and dull sentient beings do not perceive it...
Know that you possess the original true nature, yet you have willingly dwelt in poverty and endured the cycle of rebirth in vain.
For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs appeared in the world, provisionally establishing verbal teachings for cultivation and realization, and instituting temporary stages and ranks.

Taking wisdom as the furnace, samādhi as the fire, and the severing of delusions as the hammer, they shatter the mountain of the five aggregates and break open the ore of afflictions to reveal the true gold.
The nature is refined into the precious Dharma-body, universally relieving impoverished sentient beings so that each may obtain the treasure of their own nature and attain great enjoyment.
Therefore, when my Buddha first attained enlightenment, he exclaimed: "How marvelous! How marvelous!
All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, due to attachment to delusive appearances, they do not realize it."

I shall instruct them in the Right Path so that they may forever be free from delusive thoughts and attachments, and within their own bodies perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata, becoming no different from the Buddha. Regarding the ritual manual (*kēyí*): *kē* means to sever.
When the grain is measured by the peck, its quantity becomes known; when the scripture is divided into sections (*ke*), its meaning naturally becomes clear. "Ritual" (*yi*) means "method.
The Buddha preached this sutra as a method for all sentient beings to sever delusion and clarify the truth.

Now, the commentator (*ke-jia*) takes the words, meanings, events, and principles within this sutra, and further incorporates the speech of the sages of the Three Teachings, synthesizing them into a single body to form the commentary.
The judgment [of the text] forms its chapters; thus, a ritual outline (*kayi*) is established as the title.

The general intent is to cause sentient beings to know that their inherent nature (*prakṛti*) exists within the midst of daily life. If one can simply perceive and hear without delusion, it will be empty, penetrating, and spiritually resonant;

from the gates of the six sense faculties, light will be emitted and the earth will tremble. Regarding the *Huìyào zhùjiě* (Essential Commentary on the Compendium), "compendium" means to extract the most expedient and essential points from various schools.
I have appended annotations beneath each section of the scripture, calling them "Commentary and Explanation" (*zhùjiě*). My aim is to ensure that the textual meaning is easily understood;
how could I dare to compose anything from my own arbitrary imagination? I have merely collected and recounted the established writings of antiquity, condensing them into this volume.
This is intended to ensure that [the teachings] shall endure imperishably. As for the term "scroll" (*juan*), it signifies that there are rules for unfolding and rolling up;

when one views it, it is unfolded and displayed, and when one does not view it, it is rolled and stored—hence it is called a "scroll. "Volume" (*di*) refers to sequence; "one" (*yi*) refers to the beginning.
It is the first among all the volumes.
It is said: "The Han dynasty was moved by a dream; the White Horse [Buddha] came from the West.
Kāśyapa Mātanga manifested [the Dharma] in Han. This describes the meaning of how the teachings first arrived.

The phrase "It is said" (*gài wén*) serves as the opening of the composition and is also a term of humility, expressing that the author cannot know the details but merely recounts what he has heard in a general way.
"Han" is the dynastic name. However, there was a distinction between the Western and Eastern Han.
The "Han" mentioned here refers to Emperor Xiaoming of the Eastern Han, who was the fourth son of Guangwu. "Court" refers to the imperial court.

This is the courtyard of the palace where the Son of Heaven resides and where his ministers come for audience. Regarding the one who experienced the dream: it describes the time when the Dharma was first introduced.

The Emperor was the "sender" (the one capable of being moved), and the Buddha was the "sent object" (the one moved). Through the mutual resonance of this response and stimulus, they coalesced into a dream.
As for the white horse coming from the West: this refers to the seventh year of the Yongping era, when the Emperor was sleeping in the Southern Palace and dreamed...

A golden man sixteen feet tall, with a halo encircling his neck and the sign of the "ten-thousand" (萬) inscribed upon his chest, flew through the palace courtyard, coming and going without obstruction.

Pointing to the Emperor, he said, "The establishment of the Teaching. The following morning, the Emperor assembled his ministers and ordered them to interpret the dream. At that time, the learned official Fu Yi submitted this report:

"Your servant has consulted the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Marvels in the Book of Zhou), which states that in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, in the year [of the cyclical signs]..."

Next, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jia-yin, at the hour of Zi (11 p.m.–1 a.m.), five-colored auspicious light pierced through the Taiwei Palace and then spread throughout the four directions, appearing in shades of blue and red. At that time, the mountains, rivers, palaces, and halls all shook violently;
the rivers, streams, springs, and wells overflowed with surging waters. Then the King asked his ministers the reason for this, and there was a Grand Astrologer.
Suyou replied, "This is the western region. A Great Sage was born there, and after a thousand years had passed, his teachings flowed into this land.
Your Majesty ordered that [this inscription] be carved upon stone and erected at the southern outskirts, before a celestial shrine, to record the year.
To this day, more than one thousand and seventy years have elapsed. Is it not likely that what Your Majesty dreamed of was precisely this?"
The Emperor believed this to be true and immediately dispatched eighteen men, including General of Chariots and Cavalry Qin Jing,
General of the Household Cai Yin, and Court Scholar Wang Zun, as envoys to the Western Regions to seek the Way of the Buddha.
Upon reaching the borders of India, they encountered the two Indian monks Mātanga and Dharmaratna, as well as King Udayana, in the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.
Fourth, he used white silk to paint one scroll of an image of Śākyamuni, along with the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*, the *Sūtra on Severing the Bonds of the Ten Abodes*,
the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Past Lives*, the *Sūtra of the Dharma-Ocean Treasury*, and the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Original Deeds*, totaling six hundred thousand words.
Carrying [the scriptures] upon a white horse, they returned eastward together. In the eighth year, the year Yichou (48 CE), Cai Yin and his party arrived at Luoyang;

Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the palace and presented the scriptures and images. The Emperor was greatly pleased and housed them in the Honglu Si. Dharmaratna subsequently arrived and concurrently engaged in proselytizing activities.
In the tenth year, the year Dingmao (50 CE), an imperial edict was issued to establish the Baima Si (White Horse Temple) to the west of the city of Luoyang.
He resided there. Because the scriptures were carried on a white horse, it was consequently named the White Horse Temple (Baima Si).
From this point, the Triple Gem began in this land. The concluding passage states: "When Kāśyapa Mātanga manifested [the Dharma] at the beginning of the Han transformation.

Here, "manifest" (zhāng) means to clarify, and "transformation" (huà) means instruction. Now, the voice of the Buddha serves as the substance of this transformative instruction. This refers to the transformation—
"At the beginning" refers to the time when he first arrived to begin his teaching.
Kumārajīva was moved by the imperial decree of the Qin sovereign; the Buddha-sun shone brightly, piercing through the dark alleys of ignorance, and the lamp of wisdom blazed with clarity.
To this day it has not perished; that the teaching flourishes is due to this very fact.
This clarifies the initial emergence of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Regarding Kumārajīva: in Sanskrit he is called Kumārajīva, which here means "Child-Longevity.
Although he was of a childlike age, he possessed the virtue of a venerable elder; thus he was called "Child-Longevity. He moved the imperial house to entrust him with the sacred scriptures.
"Qin" refers to the dynastic name of Former Qin. "Zong" means lord; it also carries the sense of veneration and honor.
"Dai" refers to an era. "Dian" refers to the ancient classics. Furthermore, there were four Qin states; this specifically refers to the reign of Fu Jian of Former Qin.
In the first month of the thirteenth year of the Jianyuan era, the Grand Historian reported: "A virtuous star has appeared in the outer heavens."
The distinction between the capital and the provinces shall be divided; there will surely be a man of great wisdom and virtue who enters to assist the Central Kingdom.
At that time, among the people of Zhao Wang’s state in Xiangyang, Dao’an Dharma Master was hailed as a sage, while Xi Zaochi was called a semi-sage.
Fu Jian, with a hundred thousand troops, attacked Xiangyang and subsequently captured these two men. He said to his attendants: "I..."
With a hundred thousand elite troops, he obtained only one and a half sages. His attendants asked who they were.
He replied: "One was Dao'an; the other was Xi Banren. When Fu Jian heard this, he spoke up and said:

"In Qizhi there is the Dharma Master Kumārajīva, who is skilled at explaining the Great and Small Vehicles and has extensively mastered the Tripiṭaka. Fu Jian silently took note of this. In the eighteenth year of the Jianyuan era...
In that year, he dispatched Lü Guang with an army of one hundred thousand to attack Qiu Ci four times. He said to Guang:
"I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Kumārajīva, who profoundly understands the characteristics of dharmas and is well-versed in the principles of yin and yang.
I think of him deeply. Wise sages are the great treasures of a nation. If you conquer Qiu Ci, welcome him back to the country immediately. Before Guang’s army had even arrived, Kumārajīva said:
King Quciz addressed Chun, saying, "An enemy force is coming from the east; do not oppose its vanguard. When the Guang army arrived, Chun engaged them in battle.
Guang defeated Quciz and killed Chun, then installed Chun’s younger brother, Baitin, as king. Guang and Shi turned eastward;
upon reaching Liangzhou, they heard that Yao Xian had already been slain by Yao Chang. Guang then usurped the title of King of Guan.
Outside [the capital], the era was called Dà'ān. He reigned for eighteen years before passing away.
His son Shào succeeded him, but he too was assassinated. Yáo Guāng’s nephew, Lǚ Lóng, became king. When Yáo Chāng died, his son Yáo Xīng ascended the throne.
In the third month of the third year of the Hóngshǐ era, a tree with joined trunks grew in front of the palace courtyard; in the Dàoyáo Garden, an onion transformed into...
The chǎi is an aromatic herb. In the fifth month, he dispatched Shí Dé, Duke of Lǒngxī, to raise an army for a western campaign.
Lǚ Lóng’s forces were utterly defeated. In the ninth month, Lóng submitted a memorial of surrender; only then was it possible to welcome Kumārajīva into Guān.

On the twentieth day of the twelfth month, he arrived in Cháng’ān and was received with the honors due to a National Preceptor (Guóshī). He selected eight śramaṇas from various regions who possessed talent and wisdom.
Among these one hundred [works], there are the Four Holy Ones and the Ten Sages, who together translated three hundred and eighty fascicles of scriptures.
This scripture was translated into the Chinese language at Cháng'ān Cǎotáng Monastery in the fifth year of the Hóngshǐ era; hence it is said:
"Kumārajīva, moved by the imperial decree of the Qin sovereign, made the Buddha-sun shine brightly. These two lines jointly praise the preceding text, extolling this [work].
The Sūtra says: "It is like the brightness of the sun that illuminates the day, and like the light of a lamp that illuminates the night.

The term "dark thoroughfare" (*hunqú*) is a metaphor for the clinging emotions of the afflictions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). These obscure the Buddha-sun that is inherently present and shroud the wisdom-lamp that is inherently present.
Consequently, one sinks and revolves through the seven realms of existence, as if in a long night or a dark thoroughfare, remaining ignorant and unaware. Up to this point...

Regarding the phrase "it has not perished until now": since the Buddha preached this Great Teaching of Prajñā, it was transmitted through the Han and Qin dynasties and reached the Chunyu era of Emperor Lizong of the Great Song, when its propagation flourished greatly; hence it is said that it has not perished until now.
As for the flourishing of this teaching, it summarizes the entirety of Śākyamuni Buddha’s lifetime of teachings and promotes their widespread circulation.
The phrase "it lies herein" (*qí zài sī yān*) is an expression used to point toward the Dharma. "Sī" means "this.
It was during the era of the two dynasties of Han and Qin that the Great Teaching flourished; therefore, it is said, "it lies herein."
In this age of the Final Dharma, reaching unto this very day, I, [Name], reverently address the worthy sages and holy ones of the ten directions currently seated at the site of enlightenment.
These are words of praise, celebration, refuge, and prayer. "Praise" refers to being born during the final period; "celebration" refers to the honor of encountering this sutra;

and "refuge and prayer" express the hope for secret empowerment. Within the Buddha’s teachings throughout his entire lifetime, there are the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma.
Regarding the distinctions between the three periods: the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years.
This so-called "Final Dharma" corresponds precisely to the latter five hundred years, at the time of two thousand five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
This was the occasion when the Master of the Text sighed and expressed his own joy, meaning that he was currently situated in the midst of the evil world of the Final Dharma.
To have encountered this scripture today is like a blind turtle encountering a floating log, or a needle’s point meeting a tiny grain of mustard seed;
it is no trivial or minor matter. Although I understand and comprehend it myself, I fear that future generations may find it difficult to do so.

Therefore, I have composed these topical outlines and explanations, desiring that students, upon seeing the outlines, may clarify the essential meaning of the sutra, as if suddenly finding light in the darkness.
This is the "Lamp. As I am about to compose this text, I fear that ordinary minds may lack deep understanding and find it difficult to reach the ultimate truth;
therefore, I pray for the secret assistance of the Triple Gem. Thus it is said: "I respectfully address the ten directions. "I, [Name]" refers to the presiding master himself.

"Respectful" (*gōng*) means reverence. "White" (*bái*) means to set forth. This refers to the sincerity of the three karmas. "The worthies and sages of the ten directions" is discussed in terms of the horizontal (spatial) dimension;

"presently seated at the site of enlightenment" (*daochang*) is discussed in terms of the vertical (temporal) dimension. The "site of enlightenment" (*daochang*) is the place where the worthies and sages of the ten directions and the three periods of time attain the Way and preach the Dharma.
The Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha and the two great Bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are precisely the Three Jewels of this land.
That is to say, the Buddha constitutes the Jewel of the Buddha, and the Bodhisattvas constitute the Jewel of the Saṅgha;

the Jewel of the Dharma is contained within them both. "Original Teacher" (Ben-shi) is an earnest title of respect; it is also called the "Original Teacher" (Ben-shi) because he is the original essence.
He is the model. His physical form emulates the legacy of the Buddha; therefore, he is called the "Original Teacher" (*mūla-śāstṛ*).
In the Sanskrit language, he is Śākyamuni, which here means "Able Benevolent One" (*Śakya*) and "Tranquil Silence" (*Muni*); this is his title as the Perfect Response.

In the Sanskrit language, Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (*Mañju*) and is also named "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Śrī*). As for Samantabhadra: his virtue is all-pervasive, hence it is called "Universal" (*Samanta*); he bestows blessings upon those above and benefits [those below].
The lower grade is called "Worthy" (xian). "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; in full it is *bodhisattva*, which translates as "Awakened Being" (jue youqing).
All who are born possess sentience (*youqing*); a Bodhisattva is simply one among sentient beings who has attained awakening. A Buddha possesses the nature of awakening.

Yet they are not devoid of emotion. Bodhisattvas likewise cannot avoid having emotion; therefore it is said: "Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above and transforming sentient beings below" is the designation for benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
The assembly of holy beings filling the void, all the deities and spirits—those with the divine eye behold from afar with their divine eyes;

those with the divine ear hear from afar with their divine ears; those who know the minds of others and the past lives perceive with the profound discernment of the holy mind. Out of compassion, out of compassion, out of great compassion!

This is a general prayer to all the assembly of noble ones: may you exercise the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to observe and illuminate, and give rise to the four means of conversion (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to bestow secret empowerment.

"Divine eye" and so forth refer to the five supernormal powers. The "noble mind" refers to the power of the miraculous domain (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), which serves as a metaphor for profound discernment.

Compassion (*maitrī*) is able to grant happiness; pity (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering; joy (*muditā*) is able to bring celebration and gladness; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is able to maintain impartiality. Thus, compassion inherently contains [all these qualities].

These are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Regarding the three invocations: they express the intensity of sincerity. The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is not mentioned because these are the assembly of holy sages;
only the Buddha possesses all six supernormal powers (*ṣad-abhijñā*), whereas those mentioned above all possess five supernormal powers.
Faithfully prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
"Faith" (xin) means weightiness and sincerity. "Prostration" (li) means embodiment. If there is faith without prostration, the mind will surely not be substantial.
If there is prostration without faith, the intention will surely not be sincere. When both are fully present, one may perform a rite of true sincerity. Constantly...
"Abiding" (zhu) signifies the meaning of distinction. It differs from the Three Jewels of the ten directions and this land mentioned previously;
this is the eternally abiding self-nature, the pure *dharmakāya*, which is the Buddha Jewel. This nature possesses the sense of awakening and illumination, which is the Dharma Jewel.
This nature possesses the meaning of harmony; it is the Sangha Jewel. "Jewel" (ratna) carries the meaning of being precious;
it refers to the three jewels as a single essence of true reality, eternally abiding.
I take refuge in all Buddhas of the ten directions. I take refuge in all Dharmas of the ten directions. I take refuge in all Saṅghas of the ten directions.
May the Wheel of Dharma turn forever to deliver all sentient beings.
This is a prayer offered with repeated layers of devotion; it is not a praise that can be fully exhausted.
Because one seeks refuge and entreats for life, and hopes for the bestowal of protection, it is called "taking refuge" (*namas*). Furthermore, "life" (*jīva*) is the totality of the single person.

Thus, the term "taking refuge" here encompasses the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind] as a whole, representing the rites of reverence, respect, and praise. It comprehensively includes all things throughout the ten directions in their horizontal expanse.
"Shu" (竪). "Buddha" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. In full, it is *Buddha*, which means "Awakened. This refers to one who is both self-awakened and awakens others;

it signifies the perfection of awakening and practice. "Dharma" carries the meaning of "guiding and maintaining. It refers to that which guides and maintains its own nature, causing sentient beings to give rise to understanding.
"Saṃgha" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. In full, it is *Saṃgha*, which means "harmonious assembly. To state it comprehensively, it is "harmony."
This is the assembly of the Sangha. Regarding "the Wheel of Dharma delivers sentient beings": this refers to the Patriarch’s prayer to the Triple Gem that the Four Great Vows shall not perish;

that while constantly dwelling within the Three Realms, he may benefit and rescue all sentient beings, so that they may together realize the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) and collectively attain Perfect Enlightenment.
Thus it is said, "delivering sentient beings."
Now, the Diamond Prajñā is able to open the gate of liberation; the jade-like verses of the Pāramitā are skilled at entering the path to Bodhi.
This single fascicle of the Diamond Prajñā Sūtra is that which opens the gate of liberation and enters the path to Bodhi.
A gate has the sense of entering and exiting; a road has the sense of going and returning. This serves as a metaphor for this sutra being the gateway and path for entering into principle (*li*).
Liberation (*vimukti*) is the fruit of cessation; enlightenment (*bodhi*) is the fruit of wisdom. Both are designations for the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

*Yugīparā* means "praise. It praises this sutra—the text that expresses its meaning—as being like a king among all virtues, difficult to see, difficult to hear, and difficult to encounter or meet. Therefore, it is said: "It skillfully enters the path to Bodhi."
Each line is neither empty nor existent; every phrase is without going or coming.
Altogether, these are praises for the expressive words of this sutra: each line and every phrase is neither empty nor existent, and without going or coming.
The meaning expressed therein differs from what was previously taught in the Initial Teaching (Āgama), which holds that the mind is non-existent while objects are existent.

This refers to the state where objects have no existence apart from the mind. This sutra exclusively discusses the wondrous existence of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), manifesting the fundamental true wisdom of *prajñā*.
Furthermore, it is not empty, for it differs from causelessness; it is not existent, for it differs from false causes. It has no departure, as it does not belong to the past;
it has no arrival, as it does not belong to the future. Thus, it does not fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence. Departure.
Coming from across the three periods of time, it may truly be called a teaching that negates appearances to dissolve the mind and discourses on emptiness.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* expounds thirty-two sections; in each and every section, its merit is difficult to measure.
Subhūti, upon hearing the wondrous four-line verses, the extraordinary causes behind each verse remain unfathomable.
This one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was originally spoken by the Buddha. Later, Prince Zhaoming divided it into thirty-two sections;
hence the term "section by section" (*fenfen*). Regarding the "immeasurable merit": cultivation and progress are called "merit" (*gong*), while realizing one's nature is called "virtue" (*de*).
If there are practitioners who rely upon this to cultivate and progress, they will immediately realize their nature and attain Buddhahood; hence it is said to be "difficult to measure."
This is the measure. In the Sanskrit language, Subhūti means "Good Fortune" (Śubhamati), and he is also called "Born of Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-ja). Regarding those who hear these four lines:

from the eighth chapter onward, the Buddha told Subhūti, "If a person were to take seven treasures filling the trichiliocosm and give them as a gift, although the merit obtained would be great, it would not equal that of a person who, with these four..."
Regarding the phrase "explaining the verses and gāthās to others," from this point downward there are seven instances where verses are spoken;
hence it is called "verse by verse. Inferring from this, every single character and every single line possesses extraordinary and supreme merit.
The causes and conditions are unfathomable; hence it is said that "extraordinary causes cannot be measured.

Regarding the four lines [of verse], various interpretations have been offered by scholars of past and present, each adhering to their own views without any settled consensus. For now, I shall simply rely on the record of the Bronze Stele.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven and requested instruction from Maitreya regarding what constitutes the four-line verse.
Maitreya replied: "It is this: no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span."
If one copies, reads, and recites [this], one shall be reborn in the Flower Treasury Heaven (*Puṣpasaṃcaya*). If one expounds it for others, one will certainly reach the path to *nirvāṇa*.

To record on bamboo slips is called "writing" (*shū*); to transcribe from an original is called "copying" (*shashō*); to read by facing the original is called "reading" (*dokusho*); to recite without the original is called "reciting" (*jushō*). If there is a person who...
Relying on this sutra and practicing according to the Dharma, one shall be born within the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī in the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*).
The mention of the "Flower Treasury Heaven" (*kusumatalagarbha*) serves as a general heading; this is a skillful literary device.

Within this Flower Treasury World, amidst an ocean of fragrant water of boundless wondrous flowers, there are great lotuses as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra-rajas*). Each and every one...
The flowers bloom. Within them are oceans of fragrant water as numerous as motes of dust. In each ocean, there is a world-system of lotus-jewel radiance.
Each such system consists of twenty tiers, and each tier is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the motes of dust in twenty buddha-fields;
hence it is called the "Flower Treasury" (Huazang). "Heaven" (Tian) means spontaneity and purity. The intended meaning is:
It is said that those who transcribe, recite, and hear this will certainly reach nirvana; hence, it is called "Certainty of Attainment.
Prajñā is the Mother of Bodhi and the Buddha; faith is the source of the path of merit, nurturing the holy embryo and giving birth to the sublime Dharma.
In the Sanskrit language it is *prajñā*; in the Tang language it is "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). Internally, it refers to the true mind of original enlightenment;
externally, it refers to the sublime purport of this sutra. The following passage clarifies the capacity [of the practitioner]: "Faith is the source of the path of merit.
Although there is internal wisdom and external teaching, the essential point lies in faith. Through faith, the fruit of Bodhi is realized and the teachings are disseminated. Therefore, it is said:
Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; it nurtures and develops all roots of goodness.
By practicing in accordance with this teaching, one nurtures and develops the embryo of sagehood, giving birth to the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma.
In general, by examining the scriptures to master their meaning and inquiring into the Way to reach its source, one awakens pure faith and possesses the eye of discernment.

By analyzing the phrases, one penetrates the underlying principles; by clarifying the questions, one masters the texts of debate and disputation. When mind follows mind without interruption, the principle is fully revealed;
when mindfulness is constant without forgetfulness, the text manifests of itself.
The preceding section discussed the function of the teaching; this current section discusses the role of the capacity [of the practitioner].

Nevertheless, although this sutra can nurture the embryo of the sage and give birth to the wondrous Dharma, its primary intent is that those who read the sutra must penetrate the principles and meanings expounded within it. If, however, these principles and meanings are not clear, one should...
One must extensively inquire of those who possess prior knowledge so that they may point out the Way and exhaustively investigate its source;

this is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Thereafter, one awakens the pure mind of faith. This "pure mind" is what the Sūtra refers to as "when the mind of faith is pure, the mind of the true mark (*tathatā*) arises";
this is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, the practitioner must possess the eye of discernment (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*). As for the eye of discernment:
This is precisely the eye of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). "Discernment" (*viveka*) means to select and distinguish.

This exhorts the practitioner that they must employ the eye of wisdom to eliminate the views of self, personhood, ignorance, the body, and the limits of existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and to select and grasp the principle of the Middle Way, the unconditioned *tathatā*.
Regarding the division of *jù* (sentences) and *dòu* (phrases): where the meaning is complete, it is a *jù*; where the meaning is not yet complete, it is a *dòu*.
The text (*wén*) is that which expresses; the principle (*lǐ*) is that which is expressed. A practitioner who studies the sutras must distinguish each of these individually.

Only when one understands the length of the *jù* and *dòu* and the principles are thoroughly integrated can one be called a person with "eyes" [of wisdom]. Only then may one proceed to practice the stages of cultivation. This is clear.
Regarding "questions and answers": this refers to inquiries and their corresponding responses. In this sutra, from the second section onwards, beginning with the question "How should one abide?
and continuing until the end of the scripture, there are twenty-seven instances of textual passages consisting of questions, answers, and dialectical discussions.
A practitioner must clearly understand each of these individually; only then can they nurture the embryo of the sage and give birth to the sublime Dharma.

Indeed, the masters of the *ke* (sections) possess such great compassion that they provide instructions and exhortations with such care. Thus it is said: "When mind after mind is without interval, the principle is fully revealed;
when thought after thought is not forgotten, the text manifests of itself. "Thought after thought" (*niàn niàn*) has the same meaning as the preceding "mind after mind" (*xīn xīn*);
one should simply change the phrasing, for the meaning is identical. "Without interval" (*wújiàn*) means "not forgetting"; this too is merely a variation in wording. That is to say:
Focus the mind with single-minded concentration, allowing no leakage or wandering. If you do so, the text will manifest of itself and the principle will become clear of itself.

This is precisely how one takes the holy teachings as a bright mirror to illuminate the self-mind, and uses the self-mind as a lamp of wisdom to shed light upon the profound meaning of the scriptures.

Some may ask: "The responses are profound and subtle, while the phrasing and meanings are abstruse and minute; you have investigated the fundamental causes in detail yet presented them here only in brief segments.

It would be well to ensure that for every question and answer, the clarity is as bright as the sun and stars, and through repeated discussion and inquiry, the meaning is as distinct as black and white."
Alternatively, these are indefinite terms; sometimes the Buddha asks and Subhūti answers, and sometimes Subhūti asks and the Buddha answers.
This sutra contains twenty-seven points of doubt and twenty-nine questions.

The phrasing of these questions and answers is profound and their underlying principles are subtle and wondrous, such that those of initial capacity and shallow understanding cannot fathom their limits.
Because the text of this scripture is difficult to understand, I have thus composed a topical outline (*ke-wen*) to explain and clarify it. Therefore, the description of its merit states:
"To examine in detail the original cause. "In detail" means to scrutinize; "original" refers to the fundamental source.

This refers to a meticulous examination of the various schools' explanations regarding that fundamental cause. I have then summarized and pointed directly toward them, collecting and presenting [these insights] here.

This constitutes the structural analysis (ko-wen) of the completed sections. "Shu" (庶) means "to cause. It refers to causing the questions and answers within the sutra to be repeatedly debated and investigated.
Regarding their "text" (wen) and "meaning" (yi): the meaning refers to the significance of the pointed-out dharmas; the text points to the sutra and thereby establishes the structural divisions.

As for the meaning, it is like the sun and stars, or like day and night, or white and black—these are two distinct parts. "Text" (wen) refers to the expressive words that convey [the meaning]; as for "meaning" (yi), it refers to...
This is the principle that is expressed.
Meaning follows the text, and the text follows the meaning; thus, one encounters the source from either side.
"Meaning" refers to the meaning of the sūtra; "text" refers to the topical outline (*ko-wen*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One is many, yet many..."
They are one and the same. The text follows the meaning, and the meaning follows the text. As for "moving left and right," it is like the two elbows of a body;
they do not depart from the body itself.
It is like a pearl rolling on a tray while the tray rolls the pearl; moving vertically or horizontally without obstruction.

The "pearl" (zhū) refers to a treasure. According to the *Wùlèi Xiānggǎn Zhì* (Record of the Mutual Resonance of Categories), pearls emerge from the banks of the Langyuan Pond; when placed upon a platter, they turn of their own accord.

The pearl is a metaphor for the meaning of the sutra, while the platter is a metaphor for the topical outline (*kēwén*). To be unhindered whether moving vertically or horizontally is precisely what is meant by "encountering the source on both left and right.
The intent is this: the principles and phrasing herein are profound and subtle; it is hoped that practitioners will savor them with focused attention. Should one...
Upon hearing these words, the ground of one's mind opens and becomes clear; this may then be called the ancient treasure within the fist, requiring no further sifting through sand.
One can then board the bottomless empty boat and sail upstream against the waves of the Dharma-ocean of Nirvana, so as not to fail the compassionate heart of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Regarding those who believe, understand, accept, and uphold [this teaching]:
they penetrate and clarify the true nature (*dharmatā*). When the patriarchs reached this point, they made this vow:

"Wherever this Dharma circulates, if there are practitioners who believe, revere, and understand it clearly, receiving it within their hearts and upholding it without abandoning it, they shall immediately attain penetration and clarity regarding their own true nature."
Furthermore, those who see, hear, or rejoice in accordance [with this] shall all awaken to Bodhi.
To behold with the eyes is called "seeing"; to reach the ears is called "hearing. "Sui" (隨) means to accord with; "xi" (喜) means to rejoice. This refers to the following:
In places where the Dharma circulates, if there are practitioners who see, hear, rejoice in, or praise it as excellent, they shall all awaken to Bodhi.
The preceding section clarifies the true nature as the cause; this present section establishes the universal awakening to Bodhi as the fruit.
"It circulates throughout the heavens and the human realm, pervading the oceans of lands as numerous as atoms.

The first phrase moves from the distant to the near; from the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) down to the land of Jambudvīpa, this Dharma circulates everywhere among both humans and celestial beings.
The second phrase moves from the narrow to the broad; there is no place where it does not reach.
"To arrive" means "universal. To be all-pervasive without exception is called "pervading. "Dust motes" refers to particles of dust suspended in a crevice.
"Ocean of lands" refers to the *Fuchuang* (Floating Banner) Buddha-lands, which float and abide within the Sea of Fragrant Waters; hence they are called the "Ocean of Lands.
This clarifies that this Great Dharma pervades everything from a single dust mote to the entire ocean of lands.
The great void has no boundaries; how could the gift of Dharma ever come to an end?
"Great void" is simply another name for emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Using this as a metaphor, just as space is boundless, so too is the gift of Dharma boundless.
The purport of the section’s main theme is that this Dharma circulates everywhere, without exhaustion. This is the gift of Dharma.

A single phrase or a single verse enters the field of the eight consciousnesses, becoming forever a vajra seed that remains indestructible throughout ten thousand kalpas until the attainment of Buddhahood; therefore, it is inexhaustible.
By means of these meritorious achievements of *prajñā*, I universally repay the four debts of gratitude and the beings of the three realms of existence.

By "these *prajñā*," he refers directly to this sutra. I pray that the present topical outline shall explain the merits and benefits of *prajñā* so as to repay the four debts of gratitude and the beings of the three realms.
As for the four debts of gratitude: Heaven and Earth provide shelter and support; the sun and moon provide illumination; the Sovereign...

The "soil and water" refers to the physical body produced by one's parents. The "three realms of existence" (trai-dhātu) consist of the realm of desire (kāma-dhātu), the realm of form (rūpa-dhātu), and the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu).
Because the causes and effects of these three realms are not forgotten and one has not yet escaped from existence, they are called the "three existences.
In the preceding section, since the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, the repayment of this kindness is likewise inexhaustible; therefore, it is termed the "comprehensive repayment."
Consider this: the empty *tathāgatagarbha* shatters the barriers of the patriarchs, revealing alone the true and eternal;

there is nothing that is not *prajñā*. The phrase "consider this" is an introductory expression. There are three types of *tathāgatagarbha*, which correspond to the three truths and the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the truth of reality (*paramārthasatya*) and the *dharmakāya*. The non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
This is the *saṃbhogakāya*. The *tathāgatagarbha*—both empty and non-empty—is the *nirmāṇakāya* of the Middle Way Truth.

As for "the barrier" (*kan*), the horizontal beam of a gate is called a barrier. Regarding the "patriarchal school" (*shū*), it takes the seventeen hundred cases of causal conditions as the barriers of the Patriarchs.
Therefore it is said: "If you wish to penetrate the heavy barriers of the various patriarchs, you must press upon each one.

Now, when it says "the empty *tathāgatagarbha*," it directly reveals the *dharmakāya* of ultimate truth; where both sage and ordinary being are forgotten and both the absolute and conventional truths are extinguished—hence it is called the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
As for "revealing alone the true and eternal," this is the Master’s extreme compassion, clearly pointing the way.
This clarifies that beyond ultimate truth, not even a fragment of a thing can be found; thus it is said that "there is nothing that is not Prajñā.
The three minds are unmoving, the six metaphors are fully manifest, the seven treasures compare their merit, and the four propositions are doubly superior.
The former extends the functional power of Prajñā; this extends the reason for bestowing material wealth. Regarding the "three minds," the Sūtra says:
"The past mind, the future mind, and the present mind are all unobtainable. Therefore, it is said that the three minds are unmoving.
The six metaphors are: a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and a flash of lightning. "Manifest" (*zhāng*) means clear or evident. The seven treasures are:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, and amber. "Compare" (*jiào*) means to contrast. The Sūtra says:

"If one were to fill the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, the merit of that act is compared to this Sūtra when it is seen, heard, or received."
Holding to the merit of these four lines, even hundreds of thousands of millions of other merits cannot equal one part of it; therefore, it is said that these four lines are doubly superior.

If, however, one merely follows the tracks of practice or counts the ink-streaks of the texts, one’s views and knowledge will only increase further; if the eye of the fundamental principle is not clear, this is not the ultimate realization.
The above has been a praise of the teaching. Although it possesses such merit, its essential point lies in the practitioner’s application of the mind.

As for "if," this refers to the person who reads the sutra; if they do not dissolve every sentence back into themselves and ensure that every word harmonizes with their true mind, [the teaching will remain external].
To be solely preoccupied with following the lines and counting the characters is merely to increase one’s views and knowledge;

it turns one’s back on the power of *prajñā* and obstructs the wondrous function of the True and Constant. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one establishes knowledge within knowledge and vision, this is the root of ignorance;
if knowledge and vision are without [the establishment of] seeing, this is *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the "Eye of the School" (*zongyan*): "School" refers to the school of Mind, and "Eye" refers to...
The Eye of Wisdom. The mind is the sovereign of the single body and the source of all phenomena. If the mind does not attain sublime awakening, much learning is of no benefit.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Like one who counts another's treasures, yet possesses not even half a coin of his own;
so it is with much learning when one does not practice the Dharma. This exhorts practitioners: if you do not practice according to what has been taught, [you will remain in] darkness.
Those who perceive the ultimate truth all find that [their realization] is not yet final.
Alas! These are the words of the Master’s lamentation and admonition; practitioners must cherish them as a matter of vital importance. Below follows the section on the Dharma and its analogies.
"Clarifying" means causing people to fix their eyes [upon the truth].
To subtly proclaim the profound purport is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning; to secretly reveal the true mechanism is like a silver mountain or an iron wall.
"To subtly proclaim the profound purport" refers to the exposition that this sutra is indeed a subtle and wondrous Dharma, a most deep and profound purport.
Regarding this first teaching, one must ensure that the practitioner urgently fixes their gaze upon it; therefore, it is likened to fire within a stone or light within a flash of lightning.
This principle is such that a mere blink of an eye creates a discrepancy of thousands of miles, and a moment’s downward reflection involves ten thousand layers of barriers.
Regarding the "secret revelation of the true capacity": throughout this sutra, there are twenty-nine instances where the term "bodhicitta" appears;
in essence, it refers to a single True Mind. Therefore, it is said that the true capacity is revealed in secret—namely, the capacity of the True Mind, whose spiritual wondrousness is unfathomable.
It is difficult for people to tread upon; it is likened to a silver mountain or an iron wall. One cannot gain entry through inquiry, nor can one grasp or manipulate it.
It is like a mosquito on an iron ox—it is impossible to bite or chew.
To give rise to a fleeting divergent view is to stagnate midway; it leaves no door for progress and leads one astray on the path.
This is a repeated instruction and a subtle guidance, intended to cause people to arouse true knowledge and true vision.
If a practitioner gives rise to even a single moment of such divergent sentiment, they immediately contradict the true wisdom of Prajñā.
When the mind dwells upon objects, one falls into the middle way and fails to reach home; thus it is said: "Advancing, there is no gate;
retreating, one loses the path. This may be called giving rise to views of subject and object from nowhere, seeking Bodhi by clinging to appearances.

If the mind harbors even a single thought of awakening, how can one transcend the delusion of former times? This principle is such that the mere arising of a hair’s breadth of distinction between the sacred and the profane constitutes the path.
This is a discourse on the Path.
I have briefly opened a single thread for the sake of beginners; like a fine horse seeing the whip, it shall pursue the wind for a thousand miles.
This is the patriarchs’ way of expressing their own realization, yet it is also a humble expression. I have now composed this text of the *ke* (sections) solely—
This serves as a mere thread of access for practitioners; it is humbly intended for those at the beginning of their journey. How could it possibly reach those of superior capacity?

A fine horse responds to the sight of a whip—this is used as a metaphor for comparison. If one possesses superior wisdom, they know before anything is raised and understand without words being spoken;
how could such a person require these fragmentary explanations? As the ancients said: "If you are a cub of the golden-maned lion, [the roar] reaches three thousand [leagues]..."
Within and beyond the village, one sees the absurdities; there is no need to open the mouth or move the tongue.
Amitābha Tathāgata says above:
"I look down upon those of initial capacity. This refers to the reason for those of initial capacity. Thus, the master first cites that which is capable of encompassing them.
The Buddha. Next, he alerts those sentient beings who are to be converted. In the Sanskrit language, he is called Amitābha;

here it is translated as "Immeasurable Life. He is the Lord of the Land of Bliss. Because that Buddha’s radiance is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction, he is called Amitābha.
That Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and incalculable; therefore, he is named Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus).
I humbly consider that this illusory body will not endure long, and this floating world is not solid. Since it does not endure long, the physical form will undergo transformation;
since it is not solid, there is no peace within this house of fire.

I venture to say that "stealthily" (*qie yi*) carries the sense of borrowing or pilfering; one does not dare speak directly, which is likewise a term of humility. As for the "illusory body" (*huanshen*):
that which is non-existent yet suddenly appears is called "illusory" (*huan*); the accumulation of manifold phenomena is called a "body" (*shen*). Originally, this body did not exist at all;

it exists only through the provisional conjunction of three conditions. That which is formed must necessarily decay; that which exists must necessarily return to non-existence. Therefore, it is said to be "not long-lasting."
"That which is in this floating world is not solid" is a metaphor for this physical body, which is like a bubble upon the water, arising and ceasing swiftly;
therefore, it is said to be "not solid. "Before long it changes" means that this physical form will change before long.
At birth one has youthful features and vigor, yet one grows old, falls ill, and dies; therefore, it is called "changing. "Not solid and without security" is used as a metaphor.
The three realms constitute a single burning house. The karmic retributions of sentient beings all dwell within it. The heavens have the five signs of decline; humans have the eight sufferings.
Like being oppressed by many fires, what peace or joy can there be? Therefore, it is said that there is no peace. As the Sutra says:
"In the three realms there is no peace, just like a burning house. The Master [Zhiyi] required people to recognize that this illusory body will not last long, so that they might know the Dharma-body.
It endures for a long time; this burning house offers no peace. The Pure Land is eternal tranquility.
For this reason, when will the cycle of rebirth in the six realms ever cease? When will the transitions through the four modes of birth ever come to an end?
If one does not recite the Buddha’s name to seek liberation, there will ultimately be no way to attain deliverance.

"By this" is a phrase that concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. Because it was previously stated that due to the illusory body, one clings to it as a self, there arises the notion of "mine.
From this, the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), the sixty-two views, and the eighty-one grades of delusive obstructions arise.
Due to this sense of self, the six sense faculties are produced, which then become defiled by the six objects; thus, one commits boundless transgressions according to one's karma.
Receiving retribution, one wanders through the six realms of existence like a wheel, revolving upward and downward without end;
therefore, it is asked: "When will this ever finish? When will it ever cease? The "six realms" refers to the six paths of existence. The "four modes of birth" refers to—
These are precisely the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.
Taking the six realms and four modes of birth as the realm in which sentient beings dwell and the path upon which they travel, they come and go without rest.

For those who do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, O Master, for both the teacher and the practitioner, there is only the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha that can lead one out of this state. Only by this means can one attain liberation.

There are six realms of existence and four modes of birth. Therefore it is said: "If one does not recite the Buddha's name to seek escape, there will ultimately be no means by which liberation can be attained.
How could one not be stirred to awakening? One must practice with the utmost urgency.
This is the patriarch’s exhortation to people to practice with urgency, as if their very heads were on fire.

Since the path to the Western Land and the Dharma-gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) is the swift shortcut and essential way for escaping the six realms of existence and transcending the four modes of birth, why not awaken quickly and practice early?
Therefore, it is likened to one whose head is on fire, who must rescue themselves with all haste.

It is late; therefore, it is said to be "urgent as fire. As for "practice and cultivation," this requires that one advance in cultivation, maintain recitation with diligence during the six periods of the day and night, remain single-minded and undistracted, visualize Amitābha, and exclusively hold the sacred name.

At the time of death, one will certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one shall see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and receive the prediction of the highest grade. Thus, it is called "practice and cultivation. —Shiwu.
The poem says: Worldly affairs swirl in confusion with no end in sight; One must urgently awaken to one’s own livelihood. Everyone sees the crab falling into boiling water;
Every individual knows the moth flying into the flame. Only when illness strikes does one realize the body is suffering;
When death arrives, only karma follows. Floating light and illusory shadows are but momentary things; Hurry to practice—do not wait until it is too late.

I vow that at the end of my life, I shall be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), transcending the Three Realms, realizing the True Void, and departing far beyond the Four Flows so as never again to fall into the realms of suffering.

This is the method of the Master [Shandao]. He exhorts people to advance in their practice, with the essential requirement that the period of study extends from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until birth in the Pure Land.
Therefore, it is said: "Exhausting this single retributive body constitutes one full term for practicing the Pure Land.
Thus, it is stated: "Taking the exhaustion of the retributive body as the limit. Regarding the phrase "vowing to be born in An-yang," "vow" refers to the making of a formal aspiration.
"An-yang" (Peaceful Nurturing) refers to the Pure Land. As it is said: "By this merit, until the end of this present body, may we be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Therefore, it is called the vow to be born in An-yang. "Transcending the Three Realms" means that this Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance is a horizontal transcendence of the Three Realms, unlike the Two Vehicles who sever the afflictions of the nine stages to realize [liberation].
The principle of the four fruits involves traversing fifty-five stages and levels; this is the vertical transcendence of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Defilements are most difficult to sever, and the fruits are most difficult to realize. This is not like the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nien-fo*), which does not require the severance of defilements, does not involve traversing stages and levels, and does not necessitate the realization of fruits.

This period of a hundred years refers to the span of thirty-six thousand days;

Therefore, the sutra concludes: "It is solely because one does not recognize the perfect luminosity of the single nature that one vainly indulges the cravings of the six faculties, unaware that what was originally a single refined spirit has divided into six harmonious combinations. (Sutra)

to attract inexhaustibly is called greed (*rāga*), while that which is favored by the five sensory objects is called desire (*kāma*).
Fame and achievement that cover the world are nothing but one great dream; wealth and status that startle the world cannot escape the two characters of "impermanence.

It is a great dream. Impermanence is but another name for death.

"When wind and fire disperse, there is neither old nor young; when mountain streams are worn away, how many heroes have perished?
This serves as a warning that birth and death do not depend on whether one is old or young. "Wind and fire" refers to earth, water, fire, and wind.
"When they disperse" means at the moment life comes to an end: warmth returns to fire, movement returns to wind, and moisture returns to water.
"Bone and flesh return to the earth. There is no fixed standard for youth or old age; therefore it is said: "Do not wait until old age to study the Way;

most solitary graves belong to the young. Those whose heroic spirits have been worn away by the mountains and rivers—such as the Three Sages of the Han, whose illustrious names surpassed all others, and the Ten Talents of the Tang, whose valor was peerless—are now but empty names.
Empty fame ultimately returns to the same dust as all else; thus it is said: "The sun and moon have no root, yet Heaven does not grow old;

Before long, the green hair fades, and white hairs soon invade; the celebrants have barely arrived when the mourners follow immediately.

"Secretly sending cold frost to invade the green hair, lightly hanging over the frail and aged physical frame. As for "those who offer congratulations and condolences":

Abiding [in this world], one is oppressed by the fires of the five signs of decline in the heavens and coerced by the fires of the eight sufferings in the human realm.

This is not for a single morning or evening, but spans kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, with suffering that is inexhaustible. Hence, it is said: "When will this end?"

Regarding the Sword-Tree Hell (*asipattravana*): the Sūtra states that there are eighteen sword-tree hells.

This causes all the sinners to climb upon them. Regarding the Mountain-of-Swords Hell (*śastraparvata*): the Sūtra states that there are separately eighteen mountain-of-swords hells.

This is because in previous lives they placed spears and spikes in mountain wilds to injure and harm sentient beings, and thus have invited this retribution.

Some are gathered beneath the *Vajrāśani* (Wojiao) Stone, while others reside between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).

"Or those who are within the Iron Ring Mountains: the Great Iron Ring Mountain encircles the trichiliocosm, reaching as high as the third dhyāna heaven;

The hell-wardens glare with eyes wide open, seize the feet of the offenders, and cast them headfirst into the cauldrons, where they rise and fall with the boiling water.
The body rots and the bones become visible; the suffering is unbearable. One seeks death but cannot find it, and though one seeks life, there is no way to do so.

As stated in the *Jiàohuà Dìyù Jīng* (Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming in Hell): "There is the Mountain-Pressing Hell and the Stone-Pressing Hell."
