When he first traveled through the four gates, he encountered old age, sickness, and death;
upon seeing a mendicant, his heart gave rise to weary detachment. The Prince was then nineteen years of age. The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven led the celestial hosts.
The Four Kings guarded him as he departed from the palace; they supported the horse’s hooves while Chandaka leaped into the air and crossed over the city walls.
Having traveled three *yojanas*, they reached the Vāṭa forest. There, the Prince used his sword to shave off his own beard and hair.

A deity of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested in the form of a hunter wearing a *kāṣāya* robe; the Prince traded his seven-jeweled garments for it and put it on. He then practiced the nine successive stages of meditation.
He knew with certainty that his meditative absorption was not the ultimate truth and abandoned it. He entered the Snowy Mountains once more and practiced austerities for six years.

Upon beholding the morning star (Ursa Major), he attained enlightenment; this occurred precisely at the hour of the rat on the eighth day of the twelfth month in the year of Jia-mao, the forty-ninth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty in this land.
It may be said: "He renounced the precious throne of the Golden Wheel and relinquished the position of the Nine and Five."
He abandoned the imperial palace and did not crave worldly glory or pleasure; he practiced austerities on Mount Himavat until crows nested upon his head and spiderwebs hung between his eyebrows.
Without leaving his grass mat, he attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. This is the very model for how our Buddha, the teacher outside the world, transforms sentient beings.
The Layman Pang Gong: He sank his family wealth entirely into the blue sea.
During the Tang dynasty, there was a layman named Pang Yun, style name Daoxuan, from Hengyang County in Xiangzhou. His family was wealthy and noble, with accumulated riches filling their rooms.
By hereditary tradition they practiced the Confucian arts, but in his youth he awakened to the toils of worldly existence and resolved to seek the ultimate truth. He was compassionate...
Reflecting on his own poverty, he encountered two merchants who came to borrow capital. Having taken their wealth and returned it to them, they were unable to carry it back themselves.

The man carried them on his own shoulders until they reached the foot of a tree, where they rested. As they sighed, he said, "I possess a heart of compassion, yet I do not know how to remember those from whom I borrowed in the past;
today I may deceive them. Having spoken, the donkey spoke in human voice: "In the past, I borrowed..."
The official had embezzled public property. When the merchant returned as a donkey to repay his debt, the official heard this and was greatly astonished.
He immediately sent back the wealth and silks to the public treasury. The official asked, "Why have you returned so suddenly? The merchant replied, "How could you possibly know my intention?
I wished to embezzle it, but I have related the circumstances and reasons spoken by the donkey, which is why I am returning it. I fear that those who come after me will act likewise. The official...
During the night, he went to the stable and listened silently to the extent of the conversations and exchanges between the animals.
Upon returning to his seat, the Duke sighed and said: "I originally intended to save others, yet I did not realize that I was instead burdening them to such an extent.
What I have accumulated is calamity; it would be a blessing to discard it. It would be better to spend my days in pure poverty than to scheme for turbid wealth."
Xuming then transported his family wealth by boat until it was full, and sent it to the Han Yang River where he sank it.
His daughter, Lingzhao, made bamboo baskets and mats, while his son, Pang Da-ge, farmed the fields to pass their time.
Zhenwu did not assume the royal throne, but devoted himself solely to spiritual cultivation.
Xuandi (the Dark Emperor) declared: "He was the crown prince of King Jingle.

He corresponds to the celestial division of the two lunar mansions Kui and Lou, and above he accords with the Qunlong (Multitude of Dragons) Heaven of the Brahma-world. His queen’s name was Shansheng; she dreamed of swallowing the sun."

She became pregnant and, after ten months and four days, gave birth in the royal palace on the day of Jia-yin, at the hour of Geng-wu, in the month of Wu-chen, during the year of Jian-jia-chen (the first year of the Kaihuang era). He was born from his mother’s left side, while auspicious vapors shrouded the kingdom.
Celestial flowers were scattered, and a wondrous fragrance perfumed his body while precious light filled the land, which all turned the color of gold.

After his birth, his face was like the full moon, his eyes had the gaze of a phoenix, his ears were like autumn lotuses, his eyebrows were parted in the shape of the character "八" (eight), and his lips were as crimson as vermilion.

At the age of seven, he was extensively versed in the classics and histories; at fifteen, he took leave of his father to renounce the household life. With a resolute mind, he contemplated the Way and constantly made this vow:

He did not ascend the throne, but devoted himself solely to spiritual cultivation. When his father, the King, would not permit it, he secretly retreated to the deep mountains where he happened to encounter the True Lord Zi-yuan, who bestowed upon him the Wondrous Way of the Infinite (Wuji Miaodao). The Lord said, "You shall choose a mountain peak above the purple qi that pierces the heavens;
only there may you dwell. The Crown Prince then crossed the sea to travel eastward. On the way, he met a youth who gave him a sword, saying:
This was a black snake-patterned sword with a horn-shaped hilt, a weapon for severing the malevolent forces of Māra; it was seven chi and two cun long and four cun and eight fen wide.
Having received it, he traveled eastward until he reached the south of Junzhou, a place named Wudang, where he went into seclusion.
Prince Wang Si led five hundred soldiers in pursuit as far as Wudang, entering the mountains and crossing rivers nine times before finally seeing him.
The Crown Prince, [found that] the waters of the mountain torrent had overflowed all around so that they could not proceed. Suddenly, the feet of the five hundred men found it difficult to lift them.
They said to one another, "This is caused by the power of the Crown Prince's vows. In unison, they cried out, "Let us return to our country."
"I wish to follow the Prince here to study the Way. Having spoken thus, [the attendants] returned as they had come; only the King wept as he turned back alone.
The Prince dwelt in the mountains, where a spiritual crow announced the dawn and a black tiger guarded the crags. The crows had red beaks:

those who followed them would prosper, while those who opposed the black tiger’s expulsion of the wicked would meet with calamity. Although he practiced there, he did not yet attain realization and desired to descend the mountain. Upon arriving—
By a mountain stream, he saw an old woman grinding an iron pestle. The Prince asked, "For what purpose do you grind this pestle?
The old woman replied, "To make needles. The Prince said, "Is that not difficult? The woman said, "When one's effort reaches its limit, it will naturally succeed;
what difficulty could there be? The Prince understood her meaning. A seer of the foothills inscribed: "Much labor spent on sharpening results in the coarseness [of the needle]."

The Sage Master, refined and holy, invited me to visit the celestial capital. My heart was not as firm as stone, yet it became firmer than stone. When my small vessel was perfected, the Great Way was accomplished.
Thereupon, returning on the road, he plucked a plum blossom from a wondrous willow and vowed: "If I shall accomplish the Way, may this flower bloom and bear fruit.
Having spoken these words, he reached a cliff and sat upright in meditation. He moved a beautiful woman, who came frequently to look upon him. One day he said:
He said, "I am but one of the many immortals who have come specifically to test you. Having spoken, he flew away. That which had been broken transformed into a *jilu* (cudrania) tree;
its fruit resembled a plum, an apricot pit, and an almond, and was named "Jiumei" (Cudrania Plum). Its flavor was sour and sweet, capable of curing a hundred ailments. The Real Man of Yuxi said:
"When the High Perfected One studied the Way and dwelt in seclusion on the mountain, he personally broke off a plum branch and sent it to the willow."

The branches flourish; when merit is fulfilled and the time for the imperial examination arrives, the flowers bloom and the fruit forms—this shall be known beforehand. The immortal elder protects the realm, keeping a hundred evils at bay;

the holy fruit bears its name, hanging down through ten thousand generations. By taking these herbs one prolongs life and eliminates chronic ailments; with sincere devotion in worship, blessings follow.
Thus, as his meritorious practice was complete, the flowers indeed bloomed and the fruit formed—the Crown Prince.
He beheld seventy-two peaks; among them, one peak rose aloft toward the purple heavens.

On the day of Bingyin, in the month of Bingxu and the year of Gengzi, at the clear dawn, celestial flowers fell spontaneously and auspicious clouds gathered from all four directions for three hundred li each.
A purple vapor crowned his head as he donned robes of pine and silk; the Dragon Lords of the Five Palaces escorted him upward to the Nine Heavens to pay court at the Jade Gate.

"Devoted solely to the practice of cultivation": "Solely" (wei) means exclusively; "devoted" (wu) means single-mindedly. To sever habitual tendencies is called "cultivation" (xiu); to act without abiding is "practice" (xing).
Therefore, it is said that he did not preside over the royal throne, being devoted solely to the practice of cultivation. Thus it is said: "He was devoted solely to the practice of cultivation."
Even after Lü Gong had become an immortal, he remained diligent in seeking instruction and paying his respects.
During the Tang dynasty, the one known as Master Lü was surnamed Lü, named Yán, with the style name Dòngbīn. His alternative title was Chényángzǐ, and his literary name was Lǚyán.
He was a Perfected Man (Zhēnrén) from Púbǎn in Héyáng, Jīngchuan. He was born during the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuānzōng of the Tang dynasty.
For many years he served as a prominent official. Having failed to pass the jinshi examinations despite repeated attempts, he eventually retired from office.

While traveling at Mount Hua, he encountered Zhongli Quan, a court official of the Jin dynasty who had fled the chaos to study the arts of longevity. Before transmitting the teachings to Lü Dongbin (Chunyang), Zhongli first tested him with wealth.
One day, Zhongli and Lü were walking together; Zhongli picked up a stone and, after applying medicine to it, it immediately turned into gold.
He gave him some gold, saying, "This is for your travel expenses. Lü asked, "Will this also eventually decay?
Zhong replied, "If it frequently encounters fire, it may decay after five hundred years. Lü threw it down, saying, "It might lead people astray in the future."
After the bell had tolled, he tested her with his physical form. He then commanded Lü to enter the mountains to gather medicinal herbs.
[Lü] transformed into a small cottage, where a beautiful woman welcomed him, saying, "My husband has been gone for a long time; now that I have met you, a gentleman, I hope you will not reject me.
As the woman wished to take his hand and draw near, Lü pushed her away with his hand, saying, "A woman is but a leather bag of filth to me. Having finished speaking, the woman—
The woman did not appear; it was none other than Zhongli [Quan]. Thereupon, he was granted the art of the Golden Elixir (*jindan*) and the methods of the Celestial Immortal’s Sword.
He subsequently attained the ability to travel with complete freedom. A poem says: "Morning I roam the Southern Peak, evening Cangwu;
A green serpent in my sleeve, my spirit bold and fierce. Three times I entered Yueyang, yet no one recognized me; With a loud chant, I flew across Lake Dongting. He then went to pay his respects...
When Master Longya was asked by Lü, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Longya gave him this verse: "For what reason do you grieve at dawn and grieve at dusk?
If you do not study in your youth, you will be ashamed in old age. It is not that the bright pearl is begrudged by the black dragon;
it is simply that people of the time do not know how to seek it. Later, while passing through Huanglong Mountain in Ezhou, he saw purple clouds swirling about.
There was a man of extraordinary character who had been staying nearby; he eventually entered the hall just as Chan Master Zhiji was ascending the dais.
The Master, sensing that this man of distinction was secretly observing him from below the seat, spoke in a stern voice: "In the assembly, there is one who would pilfer the Dharma.
Lu Yigan asked, "A single grain of millet conceals a world; half a pint of rice in a cauldron boils mountains and rivers. Pray tell, what is the meaning of this? The Master—
[The Master] said, "I am a corpse-guarding ghost. Lü said, "What can you do? There is the elixir of longevity and immortality within my bag.
The Master said, "Even if you pass through eighty thousand kalpas, in the end you will surely fall into emptiness and oblivion. Lü, unable to contain his indignation, departed.

That night, he flew with his sword to threaten him. The Master had already anticipated this; he covered his head with his dharma robe and sat in the abbot’s quarters. The sword circled him several times, but the Master—
The Master pointed with his finger; the sword immediately fell to the ground. Lu bowed in apology. The Master then interrogated him, saying, "I shall not ask about the half-pint cauldron.
How is it that within a single grain of millet the world is concealed? Upon these words, Lu attained realization and composed a verse, saying:
"The gourd-bag is shattered and the lute is broken; In this life, I shall no longer seek within quicksilver."
"Today I have realized the Dharma of Huanglong; I now perceive that all my previous efforts were in vain. This passage is from the *Xianyuan Yishi* (Account of Remnants from the Immortal Garden).
Scholar Su was a frequent personal associate of Foyin.
The scholar Su was surnamed Su, named Shi, styled Zizhan, and titled Master Dongpo. Because he was exiled to Huangzhou, he built a raised earthen mound (po) where he lived;
thus he was called Dongpo. He was a frequent associate of Foyin. Foyin was the name of Liao Yuan, whose courtesy name was Jue Lao;
he was a native of the Lin family of Fuliang in Raoyou and resided at Yunju Mountain in Nankang Prefecture.
Originally a student of Confucianism, he left secular life at the age of twenty-one at Baoji Temple.

He took the śramaṇa Riyong as his teacher, passed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* examination, and received full ordination. He traveled to Mount Lu, where he visited Chan Master Xian of Kaishan and attained the Dharma.
At the age of twenty-eight, he first resided at Chengtian Temple in Jiangzhou, and later lived at Guizong on Mount Lu, which faces Huangzhou.

Shore engaged with his teacher in the exchange of verses and commentaries. Later, while residing at Jinguangsi Temple, when Dongpo was appointed as the Governor of Hangzhou, he again traveled back and forth to inquire about the Way.
On one occasion, he encountered Foyin entering his room; Foyin said, "There is no place here for Wenming to sit."
Slope said, "I shall borrow the Great Elements of the Master as my seat. Yinzhu said, "The old monk has a question for you.
If you can answer it, I will give you my four great elements as a seat; if you cannot answer it, you shall forfeit the jade belt at your waist.
He immediately unfastened his belt, placed it upon the table, and said, "I request the Master to ask. Yinzhu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates do not exist."
"Endong, where do you sit? Su Dongpo was speechless. Zhenke called to his attendant, "Leave this jade belt here to permanently adorn the mountain gate," and he rewarded him with a monk’s skirt.
Dongpo composed two quatrains, saying: "My sickly bones cannot endure the girdle of jade;
My dull faculties still fall short of the arrow-pointed wit. In time, I shall beg my food at the courtesans’ quarters, To trade for a cloud-robed robe."
This mountain monk’s old patched robe—some say this sash has seen as many people as travelers passing through an inn; its transmission down to me is also leisurely.
The brocade robe, with its scattered patterns, fits it perfectly; I beg it for the old man Wan-hui, who feigns madness.
Han Wengong finally performed the rites for Dadian.
Han Wengong’s surname was Han, his given name was Yu, and his style name was Tui-zhi; he was posthumously titled Wengong and served as the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
In the first month of the fourteenth year of the Yuhuan era of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty—the Jihai year—he dispatched the Imperial Messenger Du...
Yingqi took incense and flowers to the Faguang Temple (Fayun si) in Fengxiang Prefecture, to the site of the National Protection True Body Stūpa.
He requested that the finger bone of Śākyamuni Buddha be brought inside, where the Emperor personally went to the Anfu Gate to welcome and pay homage to it.

He kept it within the palace for three days of offering, during which five-colored lights appeared and the hundred officials offered their congratulations. It was then escorted through various temples, accompanied by the full ceremonial protocol of the Buddhist clergy.
The music, banners, and drummers of the Taichang, Chang’an, and Wannian [bureaus] were magnificent and extraordinary.

Han Yu, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, submitted a memorial to offer remonstrance, citing ancient precedents to contrast with the present, asserting that the Emperor’s longevity and the duration of the state’s mandate would not be extended.
The Emperor was greatly enraged; he showed the memorial to his ministers and intended to sentence him to death. Pei Du and Cui Qun interceded on his behalf.

The Emperor said: "Your words, Miu, are indeed acrimonious and contrary; you truly deserve punishment for them. Nevertheless, were it not for your innermost loyalty, how could you have reached such a point?
I hope you will grant me some leniency so that I may receive further remonstrance. Miu replied: "Your Majesty says that my statement that you practice Buddhism too excessively is still forgivable.
But as for saying that since the Eastern Han dynasty's devotion to Buddhism, all emperors met with premature deaths—how can such words be so perverse?"
"Yue, a subject, has been so audacious and reckless! Thereupon, the members of the imperial clan, the various princes, and the veteran ministers all pleaded for Miu on his behalf.

Consequently, he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou. Upon arriving at the commandery, Miu submitted a memorial expressing his grief and gratitude, and urged the Emperor to perform the Feng sacrifice at Mount Tai.
After a long time passed without a response, he became despondent and unhappy. Hearing that there was a Chan Master named Dadian in the commandery, he went to visit him.
Moral integrity was highly esteemed. He sent a letter to summon him; after three invitations, Dadian arrived. Dadian’s discourse was transcendent and superior.
He remained for several dozen days, sometimes entering meditative absorption for several days before rising. Muzhi respected him even more deeply. When the Master took his leave, he departed.

Li Yü was performing sacrifices to the gods by the sea when he ascended Mount Ling. He visited the Master’s hermitage and asked, "My disciples' affairs regarding the army and the prefecture are numerous and complex;
I beg the Master for a single phrase that captures the essential. The Master remained silent for a long while without looking at him.
Li Yü was at a loss. At that time, Sanping was serving as attendant; he struck the meditation seat once. The Master said, "What is this? Sanping replied, "First, through concentration..."
[The monk] moved. Later, he was extricated by means of wisdom. The Duke then bowed to Sanping and apologized, saying, "The Master’s school tradition is lofty and steep;
it was only through your attendant that I gained an entrance. From then on, he took Dayuan as his teacher.
That he eventually paid homage to Dayuan—who had initially been disparaged by him—shows how things changed. Later, he was appointed Governor of Yuanzhou and visited [Dayuan] once again.

Dianlu presented him with two sets of robes and requested a parting word, saying, "I, Yu, am about to leave my teacher; I would be fortunate to hear a single word from you to serve as a final admonition.

Dianlu said, "I have heard that those who easily trust others will surely find their integrity easily altered, and those who easily praise others will surely find their slander easily unleashed. You have heard my words and easily trusted them; how can you know [otherwise]?"
Furthermore, I heard others say, "He no longer regards me as wrong. Consequently, I did not inform him further of my views, knowing that he would not be able to hear them.
Thereupon, I departed for Yuanzhou. Minister Meng Jian learned that I had been associating with Dadian;
he sent a letter to me commending my sincere devotion, to which I replied, stating that Dadian was quite intelligent and possessed an understanding of the Way.
In truth, he was able to transcend his physical form through principle, overcoming himself with reason so that he was not disturbed or confused by worldly affairs.
Although I did not fully understand the essential points of his speech, my mind remained free from obstruction as I associated with him. This passage is from the *Collected Works of Hanzi*.
Lord Pei seized the ceremonial tablet from Shishuang.

Lord Pei’s surname was Pei, his given name was Xiu, and his courtesy name was Gongmei; he was a native of Jiyuan County in Hedong. Chan Master Qingzhu of Mount Shishuang in Tanzhou was the son of Chen of Xintu;
after leaving the household life, he went to Miu... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly at "到溈" [arrived at Miu], so the translation reflects this truncation.)
Shan Zuomitou revealed the Great Matter. Later, while he was residing at Shishuang Mountain, Lord Pei came to pay his respects.
The Master took Lord Pei’s ceremonial tablet and asked him, "In the hands of the Son of Heaven it is called a *gui*; in your hand it is called a *hu*.
In my old monk's hands, what do you call it? Lord Pei was unable to answer. The Master said, "Then leave this tablet behind."
This is a scenic view from within the mountain gate of the temple.

He asked, "May I leave the household life? The Master said, "Leaving the household life is the work of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish.
At these words, the official attained realization. The Master’s name was Daochin; he was the son of the Zhu family from Kunshan, Suzhou.
He had originally studied Confucianism, but at the age of twenty-eight, he met Chan Master Su of Helin in Runzhou, who encouraged him to shave his head and receive the precepts.
He said to himself, "I shall follow the current and stop whenever I encounter a path," and so he proceeded southward.
In the third year of the Tianbao era of the Xuanzong reign, he reached a mountain to the northeast of Lin’an. Asking a woodcutter, "Is this Mount Jing?
he then halted there to establish his residence. That mountain contained a dragon pool, and the Dragon King manifested in human form and offered the land to the Master.
It was thus established as a monastery. In the third year of the Dali era of Emperor Daizong, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital; the Emperor personally came to pay his respects.
The Emperor said to National Teacher Zhong, "I wish to bestow a name upon Master Qin. The National Teacher joyfully accepted the decree.

He was subsequently granted the title National Teacher Guoyi (Guo-i Chan-shi). Later, he took leave and returned to Mount Jing; there, in the twelfth month of that year, he manifested illness, preached the Dharma, and passed away.
The Emperor posthumously conferred upon him the honorary title Chan Master Dajue (Da-jué Chan-shi).
Miaoshan did not seek a prince consort and will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.

Formerly, Vinaya Master Xuan resided at Linggan Monastery on Mount Zhongnan practicing the Way, where he was moved by the appearance of celestial beings to serve him. The Master asked the celestial being:
"I have heard that the Great Being Avalokiteśvara has a profound karmic connection with this Sahā world; in what place does he manifest his transformations?"
"Most excellent," the deity said. "The manifestations of a Bodhisattva are without fixed direction, yet his physical incarnation on Mount Xiangshan is preeminent.
The Master asked, "Where is Mount Xiangshan located today? The deity replied, "More than two hundred li south of Mount Song, three mountains stand side by side;
the central one is Mount Xiangshan, which is the site of the Bodhisattva. To the northeast of the mountain lies the past..."
There was a king named Lord Sublime Adornment, whose queen’s name was Jewel Virtue. The king had no crown prince, but only three daughters:

the eldest was Wondrous Countenance, the second was Wondrous Voice, and the youngest was Wondrous Goodness. Among these three daughters, two were already married; only the third daughter remained unmarried.
Her deportment and bearing were transcendent and set her apart from the mundane; she constantly wore soiled garments, adorned herself with no ornaments, and [spent her days] day after day.
She observed the practice of eating only one meal a day, abstained from pungent vegetables and spices, and maintained her vows and spiritual cultivation without ever wavering in her resolve.

The King said to Miaoshan, "Now that you have reached maturity, you should take a husband. Miaoshan replied, "The waves of the river of desire are vast and the depths of the sea of suffering are profound;
how could I covet the glory of a single lifetime and thereby sink into suffering for many kalpas? My heart’s intent is to seek renunciation and practice the Way."
King Daowang became enraged. He banished her to the rear garden and cut off her food and drink, yet his mother urged him with great persistence to summon the Princess as a royal consort.

Miaoshan said, "If space has an end, my vow shall have no end. When the King heard this, he was greatly incensed and issued an edict for the nun Hui-zhen of Baique Monastery to take her away to the temple to grow vegetables, devising a plan to persuade her to return to the palace. Miaoshan...
He said, "Have you not heard that those who obstruct others from leaving the household life shall suffer the consequences of their actions for ten thousand kalpas?

How dare you defy the benefits of the Buddha's gate, only to willingly accept the karmic retribution of the three miserable realms? The nun replied, "I am obeying the King's command; it is no concern of mine.

Miaoshan did not consent, yet she remained firm in her desire to leave the household life. The nun reported this to the King, who was greatly incensed and ordered his army to surround the temple and execute all the nuns.
A great fire consumed the monks’ quarters. The princess was taken by a dragon deity to the base of Mount Xiangshan, where she remained for three years;
not even a hair or a thread was harmed. She dwelt in a thatched hut, clothing herself in grass and subsisting on wood and water, unknown to anyone. At this time, the King...
Due to the karmic retribution of his crimes in destroying monasteries and killing monks, he was afflicted with kāmalā disease; his rest was disturbed and medical treatments failed to cure him.
An edict was issued to all four quarters of the land to seek a cure. At that time, a strange monk said, "I possess a divine remedy that can heal the King's illness.
The King asked, "What medicine do you have? The monk replied, "It requires the hand and eye from the hand of one who is free from anger."
Upon taking the medicine, he was immediately cured. The king said, "This medicine is difficult to obtain. The monk replied, "It is not difficult.
Within your kingdom, at the summit of Mount Gandhamādana in the southwest, there is a rishi who has perfected his cultivation of the Way. This man is free from anger."
"If you seek it, I shall surely give it. The King then commanded his attendants to carry incense into the mountains. Prostrating before the Rishi, he said, "Your Majesty has fallen ill;
we venture to trouble the Rishi for his hands and eyes to save the King’s life. May you grant us your resolve.
Having heard this, the Rishi gouged out both his eyes with a blade and severed both his hands, delivering them to the attendants. At that moment, the great earth...
All were shaken, and the attendant ministers returned to their country. They had the monks prepare a medicinal compound, which the king then took and was cured of his illness.
The king prepared a grand carriage and traveled to Mount Gandhamādana to pay his respects and offer thanks.
Upon seeing that the immortal lacked hands and eyes and was incomplete in his physical form, the king, his consort, and those around them gazed upon him and felt deep compassion for his appearance.
"She bears a striking resemblance to my daughter. The seer said, "I am indeed Miaoshan. My child, I offer you my hands and eyes to repay my father's kindness.
Upon hearing this, the king embraced her and wept bitterly. The king said, "I have been a man of no virtue, causing my daughter to endure such great agony.
The seer replied, "I do not feel pain; by casting aside my fleshly eyes, I have attained the adamantine eye (*vajra-cakṣus*)."
"By casting away the hand of an ordinary man, one obtains a golden arm; since this vow is not in vain, its fruit shall surely be attained.
Thereupon, heaven and earth shook, and the Immortal appeared—the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion, with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes.
His physical form was dignified and majestic, his radiance dazzlingly brilliant, towering and sublime like the moon among the stars. [He spoke thus] to the King and his consort.
The people of the entire country all gave rise to wholesome minds and took refuge in the Triple Gem. The Bodhisattva then entered samādhi and passed away in a state of dignified stillness.
When the Sixth Patriarch encountered travelers, they heard the sutra and attained sudden enlightenment.
The Great Master of the Sixth Patriarch was named Huineng. His father’s surname was Lu and his mother was of the Li clan.
At the time of his birth on the eighth day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era (the Wuxu year), a beam of light soared into the sky and a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
At dawn, two monks came to visit and said to the Master’s father, “A light has appeared in the night.”
The child was named Huineng. His father said, "Why 'Huineng'? He replied, "As for 'Hui,' it means bestowing the Dharma upon sentient beings;
as for 'Neng,' it means being able to perform the work of a Buddha. Having spoken these words, he departed and could not be seen again. The Master did not drink milk;
at night, he encountered a divine being who poured nectar over him. This was the Patriarch’s origin.
Guàn was originally from Fanyang Commandery. Later, he was exiled to the south of the Ling Mountains, where he became a commoner in Xin Prefecture.
His father had died early, leaving his elderly mother orphaned; they moved to Nanhai, where they lived in hardship and poverty. He made his living by selling firewood in the marketplace.
Once, a traveler purchased some wood and ordered him to deliver it to an inn for collection. When he received the money and was about to leave the gate, [the story continues].

How is it that the Venerable One, through the power of his wisdom, can teach the Dharma in such a way? The Venerable One replied, "Śakra, I do not even know how to teach the D
"Is it attained from the earth, or is it attained from humans? The Emperor replied, "No. [The Venerable One asked,] "From what, then, is it attained?
The Emperor then raised his hand. The Venerable One said, "So it is, so it is."
Bodhidharma took his sandals and returned to the West.
As for Bodhidharma, he was the third son of the King of Xiangzhi in South India; his clan name was Kṣatriya.

His original name was Bodhidhara. Because the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, arrived in that country and received the offerings of his father, the King, he obtained the pearl bestowed upon him. To test what [the King] had said, the Patriarch addressed him, saying:
"Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery. Now, 'Dharma' (達磨) carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration' (通大); it is fitting that you be named Bodhi."
Dharma asked the Patriarch, "Now that I have attained the Dharma, to which country should I go to perform the Buddha-work?
The Patriarch replied, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not travel far yet. Stay in South India for now;
seventy-six years after my passing, you should go to China (Zhendan) to administer the great medicine of the Dharma, where those who attain Bodhi will be beyond counting."
[He] counted [the years]. He pointed directly to those of superior capacity. Be careful not to act too hastily, lest you decline beneath the sun.
Furthermore, when you arrive, do not stay in the south; that place values only conditioned merits and does not perceive the principle of the Buddha.

Even if you go there, you must not remain for long. [Dharma]mo was thus respectful; he received his teachings and served him diligently by his side for nearly forty years, awaiting [his instructions].
The Patriarch passed away and propagated the teachings in his own country. Subsequently, he reflected that the conditions for China had ripened and the time for his mission had arrived.
He took leave of his nephew, and the King provided him with a large ship to sail eastward across the sea. After three cycles of winter and summer, he reached the South Sea.
This was during the reign of this country, on the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty. There was a broad...
The Provincial Governor Xiao Ang received him with ritual courtesy and reported his arrival to Emperor Wu. However, their dialogue failed to reach a point of accord.

Hengwei crossed the Yangtze River and went to Shaolin, where he sat facing a wall for nine years. Later, he attained realization under Shen Guang, who stood in the snow; he severed his own arm as a token of transmission.

Having passed on the robe and the Dharma, and having fulfilled his karmic conditions through his transformative work, he wished to return to the Western Heaven. Thereupon, he entered *nirvāṇa* at Xiong’er Mountain during the Liang dynasty.
This was the fifteenth day of the second year. A stupa was erected at Dinglin Temple.
The Wei dynasty then informed Emperor Wu of Liang of his passing and presented precious silks for the funeral rites and offerings.

Three years later, a Wei envoy named Song Yun, returning from a mission to the Western Regions, encountered Sengzu on the Pamir Mountains as he walked alone with a single shoe in hand, departing gracefully.

When asked where the Master was going, he replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven. When Huìyún arrived in Luoyang, he recounted these previous events in detail. The disciples opened the tomb and found that only a single shoe remained there.
At that time, Emperor Xiaozhuang of the Wei dynasty issued an edict to take the left-over shoe and enshrine it for veneration at Shaolin Monastery.

Upon hearing of the Master’s transformative legacy, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty personally composed an inscription for his memorial stele. During the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously granted the title: *The Great Master of the Dharma Jewel, the Venerable Bodhidharma of the East* (Dàfǎbǎo Dàzūn Dōngtán Pútí Dámó).
The Great Master Yuanjue’s stupa was named Kōngguān (Empty Contemplation).
Puhua shook his bell and ascended into the air.
The Venerable Puhua of Zhenzhou was a man of unknown origin who received the secret transmission of the mind from Bāoshan.

This was Zen Master Ji. In the first year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty, as he was about to manifest his passing, he entered a marketplace and said to the people, "I beg for a *zhidu* (a monk’s robe).
Give me either a leather jacket or a cotton shirt. He refused them all and departed, shaking his staff.
Linji sent someone to deliver a coffin for him; the Master sighed, saying, "Linji, that little fellow, is so talkative. Then he passed away.
He accepted [the invitation] and then took leave of the assembly, saying, "Puhua will pass away tomorrow outside the East Gate. The people of the district drew one another out of the city.
The Master responded with a cry, saying, "Today it is not auspicious for a blue bird"; he then said, "Tomorrow I shall pass away outside the South Gate.
The people went to escort him there as well. Again he said, "Tomorrow, it will be auspicious only outside the West Gate. The people escorted him there.

The sounds gradually grew fainter. Having emerged, he returned once more. People’s resolve began to slacken slightly. On the fourth day, he personally carried his coffin out through the northern gate.
Shaking a *ghaṇṭā* (bell), he entered the coffin and passed away. The people of the commandery rushed out of the city; when they lifted the coffin to look, there was no trace of him at all.
Only the sound of the bell was heard in the air, gradually fading into the distance, its cause unfathomable. A verse says: "The three realms are..."
The Traveling Pavilion: The four modes of birth are its pathways. Coming into life is like putting on a shirt; departing from life is like taking off trousers.
Neither rejoicing nor weeping, there is neither new nor old. Unbound by the transformations of the cosmos, everything is created by me.
The Arhat came to visit Master Yangshan.
As for Yangshan, he was known as the "Second Coming of a Lesser Śākyamuni" by the Arhat. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Shou of Mount Gui, and his school is called the Guiyang School.
It possesses nine and six types of circular diagrams (*yuánxiàng*) as its fundamental tenets. Later...
A certain Brahman monk came to visit Yangshan and asked, "Do you know how to write characters? Yangshan replied, "I do so according to my capacity.
The monk then circled him once clockwise and asked, "What character is this? Yangshan drew a cross on the ground.
The monk then circled him once counter-clockwise and asked, "What character is this? Yangshan then changed the cross into a *svastika* (卍). The monk—
He drew a circle and, with both hands pressed against it like the asuras grasping the sun and moon, asked, "What character is this?
Shanshan wrote a circle enclosing a *swastika* (卍). The monk made the gesture of *louti* (婁至). Shanshan said, "So it is, so it is. You must protect and uphold [this] well.
After the monk had finished his prostrations, he left the gate and ascended into the air to depart. At that time, there was a certain path...
The practitioner asked Yangshan, "Five days ago, you asked about the monk who recognizes characters; where is he from?
Yangshan said, "Have you seen him? The practitioner replied, "I saw him just now as he was leaving the gate, soaring up into the air and departing."
Shan said, "This is an Arhat from the Western Heaven; he has come specifically to investigate my school's fundamental tenets.
Regarding Mount Yue’s Emperor receiving the precepts from Chan Master Sidamo:
according to the *Denglu Jiaozheng* (Corrections and Verifications of the Lamp Records), there is no record of Mount Yue’s Emperor receiving the precepts from Chan Master Sidamo.
The text states: The Master was originally Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song. He was born into the Li clan of Ique.
Having left home at a young age, he received full ordination at Xianju Temple during the Yongchun era of Emperor Gaozong and studied the Vinaya.

He visited National Teacher An, through whom he attained sudden enlightenment regarding the profound essence. He subsequently built a hermitage at Pangwu on Mount Song. One day during that year, there occurred—
An extraordinary person appeared; he was the deity of Mount Song. Wearing a tall crown and trousers with sleeves, he arrived with an immense and magnificent retinue.
He announced his visit to the Great Master. The Master, perceiving that he was no ordinary being, addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, benevolent one! For what purpose have you come? The deity replied, "Do you not recognize me? The Master said, "In my view, living beings and Buddhas are equal before my single eye."
"Is this not discrimination? He replied, "I am this mountain deity, capable of bringing people to life or death.
How can you, Master, look upon me with such equanimity? The Master said, "I am fundamentally unborn; how could you bring me to death?
I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you. Can you destroy space or yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself," [he continued].
"I am neither born nor do I perish. You are not yet able to be thus; how then could you undergo birth and death?
The deity of Mount Yue bowed his head and said, "I am also wise and upright compared to other deities, yet I did not know that you, Master, possessed such vast wisdom and eloquence.
I pray that you will accept me into the true precepts and enable me to cross over into liberation. The Master said, "Since you have requested the precepts, then..."
"Now that you have received the precepts, why is this? Outside of the precepts, there are no precepts; what further precepts could there be? The spirit said, "This is the principle.
What I have heard has been vague and obscure, so I specifically sought a master for the precepts. I am now your disciple.

The master then prepared a seat, took up the incense burner, and set out a formal table, saying, "I confer upon you the five precepts. If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you must speak the truth."
The spirit said, "No. The Master said, "Be careful to receive my teaching. The Master asked, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct?
The spirit said, "I am also married. The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean that you must have no lustful attachments. The spirit said, "I can.
The Master asked, "Can you refrain from stealing? The spirit said, "What would I lack? How could I ever take anything by theft? The Master said, "I do not mean this—"
This is it. It means that blessings come to the profligate for their feasting, while calamities befall the virtuous for their lack of offerings.
The spirit said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from killing? The spirit said, "I truly preside over its handle; how could I refrain from killing? The Master said, "I do not mean this.
I mean whether there are errors, oversights, doubts, or confusions. The spirit said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from being deceitful? The spirit...
The spirit said, "I am upright; how could there be any falsehood? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that your words before and after do not accord with the Will of Heaven.
The spirit said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from drinking wine? The spirit said, "I receive offerings."
The Master said, "How could one not drink? The deity replied, "I do not mean this; I meant that one must not allow it to disturb one's nature.
The Master said, "To be able to do so is the Buddha’s Five Precepts. The deity immediately performed a prostration and took his leave.
The Master then saw him off at the gate and watched him go; he saw the ceremonial guard trailing along like the grand retinue of a sovereign, amidst mists, vapors, and rosy clouds.
The banners, streamers, and jeweled pendants vanished into the void.
At Mount Jing, even today, the Dragon King continues to receive offerings.
Chan Master Daoqin of Mount Jing in Hangzhou was the son of the Zhu family of Kunshan in Suzhou; he initially followed the teachings of Confucianism.
At the age of twenty-eight, he encountered Master Su. The Master said to him, "Observing your spirit and temperament, you are truly a treasure of the Dharma.
He requested to become his disciple and have his hair shaved. Master Su said, "Follow the current as you go; stop whenever you encounter a path.
The Master then traveled south and reached Lin’an. Seeing a mountain to the northeast, he asked a woodcutter, "What is this?"
"Mountain! the woodcutter replied, "It is Mount Jing. Thereupon, he halted his staff [to settle there]. To the west, facing a precipitous peak, he spread his seat upon a stone cliff.
An old man came forward, paid his respects, and said, "I wish to offer this dwelling as a place for the Master to halt his staff."
The Master proceeded southward with him. Upon reaching the area between the Five Peaks, there was a large pool of water which [the deity] said to the Master:
"When I depart, this pool shall swell; leave a single opening for the water and do not fill it in. I will come here often. Having spoken, he vanished.
Thereupon, clouds and mist darkened the sky, and a great wind and rain broke out, continuing without ceasing throughout the night. By dawn—
When the rains ceased, the waters of the pool were completely dried up and the swelling sands became level; only one small pool remained, which was called the Dragon Well.
The Master resided there, and strange people would constantly come to present offerings and then vanish.
This occurred every day, leading him to realize that these must all have been the Dragon King sending people to deliver the offerings.
In the past, Xuefeng was able to cause a wooden man to open the mountain.
Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng in Fujian was the son of the Feng family of Nanan County, Quanzhou. From birth, he loathed the consumption of meat and pungent vegetables.
Even as an infant, he would be moved to joy upon hearing the sounds of bells and chanting, and his countenance would brighten whenever he saw banners or flowers. At ten [years of age]...
At seventeen, he left home and shaved his hair. He served as a disciple of Vinaya Master Qingxuan.
Initially, he visited Chan Master Xuanjian of Deshan and asked, "Within the matter of the ancestral vehicle, does a student have any share in it?
Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "What are you saying? The Master recounted this to Yantou, saying, "At that time, it was as if the bottom had fallen out of my bucket."
Xiangsi shook his head and exclaimed, "Have you not heard that what enters through the gate is not the family treasure? The Master said, "How will it be after this?
When it flows forth from one's own breast at every moment, only then does it cover heaven and earth.
Xiangsi attained great enlightenment and said, "Only now is Mount Aoshan completed. As for the wooden man, he is simply wood.
It was a wooden ball. Whenever the Master called for a monk, he would invariably roll the wooden ball away; the monk would then come of his own accord.
If he wished to request a donation, he would attach a note to the ball, which would travel directly to the donor’s house, bringing back the offerings one by one.
Zuo of Zhimen composed a verse on this: "Xuefeng rolls the ball—whom can they discern the function? Of the fifteen hundred, how many truly know? He then raised his eyebrows.
"Eyebrows spanning thousands of miles—these must be the lion cubs of our school.
These are all proven precedents; do not harbor any self-doubt or despondency."

This refers to the meaning summarized from what preceded. The more than ten sages and worthies mentioned above all demonstrated through the efficacy of the scriptures that such causes produce such effects. "By no means yield" means: "yielding" (*tui*) refers to retreating;
"yielding" (*qu*) refers to being bent or broken. This is the master’s exhortation to the practitioner; one must not harbor self-pity.
"Retreating and yielding" refers to being cowed and submissive. An ancient worthy said: "Since he is a man of stature, so am I;
one should not disparage or deceive oneself by retreating and yielding."
Commentary on the Essential Ritual Manual of the Vajra, Scroll One;
Commentary on the Essential Ritual Manual of the Vajra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yao Tai and Kumārajīva.
Composed by Chan Master Zongjing of Baifu Monastery in Longxing Prefecture.
Recompiled by the Caodong Orthodox Lineage Successor and Śramaṇa Juelian.
The Wild Fox still listens to the Dharma of Baizhang.
Chan Master Baizhang Huaihai of Hongzhou was a native of Changle, Fuzhou. Having received the Dharma from Mazu, he would sit in the Dharma hall every day;
there was always an old man who listened to the teaching and would disperse with the assembly. One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, the old man alone did not leave.
The Master asked him, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am no human being; I am a wild fox."
[The Buddha] said, "Listen. In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain and gathered the assembly to expound the Dharma.
A student asked whether those who practice the Great Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect. I replied, 'They do not fall within cause and effect.'"

Consequently, for five hundred lifetimes, he fell into the body of a wild fox. Now, he requests that the Master provide a turning phrase on his behalf to shatter his doubts and liberate him from the fox’s body.
The Master said, "Try asking me one. The old man said, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
The Master turned the phrase and said, "Not obscuring cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.
"Only then do we know that 'not falling into cause and effect' is the nihilistic view of denial; 'not obscuring cause and effect' is attaining the wondrous while following the flow.

Therefore, the awakened one prostrated and said, "I have now cast off my wild fox body. I dwell behind the mountain; I beg the Master to permit me to be buried according to the rites for deceased monks.
The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to announce to the assembly: "After the meal, we shall escort the deceased."
The monks gathered for a communal consultation, and the entire assembly was at peace. There were no patients even in the Nirvana Hall. "For what reason is this so?
[the Master asked]. The Master led the great assembly to a cliff behind the mountain and, using his staff, pried out a dead wild fox.
He then performed the cremation according to the Dharma and buried it.
The Snail: Like the case of one who protected the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*.

During the Tang Dynasty, a certain *Daizhi* (Court Attendant) was traveling by boat on the Han River when he was held up by adverse winds. As the waves surged and roared, everyone on board was struck with terror.
He hurriedly took the single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā* he had habitually recited and cast it into the river; immediately, the wind abated.
The waves were calm and the waters still. The Waitzhi (Court Attendant) said, "I have long remembered this sutra; having held it for many years, I have been deeply distressed and unhappy.

It has taken two months of travel to reach Zhenjiang. About a hundred paces behind the stern of the boat, there was something shaped like a fur robe, appearing and disappearing at irregular intervals.
The people were suspicious, so the Waitzhi ordered a fisherman to retrieve it. It was then—
The snail shells rolled into a single mass; when split open, they were moist on the outside but dry within.

When the Attendant-in-Ordinary separated them with his hand to examine them, they were found to be the very sutra he was holding, without the slightest damage to a single hair’s breadth. The Attendant-in-Ordinary was filled with wonder and joy;

he prostrated himself, received it upon the crown of his head, and sighed in praise: "The Han River meets the Nine Bends, and from there to Nanxu is several thousand li; yet ships have come and gone [between these places]."
How could there be such a number? Yet we have not heard that the sutra he held was brought from there to here; a single snail saw it and did not let go of it.
Was it for fame? For profit? For wealth? Or for beauty? Surely it must have been so that they might escape saṃsāra and be spared the cycle of birth and death.
Alas! Among all things, man is the most sentient. There are those who ultimately do not...
Regarding this sutra, there are those who hear it but do not see it, and those who see it but do not believe it.
Even among those who believe, if their faith is subsequently tied to fame and profit, they are not even equal to a snail.
Ten thousand wandering fish, upon hearing the Buddha’s name, were transformed into deva sons.
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, the Buddha told the Bodhi-tree deity:

"In the past, within the kingdom of King Divaukasa-svayambhu-prabhāsa, after the Elder Jalavāhana had treated the sickness and suffering of the multitude, the Elder’s wife was named Jalottarabāhu-kośā; she had two..."
The two sons were named Jalam-pūrṇa and Jala-nidhi. When the elder brother and his two sons arrived at a vast marsh, they saw that it was parched and devoid of water;
fish were on the verge of death. A great heart of compassion arose within him.
At that moment, a tree spirit manifested half its body and said to the elder brother, "These fish are pitiable; you should give them water. The elder brother replied, "The fish have..."
"How many are there? He replied, "There are ten thousand of these fish. Exposed to the sun, the water has diminished and they are on the verge of death.
The elder paced back and forth around the pond; as the fish watched him, he gathered tree branches and covered them over the pond to provide shade.
Looking toward the four directions for water, he suddenly saw a river named Jāyodaka. The elder was filled with both grief and joy, and arrived at the great [river].
He went to the king’s residence, prostrated himself, and reported the aforementioned matter to the king.

The king ordered him to select twenty powerful great elephants from among his own and to borrow leather bags from within the city. Upon reaching the river, they were to carry water quickly to the edge of the pond and fill it;
then, one particularly strong elephant was to be selected for the son to request for use in his grandfather’s household.
The food was all transported to the edge of the pond and placed within it.

Following the instructions he had been taught, the elder called out in a loud voice, reciting the ten titles of the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, such as "Arhat," and chanting the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Because of this, the ten thousand wandering fish heard the Dharma and received food; they were reborn by transformation in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all becoming [devas].
The sons of heaven, each realizing their former causes, all came to offer their thanks. Ten thousand sons of heaven each brought celestial necklaces to the house of the elder;
they placed ten thousand exquisite celestial necklaces at the head of the bed, and ten thousand necklaces at the feet.
They did likewise for the left and right sides. Furthermore, they rained down four kinds of flowers and played celestial music.
At dawn, the king asked his ministers, "For what reason was there such an auspicious omen last night? The ministers replied, "The reasons are as explained above.
The king issued an edict for the elder to inquire into the circumstances as described. The elder reported to the king, "I fear that ten thousand fish may have attained rebirth in heaven.
I shall wait until I reach the pond to verify whether the fish are dead or alive, and then return to report to Your Majesty. He then proceeded to the pond.
The fish of the extreme views all died. Many four-petaled lotuses filled the pond. [The gatekeeper] returned and informed the Great King:
"These ten thousand swimming fish will certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When the King heard this, he was filled with joy; the elder was likewise delighted.
The Buddha told the great assembly: "This elder was my own self. His eldest son was Rāhula, and his second son was Ānanda. As for the tree..."
The deity was none other than the present-day Goddess Bhadra; the ten thousand wandering fish were the present-day ten thousand devaputras;
and the five hundred bats who heard the sound of the Dharma all became sages and worthies.
Long ago, during the time of the Buddha’s True Dharma, five hundred bats lived in a hollow in a withered tree.
At that time, some merchants were kindling a fire beneath the tree. Because a certain practitioner was constantly reciting the Abhidharma treatises, he ran toward the fire and set the tree ablaze.
The five hundred bats, greedily listening to the sound of the Dharma, were burned to death by the flames. On the following night, they saw five hundred men.

They came to pay their respects and said, "Having previously received the power of the Dharma, we have now been liberated from our evil retributions. We have all been reborn among humans and are all wise and intelligent.
Having left our homes to study the Way, we have all attained the fruits of sainthood. Later, Kaniska and the Venerable Pārśva...
He summoned five hundred noble sages to the kingdom of Kaśmīra to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

These five hundred noble sages were, in fact, five hundred bats; having recollected their past lives, they collectively composed the treatise to repay the kindness of the Dharma Master’s spiritual power.
A python heard the repentance and was reborn in heaven.
Formerly, Empress Xi, the mother of the state of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, passed away several months prior. The Emperor mourned her;
by day he was restless and unhappy, and by night he was anxious and could not sleep. Hearing a sound outside, he looked and saw it was a python.
He turned his ears toward the Emperor, his eyes glaring and his mouth agape. The Emperor was greatly alarmed and said to him, "My palace is strictly guarded; you must have been a high official.
The python spoke in human speech, saying, "I am the one who was formerly of the Xi clan. While alive, I was jealous of the ladies of the six palaces;
my nature was cruel and venomous, and I harmed many people. Therefore, I have been punished with this python body and am without food."
His mouth was filled [with worms], and having no cave to shelter his body, his suffering was unbearable. Small-scaled insects bit and gnawed at his flesh as if with needles and knives.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor sighed in lamentation and suddenly vanished. The following day, the Emperor assembled the śramaṇas in great numbers and asked for the reason.
Baizigong said, "If he does not pay homage to the Buddha and repent, there is no way to save him."
Ji then compiled ten volumes from the Tripiṭaka and performed repentance rites according to the Dharma. After a long time, a rare fragrance was perceived within the palace.
Suddenly, a celestial being appeared in the clouds, his countenance and deportment beautiful; he said to the Emperor, "I am the final incarnation of a python.
By the power of Your Majesty's Dharma, I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Having offered his thanks repeatedly, he vanished after he had finished speaking.
It was not manifest.
The dragon listened to the Dharma and attained enlightenment.
This "dragon" was, in fact, a dragon girl. At that time, from the world below, there was a bodhisattva who followed the World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna, named...
[He] said, "Zhijí. He addressed the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, saying, "I shall return to my native land.
Śākyamuni Buddha told Zhijí, "Wait but a moment. Here is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī; you may meet him and discuss the wondrous Dharma.
You may then return to your native land. At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with an immeasurable assembly of the three vehicles, [emerged] from the sea.
Emerging from the water, she approached Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where Prajñākūṭa asked, "Virtuous one, what essential Dharma did you preach within the palace of the ocean?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Prajñākūṭa asked, "Are there any sentient beings who, by practicing this sutra, can quickly attain Buddhahood?
Mañjuśrī said, "There is the daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara; she is only eight years old..."
He was of great age, possessed of wisdom and keen faculties, and well-versed in the faculties, karma, and conduct of sentient beings.
He had attained dhāraṇīs and was able to receive and uphold the entire Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. Having entered deeply into dhyāna, he thoroughly understood all phenomena.
In a single kṣaṇa, he gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained the stage of non-retrogression. With compassion, he regarded all sentient beings as his only child. Zhizhi said: "I..."
They saw that throughout the trichiliocosm, there was not even a space the size of a mustard seed where Śākyamuni Tathāgata had not sacrificed his body and life in pursuit of the Buddha-way;
yet they did not believe that this girl could attain Buddhahood in a mere instant. At that time, the dragon girl had a precious jewel, which she offered to the Buddha. The Buddha—
The Dragon Girl who had received it addressed the Bodhisattva Zhijì (Jñānākūṭa). The Venerable Śāriputra said, "I offered a precious jewel to the World-Honored One, and he accepted it;
was this matter not swift? She replied, "It was exceedingly swift. The Dragon Girl said, "Observe my attainment of Buddhahood through your own supernormal powers;
it shall be even swifter than this. At that moment, the entire assembly saw the Dragon Girl suddenly—
In that interval, he transformed into a man, perfected the bodhisattva practices, and immediately proceeded to the stainless world in the south.
There, sitting upon a precious lotus flower, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment, receiving the name Tathāgata Puṣpasena.
If even those beings can comprehend and realize [the truth], how much more so should humans not turn their minds?

This concludes the meaning of the preceding section. If those of different species, upon hearing the sublime Dharma once, can still comprehend it and attain the Way, how much more so should we, who are human?
Our nature is the most sentient; why do we not turn the lotus of our minds [toward enlightenment]?
This is the Way.
There are those who bury their heads in eating and thus pass their entire lives in vain;

these are indeed the "sectarians" (keka) who perpetuate the ailments of later generations. Or there are certain monastics and laypeople who, though dwelling within the Buddhist fold, [fail to practice].

Within the gates of the teachings, they do not cultivate the Tathāgata’s precepts, concentration, and wisdom; they merely indulge in worldly affairs and engage in strife, burying their heads to eat and pass the days.
As the *Jingsu* (Exhortation) says: "It is a pity that one's life passes in vain; regret is difficult to pursue once it has come."
They have never applied their minds to the teachings and principles, nor have they found any means to realize the profound Way. How tragic this is!
Some may even practice along mistaken paths without reflecting upon this very point.

This section extensively elaborates upon the maladies of Chan. Although one may study the Way within the Chan school, if one does not receive instruction from an enlightened master and instead encounters a teacher of biased views who imparts a deviant teaching, one will practice on a mistaken path and fail to realize the Great Way.
Thus Yongming said: "Sometimes one gives rise to extraordinary knowledge and understanding, which is like gouging a sore into healthy flesh; or one remains..."
The nature is originally pure, yet by grasping at medicines, one creates illness. Some seek out the words and probe for the meaning, thereby drinking "guest water.
Some maintain stillness and dwell in seclusion, yet sit amidst the "dust of dharmas" (*dharmaraja*). Some recognize the bright and luminous as their own self;
others recognize the conscious spirit as the original person. Regarding this, Master Changsha composed a verse: "Those who study the Way..."
To recognize the truth is simply to realize that from time immemorial, the very root of birth and death has been called by the deluded "the original person.
This clarifies that within the midst of ultimate truth, if even a hair’s breadth of clinging view arises,
one is practicing on a mistaken path.
How could they recognize that the nature of bodhi-awakening is perfectly complete in every individual? How could they know that the roots of goodness of prajñā are fully possessed by everyone?
This refers to those who, as previously described, bury their heads while eating their meals—those who practice on a mistaken path. Such are these two types of people.
How could they recognize that Bodhi is fully possessed by every person? "How could they recognize" refers to their striving for knowledge.
"The nature of awakening (bodhi)" is precisely the root of goodness that is prajñā. "Each and every one is perfectly accomplished" means that it is fully possessed by every person.
The expressions differ, yet the meaning is the same.
Do not ask about "great reclusion" and "minor reclusion.
If you understand this one great matter, then both great reclusion and minor reclusion are acceptable; if you do not understand it, neither is.
The "great hermit" and the "minor hermit"—both are merely laborious pursuits. As for the great hermit:

dwelling amidst the dust of the world yet remaining unstained, facing external objects with no fixed mind, neither yearning for the ranks of the sages nor esteeming one's own spiritual essence—only such a person may truly be a great hermit.
If one is a practitioner at the initial stage, one must dwell as a minor hermit. Thus, Bai Juyi said: "The great hermit dwells in the court."
The city is small; I shall hide away in the hills and orchards. The hills and orchards are vast and desolate, while the morning markets are loud and clamorous.
It would be better not to seek such seclusion, but rather to remain as an official in the capital.
Farewell. Regarding householders and those who have left the home life, the Buddha praised Vimalakīrti, saying: "Though he is a layman, he upholds the pure monastic discipline;
though he dwells in a household, he is not attached to the triple world; though he appears to have a wife and children, he constantly practices the holy life (brahmacarya); though he has kinsmen..."
"Delighting in seclusion. One day, while Mazu Gu and Nanquan were traveling on the road to Jingshan, they encountered an old woman.

Nanquan asked her, "Where does the road to Jingshan lead? The woman replied, "Go straight ahead. Mazu Gu asked, "The water ahead is deep; can one cross it? The woman answered, "Without getting one's feet wet.
Mazu Gu said, "The rice on the upper bank is good, but the rice on the lower bank is poor. The woman said: [The text here is incomplete in the source.]

She has been entirely devoured by the crab. However, if one were to discuss this old woman as a layperson, how could she possibly be said to observe the precepts, cultivate pure conduct, or skillfully know how to cross a river without getting her feet wet?
Although the crab has eaten the rice and she possesses the outward appearance of a householder, she cannot be discussed as a mere layperson.
Regardless of whether one is a monastic or a layperson, it is necessary only to discern the mind.
As for the mind, there are four types: the first is the physical heart, which is located within the five viscera; the second is the ālaya-vijñāna (storehouse consciousness).
The third is the discriminating mind; this is that which can discern external objects. The fourth is the solid and substantial mind;
this is the *bodhicitta* of original enlightenment (*mūla-āśraya-bodhicitta*). This mind is inherently possessed by both the holy and the ordinary. Therefore, it is said:
It is simply a matter of discerning the mind. Once, there was a monk who went to visit Mihu. On the road, he encountered an old woman. The monk asked, "Do you have any kinsmen?

The woman replied, "I do. The monk said, "Where are they? The woman said, "The mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, and the trees—all these are my kinsmen. The monk said, "Are you not a nun? The woman replied: [The text ends here.]
"What kind of person do you see me to be? The monk said, "A layperson. The old woman said, "Then you are not a monk.
The monk said, "Do not confuse and muddle the Buddha-Dharma! The old woman said, "I have never confused or muddled the Buddha-Dharma.
The monk said, "Speaking as you do, is that not confusing and muddling the Buddha-Dharma? The old woman said, "You are a man; I am a—"
"Women, how could you ever have been so confused as this old woman? Although she is but a worldly person, her mind has already attained realization.
Fundamentally, there is neither male nor female; why then must one cling to appearances?"

This clarifies that apart from the true wisdom of *prajñā*, the conditions of illusory phenomena are empty. If one discriminates with the consciousness of views, there appear characteristics of differentiation;
yet if one contemplates with actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), all dharmas are transparently clear—how could there be any distinction between male and female?
Since fundamentally there is neither male nor female, consider, for instance, the heavenly maiden who scattered flowers within the chamber of Vimalakīrti. This...
The woman was in fact a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body manifesting in form. When the flowers reached the sides of the various Bodhisattvas, they all fell away;

this is because the Bodhisattvas have eternally severed the habitual tendencies of delusion, which is why the flowers fell. When the flowers reached the bodies of those of the Two Vehicles, [they remained].
Consequently, they become attached and do not fall away. This is because those of the Two Vehicles have not yet exhausted their delusions and habitual tendencies; therefore, they become attached.

The woman said, "For one whose fetters and habitual tendencies are exhausted, flowers do not adhere to the body; for one who has not yet exhausted them, the flowers adhere to the body. The woman spoke again:
"I have resided in this chamber for twelve years, and have only smelled the fragrance of the Buddha's merits;
I have not smelled the fragrance of the two vehicles. Śāriputra said, "Why do you not transform your female body into a male?

The goddess replied, "For twelve years now, I have sought the characteristics of a woman and found them utterly non-existent. What, then, is there to be transformed? This clarifies that all [phenomena]...

"Phenomena have no fixed characteristics. They are like a magician who conjures the forms of men, women, and so forth; since these illusions have no substantial reality, what could possibly be transformed?

At that moment, by means of her supernormal powers, the goddess caused Śāriputra to transform into the body of a goddess, while she herself transformed into the body of Śāriputra. Then, as the goddess, she asked Śāriputra: "Why do you not..."
She transformed her female body into that of a man. Śāriputra, responding with his female form, said, "I do not know for what reason I have been transformed into this female body.
The goddess said, "If you can now transform this body, then all female bodies can likewise be transformed.
Just as Śāriputra is not a woman yet manifests in a female body, so too it is with all women."
It was likewise so. Although she manifested in a female body, she was not actually a woman. Therefore, the Buddha said that all dharmas are neither male nor female.
At that moment, the goddess withdrew her supernatural power, causing Śāriputra’s body to return to its former state.
The goddess then asked Śāriputra: "Where now is the form and appearance of a woman's body? Śāriputra...
Vimalakīrti remained silent; he was neither present nor absent. The goddess said, "All dharmas are likewise thus: they are neither present nor absent.
It may be said that fundamentally there is no male or female. By means of her supernatural power, she transformed her own body into Śāriputra, changing her male form into a female body.
At this point, even with the eyes of a *deva* or the vision of a dragon, one could not perceive it otherwise.
One cannot look upon him and grasp him. As it is said: "The Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands is difficult to fathom; the Śakrāloka eye has no door through which to look.
Therefore, the Master of the Text (Kejia) says: "Fundamentally there are neither male nor female; why then must one cling to appearances?"
Those who have not yet attained clarity falsely divide the teachings into three. Those who have realized the truth awaken to the same single mind;
this clarifies that what is revealed by the three teachings is, in fact, one and the same principle. Failing to understand this Way, they falsely divide it into three.
Master Liu Mi said: "I have often observed that the so-called 'three teachings' of China originated from Fuxi."
When the Duke of Zhou drew the Eight Trigrams, Confucianism began from this point. When Laozi expounded the *Daodejing*, Daoism began from this point.
When Emperor Ming of Han dreamed of the golden man, Buddhism began from this point.
Thus, within China, there arose the sequence of the Three Teachings. Yet those who do not understand humanity each cling to their own [doctrines].

When one observes their mutual claims of right and wrong, those who have attained true understanding realize that, fundamentally, there is no duality. Generally speaking, the Confucians establish their teachings through rectitude;

the Daoists establish theirs through reverence; and the Buddhists establish theirs through magnanimity. When one examines their love of life and abhorrence of killing, they share the same benevolence (*ren*);
when they regard others as themselves, they share the same impartiality (*gong*). They alike punish anger, stifle desire, restrain transgressions, and provide prevention.

It is not so; for they share the same cultivation and practice. That thunder deafens the multitude of those with hearing and the sun and moon blind the multitude of the sightless is the same transformative wind.
Judging from coarse traces, the principles of the world do not exceed the two paths of good and evil;
yet the intent of the Three Teachings is none other than to urge people to abandon evil and transform toward goodness. Thus, it is said that performing good brings down auspiciousness.
Those who do evil receive calamity. An ancient sage said: "In the world there are not two paths; the sages and worthies have but one mind.
These words mean that those who realize the One Mind together understand that the mind can become a Buddha, the mind can become a sentient being, and the mind creates heaven.
The mind creates hell; when the mind differs, a thousand divergences arise. When the mind is equanimous, the Dharma-realm is expansive and level.
If one realizes that all phenomena are empty, there is nothing that is not the true mark of the One Mind. Therefore, it is said: "Together awakening to the One Mind."
If one can reflect back and turn the light inward, all shall attain the vision of their nature and achieve Buddhahood;
this concludes the meaning of what preceded. Whether lay or ordained, monastic or secular, male or female, none possess a substantial reality.

If one can reflect back and not pursue the false appearances of the five aggregates, the sense organs, and the sensory objects, and subsequently turn the light inward, one will spontaneously awaken to the source.
...the nature [of all beings]. Therefore, it concludes by saying: "All shall attain the seeing of their nature and become Buddhas.

Furthermore, since the human body is easily lost and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter, the following passage praises how easily the human body is lost and extols the difficulty of encountering the Great Dharma. Regarding that which is easily lost:
The body is like the morning frost or the dawn dew; in an instant it vanishes, like a tree on a riverbank or a vine by a well—how could it endure for long?

That which is difficult to encounter is rarely met: the Great Dharma is as hard to find as a tortoise encountering a floating log, and a superior affinity is as rare as a mustard seed falling into the eye of a needle.
It is like the udumbara flower; it is truly rare indeed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"It would be better to suffer for many kalpas within the hells than to leave the three miserable realms to be born in a place where there is no Buddha or Dharma."
To transcend the cyclical flow of the six realms, there is only the single vehicle (Ekayāna) as the swift path.

This is an exhortation for practitioners: those who wish to transcend the six realms must rely upon the single vehicle. As for the six realms, they are: devas, humans, [asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings].

Asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—these are they. For those who wish to transcend the six realms of existence and escape the cycle of wandering, there is only the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which is the dharma-gate of the swift path. The One Vehicle reveals the true emptiness of *prajñā*.
As it is said: "The real is not established; the delusive is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside—not empty, yet not non-empty."
This is precisely the Middle Way of the One Vehicle; how direct and swift it is!
One must seek right view and not trust false teachers.
This is the instruction of the patriarchs for future generations: those who wish to investigate the One Vehicle must obtain the guidance of an enlightened master before they can truly proceed.
There is no fault. Those with correct vision directly manifest the Middle Way, without falling into the two extremes.
As for false teachers, they do not embody the True Path and recklessly transmit deviant teachings. Chan Master Yuanwu addressed the assembly, saying: "Alas!
I see those of the Dharma-ending age who are blind and belong to the lineage of wild foxes; they have never even dreamed of the Way of the Patriarchs, yet they recklessly..."
The Sixth Patriarch transmitted *tai-xi* (embryonic respiration) to others, calling it "the transmission of the Dharma to save deluded sentiments. This led to further false citations;
from the time of the late High Ancestor, such as National Teacher An and Zhaozhou, all practiced this breath-work to attain the Way.
