Furthermore, they boasted that the First Patriarch returned to the West with his single shoe and that Puhua departed in an empty coffin—all of which they attributed to this technique.
Having attained verification, they eventually achieve liberation throughout their entire bodies; this is called departing with both body and spirit exquisitely refined.

Fools who cherish this deeply fear the day of the thirtieth of the twelfth lunar month, when they will be filled with panic. They zealously transmit the method for returning to the Truth, gazing at their shadows on New Year’s Eve and calling out to their "original lord" to divine the passing of days and months.
They listen for the drum atop the tower to verify the water in the Jade Pond, and peer into it...

They take this as the method for escaping birth and death; this is truly a means of deceiving the common folk, fabricating falsehoods to establish a nest of their own, and inviting the derision of those of high standing.

Furthermore, there is another class of people with deviant views who falsely claim to represent the First Patriarch Bodhidharma, practicing this "fetal breath" (tāi-xī) and propagating Zhaozhou’s “Songs of the Twelve Hours” and Master Pang’s “Verses on Turning the River Cart,” passing them down...

They transmit secret instructions to one another regarding the practice of longevity, seeking to preserve their bodies for a long life or hoping to attain an age of three, five, or even five hundred years.
Little do they realize that these are merely true delusions born of craving and false views. What was originally a wholesome cause instead brings about an evil fruit;
they remain unaware as they fall into the weeds of the wilds. This is the case for those who are merely men of talent and eloquence, engaging in lofty discourse and grand sophistry.
People often believe this; such a person is a false teacher. An ancient worthy said: "Returning to emptiness is a perverse delusion that deceives the ignorant;
circulating the breath and applying effort pierce through the crown of the head and skin. Pressing the eyes causes flowers to appear, which they claim is the manifestation of the Buddha;

plastering windows to transmit the Dharma, they fear others will know. Those who allow a draft of air shall receive three thousand blows; those who leak [the secret] shall personally suffer eight hundred strikes. Do not [believe them].
Those who study in this manner—men and women alike—will encounter royal calamities in life and fall into the Avīci Hell at death.
Only upon awakening can one truly enter the Way; only through practice can one transcend the mundane.
Since you possess right view and cultivate practice, you must take awakening as your goal, penetrating to the very source of the Dharma and realizing the truth.

Wisdom is precisely the point of entry. For one who has transcended the mundane, having already awakened to this principle, it is necessary to practice in accordance with that principle and act as one speaks;
only then can one truly escape the birth and death of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Yongjia said:
"How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), which directly transcends and enters the stage of the Tathāgata?"
At every step one treads upon solid ground; at every turn one bears the void upon the head.
This clarifies the practitioner who, having realized this principle, understands death and liberation from birth as not departing from the ordinary course of daily life.
Thus, when walking, one’s feet tread upon solid ground and the head bears the void; it is never separate from eating, drinking, dressing, and wearing clothes. In short—
This is the wondrous intent of the One Who Came from the West. It may be said that in every thought-moment Śākyamuni appears in the world, and with every step Maitreya descends to be born.
In discernment, one manifests the mind of Mañjuśrī; in movement and stillness, one carries out the conduct of Samantabhadra.
When in active engagement, the myriad realms are fully manifest; when set aside, not even a single speck of dust remains.
When a practitioner reaches this state, they can respond to all conditions without following after the various realms of existence.

That the myriad realms are fully manifest is the principle of the single thread: it may be said that "every dharma is unrevealed in hiding; from ancient times to the present, it has always been manifest. Mountains and rivers...
This extends throughout the great earth, fully revealing the body of the Dharma King. As for "not establishing even a single speck of dust":

if one gathers it back, a single thought is fundamentally empty, yet all conditions remain unobscured. An ancient worthy said: "On the ground of the ultimate principle (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is received;
within the gateway of the myriad practices, not a single dharma is abandoned."
Transcending the realm where birth and death do not apply, one realizes the mechanism that ghosts and spirits cannot perceive.
This is the verification of cultivation for a person of clear realization; indeed, it is the attainment of great mastery within all phenomena.

One is then able to transcend birth and death; ghosts and spirits find it difficult to restrain such a person. An ancient said: "If one discusses this matter, it lies beyond the participation of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
It departs from the paths of sages and ordinary beings. A thousand sages can hardly fathom it, and even the five eyes cannot perceive it."
Therefore it is said: "Birth and death do not concern one another; ghosts and spirits cannot see through them.
Whether ordinary or sagely, they share the same path; whether enemies or kin, they share the same nostril.
This clarifies the matter that transcends [the mundane]: ordinary beings and sages share the same path; enemies and kin are of one essence. Thus it is said, "One single roadhead;
one single nostril. Master Fu Daoshi said: "Sentient beings are no different from Namo; great wisdom is not distinct from folly. Why seek jewels outside the self?
Within the field of the body, there is naturally the bright pearl. Whether the path be right or wrong," [it is all within].

Non-dual. One thoroughly understands that ordinary beings and sages share the same path; that delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction; and that nirvana and birth-and-death are of one suchness.
Ultimately, all conditions are empty and still; when one investigates thoughts and perceptions, they are pure and void, and not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Suddenly entering the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (the realm of no-remainder) by oneself—such is true awakening. Yet even this may still be lingering halfway.
"Such as this" (*ru-si*) is a term used to point to the Dharma. "Such as" (*si*) means "this. It points back to the aforementioned suchness of reality.
"Truly understanding" is still the talk of a second head; it is called discourse on the path.
Since one has not yet arrived home, it is said to be "halfway."
Do not remain submerged; realize the three essential mysteries that point upward and master the final stroke.

"Do not remain submerged" means that the Master, for the sake of future generations, urges them not to cling to their previous states of awakening, as these are all matters pertaining to the periphery of the three mysteries.
One must not be attached to them. As for the three mysteries: the mystery within the essence, the mystery within the phrase, and the mystery of the mystery itself.
The Middle Mystery (*zhōng xuán*). These three mysteries are taught according to the capacities of sentient beings; they are not yet the Way prior to sound. Therefore it is said:

"Rest, do not sink into the three mysteries above. As for "the final stroke," this refers to the single stroke of the person themselves in both movement and stillness, which transcends language and mystery.
It is like the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa smiling—a seeing of principle right before one's eyes.

This is clear and distinct; it is called "the final stroke. Furthermore, when Bodhidharma settled the mind and Shen Guang sought the mind, finding it utterly unobtainable—this too is called "the final stroke.
This is the final stroke of the enlightened Buddha and the enlightened Patriarch.
As for the practitioner’s final matter, the karmic deeds performed throughout one's life must reach their culmination at the moment of death.
At the moment of casting off life, when one’s single thought accords with principle and one clearly penetrates true nature to depart in peace—this is the final stroke for the practitioner.
Thus it is said: "Do not remain submerged in the three mysteries above; you must resolve the final stroke."
Now tell me: which one would you call "the final stroke" right now?
These are words for critical examination; they urgently require the practitioner to apply their mind and investigate thoroughly. What follows shall reveal it.
"From the low ridges of the green mountains, one sees the vastness of the sky; when the red lotuses bloom, one smells the fragrance of the water.
These two lines clarify the fundamental principle and bring forth the final stroke.
If a practitioner, while seeing the vastness of the sky and smelling the fragrance of the water, does not obscure this principle through their seeing and hearing, is this not indeed the final stroke?
This refers to Chan Master Sanping. His verse says: "Seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are fundamentally not causes;

their very substance is void and profound, transcending delusion and being true. When appearances are seen, they do not give rise to the karma of ignorance or craving; all is transparently the body of Śākyamuni.
This is indeed the model for the "final word" (mo-hou-ju).
Casting aside the gourd and bag, smashing the zither— Now I have no longing for mercury within gold.
Since first seeing Huanglong, I have finally realized my former efforts were in vain.
These four lines were originally the verse by Lü Dongbin upon his realization of the Way after meeting Huanglong. The Master of the Ritual (Kojia) has taken them here to [be used as]...

The practitioner picks up the essence and resolves his doubts. He says that although Lü Dongbin had already attained the rank of an immortal, it was only upon studying under Huanglong and realizing the true nature that he first understood:
the Way of the Immortals does not transcend the Three Realms; even if one lives for a thousand years, one cannot avoid sinking into the cycle of rebirth.

Therefore, he cast away his gourd and pouch, no longer clinging to the "mercury-gold" [elixirs], and realized for himself that all the methods of immortality he had previously studied were misapplied.
Thus it is. This describes how the immortals possess a lifespan equal to that of heaven; even those who could turn iron into gold still sought the Way before returning to Chan.
How much more so for ordinary people caught in the cycle of birth and death—how could they afford to miss this?
Only then does one come to know that birth and death are impermanent; do not say that only those who have grown old shall first perish.
When the great limit arrives, there is no fixed standard; even the young and newly born must remain on their guard.
This is the meaning of citing what has preceded: once the true mind of one's own nature is clarified, one will then know that birth and death are impermanent.
The first two lines serve as an exhortation for the practitioner; the latter two lines illustrate the meaning of the preceding points. Regarding the impermanence of birth and death:
beginning from youth, which marks the start of life, one’s physical form inevitably undergoes transformation through old age, and is ravaged by illness;
finally, at death, the vital breath ceases and the spirit departs—hence it is called "impermanence. Do not say that only those who have already grown old will perish first; this cannot be fixed.
This means that the elderly pass away first, while the young pass away later. Yet, when the great limit of one's lifespan arrives, even those born later cannot escape the suffering of death.
Therefore it is said: "Do not wait until old age before you study the Way; most solitary graves belong to the young."
Wealth and nobility, poverty and destitution—each has its own cause; Past conditions and karmic allotments are fixed, so do not seek them with force.
If you have never sown seeds in the springtime, You will sit idly watching a wasteland, hoping for an autumn harvest.

These four lines of verse are by the Layman Ruru (Rurujushi), an exhortation to laypeople regarding the cultivation of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). The preceding two [lines] are the first part.

The first phrase refers to the phenomenon (*dharma*). The latter two phrases serve as the analogy. Each has its own cause: whether one is wealthy, noble, poor, or destitute, each has a fixed allotment.
As the verse from the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If you wish to know the causes of your past lives, look at what you receive in this life;

if you wish to know the fruits of your future lives, look at what you cultivate in this life. Taking this and observing it in the present, we see that among human beings there are those who are poor and those who are wealthy and noble.
The lowly, the long-lived, the short-lived, the flourishing, and the withered—these various differences are all nothing other than what has been trodden by past karma. For example:

having practiced generosity and bestowed kindness upon others in a previous life, one is born wealthy and noble in this life; having been stingy and greedy in a previous life, obstructing others from practicing generosity, one is born poor in this life;
having killed and harmed living beings in a previous life, one is short-lived in this life; whereas having refrained from killing in a previous life, one is long-lived in this life.
Long ago, a virtuous elder said: "Wealth and honor, poverty and destitution, each have their own conditions; when one encounters peril and calamity, it is entirely due to Heaven.

When one's merit declines, even achievements turn into offenses; when the times decay, even good deeds become faults. That one has little fortune is not because they are as foolish as a thousand others;
that a family is wealthy does not depend on wisdom or virtue. From antiquity, nobility and meanness have all depended on fate; among the myriad matters, there is nothing that surpasses this."
Listen to this principle of nature: for one who has never sown seeds, it is like having nothing to sow in spring and nothing to harvest in autumn.
If one did not plant the seeds of merit in previous lives, how could one obtain merit in this life? Therefore it is said: "Vainly guarding a fallow field while hoping for an autumn harvest.

This means that as humans living in this world, one must extensively cultivate the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). As the saying goes: "Plant melons and you will get melons; plant beans and you will get beans."

One obtains beans. Therefore it is said: "In spring one plants a single grain of millet; in autumn one harvests ten thousand seeds. For human beings, good and evil deeds yield fruits and retributions in just this way."
*Sūri sūri mahāsūri*. This section is the mantra for purifying verbal karma.
The ten phrases that follow constitute the structural outline established by the master of this section.
Before each section of the scripture, the phrase *namo kāyai* is established to introduce and highlight the meaning of the sutra.
Without becoming distracted, one universally makes offerings to me, the Muni.
This is the mantra for universal offering; it universally offers to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Thereafter—
"The one who makes offerings to me, the Muni," refers to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
When about to recite the sutra, one first establishes the local deities (*bhūmidevatā*).
Regarding this section, the *Bhūmidevatā-mantra*: whenever one wishes to read or recite this sutra, one must first comfort the local deities.
This is for the purpose of seeking empowerment and protection.
The Vajra Bodhisattvas eternally protect the ritual procedures of the maṇḍala.

Regarding this section, there are the eight Vajras and the four Bodhisattvas. As for "ritual procedures of the maṇḍala" (壇儀), it refers to the liturgical protocols of the maṇḍala site. According to [the standard]:
The *Sahasrabhuja-sahasranetra Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Kalpa Sūtra* states:
"Now, taking the Vajra as the outer protection and the Bodhisattva as the inner protection, external māras will be unable to invade, and internal māras will be unable to arise."
Because both the internal and external are thus purified, this may be called the practice of cultivation, recitation, and upholding.
What is the "Brahma-vow"? It is the vow to reverently receive and uphold this section.
The text for making the vow begins: "I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms; I take refuge in the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. I now make this great vow..."
Vow: Having upheld this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one should then perform the Brahma-Invocation to request the Buddha to expound the Dharma:

The single characteristic is fundamentally without defilement; Its essential nature is free from worldly conditions. With a concentrated mind, uphold these four lines, And furthermore, recite the mantra.
These four lines are the topical outline (*kośa*). Furthermore, they are placed at the beginning of each section of the sutra text to serve as its essential purport (*yaozhi*).
Just as a garment has a collar by which the garment is guided, these are called the "essential purport. As for the first two lines:
Regarding the principle of the verse: what cultivation is there that is not practiced? It concerns upholding or not upholding. That which is called "one mark" is the mark of no-mark;
it is named the one mark because it directly points to the true principle of the Dharmakāya, which from the beginning has been free from the defilement of afflictions.
Therefore it is said: "The essential nature is free from sensory objects and conditions. As for the latter two phrases:
since one has received and upheld this sutra, one must first recite the mantra. This mantra is the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) employed by all Buddhas;
if one upholds it, its merit is immeasurable, and if one recites it, one will obtain benefits in this very life. Therefore, it is necessary to recite and contemplate it.
Invocation for the Vajracchedikā Sūtra: If there is anyone who receives and upholds the Vajracchedikā Sūtra, they must first, with a sincere mind, recite the Mantra for Purifying Oral Karma.
Thereafter, they should invoke the names of the Eight Vajras and the Four Bodhisattvas, and the locations where they reside.
One should always protect this practitioner who recites the mantras.
For those who wish to recite sutras and seek added protection, here is the Mantra for Purifying Verbal Karma: *Svāhī svāhī mahāsvāhī svāhī svāhī svāhā*.
For one who recites this mantra, all verbal karma becomes entirely purified. Even if one does not recite the mantra, rinsing with the waters of the Ganges will likewise fail to bring purity.
The Mantra for Pacifying the Earth: Namo samantabuddhānām. Oṃ dhu ru dhu ru dharaṇi svāhā.
Regarding the term "earth" (dharaṇi) here, it refers to the Earth Deity, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī. Whenever the Three Jewels establish a site for practice (maṇḍala), [this mantra is recited].

In places where sutras are recited, seated meditation is practiced, or commentaries are expounded, this Earth Deity Sthāvarā reports these matters to the heavens and constantly comes to provide protection;
for this reason, one recites this mantra.
The Universal Offering Mantra: Oṃ gagaṇa-svabhāva-vajra hūṃ.
When the practitioner recites this mantra, they should direct their mind toward visualization.
These offerings are empowered twenty-one times using the *gaṃ* syllable mantra of the pure dharmadhātu and the auspicious hand gesture (*śrīvatsa-mudrā*).
One should regard this as the pure food of the Dharma, which naturally pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
As for the hand gesture (*mudrā*): with the right hand, join the thumb and the ring finger together, while the remaining three fingers are extended and relaxed.
Next, recite the mantra for transforming the food: *Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo vilokite | Oṃ sabara sabara*.
RAḤ. HŪṂ. The practitioner recites this mantra three times, seven times, or twenty-one times.
By the power of this mantra, the offered substances naturally transform into various kinds of divine delicacies.
The food offerings all possess five kinds of colors, fragrances, and supreme flavors, each as vast as Mount Sumeru. Subsequently, one recites this Mantra of Universal Offering.
By the power of this mantra, offerings are naturally made universally throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.

Therefore it is said: "This food, with its color, fragrance, and superior flavor, is offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions, presented in the middle to the various worthies and sages, and extended below to the six [classes of beings]."
Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment. Equal giving without distinction; all who respond to the invocation are fully satisfied.
Invocation of the Eight Vajras:
Invocation of the Blue Vajra for the Elimination of Calamities; Invocation of the Vajra for the Dispelling of Poison.
I respectfully invoke the Yellow Parnashavari Vajra; I respectfully invoke the White Vimala Vajra;
I respectfully invoke the Red Shabdavajra; I respectfully invoke the Samayavajra who Eliminates Calamities;
I respectfully invoke the Purple Bhadra Vajra; I respectfully invoke the Mahadeva Vajra.
The Blue Disaster-Averting Vajra is the blue-colored Vajra, capable of eliminating calamities and misfortunes.
The Poison-Averting Vajra is capable of subduing all malevolent poisonous spirits, ghosts, and evil dragons or beasts that cause harm to all sentient beings.
The Yellow Sarvatathāgata-prasādakarī Vajra is the yellow-colored Vajra, capable of [fulfilling] all that is...
Whatever one seeks shall be fulfilled according to one’s wishes: seeking the promotion of office, the extension of life, merit, virtue, and intelligence; wealth, wife, and children;
hidden treasures, precious jewels, elixirs of immortality, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and so forth.
As for the White Pure Water Vajra, this is the White Vajra which can purify turbid water and eliminate evil karma, grave offenses, afflictions (*kleśa*), and various calamities.
[This refers to] legal disputes, verbal quarrels, possession by malevolent spirits, and the oppression of evil stars. As for the Red-Sounding Fire-Vajra, this is the red-colored Vajra;

it is for the sake of seeking the protection of the worthy and holy ones, so that devas and nāgas may rejoice, and one may possess eloquence in preaching the Dharma with clear and refined speech and sound.
As for the Vajra that Certainty-Removes Calamities, this is the azure-colored Vajra, which is able to eliminate [misfortunes].
All poisons, calamities, and obstacles are themselves supramundane dharmas; those who wish to swiftly fulfill their merit and wisdom shall succeed in their intent.
As for the Purple-Worthy Vajra (*Pīta-bhadra-vajra*), those who seek the rank of a noble sage shall all achieve their desires.
As for the Great Deity Vajra (*Mahādeva-vajra*), those who seek vast supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) shall likewise achieve their desires.
I entreat the four bodhisattvas:
I respectfully entreat the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; I respectfully entreat the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa;
I respectfully entreat the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga; I respectfully entreat the Bodhisattva Vajrabhāṣa.
Vajrapāṇi: this bodhisattva possesses a vast retinue. Vajrapāśa:
this bodhisattva holds a lasso in his hand and is able to bind demons and malevolent spirits. Vajrarāga:
this bodhisattva is able to love sentient beings with compassion, such that there are none whom he does not deliver. Vajravāk: this bodhisattva is able to use gentle speech.
This is to exhort and transform sentient beings.
Regarding the text on making vows:
as for "making vows," within the teachings there are two paths—practice and aspiration. As it is said: "If there is practice without aspiration, the practice will surely be aimless."
However, if there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration is established in vain. One must rely on the mutual correspondence of practice and aspiration before one can be free from fault;
therefore, one generates the aspiration.
I bow my head to the Honored One of the Three Realms; I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions. I now make this great vow:

by upholding this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I shall repay the fourfold heavy debts of gratitude above, and deliver those suffering in the three miserable realms below. May all who see or hear of it give rise to the Bodhicitta;
at the end of this present life, may we together be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the text of this section: before reciting the sutra, one must first make a vow.

As for the phrase "the Buddhas of the ten directions, honored ones of the three realms," one first pays homage to the single Buddha Śākyamuni, and subsequently pays homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
One who vows to uphold the sutra first makes the Four Great Vows, and only thereafter receives and upholds this scripture. [One does so] to repay the four debts of gratitude above, and... below.
"To deliver those in the three miserable realms" clarifies the purpose of making this vow:
to employ the merit of taking refuge in the Buddha and reciting the sutra to repay the fourfold debt of gratitude and universally deliver those suffering in the three miserable realms.

"Those who see or hear and resolve their minds" refers to the meaning of self-benefit through the present vow and recitation of the sutra; "those who see or hear and resolve their minds" refers to the meaning of benefiting others.
Thus it is. "When this reward-body (vipākakāya) comes to its end, may one be born together with others in Sukhāvatī"—this is the general dedication of merit.
Should anyone recite, uphold, see, hear, read, or chant [this], when their life as a reward-body in this world ends, their consciousness shall certainly be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
What is meant by "Brahmā"?
"Brahmā" is a term from the Indic language; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "purity. It refers to the meaning of the Brahmā Heaven—abiding in emptiness, free from desire, and pure.
At the time when the world first began to form, during the initial period of the kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to be born among humans.
The sounds that issue forth are none other than the Brahma-voice, with its winding and meandering cadences.
In ancient times, the *dujiang* (chief lecturer) and the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) would use these eight phrases to request the Dharma Master to deliver a lecture.
How does one attain long life and an indestructible vajra body? Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain great, firm, and solid power?
How does one reach the ultimate further shore regarding this sutra? We pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle mysteries and explain them extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Longevity that is indestructible" refers to the first inquiry. This passage is from the "Chapter on Longevity" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "Those who wish to attain longevity should protect and mind all sentient beings as if they were their only child, giving rise to great compassion, joy, and equanimity, and bestowing upon them the precept against killing. By these causes and conditions..."
One shall then attain immeasurable life and a vajra-like indestructible body. This passage appears in the Vajra Chapter. The Buddha said:
"The body of the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding, vajra-like, indestructible body.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain great, firm power? This is the second inquiry. The Buddha said: "In the past, I protected..."
The causal conditions for the Dharma have now been fulfilled, resulting in this adamantine, firm, and indestructible body.
Regarding the question of how one reaches the ultimate further shore through this sutra—this is the third inquiry. The text appears in the "Chapter on the Merits of Names.
The Buddha said: "If there is anyone who hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and practices according to its teachings, they will be able to..."
"By severing afflictions and all demonic influences, one does not fall into the evil realms; thus, one reaches the other shore.

"I pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle and secret [teachings] and explain them extensively for the sake of sentient beings"—this is the fourth inquiry. The text appears in the "Chapter on the Four Marks" (Sishangpin).
"To open the subtle and secret" refers to the secret of speech; that is, requesting the Buddha to extensively preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
It opens the verse of the sutra:
"The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma Is difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas."
"I have now seen, heard, and received this teaching; may I understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
The first two lines praise the sublime Dharma as something difficult to encounter and difficult to find. "Unsurpassed" refers to the cause for transcending the world.
It alone is supreme; there is nothing that surpasses it. As for its profundity: it is not like worldly dharmas, which are commonplace, superficial, easy to encounter, and easy to understand.
This supramundane dharma is profound and difficult to encounter, difficult to comprehend, subtle and difficult to fathom or conceive.
It may be said that it is as rare as a tortoise encountering a floating log over ten thousand kalpas, or as once in a thousand lifetimes.
"Rarely encountered, like a mustard seed passing through the eye of a needle. The latter two lines express gratitude and the making of a vow: "I have now encountered this sutra;

it is like a poor man finding treasure, or like one who is thirsty encountering a refreshing drink. "Wishing for understanding" (*yuan jie zhe*) carries the sense of aspiring to and looking up toward [the truth].
It means wishing to fully comprehend the Tathāgata’s true principle.
I reverently hear that the Dharma-body is without marks; it cannot be observed through marks. The ultimate principle transcends speech; it is beyond the reach of words.
The following text is established by the commentator as a brief commentary on the long prose. Regarding the "Dharma-body without marks":

this refers to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) nature of the Dharma-body, which does not fall into any numerical categories; hence it is called "without marks. Although it is said to be without marks...

This is not a non-existence that is merely the cessation of something; it is not a state of absolute nothingness. This is precisely the characteristic of the signless, which is called the "true characteristic" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is said: "It cannot be perceived through characteristics. As it is further stated: "The three lights have not yet shone, and even the five eyes find it difficult to discern.

Regarding the phrase "the ultimate principle transcends words," "ultimate" (*zhi*) carries the sense of definitive discrimination; it is not a principle that corresponds to or is contrasted with mundane phenomena.
Yet there exist names, marks, and verbal expressions. A name is the path of speech; a mark is the path of the mind.
Since the Dharma-body and ultimate reality are devoid of names and marks, they transcend all words. As it is said: "The path of language is cut off; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
This is precisely what is meant.

This is because, by virtue of having aroused the four vows as the cause, the fruit of the three bodies was perfected. To repay those vows, he manifested his physical form and spoke to transform sentient beings.

While the preceding section clarified that within the ultimate principle words are cut off and forms are forgotten, this section clarifies the phenomenal reality of the four vows and the three bodies.
The intention of the commentator is that our Śākyamuni Buddha, while in the stage of causal practice, gave rise to the four vows—namely, the four...
Through the fulfillment of great vows over the course of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one finally attains the fruit of Buddhahood and thereby manifests the three bodies (*trikāya*).

These three bodies are precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Upon first attaining enlightenment, the Buddha manifests these three bodies.
First is Vairocana, which is the pure Dharmakāya. Second is Rocana, which is the perfect Sambhogakāya.

Third is Śākyamuni, which is the hundred-billionfold Nirmāṇakāya. Furthermore, because the capacities of those to be reached by these emanations vary in quality, there are three types of emanating bodies:
first, the Great Emanation; [second, the Universal Emanation; and third, the Individual Emanation].
First, he manifests a body one thousand *zhang* tall, wearing the robes of a Bodhisattva at the stage of the four preparatory practices (*catur-prayoga*) of the Mahāyāna.

Second, he manifests a small transformation body sixteen *zhang* tall, wearing the robes of a Bodhisattva at the three stages of the path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*), as well as for those of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Third, he manifests transformation bodies according to the various classes of beings; thus, he universally reaches those with the three faculties, and all six realms of existence receive his grace. For example, for the sake of the elder of Kuśinagara, he manifested three [bodies].
The "one-footed body" refers to this very [body]. As for "manifesting a body to fulfill vows," it means manifesting the three bodies (trikāya) to fulfill the vows made within past causes;

thus, one must rely on the manifestation of verbal teachings to transform sentient beings and benefit them. Although these benefits are inherently present within the nature of all things, they necessarily depend upon the instruction of an enlightened master.
Therefore, it is said: "For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a lamp; if there is no person [to teach] the Buddha-dharma..."
Although it has been spoken, even with wisdom one cannot fully comprehend it.
I, Śākyamuni, the Holy Lord, out of profound compassion for benefiting sentient beings, take pity on this world of Saha’s wandering and praise the realm of the Pure Land’s eternal bliss.
The preceding passage generally revealed that the appearance of all Buddhas in the world occurs through four vows, manifesting the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This section speaks specifically of Śākyamuni, who dwells in this defiled land because his compassion for benefiting sentient beings is profound.

Thus he resides in Sahā—*Sahā* being a Sanskrit term translated into Chinese as *Kānshěn* (Endurance)—this world of five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) where there are manifold sufferings, and wherein all sentient beings willingly [endure them].
The mind endures it and does not give rise to weariness or detachment; hence it is called "endurance" (*kṣānti*).

Like water flowing eastward, with waves succeeding one another, moving on without returning, ceasing only to be born again—out of compassion for this suffering, the Buddha earnestly exhorts and guides us.

Regarding the praise of the adornment of the Buddha-land: as stated in the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*, Śākyamuni Tathāgata extensively expounded upon its sublime, wondrous, and extraordinary matters, and further described its forty-eight kinds of pure great vows.

The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extol the inconceivable merit of Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, this is also taught in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*).
In the midst [of this], the Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues and speak words of truth:
"You all should believe in this praise of inconceivable merit. "Adorned" (*yan*) means "decorated.

Within that land, the dwellings, palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, streams, flowering trees, and so forth, are all made of immeasurable varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense.
These are combined to form this one kind of adornment. Other adornments are likewise immeasurable. Regarding "eternal bliss":
because one constantly experiences happiness throughout incalculable kalpas, it is said that this praises the realm of eternal bliss within the adorned land.
The land is named Sukhāvatī; the Buddha’s title is Amitābha. His forty-eight vows are profound and far-reaching, and his hundred thousand gates of practice are vast and extensive.
The *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* states: "At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra:
'To the west of here, beyond a hundred trillion buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī. In that land, there is a Buddha whose name is Amitābha.'"
...now currently preaching the Dharma. Śāriputra, for what reason is that land named "Supreme Bliss" (Sukhāvatī)?
Because the sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore called "Supreme Bliss.
Regarding the Forty-Eight Vows: there are two types of vows, general and specific. The first four vows mentioned above are those shared by all Buddhas; they constitute the general vows.
These are specific vows, such as the twelve supreme vows of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha, which are likewise specific vows.
Regarding the present forty-eight vows, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "In the distant past, eons ago, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Dīpaṃkara...
[and so on] up to the fifty-third Buddha, named Lokeśvararāja Buddha. That Buddha extensively [taught] for..."
The Bhikṣu Dharmākara described the adornments of two hundred and ten billion Buddha-fields.

Having heard these accounts, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara beheld them all clearly; he then selected from among those fields the most supreme, subtle, pure, and extraordinary adornments—immeasurable and boundless in number—and synthesized them into forty-eight types to form [his own vows].
The forty-eight kinds of great vows comprise, in total, two hundred and ten billion adornments of Buddha-fields.

Regarding the "vastness of the one million gates of practice": at that time, after the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these vows, he entered samādhi and practiced the bodhisattva path for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; therefore, they are called "vast."

Thus it is. Both the true body and the transformation body are clearly elucidated, responding to beings of high and low capacities. Those below the stages (*bhūmi*) and those on the stages are all born [therein]; both the holy and the ordinary go together.
"Both clearly elucidated" refers to the true response-body and the transformation response-body; that is, the superior response-body and the inferior response-body. "Responding to beings" means:
There is that which can respond to what should be responded to, and that which can receive what should be received; it responds universally to both the high and the low.

Regarding those born in both the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and upon the grounds: the Buddha told Maitreya, "In this realm, there are seventy-two billion Bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression who will be reborn in that land.
Furthermore, those like Maitreya shall all become Buddhas," as well as those who have practiced even slightly.
As for those with merit, their number is beyond calculation; all shall attain rebirth there.

Regarding the statement that "sages and ordinary beings alike go," the meaning is that not only do Bodhisattvas below and above the stages of the grounds attain rebirth, but even the four classes of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings all together attain rebirth in that land.
Thus, the causal vows of Amitābha are manifested; through this, the true exposition of the Pure Land is revealed. Regarding "the causal vows of Amitābha":
"causal" (*yuan*) refers to causes and conditions. This refers to Amitābha, at the time of the World-Honored Buddha Sovereign King (*Lokêśvararāja*).
This refers to the causal conditions such as first hearing the Dharma and leaving the household life. "Vows" refers to the forty-eight great vows.
"In this regard" is a term used to point toward the Dharma; it points to what is explained within the sutra, making it manifest and clear, evident and prominent.
What is called the "True Exposition" (Zhenquan) refers to the teaching of ultimate reality; therefore, it is termed the "True Exposition."
This sutra has come down from ancient times; for a long duration, its proclamation has been lacking. To repay the Buddha’s kindness, one must clarify the intent of the sutra;

this is precisely what the masters of the lineage do when they point to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Because it has existed since the Han and Tang dynasties, it is said to have "come from a long time ago.

Although there have been those who provided commentaries and verses, none have yet summarized and pointed the way to the Peaceful Nurturing Land (An-yang). Therefore, it is said that "for a long time its proclamation has been lacking."
Furthermore, "repaying the Buddha's kindness" refers to this preface composed by the presiding master (*ke-zhu*).
"Briefly manifesting the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land" simply means employing it to repay the grace of Śākyamuni Tathāgata for his guidance and instruction.

"One must clarify the intent of the sutra" means that although a practitioner may have attained mastery of the loftiness and excellence of this Dharma-gate, they must necessarily illuminate the meaning of the sutra.
"The central purport" refers to the self-questioning that is answered by the subsequent text.

The two lines, "Penetrating the barrier, one wondrously reaches the realm of the Tathāgata / Passing the examination, one ascends high to the native land," are words that conclude and categorize the preceding meaning. The intention of the commentator is to say: "The words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs..."

The Teaching clarifies only that the Pure Land is Mind-only and that Amitābha is one’s own original nature. Because practitioners do not understand their own numinous light and instead rely on words and letters, it is called a "barrier.

If one can suddenly detach from the sense organs and their objects so that the numinous light shines alone, then whether it be the Western Land or this Eastern soil, what difference is there between the pure and the defiled? Whether it be a chamber or a place of thorns, they are fundamentally no different. This is what is meant by: [The teaching clarifies only that the Pure Land is Mind-only and that Amitābha is one’s own original nature. Because practitioners do not understand their own numinous light and instead rely on words and letters, it is called a "barrier. If one can suddenly detach from the sense organs and their objects so that the numinous light shines alone, then whether it be the Western Land or this Eastern soil, what difference is there between the pure and the defiled? Whether it be a chamber or a place of thorns, they are fundamentally no different.]
This is to be wonderfully proficient in the realm of the Tathāgata. Regarding "passing the examination" (jidi): it is like the three-tiered waves at the Dragon Gate;

those fish that leap over them ascend as dragons and depart—this is called passing the examination. Using this as an analogy for what follows, the practitioner must be wonderfully proficient in the Buddha-mind and solely clarify their own nature (*svabhāva*).
As for "one's fundamental portion" (bendun): it is the ultimate [reality] inherently present within the division of one's own nature.
It is joyful; therefore it is said: "This is one's original native place.
The Buddha is on Mount Ling; do not seek him afar. Mount Ling is right here within your own mind.
Every person has their own Ling-shan Pagoda; Go with joy to cultivate beneath that Ling-shan Pagoda.

These four lines are the Master’s [verse] commentary. He directly brings forth the Primordially Existing Spirit Mountain and the Primordially Existing Buddha-nature, intending that people not seek them outwardly.
Pointing distantly, he says the Buddha is on the Spirit Mountain; pointing closely, he says both the Buddha and the Spirit Mountain are entirely within your own mind.
This is what is called the non-duality of the Mind and the Buddha. That "everyone possesses it" refers to the Master’s extensive [explanation].
This is revealed for the sake of instruction: it is not only this Buddha and this mountain that belong to a single person alone;
rather, from the four modes of birth to the six realms of existence, every individual possesses them. Those who wish to go to the Ling Shan pagoda to practice must strive with diligent effort.
Turning toward the body of the five aggregates, one’s consciousness grasps the True Person of No-Rank. This shall be revealed in the following text as the fruit of diligent cultivation.
Even externalists and celestial māras will fold their hands in submission; Brahmā and Śakra will present auspicious omens.
"May all men and women now assembled together / Jointly realize the Great Vajra Maṇḍala.
These four lines clarify that the practitioner realizes their own mind is the Buddha.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—in every thought and every moment, they remain detached from external objects. Whether encountering the good or the evil, it is all the Buddha. If...
Being able to act thus, one causes the non-Buddhists and celestial Māras to submit with folded hands, while Brahmā and Śakra present auspicious omens and rare treasures.
As it is said: "Heavenly dragons pay respectful homage; spirits and ghosts venerate him with awe.
May all those gathered here—since the practitioner has already attained such benefits—universally cause this assembly of men and women to together realize the Buddha of the Mind.
The second dharma-gate is the Great Wisdom of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore it is said: "Together we realize the Great Vajra Dharma-Assembly.
From dawn until dusk one is busily occupied; One does not fear birth and death, but only fears poverty.
Even if you were to exhaust a thousand schemes, Until the moment of impermanence, they will not satisfy the heart.
These four lines clarify that all sentient beings are greedily attached and never find satisfaction. The *Dharmapada* states:
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a brāhmaṇa who built himself a front hall and a rear chamber, as well as a cool terrace and a warm room.
Even at eighty years of age, he still personally oversaw the construction. The Buddha perceived that this old man would soon reach the end of his life; moved by compassion, he [instructed him].
Having heard the Dharma, he realized that both the living and the deceased would benefit; he then went to the old man’s house to inquire after his well-being and ask whether he was free from fatigue.
He further asked, "What room is this? The old man replied, "This is where I usually receive guests. He asked again, "What is this place for?"
The answer is: The rear hall is for his own residence; the eastern and western wings are where men and women, the elderly and the young, wealth and property, and servants dwell.

In summer he ascends the cool terrace, and in winter he retreats to the warm chamber. Only these [practices] distance him from the sun and contain what has not yet been fully realized. Thus spoke the Buddha.

"I have long heard of your venerable virtue and have been longing for the opportunity to engage in discourse with you. I possess an essential verse that brings benefit to both the living and the deceased;

I have come specifically to urge you to consider it. He replied, "I wish to find a moment of leisure; I shall return another day to discuss this together. Thus he declined the Buddha's request two or three times.

Not long after the Buddha had departed, the old man himself leaned over a rafter; the rafter fell upon his head and he died. The entire household wailed and wept. The Buddha said, "How utterly foolish!
Death stands before him, yet he still does not turn his heart [toward the Dharma]. By what means could he escape birth and death? Therefore it is said:
"Until the moment of impermanence, one’s heart is never at ease. This is the Master of the Section citing from the sutra.
In meaning, this compares to all living beings who, from dawn until nightfall, do not contemplate birth and death, but only grieve over poverty.
They employ their minds to devise schemes until the moment of impermanence arrives, yet these do not satisfy their hearts.
The Great Teaching of Prajñā consists of more than six hundred fascicles, proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Buddha Tathāgata.

This section constitutes the essential framework of the textual meaning, elucidating the eight divisions of Prajñā, totaling six hundred and two fascicles and comprising two hundred thousand verses (*gāthā*) in all. It is solely the Great Wisdom of Prajñā that expounds these eighty-one [sections].

This section alone reveals the principle of true emptiness. Of the remaining six hundred fascicles [of the Mahāyāna scriptures] that were proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Buddha, many were spoken by Śrāvakas who, by the Buddha’s command, transmitted the teachings to Bodhisattvas.
This single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, however, was spoken directly by the Buddha’s own mouth;
therefore, it is said: "The Tathāgata, the Buddha, proclaimed it from his golden mouth."
"Translated during the Six Dynasties; circulated in the Eastern Land.
Regarding "translated during the Six Dynasties," this refers to how this one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* underwent translation throughout the Six Dynasties.
First, the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty translated it at Cháng'ān Cǎotáng Temple in the fifth year of the Hóngshǐ era.

Translated into fifteen sheets; titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Second, the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei translated it into fourteen sheets at Luoyang in the second year of the Tiānpíng era; it is also titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Third, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty [translated it] in the first year of the Tàikāng era...
1. During the [Liu] Song dynasty, in Jinling Commandery, it was translated into fourteen sheets; it is titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. 2.
During the Sui dynasty, Dharmagupta, in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, at Luoyang, translated it into sixteen sheets;
it is also titled *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. 3. During the Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Xuanzang, in the Zhenguan... [text ends]
In the twenty-second year [of the Zhenguan era], while at Yuhua Palace, it was translated into eighteen sheets and titled *Nengduan Jingang Banruo Boluomi* (The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā that Cuts Off).
In the second year of the Zhenxing era, the Tang monk Yijing, while at Foshouji Monastery, translated it into twelve sheets, also titled *Nengduan Jingang Banruo Boluomi*. Therefore...

It is said: "The translations of the Six Dynasties. As for *fan* (translation): it means to turn the Sanskrit language into the Chinese language; hence it is called *fan*. As for *yi* (interpretation/translation):
it means to take what exists in that [foreign] land and interpret it into what was previously absent here; hence it is called *yi*. Regarding "the Eastern Land":
this country is referred to as the Eastern Land in contrast to the Western Heaven (India). This sutra was translated and transmitted throughout the world, so that the teachings were widely practiced.
Therefore, it is called "circulation.

To recite these four lines of the true exposition repeatedly brings merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that surpasses all else, and its karmic fruit benefits beings in the realms of humans and devas.
This passage clarifies the places where this sutra should circulate; if there are practitioners who recite it with earnest devotion, then by means of this alone—

This four-line verse is indeed the merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The merit thus obtained ensures that, in every life and every birth, one shall always dwell among humans and in the heavens, enjoying inexhaustible rewards.
Therefore it is said: "The fruit and retribution of unconditioned merit surpasses [all others], benefiting both humans and devas.
Within this sutra, there are five instances where the merit of giving the seven treasures as alms does not equal even a quarter of [the merit of this verse].

Regarding the merit of these phrases: giving is with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas upholding this sutra is without outflows (*anāsrava*). Therefore it is said: "The merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is supreme.
I bow my head to the Lord of the Three Realms, To the Greatly Filial Śākyamuni Honored One, Who throughout successive kalpas repaid his parents' kindness.
"Having accumulated causes, he attained Perfect Enlightenment;
I bow my head to him. This refers to the nine grades found in the *Rites of Zhou* (*Zhouli*), of which this is the first.

"Bowing" (*jie*) means to touch one's head to the ground and remain there for a short duration, according to the ritual of a subject prostrating before a sovereign. "Great Filiality" (*Daxiao*) presents the preceding phrase while also serving as a term of praise.
It is said: "The Honored One Śākyamuni is the Great Filial Son. This is a turning phrase that describes the causes for practicing great filial piety.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddha practiced filiality in every place among the four modes of birth and the twelve classes of beings. He manifested such great filial acts as King Śatrujit (Jieti), who cut his own flesh to provide for his parents;
Xiǎnzi, who attended to his blind parents; and the Parrot, who carried grain in its beak—such instances of great filial piety, continuing until he attained Buddhahood.
In Kāpiśī, he visited his father; in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he comforted his kin.

He lifted the foot of Queen Māyā’s couch and carried King Śuddhodana’s golden coffin, which is said to be the repayment of kindness accumulated over kalpas. This concluding verse is thus the fruit of great filial piety.

By means of the cause of filial conduct throughout kalpas, he has now realized the fruit of attaining Buddhahood. Confucians say that filial piety is the foremost of all virtues; this is the teaching of the Śākya.
That is to say: filial piety is the root of all practices; hence it is said that by accumulating causes one achieves perfect enlightenment.
This sutra is a Mahāyāna teaching, which is to be cultivated by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"This sutra" refers to this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna.
"Mahā" (Great) has the meaning of distinguishing [this vehicle] from the "small" (Hīnayāna); "yāna" (vehicle) is named for its function of transporting [beings]. There are two types of Mahāyāna:

first, the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, which merely teaches that all phenomena are empty but does not yet exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma; therefore, it is called "initial. Because it is initial...

This refers to entering the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, among the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching], the third is the Perfect (Samyak) Mahāyāna, so called because it is correct, square, and impartial;

it universally benefits those of the three faculties and clarifies all four teachings simultaneously. Second is the Final Teaching of the Mahāyāna, which explains that the *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions to become the *ālayavijñāna*, and that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), such that all things are as they are. It teaches that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures are without [Buddha-]nature.
Icchantikas shall all attain Buddhahood; this is precisely the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna, and is therefore called "final.
It is also called the "True Teaching" (Shijiao), for it accords with the true principle, and is thus termed "true. This *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* belongs among these five teachings.

This concludes the inclusion within the Final and Perfect Teaching (*niṣṭhā-naya*). As for "Bodhisattvas," this refers to both Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and those who have attained the stages.

Bodhisattvas prior to the stages cultivate the Dharma of the Initial Mahāyāna Teaching, while Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages cultivate the Dharma of the Final and Perfect Mahāyāna Teaching.
Regarding the Middle Way within these teachings: the Bodhisattva is like the cool moon, constantly traversing ultimate emptiness within the water of the sentient beings' minds.
Zhan: Within the manifestation of the shadow of bodhi, prajñā is the most supreme among the six pāramitās. For this reason, it is named Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding the six perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom, it is only the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that serves as their unifying principle.
It is like a woman who is beautiful and very wealthy; if she is not protected by a husband, she is easily insulted and oppressed by wicked men.
The five perfections, such as giving and the rest, are exactly like this: if they lack wisdom...
Because it is easily corrupted by Māra when not sustained by its majestic power (*prabhāva*), it is called "the most supreme" (*parama*).
Why is this? Because this *prajñāpāramitā* is the sovereign of the six perfections; therefore, this *prajñāpāramitā* is established as the title.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
This citation of scriptural meaning serves as proof for this point and explains the preceding passage. Thus, this sutra is intended for those who are Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.

This is what was practiced and taught. It is for the sake of those who have set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle (agrayāna) that the preceding text is explained and established: Prajñā is the most supreme.
This was taught for the Buddha, the person of the Bodhisattva of the Supreme Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden Teaching (yuan-dun-jiao).
According to this teaching of the Buddha, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* consists of six hundred fascicles in total across sixteen assemblies.
This sutra is the fifth hundred and seventy-seventh fascicle; it was preached at the second location, the Jeta Grove, during the ninth assembly.
This is indeed the work of a master of the school (kejiā). It records the Buddha’s preaching of this *Prajñāpāramitā*, including the number of fascicles, the location, and the name of the assembly;
it follows such precedents and is thus clear and evident.
Therefore it is said: "In the past, the Tathāgata expounded it with his golden mouth; To this day, picking it up again, it is renewed once more."

As for the term "Commentary" (kē), this is what the author himself calls it. Since these are the Prajñāpāramitā teachings spoken by the Buddha, I have therefore commented upon the text and also referred to them as "the Way.
In the past, it was clearly stated that the Buddha was in the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden personally speaking these words of the Prajñā from his own golden mouth.
As for the present, from the time the Buddha preached this sutra until the fourteenth emperor of the Great Song dynasty:
In the second year of the Chunyou era of Emperor Lizong, this ritual protocol was established. It is similar to the Buddha’s own re-proclamation of the teachings while he was in the world;
thus it is said: "To this day, when [the whisk] is raised, it is once again renewed."
This sutra was spoken by the Buddha over three thousand years ago; immeasurable humans and devas have received its transmission and remembered it.
One must further understand that which existed before hearing it—referring to the first two lines.
These clarify that from the time this sutra was first spoken by the Buddha until the Chunyu era of the Song dynasty, [three...]
More than one thousand two hundred and twenty years have passed; thus it is said, "several thousand years. Since the arrival of our Great Ming Jiajing era, more than four thousand years have elapsed.

As for the upholding, recitation, and transcription of this sutra, whether by humans, devas, or heavenly beings, there have been immeasurable and boundless instances such that its transmission remains inexhaustible;
hence it is said: "It circulates throughout the heavens and the human realm, pervading the oceans of lands as numerous as motes of dust."
The latter two lines reveal the realm of the patch-robed monk (nanseng). Regarding the phrase "one who remembers the ancients," it means that this sutra exists within each and every person;
do not seek it elsewhere. One must realize the essential meaning before the voice and clarify the fundamental principle beyond the words.
Thus Yongming said: "If you wish to investigate the Buddha-vehicle and explore the precious treasury, let every single thing be resolved and returned to yourself."
Every word is in profound accord with the true mind; one must simply not cling to the literal expressions of the meaning and allow understanding to arise merely from following the words.

One need only investigate the underlying intent beneath the explanations and harmonize with the fundamental school. Then, teacherless wisdom will manifest before you, and the natural, celestial Way will no longer be obscured.
Human life is truly difficult to obtain; An inch of time is an inch of gold.
Do not wait until old age to study the Way; The solitary graves are all but the young.
These four lines of verse lament the impermanence of the world. The first line laments that time passes easily and that one’s lifespan does not endure long.

Pause. The second line exhorts people: a single inch of time is like an inch of gold; one must value it and maintain clear awareness, never allowing the years and months to pass in vain or letting this light of life be wasted.
As the ancients said: "A foot-long jade disc is not a treasure; an inch of time is what one strives for.
The meaning of the third line is that the practice of cultivation does not depend on whether one is old or young, nor on [the duration of] birth and death.
How could this depend on morning or evening? An ancient worthy said: "A single lamp illuminates the night tomb;
/ Upon the bed, one strips off both socks and shoes. / The three souls and seven spirits depart in a dream; / It remains unknown whether they will return tomorrow.
This concluding verse speaks of birth and death, making no distinction between old and young; therefore, it is said that most solitary graves belong to those who died young.
The wisdom of a lay bodhisattva is not [fixed] as permanent; Even amidst the bustle of a marketplace, they establish a site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa).
If the ground of the mind is free from hindrance, Then high mountains and level plains are all the Western Land [of Sukhāvatī].
The opening verse states: "Regarding those who live at home and practice the six perfections of a bodhisattva, these are people of wisdom. As it says:

This is precisely Vimalakīrti and Layman Pang. Thus, the Layman Ruru said: "One whose body does not leave the household life, yet whose mind has left the household life, is called a Bodhisattva within the teachings.
As it is said: "Practicing dhyāna while amidst desire through the power of knowledge and vision;
a lotus born from fire is never destroyed. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas possess wives, children, and retinues, yet they cultivate [the path]."

Regarding the conduct of Bodhisattvas: there are some Bodhisattvas who first experience the five desires and subsequently renounce them with weary detachment, diligently cultivating pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).

There are also some Bodhisattvas who, through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), manifest the acceptance of the five desires for the sake of maturing sentient beings, yet in reality they remain free from any defiled attachment.
The second phrase presents the aforementioned meaning, stating that this is not within the scope of ordinary human intelligence.
The practitioner must take the bustling marketplace as the site for cultivating the Way;

this may be described as "establishing oneself within a sea of right and wrong, planting one's feet amidst thorns and brambles. These latter two lines are the Master’s clear instruction, completely overturning [all delusions].
If the mind-ground is unstained by any conditions and remains dispassionate toward all phenomena, there will be no further entanglements.
Whether obstructed by barriers, hidden on high mountains, or dwelling on level plains, all are the Pure Land of the West.
As it is said, "The Pure Land pervades the entire dharma-realm; why then point specifically to the west? When the mind is ever-awake at every moment, everywhere is Amitābha.
Therefore it is said: "High mountains and level plains are all the Western Land."
The essence of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is suchness; Green bamboos and yellow flowers fill the road.
More than eight hundred houses display their wondrous hands, Everyone copying the gourd by following the model.
The first line states that the great essence of wisdom is precisely true suchness (*tathatā*). For within the essence of true suchness, there is inherently...

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is able to know both movement and stillness. The second phrase points out the essence of the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), which pervades all places, whether material or immaterial;
that is to say, "the verdant green bamboo is entirely *tathatā*, and the luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than *prajñā* (wisdom).
The third phrase refers to the "eight hundred or more families," meaning there were eight hundred students under the gate of Kumārajīva.
The Qin ruler issued an edict to Sengqie and others, eight hundred śramaṇas, to receive Kumārajīva’s instructions and translate sūtras and śāstras.
It consists of three hundred and eighty fascicles. Among the eight hundred people [involved], there were four sages:
Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, and Sengrui. There were also ten eminent scholars, including Tanyi, Huiyan, Huiguan, Senglüe, Daochang, and Daobiao.
In the fifth year of the Hongshi era, at Caotang Monastery, they translated this sutra; thus it is said that "over eight hundred families" [participated].
Regarding the phrase "presenting works to the masterful hand," this praises the eight hundred translators who were proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit.

Whether translating single texts or re-translating existing ones, they standardized the terminology and polished the prose, adhering strictly to the guidelines of the scriptures. Their literary style and meaning were so precise that they all accorded with the Buddha’s intent;

thus, they are lauded as "masterful hands. As for the concluding phrase, "painting a gourd according to the model," this is a term of disparagement. It implies that although these eight hundred individuals...
Those of wondrous skill always interpret the meaning according to the sutras, much like tracing a gourd by following its outline.
Yet those who seek the true person among the masters must realize the wisdom that is inherently present beyond the scriptural texts spoken by the Tathāgata. Now tell me:
what is this inherently present wisdom? The essence of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is suchness; emerald bamboos and golden chrysanthemums fill the road.

This is it. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is inherently possessed by every person. With the wisdom that severs [delusion] as the beginning, where the white clouds disperse, the single orb is revealed.
The preceding passage provides a general assessment of the six hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. This present passage provides a specific assessment of the title of this sutra:
the eight characters of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thus, by manifesting both the Dharma and its metaphor, it points back to the person who is its intended recipient.
Regarding "taking the wisdom of severing as the beginning," this is a designation based on the meaning of a metaphor. Because the diamond tip is sharp, it can sever everything;
likewise, the metaphor of *prajñā*-wisdom being most sharp indicates its ability to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Thus, among the six translations, the third by Paramārtha and the fourth by Guṇabhadra both translated it as "severing" (*duànge*), while the fifth by Xuanzang and the sixth by Yijing [translated it differently].
Both are translated as "capable of severing. Regarding the phrase "where white clouds disperse": the preceding text stated that *vajra-prajñā* is the essence and "severing" is its function.
These two lines describe the efficacy of that function; therefore, it is metaphorically likened to the dispersal of clouds and the emergence of the moon.
When delusion is exhausted, truth manifests;
reflections fall upon a thousand rivers, neither coming nor going. All you people, take this up! Ordinary and holy beings dwell together as one.
To present what was before—delusion exhausted and truth manifest—is like clouds dispersing and the moon standing alone. This textual metaphor is like clear water reflecting the moon.
Coming and going are without sentience. Water never invited the moon from the heavens to descend into it;
the moon never came from the heavens to cast itself into the depths of the water. As it is said: "The mind is like the bright moon, pure as the sky;
its nature is tranquil, as clear as a cold pond to its very bottom. Thus, there is neither coming nor going. The latter two lines are the master’s explicit clarification.
Instruction: I have come here in this manner. The Dharma and its metaphors are clear; I have expounded this principle.

Why do you all not realize and take it up? Only then will you know that ordinary beings and sages are of one essence, and that phenomena and principle are without distinction. Therefore, it is said: "We dwell together as one."
The Mahā-dharma King has neither shortness nor length; originally neither black nor white, he manifests blue and yellow wherever he may be.
"Mahā" (Great) is a term that combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit designations. "Dharmarāja" (Dharma King) refers to the wisdom of *prajñā* as the king.
It possesses mastery over all phenomena; internally, it is not buried by the sense organs and consciousnesses, and externally, it is not deluded by sensory objects.
Therefore, it is called "mastery. This essence of the Mind-King has no characteristics of length or shortness, nor any colors such as black or white.
That which manifests as blue or yellow in various places is because this Mind-King, though devoid of physical form, internally contains the three [natures].
Like a seed, when encountering objects and meeting with conditions, it is able to manifest the phenomena of the sense organs, the body, and the physical world;
hence it is said that "it manifests blue and yellow wherever it goes."
[Sūtra] The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
This sūtra is titled according to both its dharma and its metaphor. "Vajra" is the metaphor; "Prajñā" is the dharma. As for "vajra":

Gold is that which is most refined and solid among metals. Hardness arises from within gold; even after a hundred refinements, it does not diminish. Taking this hardness and sharpness, one can sever and destroy all things.
In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā*; in the Tang language, "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). Its essential nature is empty and harmonious, while its illuminating function is sovereign.
It is able to sever the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion, as well as all inverted views. [In the Sanskrit language...]
Pāramitā means "reaching the other shore" in the language of Tang. By not clinging to various marks (lakṣaṇa), one attains and realizes nirvāṇa, which is precisely reaching the other shore.
If one clings to various marks, one transmigrates through birth and death; this is the "this shore.
To reach the other shore, one must rely upon Prajñā. Sūtra means "path"; this sūtra is the path for realizing one's nature and becoming a Buddha.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "This single fascicle of scripture is fully present within the nature of all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
The two characters 'Zongjing' (Mirror of the Source) are based on the ancient commentary by Vajra; they were originally the title of the scripture annotated by the layman Yan Bing, known as Ruru.
This single fascicle of scripture is fully present within the nature of all sentient beings throughout the six realms, even unto the point of clearly realizing the self.
This is the very nature. From the moment one avoids chasing after the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*), one is no longer bound by the six sense organs and the six sense objects.
Even when the flower of the mind (*citta-puṣpa*) shines forth, where is it? This passage is a text spoken from the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source); it is the work of a master of the school.
He is well able to provide illumination and transformation, cutting what is long and supplementing what is short to complete a single passage of text and meaning;

this is simply to reveal one's own nature (svabhāva) to others. As for this single fascicle of the sutra, not only are the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) fully present within it, but even sentient and insentient beings are all fully present therein. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "There is a great scroll of a sutra, its size equal to the three..."
A thousand worlds exist within a single mote of dust, and it is the same for all motes. The Venerable Old Master Yudam composed a verse:
"A single scroll of the True Sutra is the reality of the foundations of mindfulness; Every word that flows forth is pure gold.
How many seek the literal meaning upon paper, Only to miss the mind of the Buddha who came from the West. This is indeed so.
It is because after receiving this body, one delusively allows the six sense organs and six sense objects to bury and obscure this segment of numinous light;
throughout the day, one remains in darkness, neither knowing nor perceiving it.

This is the Master’s own formulation of a question and answer. He asks: "Since this sutra is complete in itself, why does it not manifest signs such as the emission of light or the shaking of the earth like the Sages do?
He answers: "It is because after receiving a physical body, one is falsely submerged by the sense faculties and their objects.
"Falsely" means that which does not exist in reality. As the Heart Sutra says: "Therefore, within emptiness, there is no..."
There is no form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.

This clarifies that within the essence of Prajñā, there are neither sense organs (*indriya*) nor sense objects (*viṣaya*). Therefore it is said: "Alas, the priceless jewel is buried and obscured by the six sense organs and six sense objects.
As the ancients said: "What a pity! A jewel of inestimable value lies hidden in the pit of the *āyatanas*. On what day..."
One attains the solitary radiance of numinous light, which is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects.

As for the phrase "remaining in perpetual obscurity throughout the day," it means that although these sentient beings possess this scripture, they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects; deluded about themselves, they pursue external things, and thus it is said they are neither aware nor conscious.
Therefore, our Buddha gave rise to a heart of compassion, vowing to save all sentient beings so that they might collectively transcend the sea of suffering and together realize Bodhi.
"Therefore" (*gu*) means "for this reason. It is because sentient beings inherently possess this segment of radiance, yet remain deluded and unaware of it.
The Buddha gives rise to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*): through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he bestows happiness; through compassion (*karuṇā*), he uproots suffering;
and through the vow, he seeks to save all sentient beings. He gives rise to the Four Great Vows (*catvāri mahāpraṇidhānāni*) to transform the sentient beings of the five vehicles.

As for the "sea of suffering," because the sufferings of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are boundless, they are metaphorically likened to an ocean. Therefore, when our Buddha appeared in the world, he provided various teachings to cause all beings universally to attain [liberation].
To cross the ocean of suffering and together realize the path to Bodhi.
The reason for preaching this sutra in the kingdom of Śrāvastī is as follows:
"The reason" refers back to what preceded; "for the sake of preaching" introduces what follows. This is because the sentient beings who came before—
This sutra was originally present but had become buried and forgotten; it is for this reason that I preach this sutra, to reveal the wisdom that is inherently possessed.
Its general meaning is simply to untie the knots and loosen the bonds for people, so that they may directly and clearly realize their own nature and avoid pursuing the cycle of saṃsāra.
One is not deluded by the six sense organs or the six sense objects.

As for the general purport: it clarifies that the Buddha’s primary intent in preaching this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was to lead people to understand and eliminate the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life, as well as the notion of "mine," so that they may directly and clearly realize the nature of true emptiness and transcend [all attachments].

Regarding "transmigration": one is not deluded by the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). As for "adhesion and bondage": when sentient beings recognize a self (*ātman*), the six sense organs adhere to the profound stillness;

when they falsely recognize what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*), the six sense objects bind them. Since the self is ultimately empty and non-existent, how could the sense organs and their objects exist?
Both self and dharmas are empty; thus it is said: "to untangle the clinging and remove the bonds.
