how then is it upheld? It may be said: even if one’s eyes are like shooting stars, one cannot avoid having a mouth like a wooden door-bolt.
The Vajra-jewel sword leans against the cold heavens;

the brains of externalists and malevolent spirits are all split asunder—these two lines reveal the meaning of being without anything to uphold. The commentator [uses] the "Vajra King Jewel Sword" [as a metaphor].
This is a metaphor for prajñā-wisdom. Beyond this wisdom, not even a fragment of a thing can be found. Apart from the one mind, there is no other dharma that can be transmitted or received.
Like the cold radiance of a precious sword that shatters the courage of all demons, the so-called Great Man wields the sword of wisdom;
the blade of prajñā has the brilliance of a vajra flame. It does not merely destroy external [phenomena] in vain.
The Mind of the Way has long since caused the demons of heaven to lose their courage—so it is.
Herein, fundamentally, there is no trace of a name; who would dare to forcibly impose a title upon the void?
With ease, the adamantine eye is revealed, piercing through the eighty thousand cities of the Mara King.
The first two lines of the verse summarize the meaning within the sutra. It states that Prajñā is nameless and True Emptiness is formless;

therefore, the Master of the Text (the *kejiashi*) reveals it directly and does not conceal even a hair’s breadth of its reality. Thus it is said: "Within this, there is originally not a single word."
Regarding the principle of the true emptiness thus explained, who would dare to assign it a name? It may be said that where there is a name, it cannot be invoked;
where there is no position, there is nothing to be arranged. As for the latter two lines:
if a practitioner can directly realize the true wisdom of Prajñā, it is like casually pointing out the Vajra Eye. This Vajra Eye is precisely what is inherently possessed by each person.
This is the eye of wisdom. When this eye is opened, it can shatter the eighty-four thousand delusions of the afflictions and defilements of all sentient beings.
Thus, the Heart Sutra says: "Illuminating and seeing that the five aggregates are all empty, one transcends all suffering and calamity."
Thus one shatters the eighty thousand cities of the Māra kings.
Do not be startled by the passage of a hundred years; When old age comes, what thing can serve as your future?
Rely solely upon the three thousand treasuries of the scriptures; Do not spend a lifetime in vain and empty pursuits.
The first two lines praise human life in this world: there is but a hundred-year span of light.
From dawn until dusk, one only craves fame and profit, refusing to be startled by oneself; that time is limited and worldly cycles are few. Once old age arrives—
What do you intend to take with you as provisions for your journey ahead?

Just as a traveler first prepares his supplies so as not to suffer the pangs of hunger, so too must one who cultivates the Way inevitably avoid the perils of the three miserable realms. As an ancient worthy said:
"Two-thirds of one's life have already passed; the single point of the numinous mind remains unpolished. One pursues the days in vain, driven by greed for life."
"Go! If one calls out but does not turn back, what can be done? Such a person has likewise not yet discerned their future path.
The latter two lines praise the reason for discerning the future path:

they intend to cause the practitioner, in the midst of daily life, not to waste time or let the years pass in vain, but must instead be diligent in the six recollections and carefully maintain a single mind while chanting.
The profound texts of the Tripitaka exhaustively investigate the deep meanings of the five vehicles; thus it is said: "Rely solely upon the three thousand volumes of the canon.
Do not spend a lifetime in vain pursuit of the empty and flowery. This is the admonition of the commentators to practitioners:

do not mistake the empty and flowery phenomena of the triple world for something truly existent. It is a pity to let a lifetime pass in vain; regret will be difficult to undo once it is too late. One should heed this.
That is to say: reciting a thousand sutras while deluded is merely a small matter; yet a single moment of awakening must be vast. Therefore, a sutra says:
"All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them in this way."
Prajñā manifests before one, free from obstruction; Transcending the universe, do not harbor doubt or suspicion.
The void is squeezed through, impossible to conceal; The Great Way is manifest—return! Return!
The first two lines clarify that the phenomena of the triple world are born from a single Prajñā. Now it says: "Prajñā manifests..."
Previously, it was said that all phenomena are entirely empty; this is precisely Prajñā. Therefore, it is called "unimpeded. It can be said:

"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—fully reveal the body of the Dharma King. Regarding the phrase "stretching its body across the universe," this means that because this Prajñā is free from all obstructions, it extends its body across the universe, filling the vast void. It can be said that it vertically exhausts the three periods of time.
It extends horizontally throughout the ten directions; therefore, it is said: "Do not harbor doubt or suspicion.
The latter two lines mean that the great function of Prajñā manifests before one, causing all of the empty space of the ten directions to utterly vanish.

"The Great Way is manifest" means that when Prajñā appears, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—none of these can be grasped in the slightest degree. As an ancient said: "Floating..."
Life is easy to pass, but do not let it pass in vain. The Great Way is difficult to clarify; one must strive to explain and understand it. Therefore it is said:
"The Great Way is clear—return! Return!

"Transcending form and abiding in extinction—who could make distinctions? Even with a mouth, it is difficult to speak. For five hundred lifetimes, my limbs and joints were severed."
This section was elucidated by Prince Zhaoming, who designated this passage of the sutra as "Chapter Fourteen: The Section on Detachment from Characteristics and Quiescent Extinction.
This is because the Buddha taught that to give rise to the bodhicitta while detached from all characteristics is precisely what constitutes hearing this scripture.
To be free from the four marks of self, person, and so forth is precisely what is called the Buddhas. Having realized the principle of quiescence, they are given this name:
"quiescence free from marks. Who is it that makes such distinctions? Since it is quiescence free from marks, it is the state free from the two attachments to persons and phenomena;
this is called the true mark of quiescence. Since there is no longer the view of attachment to a person, furthermore—
What discriminating emotions could there be? Therefore, it is perfectly round, without interior or exterior; it harmonizes above and below, and is level.

Since that which is difficult to express with words has already spoken the principle of quiescence, the mind is empty of the four marks, and one must depart from the attachment to persons—this is the non-discriminating mind.
Departing from the marks of dharmas and departing from the attachment to dharmas, what would there be to say? Hence it is said:
There is a mouth, yet it is difficult to speak; that is to say, the path of speech is severed and the sphere of mental activity has ceased.
The phrase "throughout five hundred lifetimes" extends this preceding meaning, for it is the reason why one is detached from marks and abides in quiescence.

"Who would engage in discrimination? means there is no grasping at a person (*pudgala*). "There is a mouth, yet it is difficult to speak" means there is no grasping at phenomena (*dharma*). Because these two types of grasping are absent, [it is thus].
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is able to practice patience. For example, when the Buddha was once King Kali, his body was cut and dismembered;

yet it was not only in this single lifetime that he was free from the two attachments. Throughout five hundred lifetimes as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, he was likewise free from the two attachments, and thus was able to practice patience. This is why his limbs and joints were severed.
Yet there is not a single thought that gives rise to false or empty speech regarding the attainment of the Way or the realization of the fruit.
"The clouds disperse, yet the moon is present in every house"—this means there is not a single thought that gives rise to false or empty speech.

This clarifies that the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, speaks reality, speaks as it is, speaks without deception, and speaks without variation. The intent is that the Tathāgata is not merely [one of] the five...
Throughout a hundred lifetimes, he performed these deeds of asceticism that are difficult to practice and difficult to endure.
Furthermore, for immeasurable eons, he has not uttered a single thought or word of deception or falsehood; this demonstrates that the Buddha’s words are entirely true and devoid of falsity.

Moreover, it is said: when the Buddha speaks of sentient beings having happiness, they definitely experience happiness; when the Buddha speaks of sentient beings having suffering, [they definitely experience suffering].
One will certainly undergo suffering. It is as if one were to say that the sun could become cold or the moon could become hot;
no demons can destroy the True Teaching. The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "O Brahmins, they collectively established a regulation not to give food to the Buddha.
If anyone gives food to the Buddha, they shall be fined five hundred gold coins. At that time, when the Buddha entered the city to beg for alms, everyone closed their doors, leaving him empty-handed.
He went out with his bowl. There was a woman who, having filled a broken vessel with foul, dregs-like gruel, was going out her door to discard it.
Seeing that the Buddha’s bowl was empty, this woman immediately conceived faith and wished to make an offering. She thought, "This food is foul-smelling; I fear he will not accept it.
The Buddha, knowing her intention, accepted her gift and bestowed upon her this prophecy: "For fifteen kalpas, you shall dwell among the gods..."

In the human realm above, he will receive blessings and happiness, not falling into the evil paths; later, he will obtain a male body, leave the household life to study the Way, and become a Pratyekabuddha.
The brahmins said, "For the sake of food, the Buddha speaks such falsehoods.
The Buddha then extended his tongue until it covered his face and reached up to the hairline, saying to the brahmins, "Have you seen in the various scriptures..."

"Is it possible for such a tongue to utter false speech? "O Brahmin, prostrate before the Buddha and repent of your transgression. By comparing this with that, one sees that the Buddha has no false speech;

therefore, he possesses the mark of the long tongue. As for those who have attained the Way and realized the fruit—meaning the Buddha, who throughout five hundred lifetimes has already abandoned the two attachments to persons and phenomena, as well as all signs—it is through such cultivation and progress that he has now [attained this].

Having attained the Way and realized the fruit, one manifests bodies throughout the ten dharma realms and preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings. This is like clouds dispersing across the vast sky, such that every household has its moon.

This illustrates how, while seated in a single place, one appears simultaneously throughout the ten directions; with a single voice, it is heard equally across all lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus it is said: "Clouds disperse, and every household has its moon. Master Guangzhi said: "Clouds disperse, and every household..."
The moon: where emotions are cleansed, it is manifest everywhere. In a state of neither dependence nor utility, one is the King within the Dharma.
Free from characteristics, there is no teaching; ancient and modern, eternally quiescent and extinguished. Without a single thought-moment, let you divide and branch out as you will.
"Free from marks" means being free from the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

"It is not that which can be spoken" means that since one is already free from these four marks, what further dharma could there be to speak? Therefore, it is said: "it is not that which can be spoken.

"Constantly quiescent throughout past and present" means that since the four marks do not exist, there is no speaking regarding dharmas; spanning from antiquity to the present, it is neither shifting nor changing—only this.
This is the principle of the single true reality; hence it is said, "eternally quiescent.

As for the phrase "without a single thought-moment," it means that since the Tathāgata is free from the two attachments to self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*), even if others were to dismember him limb by limb, he would not give rise to a single thought.
[He thinks: "Though you cut and slice my body into pieces, I have no thought of discrimination or calculation regarding this."
If one harbors even a single thought of discrimination between self and other, then resentment will arise. Since there is no resentment, both person and phenomena are empty;
one thus realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore it is said: "Let them sever your limbs as they please."
Yongjia said: "My Master met Dīpaṃkara Buddha; for many kalpas he was once the Immortal of Endurance. Section Fourteen:
The Division on Detachment from Marks and Quiescent Extinction.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sūtra being preached... [up to] "being free from all marks is itself called the Buddhas.
[Commentary] This section of the sūtra is titled the "Section on the Quiescence of Freedom from Marks.

It is because Subhūti, upon hearing this sūtra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent—that he deeply understood what was previously established through the giving away of body and life.
The merit [derived from that] is not equal to the excellence of receiving, upholding, and expounding these four lines of verse. Now, having heard this sutra, he was moved by its profound kindness;
he wept with tears streaming down and praised it as rare, saying to himself: "Since time immemorial, although I have attained the eye of wisdom..."
The reasoning proves the emptiness of persons; however, they have not yet heard the profound meaning of this sutra. Furthermore, it says:

"If a person hears this sutra and their faith becomes pure, then the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) will arise. The intended meaning is that upon hearing this sutra, one immediately believes in the Prajñāpāramitā and does not believe in [the substantiality of] all phenomena;
this is what is meant by "pure faith. Once the mind is pure, the true mark arises.
Therefore it is said: "Thus one gives rise to the true mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Someone asked Yongming: "What is called the true mark of all phenomena? He replied:
"That which is called 'all phenomena' is ultimately empty and non-existent. Because they are thus non-existent, this is called the true mark of all phenomena.
One should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
The meaning is this: because these people hear this sutra, they realize the principle of the true mark (lakṣaṇa) and accomplish the merits of the Dharma-body;

therefore, it is called the foremost rarity. Subhūti, furthermore, when the World-Honored One says that this "true mark" is actually "no-mark," the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "true mark"—that which is called the true mark is precisely the absence of marks. This is...
It is without marks, like the great void of space, which possesses not a single form or characteristic. It is just as the taste of salt in water or the blue pigment within lacquer:
they certainly exist, yet their forms are not seen. The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is likewise. Therefore it is said:
"For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true mark. Subhūti further said: "Now that I have heard such a sūtra as this, I believe..."
To understand, receive, and uphold [this teaching] is not difficult. As for those in future ages, the meaning is this:

that I have now encountered the Buddha and heard this sutra is not considered difficult; however, that sentient beings of the future will hear this Dharma, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it—this is truly rare.
To "believe, understand, receive, and uphold" means that the mind is free from doubt; this is called faith and comprehension.

To thoroughly understand the principles is called "understanding" (解). To reverently accept them without arrogance is called "receiving" (受). To wear them upon oneself without weariness is called "upholding" (持).

That future sentient beings should thus believe, understand, receive, and uphold [this teaching] is truly rare. Furthermore, it says: "For what reason? This person has no marks of self," and so forth.
This means that Subhūti is inquiring about the preceding meaning: for what purpose [is this said]?

That one should be able to hear this sutra is truly rare. Such a person practices according to this sutra and does not give rise to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. Why is this? Because the mark of self is precisely the absence of marks.
That which is "non-characteristic" is precisely the "true characteristic. By being free from all characteristics, one achieves perfect enlightenment;
therefore, it is said that this is what is called the Buddhas. Wuzhuo says: "This person has no marks of self" indicates the absence of attachment to the grasping of a person.
"The mark of self is precisely non-characteristic" indicates the absence of attachment to the grasping of dharmas. Free from all...
"Characteristics" refers to the manifestation of attachment to the characteristic of the emptiness of emptiness. One should know that such a person is pure by being free from characteristics;
they have realized and awakened to the three kinds of emptiness, do not cling to the two extremes, do not abide in the middle way, and have no dwelling whatsoever.
Thus, they accord with the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), attain ultimate *nirvāṇa*, and are named "Buddhas. Master Fu said: "When Kūṭadanta heard the wondrous principle..."

Like tares growing among hemp, the common masses believe in this teaching; yet it is like fire producing lotuses. Fearing that people might give rise to the view of nihilism, the Great Sage preemptively established prohibitions and permissions.
If one can remain free from all conceptual marks, they will certainly enter the royal house of the Dharma.
[Sūtra] The Buddha told Subhūti: “It is so, it is so... (up to) there is no mark of a sentient being, no mark of a life-span.
The Buddha said, “It is so, it is so,” which is a term of assent. Changshui said:
From the passage “At that time, Subhūti heard this sūtra being preached” down to “being free from all marks is called all Buddhas,” these are all [quotations].
Regarding the words of Subhūti, there are six main points within them: first, weeping with grief upon hearing the Dharma; second, the arising of faith in the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*);
third, the contrast between the difficult and the easy; fourth, clarifying the absence of self and person (*pudgala*); fifth, the simultaneous elimination of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Because all six will attain Buddhahood, these words are entirely true and authentic. Thus the Buddha’s seal says:
"So it is, so it is. It further says: "If there be a person who hears this sutra and is not startled, not terrified, and not afraid, such a person is most rare.
This is because the Dharma of the Mahāyāna is difficult to believe and difficult to understand; yet if such a person hears this sutra...
Within [this teaching], there are no four marks such as self or person. One who hears that all dharmas are empty is not startled;
one who hears that even emptiness is empty is not afraid. You should know that such a person is truly rare. Furthermore, it says: "For what reason?
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of the foremost pāramitā," and so forth. The Buddha himself poses this question: for what intention does this person [act]?
It is truly rare that upon hearing the Dharma one does not give rise to fear or alarm; therefore, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

"The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*," thereby manifesting its supremacy among all causes. As previously stated: "If such a person hears this sutra and believes and understands the *prajñā*, they are immediately the most rare of the rare.
Because they hear the *prajñā*, they immediately give rise to the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); this is the rarity.
This Dharma has no equal; therefore, it is called "foremost. If one realizes that there are no marks and remains unattached to phenomena, one immediately reaches the other shore.
Because one benefits sentient beings within the realm of conventional truth, it is called the foremost *pāramitā*.
When one fully awakens to the emptiness of both person and phenomena, there is no birth-and-death to be crossed, nor is there an "other shore" to be reached.
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is further said that [this perfection] is not the foremost *pāramitā*.

Furthermore, fearing that people might cling to the two extremes, [it is taught that] within the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), one is detached from the conventional and detached from the real; thus, phenomena are identical with principle.
Therefore it is said: "This is called the first *pāramitā*. It is further said: "The *pāramitā* of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
What the Tathāgata calls the *pāramitā* of patience is not a *pāramitā* of patience; it is called the *pāramitā* of patience. Regarding patience: among the six perfections, this is the third.

To accept [injury] with composure is called "patience" (*kṣānti*); to be subjected to defamation and harm is called "insult" (*mala*). Hence, it is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*). Thus it is called "the *pāramitā* of patience."
As stated previously: "The karmic reward for sacrificing one's body and life is a cause of suffering within birth and death; it does not equal the merit of upholding and expounding [the Dharma].
Why is it that this practice of patience (*kṣānti*) does not become a cause of suffering when sacrificing body and life?

It is because this practice of patience can penetrate the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and reach the other shore (*pāramitā*); therefore, it is called the "Perfection of Patience" (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata speaks of "non-patience-perfection," he does so to dispel attachment.
Within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), if one can practice the conduct of patience and endure that which is endurable, this is called attachment.

Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), one realizes that both the practitioner and the practice are ultimately unattainable; therefore, it is said to be "non-existent. This is what is called patience.
Regarding the term "pāramitā": this single phrase was added erroneously by later generations; let us explain it provisionally.
If one is a practitioner who does not dwell upon the act of forbearance, and even does not maintain the mind that does not dwell, only then is it the pāramitā of kṣānti (patience).
The Buddha further said: "As when I was once King Kali and my body was cut and mangled."
The Buddha himself cites a past event to corroborate the present. Such was the practice of patience that I once performed;
therefore, he cites the incident of Kali to bear witness to it. In Sanskrit, *Kali* means "Extremely Wicked King.

This refers to when the Tathāgata, while practicing the path in a previous life, had realized the stage of a first-stage Bodhisattva and was seated in meditative absorption within the mountains, when he encountered—
King Kali went out of the city on a hunting expedition. When the king reached the mountains, he grew weary and rested;

upon waking from his sleep, he did not see his attendants or the court ladies. He then entered the mountain himself and saw those many queens and court ladies surrounding and prostrating before a rishi.
The king was greatly incensed and asked, "How is it that you have indulged your passions by gazing upon my women? The rishi replied: "At..."
"Regarding the forms of women, I truly have no attachment. The King asked, "How is it that you see forms yet do not feel desire?

The Rishi replied, "By maintaining the precepts with single-minded devotion. The King asked, "What is meant by maintaining the precepts? The Rishi replied, "Patience is itself the maintenance of the precepts.
Thereupon, the King took a knife and cut off the Rishi’s ears, nose, hands, and feet, asking, "Is it painful? The Rishi replied, "It is not painful."
The king likewise had him dismembered limb by limb. He asked, "Is it painful? The seer replied, "Truly, it is not painful.
At that time, the prime minister and great ministers remonstrated, saying, "This Great Being, though encountering such suffering and affliction, has a joyful countenance and remains unshaken;
why does Your Majesty inflict such harm upon him? The king then desisted. At that time, the king was... [the text continues].
Kauṇḍinya was indeed like this. The "Seer" (ṛṣi) was none other than Śākyamuni. Because the Seer practiced the path of forbearance, even when subjected to harm, he harbored no resentment whatsoever;
this was because he was able to thoroughly realize that the four marks—the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—are all empty.
Furthermore, it is asked: "For what reason? This is a reiteration of the preceding meaning, intended to clarify the Buddha’s intent.
[Subhūti] asked: "For what reason is there no mark of self or person? The Buddha himself replied:

"In the past, when my body was being dismembered limb by limb, if there had been the four marks of self and person, I would have given rise to anger and resentment. This conversely reveals the preceding meaning:
since those four marks did not exist, there was no anger or resentment. The Buddha further told Subhūti: "Furthermore, I recall the past..."
For five hundred lifetimes, he was a rishi of forbearance. Throughout those lifetimes, there was no one equal to him in selflessness.
The Buddha himself cited his past existence as a rishi of forbearance for five hundred lifetimes to corroborate the account of King Kali;

this demonstrates that his practice of patience did not pertain to a single lifetime alone. Thus, by citing the traces of his ability to endure over five hundred lifetimes, he manifested the Buddha’s [virtue].
There is no false speech. Did I not say previously? Not even for a single thought does one give rise to delusion or utter empty words.

By practicing the patience of the Buddha, one is not only free from suffering, but moreover possesses joy. What is called "joy" is because the mind is detached from the four marks and both types of grasping are empty, thereby realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Master Fu’s verse says: "Violence and cruelty belong only to the unrighteous."
At that time, he was King Kali. Encountering you as you went out on a hunt, the seer was unjustly wounded.
This occurred throughout five hundred successive lifetimes, spanning an exceedingly long duration. By virtue of the seer’s power of forbearance, he has now realized the true and eternal.
[Sūtra] Therefore, Subhūti, [from this point until] they all achieve immeasurable and boundless merit.
For this reason, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) while remaining detached from all marks (nimitta). "For this reason" means:

This is a transitional phrase that concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one. It concludes the account of his practice over successive lifetimes and his endurance of insults from the Bodhisattva of Patience;
because he attained *bodhi* through the absence of self and person, he has now become a Buddha. Therefore, it causes [the listener] to resolve upon *bodhicitta*.
A Bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon the Great Way of unsurpassed *bodhi*. "Do not dwell on the mark of form when generating the mind," and so forth.

This refers to the Bodhisattva who has resolved to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). To "not dwell in the six sensory objects"—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—is precisely to be free from all marks (*nimitta*).
"One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere" means that this Bodhisattva’s mind has no place of dwelling;
it is precisely by this that one can abide in enlightenment (*bodhi*). If the mind were to have a dwelling, then this Bodhisattva—if the mind [were to dwell] upon...
If dharmas have abiding, then one is not abiding in the bodhi of the Buddha-way. Therefore, the Buddha said that the mind of a bodhisattva should not abide in form when practicing giving.
"Therefore" concludes the preceding discussion on the six perfections practiced by bodhisattvas;
these are all formless giving, and their merit is equal in measure to the dharma-realm, being inexhaustible. [To take] form as [the object] is to [cling to] the six sense-objects.
First, giving is the beginning of the six perfections; therefore it is said: "One should not dwell on form while practicing giving.
Furthermore, the Buddha told Subhūti: "A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner.
This means that when a bodhisattva practices giving in this way for the benefit of all living beings, they perform entirely signless (animitta) giving.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata says, "All marks are themselves non-marks," this statement was spoken by the Tathāgata himself to dispel attachment.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "The Tathāgata says that all marks, such as self and person, have no substantial reality;
they are ultimately subject to destruction and do not truly exist—this is what is meant by 'non-mark. All sentient beings..."
Birth and extinction are merely provisional names. If one is free from the deluded mind, then no sentient beings can be found;
therefore, it is said that they "are not [truly] sentient beings. The *Jíjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) states: "All phenomena" refers to the realm of dharmas (*dharmaviṣaya*).
"They are not phenomena" reveals the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmaśūnyatā*). "All sentient beings" refers to the realm of persons (*pudgalaviṣaya*). "They are not [truly] sentient beings..."

"Those who are born" reveals the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Because this Bodhisattva is detached from all marks (*nimitta*), it is said that both types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are empty.
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying, "The Tathāgata speaks the true word," and so forth.

This means that the wondrous fruit of Bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is realized in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta*) and is beyond verbal expression. For what reason, then, does he repeatedly exhort [others] to uphold and explain it?
Is this merit superior to the blessings of giving and so forth? Indeed it is. For the Buddha realizes that which is not to be realized and speaks that which is not to be spoken;
yet what he realizes and what he speaks never fail to accord with the principle. Fearing that Subhūti had not yet grasped this meaning, [the Blessed One spoke thus].
Therefore, it is further declared: "The Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth. Speaking the truth refers to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma of Bodhi.
Speaking reality refers to the teaching of the Hīnayāna Dharma. Speaking as it is refers to the teaching of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
"Not speaking otherwise" refers to the teaching of predictions regarding the future. "Not speaking deceptively" refers to not deceiving sentient beings.
All five kinds of speech spoken by the Tathāgata are entirely true and devoid of falsehood. Thus, the *Jīvitakumāra-sūtra* states:
"The sun, moon, and stars may fall to the earth; mountains and rocks may fly from the ground into the sky."
"The waters of the ocean, though deep and vast, may be made to dry up; yet the words of the Buddha are definitive and free from falsehood. This is so. Furthermore, the Buddha told Subhūti:
"The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma is neither real nor unreal. When the Tathāgata realized this for himself, he said:
"The Dharma I have realized is fundamentally beyond verbal expression; therefore, it is called 'not real. Because it is taught in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, it is..."
This means there is no falsehood. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:

"If a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing. This clarifies that the bodhisattva’s practice of giving is for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
If one dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, one does not realize the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
This is called giving while abiding in dharmas. If one teaches sentient beings to abide in and cling to dharmas, there is no way for them to perceive true nature;
therefore, it is likened to a person entering darkness, where nothing can be seen. If a bodhisattva practices giving...

One does not cling to phenomena. If one realizes the essence of the three spheres (*trimandala*) and transcends names, one thoroughly understands that both the primary and secondary [receptacles] are unattainable; the entire body is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of ultimate emptiness. Regarding such a principle, it was stated previously:
"The merit of giving away as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in one *Ganges* river does not equal that of receiving and upholding [this teaching]."
"To explain even a four-line verse to others brings forth far greater merit. Having heard this meaning, Subhūti was moved by realization and compassion, and his tears fell like rain.
Regarding the phrase "the Immortal [Śākyamuni] bestowed compassion upon Hongren and others," it means that the Tathāgata, in his initial causal stage, acted as the Immortal of Forbearance;
throughout five hundred lifetimes, he practiced the path of forbearance in order to understand people.
Because the dharmas are empty of both [self and phenomena], one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Although his body was dismembered by King Kali, it was like snow-blades vainly cutting through space; this is because this bodhisattva thoroughly realized that this body is like space.
Regarding the confirmation of these words: it means that the Buddha has certified and authorized what Subhūti has previously stated, as it is consistent with reason;
thus he says, "So it is, so it is. This confirms that one is able to be free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

The intended meaning is that this person is devoid of the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span; this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The mark of a self is precisely non-existence.

"Characteristics" refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). To be free from all characteristics is precisely what is called the Buddhas; this is the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is said: "One is able to be free from all characteristics.
Regarding the phrase "I do not yet understand the point of realization," etc., this is the Master of the Text (the *kejiā*) posing a question about the preceding meaning.
He asks: tell me, in what extraordinary way did Subhūti realize and awaken to the principle? The following passage [explains this].
"Stretching forth [the hand] is the answer that reveals [the truth]. 'Opening wide the eye of wisdom, bright as the sun;

reflecting back, the world of subtle dust is seen as empty'—these two lines respond to the meaning of the preceding text. This is because Subhūti, upon hearing the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā, opened [his eyes]."
Open the eye of wisdom. Realize the non-existence of self and person and the four marks; see all phenomena as empty, like the bright sun in the sky.
A hundred years of time are but a flash of light from a flint—why did you not turn back and contemplate the mark of impermanence sooner?
Do not delay; avoid having to stand before King Yama to have your life-span measured.
The first two lines praise the fact that although a human life may last a hundred years, its passage is as swift as a spark from a flint;
it cannot be retained for long. I urge all people: why do you not turn back and reflect with urgency?
Since this body will not endure, why not hasten to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land? Cast aside this non-substantial body and realize the True and Eternal.

This refers to the body. The final two lines exhort practitioners: if you rely on the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance, you shall escape the ocean of suffering of birth and death and attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss. Even if the signs of impermanence should appear, they may be set aside;
they cannot bind or summon you, sparing you from falling into the hands of King Yama. How could one then concern oneself with the length of one's life? This may be called "understanding the ghost."
The divine eye perceives the indestructible mechanism; one transcends to a realm where birth and death do not interfere.
This is the land of true bliss, true permanence, and true purity, where jeweled ponds, jeweled trees, and jeweled flowers bloom.
There is neither cold nor heat, and no fading or change. Return, return! Return, return!
These four lines clearly indicate the realm of the West. For the people within that land of Amitābha Buddha have lifespans of countless kalpas;
in a single lifetime they succeed to the rank of Buddhahood and together realize the one state of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is the true Pure Land. That which is non-transmigratory and unchanging is called true permanence; it is free from the suffering of the two deaths.
This is called true bliss. The eight great masteries are called the true self. The total extinction of afflictions is called the true pure land.
There are ponds of the seven treasures, seven rows of trees, and lotuses of four colors;

there is no change between winter cold and summer heat, nor the seasonal transformations of spring flourishing and autumn withering. In such a place of joy, I universally exhort all people: why do you not [seek it]?
May we swiftly depart from this defiled land and proceed directly to the Lotus Land. A *udumbara* verse says: "Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and remain at ease within yourself;
With a cool eye, constantly observe the worldly realm. If you realize that what is before you is the true pure land, This mind will no longer involve itself in manifold complexities."
The merit of upholding this sutra is so vast that it is difficult to compare; even the three temporal metaphors cannot equal it. Giving while abiding in signs must ultimately lead to decline.
This section is the "Section on the Merit of Upholding the Sutra," as determined by Prince Zhaoming. This concludes the first part of the text.
Fifteen: It is named such because the merit of upholding this sutra surpasses the merit of giving in the three periods [of day and night].

Regarding "the blessings are so great they are difficult to compare": although the merit of giving away as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges during the three periods is vast, these are merely the blessings of humans and devas;
they do not yet involve seeing one's nature. Thus, they cannot be compared to the merit of upholding this sutra.
By upholding this sutra and explaining it for others, one is able to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood.

Regarding the metaphor of the three periods being unequal, this restates the meaning of the scriptural text to clarify that "the first part of the day" mentioned in the sutra refers to the hours of *yin*, *mao*, and *chen*.
The division of the day refers to the hours of *si*, *wu*, and *wei*. The division of the subsequent day refers to the hours of *shen*, *you*, and *xu*.
Suppose there were someone who, for three periods of the day over the course of immeasurable kalpas, gave up immeasurable bodies to practice giving;
yet their merit would not equal the excellence of the merit gained by hearing this sutra and giving rise to faith—how much more so for one who copies, receives, maintains, and recites it?
To recite [this teaching] and explain it to others for their benefit is millions of billions of times superior to that; thus it is said that the three periods of time are not equivalent.

Regarding "giving while abiding in marks," this refers to giving away one's body and life during the three periods of time without realizing that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence.
Such a person merely attains the blessings of gods and humans, which must eventually decline, because they have not clarified the true nature (*dharmatā*). Their mind...
Because one gives rise to attachment to existence, there is regression.
Untainted wisdom suddenly realizes Bodhi; the flower blooms and its petals fall, the sun rises in the east and the moon sets in the west.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "If there are those who receive and uphold this sutra and explain it for others, they shall all achieve inconceivable merit.
Such persons as these are indeed carrying the burden of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
This statement regarding "untainted wisdom" (anāsrava-jñāna) refers precisely to the untainted wisdom of *prajñā*.

By upholding this true sutra, one perceives one's own original nature and forever leaves the cycle of saṃsāra.
Therefore, even a hundred thousand million billion parts of the merit from making offerings to the Buddha do not equal one part of the merit from upholding the sutra in the final age;
thus, it cannot be reached by means of calculation or analogy. People in the final age merely know how to serve the Buddha, yet they do not know the Buddha.
The ultimate principle is entirely contained within this sutra; therefore, the merit of upholding and expounding it is exceedingly great.

Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty built monasteries, practiced charity, made offerings to the Buddha, and hosted vegetarian feasts, then inquired of Bodhidharma: "What merit is there in these deeds? The Patriarch replied:
"In truth, there is no merit. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit? The Patriarch said, "This is merely a minor fruit of humans and devas;
it is a cause characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*). The Emperor asked, "What, then, is true merit? The Patriarch said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect."
The essence is inherently empty and quiescent. Such merit as this cannot be sought through signs. Later generations did not understand this meaning;

they took making offerings to the Buddha to cultivate blessings as being "merit. They did not know that merit resides within the Dharmakāya, and not in what is sought through the cultivation of blessings.
The blessings thus sought do not equal true merit; offering to the Buddha does not equal upholding the sutra. The Buddha...
Furthermore, it says: "If, in the future final age, someone were to receive and uphold this sutra, as for its merit—if I were to describe it in full, the Buddha’s intention would be this:

those who uphold this sutra in my final age, even though the aforementioned comparison of the merit of making offerings to countless Buddhas does not equal even a single fraction of the merit of upholding this sutra—this is still but a brief explanation. If one were to explain it further..."
The merit of this sutra is that it is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna; it is precisely the wisdom that is primordially possessed. There may be those who, upon hearing it, immediately become deranged;
this is because one fears there are those who delight in the Lesser Dharma, and upon hearing this Mahāyāna, their minds will become confused and distressed, falling into doubt and lack of faith.
Because the Way is vast while their faculties are small, they find it difficult to reach its subtlety, and thus give rise to doubt. One should...
The meaning of this sutra refers to the wisdom of *prajñā*. This *prajñā*-wisdom is inconceivable.
That its retribution is also inconceivable means that "retribution" refers to the merit obtained;
because one awakens to the true nature through the wisdom of *prajñā*, the merit of the Buddha-fruit and *bodhi* thus obtained is therefore inconceivable.
This is the deliberation.
Due to the conditions of past karma, one falls into the evil realms; yet now, by being treated with contempt by others, one's transgressions are immediately extinguished.

To make offerings to the Buddhas and recite this sutra, the merit is so superior that no analogy can reach it. Now, as for that which is non-attached and signless—does it still have karmic retribution or not?
Regarding those with residual karma destined for the evil realms: this section refers to those who are held in contempt by others.

Although their transgressions from previous lives ought to cause them to fall into the evil realms, because they now constantly uphold this sutra and directly perceive their true nature in this present life, their offenses are immediately extinguished.

Regarding those who make offerings to the Buddha and recite the sutras: this section explains that the Buddha, when formerly before Dīpaṃkara Buddha, made offerings to eight hundred forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, yet the merit of upholding this sutra was superior and could not be matched by such offerings;
it is beyond the reach of any analogy. As for being "without attachment and without marks," this reveals the true emptiness that is markless and non-existent.
Regarding the principle of this attachment: there is no reciting of sutras that can extinguish transgressions, nor is there any making of offerings to the Buddha that can yield fruit.
As for the phrase "there is still retribution," this is the interrogative language of the master of the school;
it suggests that within such a formless Dharmakāya, there is truly no retribution to be obtained. Therefore, Yongjia said: "No sin or merit; no loss or gain—quiescence."
Within the nature of cessation, do not seek or inquire. The dust-mirrors of the past have never been polished; today, you must clearly analyze them.
The following lines provide the response:
When the deluded mind is extinguished, karma returns to emptiness; one directly realizes Bodhi, transcending all stages.

These two lines answer the meaning of the preceding passage. It is simply that according to the principle of the Dharma-body, which is without attachment and without marks, since there is neither sin nor merit, how could there be karmic retribution? When deluded mind is extinguished, sinful karma returns to emptiness;
one may say that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty because it is created by the mind. If the mind is extinguished, sin likewise perishes. One directly realizes Bodhi. Since...

The nature of sin is fundamentally empty; this is itself bodhi. Without relying on the application of effortful practice to sever delusions and clarify the truth, one directly perceives one's nature, thereby transcending the fifty-two stages of gradual cultivation and progression.
By whom does evil abide? By whom is sin summoned? The true nature is like space, unshakable;
Ignorance, spanning kalpas, is swept away entirely; Before heaven and after earth, all is silent and vast.
The first line restates the meaning found within the Sūtra. The Sūtra says: "This person’s sinful karma from previous lives ought to cause them to fall into the evil realms."
The intent of the masters of the Vinaya school is as follows: As for the cause of evil karma, who is it that creates it? As for the fruit of receiving retribution, who is it that summons it?
If one discusses this according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiang zong), it is the delusive afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) that act as the creator;
the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*), which contain and store [seeds], act as that which summons. Therefore, it is said: "Karma and its fruit can summon, lead, fulfill, and draw forth."
However, this is not the case for those of the present scholastic schools (*kojia*).

Although they maintain that causes and effects, as well as karmic offenses, clearly manifest as inducements—much like waves upon water that possess the appearance of movement—these are merely the wind of objects arising and ceasing falsely;
fundamentally, they have no substantial reality. This nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is like the vast void: profound, serene, and pure, inherently unmoving.
Furthermore, from the perspective of the Chan school (nàsēng ménxià), where karmic offenses are fundamentally empty and cause and effect do not exist, one may say: "The real is not established;
the false is fundamentally empty; both existence and non-existence are discarded, yet it is not a mere emptiness. The latter two lines restate the meaning of the sutra.
Because those of the present age treat it with contempt and disdain, their transgressions and karmic obstacles from previous lives are thereby extinguished, and they attain the realization of Bodhi.
The intent of the commentary is this: if a practitioner cultivates the contemplation of Prajñā and upholds this sutra, they will thoroughly sweep away the false ignorance accumulated over vast eons;
there remains only the true emptiness of Prajñā, which is like the great void that is originally so.
Vast and empty; thus it is said: "Before heaven and after earth, all is silent and still.
A hundred years of life pass like flowing water; Without end and without limit, when will it cease?
It is better to first realize the path to Bodhi, So as to entirely escape saṃsāra and attain freedom.
The first two lines praise human life, noting that a single lifetime lasts but a hundred years. Death leads back to birth, and birth leads back to death;
this is likened to the flow of water, where the preceding and succeeding moments continue in succession without interruption. Therefore, it is said:
"Infinite and inexhaustible, when will it ever cease? The latter two lines exhort one to practice and advance, implying that since this is the cycle of birth and death...
It is inexhaustible. A practitioner must cultivate the Mahāyāna Dharma to realize the path to Bodhi.

If one relies on the teachings of the Hīnayāna, although one may cultivate the causes and effects of humans and devas as well as the nine successive meditative absorptions (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), this does not constitute escaping saṃsāra;

one will not attain mastery. It is better to first realize the Mahāyāna, for at the very moment of the initial resolve (prathamacittotpāda), one attains perfect enlightenment and is no longer subject to birth.
Bound by death, yet unstained by the defilements of worldly toil, it is said: "All are spared from saṃsāra and attain freedom.
Return! Return! Let the one spiritual essence no longer enter a womb;
be reborn upon the body of a flower, with a golden hue. Beholding the golden countenance face-to-face—return!"
The first two lines constitute the section on Compassion. The Master’s instruction is extremely clear:

he says that "the two who have gone and returned" refers to stating it once and then stating it again, because he fears people may not believe him; thus, he repeatedly exhorts and entrusts [this teaching].
"Let the single spirit not go further" clarifies that the single spiritual true nature is precisely the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). If it departs from the parents...
At the moment of entering the womb, two initial states of mind arise: aversion and attachment. There are seven kinds of impurity regarding the entry into the womb.
First is the impurity of the seed, which refers to this body of sexual desire; it arises from the seeds of ignorance and the affliction of craving.
Second is the impurity of conception, which refers to this body arising from the two drops—the red and white—of the father and mother.

First, impurity of combination: consciousness enters into it. Second, impurity of dwelling: this body dwells for ten months in the mother’s womb, situated between the stomach (the organ of digestion) and the large intestine (the organ of maturation).
Third, impurity of the dwelling place: that is, this body dwells in the mother’s womb below the stomach and above the large intestine.
Fourth, impurity of consumption: while in the mother’s womb, it consumes nothing but the mother’s blood-clots. Fifth, impurity of birth: that is, the birth of this body.
At that time, [the fetus] emerges head-first through the birth canal along with the blood;
it is foul-smelling and filthy, like grass falling between two clashing mountains, or like a living cow being flayed. Sixth, the entire body is impure, meaning that within this body’s thin skin—
Pus and blood pervade every part. Seventh is ultimate impurity: this body, from its very birth, undergoes gradual transformation;
it passes from youth to maturity, from maturity to old age, and from old age to death, becoming bloated and putrid.
The flesh and bones lie scattered about, devoured by foxes and wolves. Because this physical body is subject to such suffering, it is said:
"Let the single spirit no longer enter a womb. The latter two lines indicate a path out of birth and death;
because one does not enter a womb, they point toward the Western World. If a person recites the Buddha's name, they will go to that land.

One is born by transformation upon a lotus flower of earth. One’s body is like the color of gold, and one immediately beholds Amitābha Buddha face-to-face, hears the Dharma, receives a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and realizes the stage of non-retrogression.
Thus it is said: "Beholding the complete form with one's own eyes, return and come forth. An ancient worthy composed a verse:
With a focused mind, contemplate Amitābha; return home and depart. Ascend afar to the nine grades and entrust yourself to the lotus womb.
When the flower blooms, behold the True Buddha face-to-face; a single radiance will pervade the nine realms.
Ultimate non-self. The four elements are entirely empty; the five aggregates are merely provisional designations. To penetrate all phenomena is to realize that they are empty everywhere.
This section, as judged by Prince Zhaoming, constitutes the "Section on Ultimate Non-Self," the first part of this scripture.
The Seventeenth Covering: The Buddha taught that all dharmas have the characteristic of selflessness (*anātman*) and so forth. Although the phrasing is the same, their meanings differ.
Previously, you asked only about the dharmas that can abide and can subdue; this was merely to destroy delusion and manifest wisdom.
The delusion to be destroyed is precisely the coarse attachment to the four marks, such as "self" and "person. The wisdom manifested is precisely *prajñā*.

This is the wisdom [of the Tathāgata]. From this point downward, the forgetting of wisdom reveals the principle, thereby shattering the subtle attachments to the four marks, such as the self and persons.

Fearing that the Bodhisattva, upon entering the path of realization, might think, "I am able to abide," or "I am able to subdue," and thus maintain this discriminating mind—which is itself the self—the following text states: "If, at the time of the Tathāgata’s presence with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there were..."
If one could obtain a dharma and thereby realize bodhi, that would constitute having a self (*ātman*). If no dharma can be obtained and no path can be realized, this is called non-self (*anātman*).
Furthermore, it is said: "If a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, for this reason this name is established as ultimate non-self.
Regarding "the four elements are entirely empty": this refers to this body, which is the basis of suffering, [composed of] earth, water, and so forth.

It is formed through the combination of the four great elements—fire and wind—and exists as a hollow accumulation of the five aggregates. Ordinary beings falsely conceptualize this and provisionally establish it as a "self.
If this self does not exist, then the four great elements and the five aggregates are also empty. One who penetrates all phenomena [realizes this].

In this section, it is stated that the Tathāgata, in reality, possesses no dharma by which he attained the realization of bodhi; therefore, he received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara. It further states:
"The Tathāgata is precisely the 'coming as all dharmas' (tathā-āgata); for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata. He taught that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharmas.
If a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, they are then free from the dharmas of the four marks: self, person, being, and life.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that one is truly a bodhisattva. Thus, they are able to see that all phenomena are empty in every respect.
What was stated above—that the four great elements and five aggregates are entirely empty as the "direct retribution" (the primary body)—refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
What is said here—that one thoroughly penetrates the myriad dharmas as the "indirect retribution" (the environment)—refers to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Green mountains and clear waters; clouds arise in the vast sky. All you people, take this up! A yellow oriole sings in the morning breeze.
This is the Master’s revelation of the principle that all phenomena have been universally realized as empty everywhere.
By means of green mountains, clear waters, and clouds arising in the vast sky—where is there that does not realize this truth? It may be said: "The mountain..."
The rivers, grasses, and trees proclaim the ultimate truth; the wind, moon, pavilions, and terraces perform wondrous music.
Before one’s very eyes, light and dark, form and emptiness—all manifest this Way. That people fail to realize it is because the Master’s compassionate heart is too urgent;
he points it out clearly, above all phenomena and amidst sounds and colors, urging everyone to realize it as if hearing the cry of a yellow oriole.

The location is sound; the morning breeze is the environment. If a traveler can realize this within the realm of sound and form, seeing what person it is and hearing what thing it is—would this not be the thorough penetration of all phenomena?

It may be said that every tolling of the bell and ringing of the drum is none other than the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle; that every short cypress and tall pine is entirely Vairocana.
The True Realm. Long ago, when a virtuous elder was reciting the Lotus Sūtra, he heard the singing of a warbler and attained awakening. He spoke this verse:
All phenomena, from their very origin, Are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction. Spring arrives and the hundred flowers are fragrant; A yellow warbler sings atop the willows.
The prediction of enlightenment is fundamentally beyond words; Thus did the Great Awakened One of True Compassion proclaim. "The four marks are not four marks"—the fruit of bodhi is naturally fresh.
The first two lines cite the meaning within the sūtra, where the Buddha himself said: "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I truly had nothing..."
If there were a dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, only then would one receive a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Therefore it is said: "The prediction is fundamentally without words.
This was spoken by the Buddha himself: "If I possessed a dharma by which I attained bodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction upon me.
Thus it is said: "Proclaimed by the Great Awakened One. The latter two lines also recapitulate the meaning within the sūtra.
If a bodhisattva perceives that there are sentient beings to be delivered, dharmas to be attained, or an enlightenment to be realized;
or perceives that there is a pure land to be adorned—possessing both subject and object—they have not realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature and are thus attached to the four marks.
That which is free from the four marks means that the bodhisattva does not perceive even a single sentient being who is truly liberated, nor do they perceive any real dharma.
One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. In the truly pure land, there is no adornment; therefore, there is no self, person, or the four marks.
As for the fruit of bodhi being naturally fresh, it is because the Bodhisattva does not cling to the four marks regarding the Buddha-fruit of bodhi.
It is naturally fresh. It may be said that both existence and non-existence are cut off, revealing alone the single true void.
○ Chapter Seventeen: Ultimate Non-Self.
[Sūtra] At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary] This section of the sūtra is for those who have realized ultimate non-self (*paramārtha-nairātmya*).

Because the Bodhisattva-mind is devoid of the four marks of self and person, it accords with the fact that no dharma can be apprehended and no bodhi can be realized; therefore, it is called "ultimate non-self."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Noble Son, O Noble Daughter, having resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should one dwell and how should one subdue [the mind]?

Why is it that Subhūti, having previously asked this same meaning in the first part of the second division, asks it again here? While the phrasing of the question is identical, its meaning is distinct.
The meaning of the initial question was merely to inquire about the dharmas capable of abiding and capable of subduing.

By asking this, [the Buddha] feared that as the Bodhisattva was about to enter the path of realization, his mind might harbor attachments—thinking, "I am able to abide securely in the Mahāyāna," "I am able to subdue the afflictions," or "I am able to bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa. If such a mind of discrimination persists, it will obstruct non-abiding.
This is the Way. Therefore, he asks this question again, saying: "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon Bodhicitta should give rise to such a thought.
The Buddha's intention is that if a person wishes to resolve upon the unsurpassed Bodhicitta, they should give rise to [this thought].
"Non-attachment and non-abiding" refers to the profoundly serene and pure mind.
Regarding the passage "I should bring all sentient beings to extinction," the Buddha realizes that true emptiness is signless; thus, both subject and object are quiescent.

Although he brings sentient beings to extinction and has himself attained extinction, he does not give rise to a single thought of being the one who delivers beings, nor does he perceive any beings who are delivered.

Therefore it is said: "There is not a single sentient being who has been truly extinguished. Thus, the mind that seeks to dwell [in liberation] or to subdue [sentient beings] is from this point forth extinguished, and one then fully possesses the four minds. To say, "I should bring all sentient beings to extinction," is the vast mind (*vaipulya-citta*).
To say, "Having already brought all sentient beings to extinction," is the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*). And...

"There is not a single sentient being who is truly extinguished" refers to the mind of permanence (*nitya-citta*). Once one possesses this mind of permanence, one naturally lacks the four marks [of self, person, sentient being, and life-span];
this is the non-perverted mind. Why is this so? The Buddha asks this as a self-reflexive inquiry:
for what reason does the Bodhisattva have no sentient beings to deliver? It is because they are free from the four marks. The meaning is: if...
The passage, "A bodhisattva who has the notion of a self, etc., is not a bodhisattva," has the same meaning as the preceding section.

However, what preceded was the refutation of deluded attachment to reveal wisdom; the delusion to be refuted was the coarse grasping at the four marks, such as self and person, and the wisdom revealed was the true wisdom of *prajñā*. From this point onward, wisdom is forgotten to reveal the principle.
This breaks through the subtle attachments to the four marks, such as "self" and "person. By means of this stage of worthiness (*bhadra*), one gradually enters the ranks of the sages.

Therefore, the Buddha conversely reveals that the Bodhisattva’s mind is free from these four marks; although they spend their entire day saving sentient beings, they do not perceive even a single sentient being who is saved.
Why is this? This is a reiteration of the aforementioned meaning: for what reason is it so?
Seeing that there were beings who could be delivered, the Buddha then addressed Subhūti again, saying: "In truth, there is no dharma by which one sets out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha feared that bodhisattvas might mistakenly recognize such a thought as it arises, taking it to be a real mind;
yet this is not something inherently existing within true nature. Therefore, he spoke thus to shatter that misconception, and it is also because [the mind] is non-existent.
It is true. Therefore it is said: Within the principle of true emptiness, there has been from the beginning no form;

truly, there is no dharma that gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For on the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single speck of dust is admitted, and not a single dharma is established.
How, then, could there be any dharma? Master Fu’s verse says: "Empty-born asked again with earnestness: 'Without mind...'"
For one who wishes to awaken the bodhicitta for their own sake, they should understand that the immediate cause is the practice of compassion, which appears to be delusive;
through wisdom, it is said to be ultimately true. To deliver sentient beings, the provisional self is established; yet upon realizing the ultimate principle, there is no person at all.
[Sūtra]: "Subhūti, what do you think? ... [up to] 'The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.

Regarding this passage, since it follows from the preceding statement that "in reality there is no dharma," it refers to those who have come forth having resolved upon bodhicitta. Its intended meaning is as follows:

If there were no one who generates the mind of awakening, then there would be no bodhisattvas. How then could Śākyamuni, while at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, have been known as the Rishi Suprabuddha?
Having spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, how did he practice the conduct of a bodhisattva and receive the prediction of enlightenment?
Fearing that Subhūti might harbor such doubts, the Buddha raised this question, saying: "Subhūti."
"What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma through which he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Subhūti’s response means:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, at that time when he was named Sudhana under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was in truth no dharma whatsoever by which he obtained bodhi."
Subhūti. Having abandoned all conceptualization and attachment, and because he realized that no dharma can be apprehended, he received the prediction.
When the Buddha said, "So it is, so it is," it was because Subhūti had already realized that dharmas are unapprehendable;
the Buddha permitted his statement and confirmed it by saying, "So it is, so it is. Furthermore, the Buddha later addressed him, saying: "Subhūti, in truth, there is nothing..."
The Dharma attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. [The Buddha] wishes to cause Subhūti to know that dharmas have no attainment, thereby causing him to deeply accord with the ultimate principle.
The verse says: "The nature of bodhi is fundamentally empty; how can one speak of its attainment? That which is without speech and without attainment is the true cause of bodhi.
The Buddha further said: "If there were any dharma such that the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*..."
Regarding "bodhi": it was not the case that Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction (vyākaraṇa) that I would eventually become a buddha named Śākyamuni.
This is because the wondrous fruit realized by the Tathāgata is precisely the dharma-gate of the mind-ground;
it is the principle of truly having nothing to attain, free from all names and marks, and devoid of grasping or attachment. As for what is now called "receiving the prediction," it is...
Within that which is without prediction (*avyākṛta*), this discourse on prediction is precisely the prediction of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Subhūti, by means of a mind of non-attainment, has attained the wisdom of non-arising; this is what constitutes the prediction of non-arising. As for the phrase "Why is this so?", it is an interrogative expression used to raise a question:
for what reason? It refers back to the previous statement: "In reality, there is no dharma that attains the fruit of Bodhi"; therefore, he receives this [prediction].
The Record of the Lamp thus dispels doubt, saying: "Since there is no Buddha-fruit, how could there be Buddha-dharma? The following passage explains the answer:
"Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. "Such" (*tathā*) refers to True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*). That which is not false is called "True."

That which is not different is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). This means that one thoroughly realizes all phenomena (*dharma*) to be suchness, the principle of reality (*tattva*), which is neither void nor existent, neither changing nor shifting;
it penetrates the three periods of time and extends horizontally throughout the ten directions. This reveals that True Suchness is the Buddha, who is the very essence of the true Dharma.
If there is anything to be attained, it is not the Bodhi of the Buddha. As the Great Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi) stated in verse: "The nature of phenomena is neither cause nor effect."
If one does not follow reason by claiming that [the Buddha] obtained the prediction of becoming a lamp-lighter, how can it be known that this was his former body?
[Sūtra]: If someone were to say that the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi... [up to] ...the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly called a bodhisattva.
This section of the sutra serves as a defense against an objection. The Buddha anticipates an objection such as this:
"If it is the case that the Tathāgata is the meaning of 'suchness' (tathatā) of all dharmas, then there must be a Buddha and truly existent dharmas.
Why, then, did you previously say that there is truly no dharma by which the fruit of Buddhahood and bodhi can be attained? Therefore, the Buddha calls out to Subhūti and provides the answer himself.
[The Buddha] said: "In truth, there is not a single dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is inherently complete; how could it be obtained from without? The Buddha again called to Subhūti and addressed him, saying:

"Regarding the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality. This is because the *bodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is beyond the reach of conceptual thought."
And it is thus realized. "Without reality" means that this principle does not possess the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
"Without falsehood" refers to the essence of *tathatā* (suchness). Wuzhuo said: "Reality and falsehood are the two extremes of existence and non-existence, and permanence and annihilation.
When both of these are discarded, the Middle Way is spontaneously accorded. Therefore, it is said to be "without reality and without falsehood. For this reason, the Tathāgata preached all dharmas.
This is the meaning of the preceding summary and inquiry. For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of all dharmas.
The phrase "the Tathāgata" summarizes the preceding point that it is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
The phrase "all are Buddha-dharmas" summarizes the preceding point regarding the dharma that is neither real nor false. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti: "As for what is called 'all dharmas'..."
This is precisely the dharma of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is "not all dharmas" is precisely the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, that which is called "all dharmas" is precisely the Middle Way, which abides in neither the ultimate nor the conventional. Yet this reality (*tathatā*) does not exist as a separate entity;
it is precisely all dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. These dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and devoid of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); this is precisely reality.

Because its essence is such, all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Although this essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is not separate from all dharmas, one must not grasp or cling to it within those dharmas; therefore, it is said: "It is not all dharmas;
it is called 'all dharmas' [only as a designation]. Yongming said: "The *tathatā* of the Tathāgata is the *tathatā* of all dharmas. All...
"The Dharma-tathatā is precisely the Tathāgata-tathatā. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti, saying: "For example, it is like a human body that is tall and large.
The meaning is that the essence of the tathatā realized by the Tathāgata, as mentioned above, pervades all places.
It may be said that [Subhūti] had become tall; furthermore, fearing that Subhūti might give rise to the view of being "tall," the Buddha again established a metaphor to inquire of him, saying:

"For example, suppose a person's body were tall. This question regarding size was posed because, within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there exists the distinction between large and small.
Is it not that while they are truly great, they are merely called "great bodies" by way of empty names? Subhūti answered him, saying:
"World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large and tall," at which point Subhūti, through this analogy, attained realization and replied:
It is not a "great body," because within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there is neither great nor small; therefore it is said, "it is precisely not a great body.
That which is called a "great body" refers to the fact that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual, and existence and non-existence mutually manifest one another;
this is the dharmakāya of the primary meaning. The Buddha further told Subhūti: "The Bodhisattva is also like this. This phrase "like this" refers to—
The preceding statement means that if a bodhisattva dwells upon these words, thinking, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," this bodhisattva’s mind harbors attachment.
He claims for himself, "I am able to extinguish afflictions" and "I am able to deliver sentient beings."
Yet, if there are four marks, and if there is both subject and object, then one is not a bodhisattva. Why is this? This interrogative phrase raises the preceding point.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Because for a bodhisattva, in reality, there is no dharma to be apprehended;
the mind is detached from the four marks, and yet one does not perceive even a single sentient being to be delivered. One realizes that all dharmas are entirely empty and quiescent."
Originally unborn, one perceives neither birth and death nor nirvana; therefore it is said: "In reality, there is no dharma that can be called a bodhisattva.
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.
The phrase "for this reason" concludes the meaning of the preceding text, asserting that in reality there is no dharma that can be so named.
He acts as a bodhisattva. This bodhisattva has already departed from the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
Although he speaks of bringing all sentient beings to extinction (*parinirvāṇa*), there is not a single sentient being who is actually brought to extinction.

Because true emptiness is markless and, in reality, no dharma exists, the Buddha taught that all dharmas lack the four marks; what is revealed therein is the dharma of true emptiness and marklessness.
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying: "If a bodhisattva should speak thus, 'I shall adorn the buddha-fields,' he is not called a bodhisattva.

The Buddha's intention was this: if a bodhisattva practices the six perfections with the desire to go and adorn the buddha-fields, yet perceives that there is a pure land to be adorned, such a person has not yet abandoned the four marks; this is precisely attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
One who does not penetrate the emptiness of phenomena is not called a bodhisattva. What is called a buddha-field is precisely the field of the mind.
Since the buddha-field is without marks, how can it be adorned? If there were adornment, then the four marks would not have been eliminated;
this is the vision of an ordinary person. Why is this so? When the Tathāgata speaks of adorning a buddha-field, it is not actually adornment. It is...
Regarding the term "adornment," the Buddha’s intention is as follows: For what reason does he speak of adorning the buddha-fields?

It is because the Tathāgata further uses the signless and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to adorn the buddha-fields; moreover, since the buddha-fields are originally pure, what need is there for adornment?
Therefore, it is said that they are "not adornments. When it is now said that one "adorns the buddha-fields," this is according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
...in the Middle Way, one may speak of adornment. That which is "not adornment" means that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), what adornment could there be?
That which is called "adornment" means that within the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), it is adorned yet not adorned; it is unadorned yet adorned.
Thus, both the ultimate and the conventional are manifested together; this is the adornment of the Middle Way. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti: "If a bodhi..."
"One who thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self—such a person the Tathāgata calls a true Bodhisattva. This section concludes the preceding points by pairing them together.
