Long ago, an ancient worthy was awakened by the sound of a bell ringing at the corner of a hall. He spoke in verse: "Copper lips and iron tongues, too sharp and new;
Hanging from the pavilion, they have forgotten spring. Beyond words are hundreds of thousands of *samādhi* dharmas; The wind speaks them for those who understand. "Do not listen with your ears!
Thus it is said that "a flake of snow flies into a red furnace" is the teaching of the patriarchs. Taking what came before—[the text here is incomplete].
The meaning spoken here is laid open with eight characters and handed over with both hands; it requires one to transcend the mind, intellect, and consciousness to realize it.
These words are intended to lead one out from the paths of ordinary beings and sages, which is why it says: "Do not listen with your ears.

If this principle is heard with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to comprehend; only by hearing sound with the eyes can one truly know it. It is like a flake of snow flying onto a red-hot furnace.
It is like this: the phrase "this great forge and red furnace—how could it allow even a flake of snow to fly past?

serves as a metaphor for the ultimate principle (tattva), which cannot tolerate speech, grasping or rejecting, nor the conceptualizations of the mental path. Therefore, it is a place beyond deliberation, difficult for the consciousness and emotions to fathom.
In the *tathatā* dharmadhātu, there is neither self nor other; this too is the red furnace that does not tolerate even a flake of snow.
This is the meaning. Chan Master Kuang of Changzhi in Tanzhou first visited Master Shitou.
Shitou asked, "Where have you come from? Kuang replied, "From Lingnan. Shitou said, "At the head of Mount Dayu, there is a shop. Has the merit been fully accomplished yet?
Kuang said, "It has been accomplished long ago; it simply lacks the dotting of the eyes. Shitou said, "Do you not wish for them to be dotted?"
Dongmao invited [Shitou] specifically. Shitou lowered one foot to indicate it to him; Dongmao immediately prostrated.
Shitou asked, "What did you see that you prostrate? Dongmao said, "My state of realization is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace."

My mind is fundamentally non-existent; to whom could a mindless one speak? That which is spoken is not that which can be spoken—this opening verse is intended for those with the capacity for the Supreme Vehicle.
Regarding "my mind is fundamentally non-existent": because non-attachment to marks and signs is itself the Dharma-body, it is so stated.
It is not existent. This is the second phrase. Since one does not grasp or cling, this is precisely "no-mind.
If there is no mind, toward whom would one speak? Therefore it is said: "With no-mind, to whom could one speak? The final two phrases mean:
although the Dharma taught throughout the various periods of the Tathāgata’s lifetime—this path of wordlessness and formlessness—is for the sake of sentient beings, they simply do not understand it.
This is the principle. Therefore, there is that which is spoken; yet, because within the principle of true emptiness there has never been a single word, it is said to be "not that which is spoken.
Such discourse and non-discourse are intended solely for those with the capacity of the Mahāyāna, not for those of the Hīnayāna.
And thus it can be shouldered. Therefore it is said: "It is for the sake of those with the faculties of the Supreme Vehicle.
Section Twenty-one: That Which Is Not Spoken Is Spoken.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, do not say that the Tathāgata... [as in the sūtra] ...the Tathāgata says that what is not a sentient being is called a "sentient being."
The commentary states: This section is titled "The Meaning of That Which Is Not Spoken and That Which Is Spoken.

Because Subhūti doubted how the Tathāgata could preach the Dharma to others when the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) cannot be perceived, this question was posed in order to sever that doubt. It says: "Do not think, O Subhūti, that the Tathāgata has such a thought as: 'I shall have...'"
Regarding the Dharma that has been taught, do not entertain such thoughts. Why is this? This is the Buddha’s own inquiry:
for what reason is there no Dharma that can be taught? If anyone should say, "The Tathāgata has taught some Dharma," and so forth...

The meaning is this: the Tathāgata’s compassionate vows are profound and weighty; he responds according to the conditions that arise. He speaks where there is nothing to speak, and though he speaks, it is as if he spoke not.
Sentient beings do not comprehend this principle and claim that the Buddha has something to say; this constitutes slandering the Buddha, for they are unable to understand what the Buddha has taught.
Thus, the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata throughout forty-nine years was entirely in response to the capacities of those present.
It is said that within the principle of true emptiness, not a single word has ever been uttered. Therefore, the quiescent mark of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed through speech.
If one clings to the notion that the Buddha has a dharma to speak, one does not understand the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddha further addressed Subhūti, saying: "One who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is what is called 'one who preaches the Dharma'. The Buddha's intention was as follows:

What was previously stated—that there is preaching—constitutes a slander of the Buddha. Now, when it is said that one "preaches the Dharma," this refers to preaching in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
When it is said that "there is no dharma to preach," this is spoken in accordance with the ultimate principle, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This is what is called "one who preaches the Dharma. Now, within the state of non-preaching, one brings forth preaching;

yet this does not hinder preaching in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, through preaching, one manifests non-preaching—this is called "true preaching," which is itself the Middle Way.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, 'at that time' refers to the moment when the question was about to be raised."
Furthermore, as for "Life of Wisdom" (Āyuṣmat): because Subhūti is foremost in understanding emptiness and is in accord with the wisdom of the *prajñā* of emptiness, he takes wisdom as his life;
therefore, he is called "Life of Wisdom. [Subhūti asked: "Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?
Subhūti had previously heard the Buddha say that the physical body is a body that is not a body.
The teaching of the Dharma is a teaching that is not-teaching. Since both the person and the teaching are sublime, there is a fear that listeners may find it difficult to believe;
for this reason, such a question arises, asking whether one can give rise to faith. The Buddha answers Subhūti’s question:
"Those who are not sentient beings" refers to ordinary, mundane sentient beings who are unable to give rise to faith in this Prajñāpāramitā. It is not [that they are non-existent].
"Those who are not sentient beings" refers to those with the body of a noble one (*ārya*) who are able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding this *prajñā*.

Furthermore, another interpretation states: "Those who are not sentient beings" does not mean ordinary sentient beings, but rather those of the Mahāyāna who are able to believe in the true teaching within the teaching-less, and who are able to give rise to faith and understanding regarding the wisdom of *prajñā*. "Not non-sentient beings" means...
"Indeed, how could ordinary worldlings, upon hearing this Dharma, be able to believe and understand it?
These two interpretations remain; let the wise examine them further. Why is this? The Buddha himself raises the preceding point as a question.
The Buddha again addresses Subhūti, saying: 'Worldlings, worldlings'—this reiterates the previous text. They are not worldlings, nor..."

"They are not sentient beings. When the Tathāgata says they are "not sentient beings," he reiterates that they are not ordinary, mundane sentient beings, but rather Mahāyāna practitioners—those who possess the essence of the noble ones and are capable of generating faith and understanding. Thus, they are called "sentient beings."
To restate the preceding: these are ordinary sentient beings; how could they possibly believe in or understand this Dharma?
The Tathāgata has nothing to say; the compassionate clouds sprinkle a dense mist of ambrosia.
Those whose life of wisdom have not yet heard it—under the bright moon and clear wind, all is empty and still. At such a time as this, tell me: what realm is this?
That the Tathāgata has nothing to say is as the Sūtra states: "There is no dharma that can be spoken; this is called preaching the Dharma.
To preach by means of non-preaching is indeed true preaching. Therefore, it is likened to compassionate clouds universally covering all and sweet dew equally moistening everything;
thus, compassionate clouds spread throughout the ten directions, and sweet dew completely drenches the great earth. The life of wisdom has not yet...
Regarding "those who have heard": it is because Subhūti, upon hearing what the Buddha taught, realized its profound meaning;
thus, though he spoke, there was no speaking, which constitutes true speaking. Though he heard, there was no hearing, which constitutes true hearing.

Therefore, it is likened to the bright moon and the clear breeze universally illuminating heaven and earth. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "As for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstrating."
As for those who listen to the Dharma, there is neither hearing nor attainment. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Listening is like a phantom person listening;
speaking is like a phantom person speaking. There is no hearing within no speaking—this is called the true Dharma. Regarding the phrase "at this very moment," the Master’s intention is to say:
when it is precisely a state of no speaking and no hearing, tell me, what kind of realm is this? This is a rhetorical inquiry.
This explains the meaning [of the preceding]. What follows below is an elucidation.
"Should you wish not to incur karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
The intention of the master is that he fears people, upon hearing the Buddha preach this Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate of neither-speech-nor-attainment, might harbor doubts.
Because they do not believe, I have thus earnestly exhorted and cautioned them: one must be careful regarding the karma of speech to avoid falling into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, a sutra says: "If anyone should say that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they are slandering the Buddha. For this reason, the commentator says:
"If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma-Wheel of the Tathāgata. This is because Prajñāpāramitā is...
The Mother of all Buddhas is none other than the nature of sentient beings; both the animate and the inanimate arise from this, and for this reason it is called the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Yongming Yanshou said: "The ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) and prajñā are fundamentally no different from the three poisons.
If one can believe and accept this, the benefits of the Dharma will be vast and boundless. If one slanders prajñā, there is no transgression greater than this. Thus it is revealed.
One will suffer calamities and misfortunes in this world and be reborn in the hells.
This Prajñā is the mother of all mundane and supramundane beings, both ordinary and sagely; it is like the great earth, from which nothing is born that does not arise from the ground.
If one slanders Prajñā, one slanders the entire Triple Gem and the Buddha-ground of Prajñā, for the ten dharma realms emerge from within Prajñā. If...
Without the majestic radiance of Prajñā, not even a single speck of dust could possibly exist.

Now, by citing those who slandered this Prajñā and received retribution in their present lives, one may warn future generations who lack faith. During the Tang dynasty, Goulong Yi was a native of Langzhou.
In the third year of the Changqing era (823 CE), he supported himself by working as a laborer in Qi County. Because a person in the district fell ill, he went there...
He reflected on this and saw that it was contained within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He slandered and rejected it, and his speech immediately became mute;
no physician could cure him for five or six years. Whenever he heard a neighbor reciting this sūtra, he reproached himself, saying, "It is because I previously slandered this sūtra that I am mute.
If I can be cured, I shall honor and uphold it for the rest of my life. Every time the sūtra was being recited, he would lean against the wall to listen.
He practiced this until his contemplation became pure and mature. One day, while entering a temple by chance, he encountered an old monk who bowed to him.
When the monk asked what was wrong, he pointed to his mouth and said, "I am mute. The monk then cut the tendon beneath his tongue with a knife, whereupon he was immediately able to speak.
He recited the sutras with a melodic intonation, much like the voice of a neighbor.
Having visited this monk for a long time without seeing him, he suddenly saw a painted image of Subhūti on the wall and said, "This is the monk who cut out his own tongue."
The Way is fundamentally wordless; calling out will not awaken it. Medicine comes from the golden flask to save the sick.
How pitiable are the multitudes of humans and devas— As before, they remain dazed, listening with ears pricked.
In this verse, the opening line is the Dharma (the principle); the second line is the metaphor. The Master’s intention is to say that, in reality, the Great Way...
Principle is fundamentally beyond words; it is fully present within all six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones. Yet sentient beings are deluded and do not know this.
Therefore, the World-Honored One extensively expounded various sutras, employing verbal expressions to reveal the wordless Way and thereby teaching and transforming them.
Sentient beings with feelings were entirely bewildered and could not understand, which is why it is said: "Calling out, they do not respond."

It is awakening. Medicine exists because of those who suffer from illness. For example, when people have illnesses, a wondrous medicine is taken from a golden jar and given to them to drink, whereby all their ailments are cured. The Buddha’s teaching of this Dharma is likewise so:

because sentient beings possess the diseases of greed, anger, and ignorance, and fail to recognize their own true nature, he employs speech to point toward that true nature, universally enabling [them to realize it].
Awakening removes the disease of afflictions; thus it is said: "The medicine causes the illness to emerge from the golden vase.

The latter two lines, "Pitiable are the hundreds of millions," lament the meaning of sentient beings' failure to awaken to their own potential (*tī*). This is like when the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak.
One day, having ascended the seat, he remained silent for a long while. Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said: "Contemplate closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. This reveals the Way of wordlessness for the assembled congregation, whether they be people or beings.
Or there may be tens of millions of devas, yet none of them know [the truth]. Those who remain as they were before, utterly dull-witted, are the "scholars" (ke-jia).
Lamenting this assembly of listeners, they all seek and investigate within the words of the World-Honored One;
they are unable to grasp the soundless Way beyond the words. This is why calling out to them does not awaken them; hence it is said they remain as they were before, utterly dull-witted.
"Listening with ears pricked up. "Dull-witted" is the appearance of the mark of delusion.

The drum sound gathers the assembly beneath the forest springs; Do not emulate Vajrapāṇi questioning Samantabhadra as he sits high upon the lion throne transmitting the secret essentials— The wondrous penetration of a single finger is the old monk’s Chan.
The first two lines cite ancient masters of the Chan school to testify to the Way beyond words. Long ago, a high monk ascended the hall and said:
"As soon as the drum sounds and the great assembly gathers like clouds, infinite celestial mechanisms are revealed all at once.
If you do not fail the True Eye, you should return to the hall immediately; do not wait for further elaborate rhetoric to bury the essential purport. Even if Śākyamuni himself were to appear...
He appeared in the world. Throughout the ages, he has always said himself: "Dharma did not come from the West; at Shaolin there is a wondrous secret.

Therefore, when the bells ring and the drums resound, every sound is none other than the gate through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle. Whether the cypress is short or the pine is tall, all are the single true realm of Vairocana.
Thus it is said: "The sound of the drum gathers the assembly beneath the forest springs"—this reveals that by hearing the sound, one sees [the Buddha].
Form—this is all the Way. Do not study the "Vajra Questions to Samantabhadra. This is the Master of the Text (Kejia) picking up on the underlying sentiment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished preaching the Dharma to the devas and humans, there was in the assembly the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, who immediately rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the vast practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra..."
"Gate! It is inconceivable. I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain it, so that all bodhisattvas may rely upon it and practice accordingly.
The Buddha said, "If one were to speak of the gate of Samantabhadra’s practices, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as atoms, one could not exhaustively describe them.
If you wish to know them in their entirety, you must enter the *dharmadhātu-garbha-kāya-samādhi* and observe; only then will you come to know them. At that time,
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered into meditative concentration and universally observed the gateways of Samantabhadra’s practices.

Pervading the entirety of space and all realms, they were as numerous as motes of dust—immeasurable, boundless, unspeakable, and beyond the reach of further description. These gateways of practice were exceedingly subtle.

It was like raindrops; no one could know them. He emerged from his concentration and reported this to the Buddha, praising the vastness of Samantabhadra’s gateway of practice as being inexhaustible and its limits unknowable.

The Buddha said, "The practices and vows of Samantabhadra are the very foundation of the practices and vows of all Buddhas. Only Buddhas and Buddhas can know them; how much less could you, a single person, possibly do so?"
It reaches its ultimate limit; thus it is said: "Do not study the Diamond Questions of Samantabhadra.
This serves to reveal by contrast that the Way beyond words cannot be reached by speech. The latter two lines present this wordless Way as utterly transcending language.

Regarding the phrase "sitting upon the lion throne to transmit the secret essentials," it refers to the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) sitting upon the lion seat (*siṃhāsana*) to transmit the essential points of the mind.
He established the written words: "The mind itself is Buddha; do not seek it elsewhere. Therefore, it is said that this transmits the secret essentials.
"Wondrously penetrating with a single finger" is precisely the meaning of transmitting these secret essentials.
Formerly, whenever anyone asked Master Jueyi about the Buddhas, the Patriarchs, Chan, or the Way, Jueyi would simply point to him with one finger. This continued for thirty years.

"Year after year, I have simply practiced in this way; there is nothing else to say. This reveals that the Way is fundamentally beyond words, leading people to realize it within the very act of pointing a finger.
Thus, the Way is manifested amidst movement and function; hence it is said: "The old monk’s Chan is a wondrous, penetrating single finger."
There is sickness and peril, leading ultimately to decline and fall;
Neither born nor extinguished, not subject to saṃsāra, the Western Pure Land is eternally peaceful and blissful. Without suffering and without grief—come back!

(The first two lines compare the two lands, the pure and the defiled, by contrasting their suffering and happiness. Regarding "there is sickness and peril": [The text continues: ...by means of... *Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.*

In this defiled land, humans endure the eight sufferings and devas face the five signs of decline. When their merit is exhausted and their lives end—whether in the human realm or the heavens—they fall back into the three miserable paths;
hence it is said, "ultimately they fall away. As for "neither born nor extinguished," those in the Pure Land have no birth-and-death;
they attain Great Nirvana, with lifespans lasting for incalculable kalpas, and upon one birth, they immediately succeed to [the rank of] [Bodhisattva].
After attaining the stage of Buddhahood, one may then enter the nirvana that is neither born nor extinguished; hence it is said, "one does not transmigrate.
The final two lines describe the bliss of the Western Land. In the Pure Land of the West, all actions and endeavors are entirely according to one's wishes;
there is no suffering of the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties, but rather immeasurable joys numbering in the hundreds of thousands. Hence it is said:
They dwell in constant peace and happiness. Furthermore, they suffer no poverty and have no anxiety regarding food or clothing.

The ground is made of gold, and the ponds are formed of white jade; there are lotus flowers of four colors, providing billions of enjoyments for all. I universally exhort all those who are of superior virtue.
Why do you not quickly and earnestly recite the Buddha’s name to be born together in the Pure Land and realize Bodhi together? Therefore it is said: "Without suffering, without sorrow—return!
Come! There is no dharma to be attained;
emotional consciousness is difficult to fathom. The fundamental substance is revealed in its majestic clarity, encompassing the entire Dharma-realm. Its marks are non-existent.
[The Section on] Characteristics. This section was designated by Prince Zhaoming as the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Non-existence of Any Dharma that Can Be Attained.
This is because, regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the Buddha has not the slightest dharma that can be realized or attained.
Because it is attained, this name is established. Regarding "the emotional consciousness is difficult to measure":

since Bodhi is a non-dharma that cannot be attained, it cannot be measured by the deluded emotions or deluded consciousnesses of ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles; hence it is said, "the emotional consciousness is difficult to measure.
Regarding "the fundamental substance is revealed in its majestic presence": the Master fears people might miss it, so he clearly states that there is no dharma.
The Way that can be attained is the originally existing essence, manifest and majestic, pervading heaven and earth, reaching everywhere without exception, appearing at all times without fail.
Thus, it encompasses the entire Dharma-realm without exterior, and even when analyzed down to the most subtle *paramāṇu*, it has no interior.

This principle of the non-attainability of any dharma includes both the phenomenal characteristics of the Dharma-realm and its signlessness. It is this very section that constitutes the truth of the non-existence of any dharma that can be grasped.
The substance of the wood is majestic and grand, encompassing and containing all: the three types of worldly gates and the four kinds of dharma-realms;
both the phenomenal and the non-phenomenal are entirely within it. Thus it is said: "Form and empty space contain the dharma-realm; its dignified perfection is the greatness of majestic spirit."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, investigate and examine with care; recognize the sound and break through the delusion.
Even as snow falls from a scorching sky, the master fears that people will find the place where the Dharma-realm is encompassed too profound and difficult to clarify.
Therefore, he points out another living path: instead, scrutinize this principle within the four modes of deportment, never letting it slip away. Hence it is said: "Walking."
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, investigate and examine this with care. Pǔshì’s verse says: "Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one is free from following conditions;
In daily life, what prevents one from traversing both the orthodox and the deviant? At the head of the shadowless tree, the wind roars; Beyond the night-bright curtain, the moon flows gently.
For those who can discern the true sound, the Master’s intention is this: if one is a true connoisseur possessing the eye of wisdom, then regarding...
Inclining toward the present moment, whether walking or staying, one attains verification through critical examination and gains conviction.

Then, suddenly, one knows: beans burst from within cold ashes; flowers bloom upon a withered tree. In the midst of intense heat, there arises refreshing moisture; at a time of icy cold, precisely what is needed is warmth.
Thus, one may take south as north, handling things upside down and using them in reverse. Within all phenomena, one attains [liberation].
This is Great Sovereignty (*Maheśvara*). Thus, a poem by Hanshan says: "Delight is supreme in the Land of Non-action; One wanders freely, dwelling in no home.
It is all because the mountain colors are so fine That the affairs of the world seem increasingly distant. Snow falls in the midsummer heat; Flowers bloom upon the ridges in the depths of winter.
Since the burdens of worldly dust have long since vanished, Where could roots or sprouts ever take root?"
Since there is no dharma that can be attained as unconditioned, what dharma could there be to be maintained? Because not even the slightest dharma exists, [it is] *samyaksambodhi*.
The first two lines of this verse restate the meaning of the question in the Sūtra: "Is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* something that cannot be attained? This is the intended meaning.

[Subhūti] asked: "Since it is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma that is without anything to be attained (*anupalabdha*), how can it be upheld? The latter two phrases also recapitulate the meaning of the sūtra.
The Buddha replied: "Up to and including the point that there is not even the slightest dharma to be attained—this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The meaning is this: since not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended, how could there be anything to be maintained?
Since there is neither apprehension nor maintenance, this is true bodhi. Therefore it is said: "Because there is not even the slightest dharma, it is samyaksambodhi."
Chapter Twenty-Two: No Dharma Can Be Attained.
[Sūtra] Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: ... [up to] ... this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The commentary states: This section of the sutra is titled "The Section on the Non-existence of Any Dharma that Can Be Attained.

It is because Subhūti, having heard in the thirteenth preceding doubt that the Tathāgata truly has no dharma by which he attained unsurpassed bodhi and received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara, [now raises this question].
How then could there be cultivation and realization? Thus, out of doubt, he asked: "When the Buddha attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, was it as one who attained nothing?
The Buddha replied: "So it is, so it is. This was the Tathāgata’s assent to Subhūti’s question. He further said:
"In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained or realized."
It is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This means that within its nature, there is not the slightest dharma to be obtained, nor is there anything to be grasped;
it is thus utterly empty and quiescent. It cannot be sought through forms or characteristics, nor can it be revealed by words or speech;
it is merely designated as "unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. A Zen Master, the Wise One, composed a verse on this: "The Great [Buddhas]..."

Awakened wisdom: the nature of awakening is fundamentally boundless. What cause for Buddhahood could there be? Is that which is attained non-existent? This wondrous nature is difficult to measure or compare;
when the principle is realized, there is no discrepancy. Those who cling to delusion and fail to awaken—how many as countless as the sands of the Ganges have they gone astray?
The Dharma is unattainable; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The Way is not something that can be transmitted; it is the direct pointing to the True Eye of Nirvana.
Yet, how is it that there is attainment without attaining, and transmission without transmitting? Ultimately, what is the essential purport?
The first section cites the meaning of the sutra, stating: "Up to and including the point where not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended—this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The subsequent section cites the fundamental tenet in conjunction with the teachings, based on the fact that the successive Buddhas and patriarchs did not establish written words, asserting that "the mind itself is Buddha. Thus, a monk asked Chan Master Deyi: "As for the path that leads upward..."
"The thousand sages did not transmit it; has the Master transmitted it or not? He replied, "An iron ball blocks the mouth;
it is difficult to find one who can swallow it. The verse says: The entire body is revealed, vast and majestic; Throughout the ten directions, there is no obstruction.
The thousand sages could not transmit it; All the myriad spirits receive it upon their heads. If you wish to deliberate together, Open your mouth and it will be crushed a hundred times. This is it.
This is the direct pointing to the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the adamantine right eye.
As for "attaining yet having nothing attained," Zen Master Huanglong Nan said: "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, Mahābodhi had not a single dharma to attain;
only then did he realize *bodhi* and receive the prediction of his future buddhahood. Therefore, it is said: "attaining yet having nothing attained. This is "transmitting without transmitting."
Formerly, Ānanda asked Venerable Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*, what else does the World-Honored One transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.
At these words, Ānanda attained great enlightenment; he then realized that this Way resides solely within the present moment.
Within the human portion [of reality], there is fundamentally no transmission or reception. Thus Kāśyapa said:

"In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to me. Now that I am about to withdraw into seclusion, I shall enter meditative absorption at Kukkuṭapāda Mountain to await Maitreya.
Furthermore, I entrust this Dharma to you; you must maintain it well and ensure it does not become extinct. And...

Wherever there is water, the moon is always reflected; wherever there are mountains, clouds never fail to arise. Thus it is said: "Where there is water, it has always held the moon."

"There is no mountain that does not harbor clouds. Using these streams and mountains as a metaphor for Zen meditation and Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*), though their names differ, the clouds and moon serve as metaphors for Buddha-recitation and Zen meditation;
the realization of the principle is identical in both. "Where is there anything that is not the Dharma of equality?
This is the master’s summary of the preceding text, concluding that Zen meditation and Buddha-recitation do not obstruct one another.

As for this principle: since the clouds and the moon are identical and manifest everywhere universally, this truth is equal across the ordinary and the sagely, and all phenomena—whether sentient or insentient—possess it.
Therefore it is said: "Where is there that which is not the Dharma of equality? An ancient said:

The teachings expounded as the Three Vehicles were proclaimed by the Buddhas; the Chan school divided into five branches was transmitted by the Patriarchs. Through the Teachings, one clarifies the ocean of nature to return to ultimate truth;
through Chan, one sings the wind of the school to reach the original source. To truly realize the Chan school, one must harmonize it with the Teachings;

yet by simply clarifying the intent of the Teachings, one naturally penetrates Chan. When both Chan and Teachings are cast aside, ten thousand miles of cloudless sky is but a single expanse of heaven.
"Knowing the state where the vertical and horizontal are unimpeded" is the master’s inquiry, intended to make the student focus their attention.

This refers to the realization that whether one practices Chan meditation or the recitation of the Buddha's name, seeing the principle is not an obstruction; this is clearly revealed in the subsequent passage beginning with "The nature is equal toward all phenomena."
"Green willows are everywhere fit for tethering horses; every house has a road leading to Chang'an.
These two lines answer the meaning of "non-obstruction" mentioned above. They clearly point out that one attains the wondrous through following the flow.
Just as green willows are found everywhere suitable for tying horses, and every household has a path that leads to Chang'an—this is the first metaphor.
All dharmas universally manifest this principle. An ancient worthy said: "The moon reaches the wutong tree; the wind comes to the willow branches.
The night is deep and people are again silent—whom can one speak of this scene with? This may be called: "Everywhere it is revealed; every thing is fully manifested.
East, west, south, and north—how could there be any need for deliberation? Therefore it is said: "Everywhere is the path to Bodhi. The Gate.
Entering the ancient gate of the Buddha-family, mountain flowers resemble brocade and the waters are like indigo. Do not inquire about the three before or the three after;
mind and object are vast and empty, forgetting self and other. The entire great trichiliocosm of sand-grains is entirely contained within form.
The first two lines cite the thesis. The metaphor illustrates that such dharmas are equal, without high or low.
These words—describing the Dharma-body and ultimate truth as mountain flowers like brocade and still waters like indigo—are all means of extolling this Way; it may truly be said:
How could mountains and rivers fail to proclaim the True Dharma? Wind, moon, pavilions, and terraces perform the wondrous music.
Do not inquire about the "three before" and the "three after. The Master of the Text has clearly pointed this out.

Since all phenomena manifest the Principle, why must one further ask about the meaning of the three before and the three after? In the past, when Master Asanga traveled to Mount Wutai, he reached the Central Terrace...
Below, in a desolate and remote wilderness, Mañjuśrī transformed a ruined temple to provide shelter for another traveler.
Mañjuśrī then asked, "Where have you recently departed from? He replied, "The South. Mañjuśrī said, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South?
He replied, "In the age of the Final Dharma, monks pay little heed to the precepts and regulations. Mañjuśrī asked, "How large is the assembly there? He replied, "Sometimes three..."
[There were] one hundred, or perhaps five hundred. Wuzhuo asked in return, "Mañjuśrī, how is the Buddha-dharma maintained here?
Mañjuśrī said, "Ordinary people and sages dwell together; dragons and snakes are intermingled. Wuzhuo asked, "How many followers are there?
Mañjuśrī said, "Three before, three after, three times three. Wuzhuo did not accord with this; he sat back down and drank tea. Mañjuśrī then held up a crystal [vessel].
Zhuanzi asked, "Is there such a thing in the South? Wuzhuo replied, "No. Wushu said, "What do you usually use to drink tea?
Wuzhuo was speechless until dawn, at which point he took his leave. Wenshu ordered the youth Juntai to see him out to the gate.
Wuzhuo asked the youth, "Just now your teacher said, 'Three before, three after.'"
"Three. "What number is that? The boy called out, "Venerable Sir! and Zhao responded. The boy asked, "What number is that? Zhao was at a loss for an answer.
He asked again, "What monastery is this? The boy pointed behind the Vajra Cave;
Zhao turned his head to look, but the transformed monastery and the boy had all vanished, leaving only an empty valley. This is why it is called Xue (Snow).
Dong Song said: "A thousand peaks winding and curling, their color like indigo. Who says that Mañjuśrī is here in person for conversation?
How laughable—how many followers are at Qingliang? 'Three before, three after.

The meaning of this master’s intent is that since the mountain flowers are like brocade, every blade of grass and every tree is none other than Mañjuśrī. Wuzhuo asked again: "The three before, the three after..."
"What are the three threes? How many are there? This is because [the questioner] does not understand the way in which ordinary people and sages dwell together, like dragons and snakes intermingled;
therefore, it is said: "Do not ask about the three threes before and the three threes after. This reproaches Wuzhuo for having missed Mañjuśrī.
The latter two phrases reveal that this Dharmakāya is devoid of the meaning of high and low; it is the state where mind and objects are vast and open.
If one realizes that this mind is equal, the mind will be free from the attachment of ordinary and sage, and objects will be free from the view of high and low.

Thus, one forgets both "that" and "this. When phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated and subject and object are both extinguished, one finally knows that mind and form are the Great Void, immeasurable.
Encompassing the sands of the ten directions; thus it is said that the great trichiliocosm of sand-grains is entirely contained within.

If you chant the name of Amitābha incessantly with your mouth, yet the sense of self and other remains like clashing swords in your heart— if you do not reform your mind from its very root, how could you possibly shatter this skull?

Regarding the first two lines, the Master’s intention is as follows: people of the present day, though they may observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name, have not yet eliminated the mind of self and other;
though they recite the Buddha’s name all day long, they do not understand the nature of that recitation.

However, there is the name of "recollection of the Buddha" (nien-fo) without the reality of "recollection of the Way" (nien-tao). Although the external appearance is virtuous, the internal mind is actually evil;
thus it is said: "In the heart, the self and others are like clashing spears and shields. The Buddha told Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva:
"Regarding the recollection of the Buddha and the practice of Chan, there may be one whose body is tranquil but whose mind is not tranquil. Or there may be a bhikṣu sitting in a quiet place..."

One who practices *dhyāna* while remaining distant from the fourfold assembly, yet whose mind constantly accumulates and habituates greed, anger, and delusion—this is called physical tranquility, but not mental tranquility.
Regarding one whose mind is tranquil but whose body is not tranquil:

there may be a bhikṣu who associates with the fourfold assembly, kings, and ministers, yet constantly cuts off greed, anger, and delusion; this is called mental tranquility, but not physical tranquility.
It is stillness. Those whose body and mind are tranquil are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; those whose body and mind are both not tranquil are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Although they may recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths, within their minds the strife of self and other does not cease.
The latter two lines are the master’s admonition to students: even while reciting the Buddha’s name, [if the mind is not still, it is in vain].

One must sever delusion to clarify the truth. If one’s mind does not fundamentally reform its evils and migrate toward goodness, and eliminate the sense of self and other, then even if one strikes one's skull until it breaks and pays homage to the Buddha or recites his name, one will ultimately fail to see one's nature;
for there remains the mind of "self" and "others."
The fools of this world lack wisdom; They know only love, desire, and greed for wealth.
How much better it would be to sever them all at once— To mindfully recite Amitābha’s name and return home!
The first two lines state that sentient beings are deluded and ignorant, possessing no wisdom, and knowing only love, desire, and greed for wealth.
The failure of wisdom to arise in the mind is called ignorance (*mūḍha*). The failure of insight (*prajñā*) to emerge within the mental faculty is called delusion (*moha*).

Attachment to the five desires is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Clinging to wealth and treasures is called greed (*lobha*). Thus it is said: "One knows only love and desire, as well as the greed for wealth.
Regarding the final two lines, the commentator exhorts one to abandon greed. If one is a practitioner of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation), yet cannot see through [the nature of] wealth—
There are two matters regarding desire: in the present life, one is bound and fettered by them all; in the past, one must inevitably enter the three miserable realms to undergo suffering.

Therefore, the teaching is that you should sever the causal conditions of these evil karmas with a single stroke of the brush, focus your mind exclusively on the Buddha’s name, and vow to be born in the Pure Land to return home.

His merit and wisdom are peerless; these two dharmas are perfectly complete. Amidst the dust and sands [of worlds], he has formed auspicious conditions, accumulating meritorious practices over successive kalpas.
With the fruit fulfilled and the cause perfected, this section is designated by Prince Zhaoming as the "Peerless Merit and Wisdom" (Fuzhi Wubifen) chapter. This passage of scripture is thus named.

Twenty-fourth: To take the merit gained from bestowing the seven treasures upon the three thousandfold world-system as a comparison, it does not equal the merit of upholding even four lines of this sutra.

This merit is peerless. Because upholding this sutra manifests the wisdom of *prajñā* and brings about the realization of Buddhahood, and because this wisdom is peerless, it is given this name. Regarding the "two dharmas being perfectly complete": by means of these two—merit and wisdom—...
The Dharma is perfected and complete, and one becomes a Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings; this is called self-benefit.

Having perfected these two dharmas for self-benefit and attained the fruit of Buddhahood, one subsequently manifests billions of bodies and enters worlds as numerous as grains of sand to teach and transform sentient beings, extensively establishing excellent conditions; this is called benefiting others. Such is the practice of merit and action.

Regarding "throughout successive kalpas": having already perfected both merit and wisdom as previously described, and furthermore benefiting both oneself and others, one knows that their practice and realization are identical to those of a Buddha;
with the three great asamkhyeya kalpas completed, the fruit is fulfilled and the causes are perfected, which is identical to the functioning of a Buddha.
The candle of wisdom shines universally; like the single moon suspended in the sky, it is perfectly bright and clear. With no-mind, it reflects the great trichiliocosm.

Regarding "the candle of wisdom shines universally": having already possessed the two dharmas of merit and wisdom, one then acts in accordance with the Buddha’s function to transform and teach sentient beings.
It is like the brilliance of a lamp of wisdom, which can dispel darkness; it is like the moon in the sky, illuminating all things high and low.
This is the meaning of equality, namely the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*). The "single moon" is that which can dispel all obscurity and serves as the light of the world;
this is the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). "Perfectly luminous" means luminous and yet more luminous; therefore, it is called "perfectly luminous."

This is the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). As for "mirroring the great trichiliocosm without mind," this refers to the stage of effortless mastery where the fruition of Buddhahood has already realized the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms;
benefiting sentient beings through non-mindfulness is precisely the wisdom of the great perfect mirror (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The nature of the emptiness of Prajñā; Cultivating both merit and wisdom together.

The first two lines of the four-line verse on the unconditioned dharma summarize the meaning of the Sūtra. "Prajñā" refers to wisdom. "Nature" (svabhāva) refers to principle (li). By means of suchness...

Rational wisdom (*nīti-prajñā*) can sever the afflictions and realize the Dharma-body; this is *prajñā*. The practice of the remaining five perfections, such as giving (*dāna*), constitutes merit (*puṇya*).
Furthermore, if there is a person who practices giving with the seven treasures for the sake of merit, yet is able to uphold this sutra, that constitutes wisdom.
If a person cultivates both merit and wisdom together, they will directly and clearly comprehend the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma of even a four-line verse upon receiving and upholding it.

Regarding "intrinsic nature," it is said that one attains Buddhahood immediately; thus, by reciting for even a brief moment, one fully possesses the three bodies through a single thought-moment of *prajñā-pāramitā*.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Incomparable Merit and Wisdom.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if [the merit of] the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system... up to that which cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy.
The commentary states: This section of the sūtra is titled "The Incomparable Division of Merit and Wisdom.
Because Subhūti had previously heard the Buddha teach that by practicing all wholesome dharmas one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he gave rise to a doubt, thinking:

"Are the wholesome dharmas now taught by the Buddha of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*); how then could they lead to the attainment of bodhi? Fearing that such a doubt might arise, the Buddha [spoke as follows].

He then concluded, saying: "Furthermore, if there were someone who took all the Mount Sumerus within the great trichiliocosm and made them into heaps of the seven treasures to bestow as alms, compared to the merit of upholding and reciting these four lines [of verse], the former gift of the seven treasures would not equal even a hundred-thousand-million-billionth part of it; therefore, its merit is incomparable."

Furthermore, although the teachings spoken by all Buddhas belong to the categories of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, *vyañjana-kāya*), they appear to be of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
However, through the wisdom of the fourfold Prajñā, one realizes that these names, phrases, and syllables are all empty in essence;

thus, they are untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) rather than indeterminate, becoming the cause for attaining Bodhi. The merit of this wisdom is incomparably superior to [the merit of] this [mere recitation], O Compassionate One.
The verse says: Although it is said that indeterminate dharmas are their cause, this single Jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable true jewels.
The meaning of this statement is not only that it is the cause of Bodhi, but because its preceding meanings are also superior, the fourfold classification is doubly superior.
Furthermore, regarding the merit obtained from giving the seven treasures as alms:
All these are characterized by abiding; they do not transcend the conditioned and must ultimately lead to decline and fall.
It is not like upholding even a single four-line verse of the Prajñāpāramitā, the merit of which is free from the characteristic of abiding.

Because it leads to the realization of the unconditioned and the attainment of Buddhahood, it surpasses the aforementioned merit by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, to the point that it cannot be measured by calculation or analogy.
Furthermore, Master Fu composed a verse: "Bestowing treasures as numerous as grains of sand Only creates causes for outflows (*āsrava*).

It is not as good as the contemplation of non-self, Whereby one realizes delusion and names it 'True. If you wish to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), You must rely on the departure from greed and anger.
Knowing that both persons and phenomena are without self, One wanders freely beyond the six sense-objects."
The merit [of this] equals that of bestowing the seven treasures upon Mount Sumeru three thousand times over.

Holding even a single four-line verse illuminates the bright pearl of the ocean of wisdom, enabling the waves of consciousness to become clear and tranquil, and suddenly causing the heavens of meaning to open and shine brightly. Its vast compassion universally rescues all, bringing immense benefit to the infinite.
"At midnight, when it is truly bright, where does it still abide?
Regarding "merit equaling three thousand," this restates the meaning of the sutra. The sutra says:

"If a person were to give as an offering all the heaps of the seven treasures from all the Mount Sumerus throughout the trichiliocosm, the merit they would obtain [is such that] it is said: 'merit equals'."
This refers to three thousand [stanzas]. Regarding the phrase "one who upholds even four lines of the sūtra," this also restates the meaning of the sūtra. The sūtra says:

"If a person receives and upholds even as few as four lines of this Prajñā[pāramitā] and explains them to others, their merit surpasses the former [merit]. This is like a brilliant, great pearl in the ocean;
for the great wisdom of Prajñā is like a vast sea—so expansive that nothing is excluded, and so deep that nothing is not received.
There is nothing, whether mundane or supramundane, that it does not encompass. Furthermore, just as a bright pearl illuminates all ten directions, so too is the light of *prajñā*:
it illuminates every single phenomenon (*dharma*). Therefore, it is said that the merit of receiving and upholding even four lines [of verse] is superior.
Regarding the phrase "it can cause the waves of consciousness to become clear and still," this refers to the aforementioned reception and upholding of the four lines of *prajñā*.

The efficacy of this is like a bright pearl that can clarify turbid water. If a practitioner brings the wisdom of *prajñā* before them, they can cause the waves of the ocean-like mind of the eight consciousnesses to become clear and still.
This suddenly causes the sky of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) to appear everywhere, open and radiant, shining through with penetrating clarity.
Therefore it is said: "The vastness of the Three Baskets is inexhaustible; the seven waves are deep and profound."
The objective realm is the wind. This refers to the eighth consciousness as the ocean and the preceding seven consciousnesses as the waves.
Stirred by the winds of the objective realms of beginningless habitual tendencies, the ocean of mind is agitated, and thus there are waves. Now, this divine pearl of Prajñā—

It is cast into the ocean of the human mind; by transforming turbidity into clarity and turning delusion into truth, it finally becomes the ocean of wisdom, also called the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
This eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is only relinquished upon reaching the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva, at which point it first attains complete clarity.
Thus, the eight consciousnesses are transmuted into the four wisdoms. It may be said: "The great perfect circle, stainless, arises simultaneously, universally..."

It illuminates the dust-like lands throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, by means of the wisdom-jewel of *prajñā*, it illuminates the emptiness of all phenomena, so that the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is revealed with brilliant clarity.
As for "vast compassion universally rescuing," the former refers to self-benefit, while this refers to benefiting others.

Furthermore, by exercising great compassion through the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one fulfills the four great vows (*catvāri mahāpraṇidhānāni*) to universally rescue all sentient beings;

hence it is said, "Extensively benefiting the boundless. Regarding "midnight is precisely luminous," the *Inscription on the Profundity* states: "Midnight" refers to the hour of Zi (the first hour of the day).
At that time, black and white have not yet been distinguished, and it is borrowed as the position of correctness. "Precisely luminous" refers to the hour of Zi. Correct...
The fifth month is bright. To manifest the correct, one does not sit in the center; the night’s empty clarity is borrowed as the partial. The meaning of the Chan school (kējiā) is this:
when it is perfectly bright at midnight, where is it? This is intended to reveal the "reaching down with a hand" from within the vast expanse, adapting to the needs of the present age.
The following text provides the full response and disclosure.
"The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the mind-ground seal.
These two lines are the response to the preceding text. As for the "three bodies," they are the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.

The four wisdoms are: the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), and the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-maṇḍala-jñāna*).
Regarding "perfect within its essence," this refers to the teaching of the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*) that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into these four wisdoms.

The four wisdoms are subsumed into the three bodies (*trikāya*). The transformation of the five preceding consciousnesses constitutes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

The transformation of the sixth consciousness, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), constitutes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*). The transformation of the seventh consciousness constitutes the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

The transformation of the eighth consciousness constitutes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Regarding the subsumption of the four wisdoms into the three bodies: by means of the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done...
The Reward Body (Sambhogakāya) consists of the two wisdoms of wondrous observation and equality; the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) consists of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom;

and the Dharma Body (Dharmakāya) is [the wisdom of suchness]. Although these three bodies have three names, there is no difference within their essence. Therefore, it is said that "within the essence they are perfect.
This means that within the single essence, the three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete, just as a mani jewel possesses perfection.
Regarding the marks: they possess the function of radiance, manifesting various forms and colors according to the directions. As for the "eight liberations," these are the eight *vimokṣas*.
As for the "six penetrations," these are the six *abhijñās*. Although there are these eight liberations and six penetrations, they do not depart from the manifestation of the one mind;
they all emerge as a single essence, sealed by the true mind of the *dharmadhātu*.
The mountain king Ratnaskandha is beyond calculation; it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
The four lines of the verse transcend the three periods of time, surpassing the merit of ten thousand times a *kalpa*.
The first two lines cite the meaning of the sutra: although one obtains blessings by giving the seven treasures as an offering to Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains...

It is inexhaustible. Because one has not yet departed from the three realms, giving with attachment to marks produces the merit of rebirth in the heavens. This is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void:
when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, resulting in an unfavorable rebirth in the future, as one returns to the three miserable paths once celestial merit is spent.
The latter two lines clarify the four lines of the sutra, illuminating Prajñāpāramitā in a single thought-moment.
Suddenly transcending the three periods of past, future, and present, one surpasses by ten thousandfold the merit cultivated and realized over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Thus it is said: "In a single thought, suddenly transcending beyond empty kalpas; originally, this was not permitted for the old barbarian to know."
On the tip of a single hair, he plucks the flower; Laughing the old master beside him down.
If you wish to ask for the essential meaning of our meeting, *Maṇidāri hūṃ phaṭ*.
The first two lines represent the hand-eye of the master of the lineage, seizing the speech. An ancient worthy once said to the assembly: "The world..."
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Honored One held up a golden *utpala* flower and showed it to the multitude;
only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. This old monk now plucks out a single golden *utpala* flower from the tip of a single hair—do you all see it?
Therefore it is said: "Plucking a flower upon the tip of a single hair."
"Laughing himself silly, the old master standing by the side. The meaning of this commentary is as follows:
To give a discourse such as yours is called "responding to the occasion and receiving the signal," following established customs. Yet, alas, those who truly know laugh.
Therefore it is said, "The old master standing by the side laughs himself silly. The final two lines shift the pivot of the discourse; the commentator takes a different path.
I do not make my livelihood upon the occasion when the World-Honored One held up the flower.
If you wish to inquire into the ultimate principle of the meeting between host and guest, I shall answer you with this single Jewel-Palace Mantra: *Maṇidhāri hūṃ phaṭ*.
Is this not the very meaning of the ultimate principle revealed at the moment of their encounter, as taught in the Gate of the Patriarchs?
Do not prize eloquent speech; simply ensure that the eye is upright. Therefore, whatever is brought forth is nothing other than the truth;
do not give rise to doubt when it is applied. The Buddha said: "Though I practiced austerities for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, I did not attain Bodhi.
Only upon hearing this dhāraṇī did my practice become correspondingly aligned, whereby I immediately attained perfect enlightenment with certainty."
Undoubtedly. The *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of Good Abiding* states: "If a person hears this mantra and receives and upholds it, or even merely hears its name;

or touches it with their hand, or wears it upon their body; or sees it with their eyes, or writes it down on paper, silk, walls, or other surfaces—[they shall be purified of] the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, slandering the Buddha, or destroying the Dharma, as well as [the sins of] butchers and slaughterers, blindness, deafness, poverty, and demonic afflictions."
External heterodox views and evil minds will all be utterly extinguished. Those who hear its name and uphold it will certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Kings, ministers, and others of the world will all joyfully offer them worship.

In this life, they will possess manifold merits and be free from the various sufferings of the world; poisons, weapons, swords, staves, water, fire, and fierce beasts shall be unable to cause them harm.

One shall be free from all malignant diseases; sleep shall be peaceful and awakening peaceful. At the time of death, the mind shall not be distracted, and one shall see the Buddhas appear before them, being reborn at will in the Buddha-lands.

If one recites this one hundred and eight times every morning, upon reaching one hundred thousand recitations, one shall see all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; at two hundred thousand recitations, one shall see all the Buddha-lands.
Reciting one million times, one beholds all Buddhas; this is the meaning taught within the scriptures: that through the empowerment of attaining bodhi, one sees all Buddhas.
I remember Amitābha as my parents; Amitābha regards me as an infant.
With every thought and every moment, may there be no interruption; father and son shall follow one another back and forth.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said: "I recall that in kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of a single kalpa, and the last of those Buddhas was named Sūryaprabhācandraprabhābhibhū. That Buddha...
Teach me the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.

If a child has fled and wandered away, though the mother remembers him, what can she do? But if the child remembers his mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or far apart.
If sentient beings with their own minds remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see him in the present and in the future.
The Buddha is not far from the Buddha. Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.

In my original ground, I entered the patience of non-arising by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. An ancient worthy said: "The Buddha remembers sentient beings more than a mother remembers her child;
sentient beings remember the Buddha and merge with the True Source. When the child has nowhere to flee, they return; these two are clearly one person.

Regarding "constantly maintaining this mindfulness without interruption," Wutian said: "If there is another person who resolutely desires to be reborn [in the Pure Land] and single-mindedly maintains one thought-moment—vivid and clear—then this very one thought-moment is my Original Teacher;
this very one thought-moment is the Transformation Buddha; this very one thought-moment is the valiant general who shatters hell; this very one..."
This mindfulness is the precious sword that severs the multitude of evils. This single thought-moment is the bright lamp that dispels darkness.
This single thought-moment is the great ship that crosses the sea of suffering. This single thought-moment is the excellent remedy for transcending birth and death.
This single thought-moment is the path that surmounts the three realms. This single thought-moment is...
The Amitābha of one's own original nature—this single thought-moment is itself the Pure Land of Mind-Only. One should maintain this mindfulness during times of peace and happiness;
one should maintain this mindfulness during illness and suffering; one should maintain this mindfulness at birth; and one should maintain this mindfulness at death.
Therefore, it is said that with every thought and every moment, never ceasing for an instant, father and son shall follow one another and together return to the Pure Land. This is because:
Amitābha is like a father; sentient beings are like children. If father and child share the same essence, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.

Though there is no object to be transformed, capacities are divided into small and great. Subhūti, do not harbor doubts or suspicions. Within the four modes of birth and the six realms, beings depart and stay, coming and going.
Liang Shaoming judged this section of the sutra as the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Transformation of Those Who Are Not to Be Transformed.

He established this title because the Buddha possesses no mind that seeks to save others, nor does he perceive any sentient beings who require saving; as the sutra says, "In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata has saved.
Thus, it is named "The Transformation of Those Who Are Not to Be Transformed. Section on Sentient Capacities (Jifen).
Regarding "small and great": when the mind possesses dualistic grasping, it is termed the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). As a sutra says:
"Ordinary persons believe there is a self"—this is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). When the mind is free from dualistic grasping, it is termed the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
As a sutra says: "When the Tathāgata speaks of a 'self,' this is the true self. Thus, it is said that the capacities [of sentient beings] are divided into small and great. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Do not harbor doubts or suspicions. In this section, the Buddha addresses Subhūti:
"You should not think that the Tathāgata has the thought, 'I shall deliver sentient beings. Subhūti, do not have such a thought. In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
This statement means that within the true Dharma-realm, all is equal and non-dual; ordinary beings and sages are one and the same, without distinction.
Because they are able to deliver those who are to be delivered, it is said: "Subhūti, do not harbor doubts.
As for those in the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence who go and stay, come and return, this is because they give rise to delusions and create karma due to the existence of a self.

Consequently, they falsely differentiate among sentient beings within the four modes of birth and six realms, and [cling to] the five aggregates as provisional names for real dharmas. Thus, they go and come without abiding, and their saṃsāra does not cease, like a chariot rolling over [the ground].
The Way is like ants circling in a loop.
When one turns the light back to reflect upon oneself, one's true face becomes clear and manifest; doubt ceases instantly. River mists spread across the nine realms.

This text presents the meaning explained previously. It was stated before that although there are the movements of coming and going within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, none of them ever depart from the true mind of the *dharmadhātu*.

If a practitioner can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light back upon itself to reflect inwardly—neither pursuing appearances nor following after objects, and with a mind free of subject and object—they will thereby perceive their original face. This is as follows:
This is the true self. Furthermore, as doubt is suddenly severed and both subject and object are forgotten, a divine radiance of the One Path pervades heaven and encompasses the earth;
the dharma-realm of the ten directions is manifested solely by the mind. Thus it is said: "The crimson clouds fill the nine realms."
The profound and subtle principles of the Mahāyāna Are understood in many different ways. Whether there is a real self or no real self, Observe this carefully.
Regarding the first line:

it states that within the one true dharma-realm, ordinary beings and sages are equal. The four classes of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings all receive [this nature] equally and are endowed with it identically.
Therefore, it is said: "Profound and abstruse. The next phrase states that although ordinary beings and sages are equal, how can one deny that there are many different levels of realization?
The six classes of ordinary beings are deluded and do not understand, and thus they transmigrate through the six realms.

Those of the Two Vehicles have awakened to this, yet they cling to partial emptiness. Bodhisattvas deeply awaken to the Middle Way, yet they still cling to the Middle Way. These are the aforementioned types of people.

They awaken to the same single reality of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā*), yet each perceives their own level of understanding as being unequal, like three animals crossing a river, where the depths they reach differ. Therefore, it is said that "there are many kinds of intellectual awakening.
As for the latter two phrases, "the real self" refers to the true self of the Tathāgata, while "the truly non-existent self" refers to the deluded self of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Carefully...
The instruction to "observe carefully and with care" is the earnest intent of the master;
it requires that one scrutinize and examine within the context of the two selves, ensuring that nothing is missed.
Chapter Twenty-Five: The Transformation of That Which Is Not to Be Transformed.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, what do you think? ... As the Tathāgata has said, they are not ordinary persons; they are called "ordinary persons."

The commentary states: This section is titled "Transforming Those Who Are Not to Be Transformed. The Buddha feared that Subhūti might give rise to doubt, having previously heard the Buddha say, "This Dharma is equal, with no high or low. He might then wonder how the Tathāgata could instead deliver sentient beings.
To prevent such a misunderstanding, the Buddha said, "Do not say that the Tathāgata has this thought: 'I shall deliver sentient beings.'"
[The Buddha] said: "In truth, there is no sentient being whom the Tathāgata delivers. The verse by Maitreya states: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings;
for their names are common to those aggregates (*skandha*), and they do not depart from the Dharma-realm. The commentary explains: "Name" refers to the conventional designation of a sentient being;
"aggregates" refers to the real dharmas of the five aggregates. Both these conventional designations and real dharmas are... [identical with the Dharma-realm].

The Dharma-realm. Therefore it is said: "It does not depart from the Dharma-realm. Since the Dharma-realm itself means that ordinary beings and sages are one and the same, how could there be any sentient beings to be saved?
Thus it is said: "The Buddha does not save sentient beings," because all sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas.
This is why mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three—are without distinction. If there were sentient beings...
"If the Tathāgata were one who 'delivers,' then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.

This means that if the Tathāgata were to think, "I am the Buddha who delivers," and "sentient beings are the recipients who are delivered," this would be an attachment to the four marks (*catur-nimitta*).
By contrast, it is revealed that the Tathāgata’s mind is devoid of subject and object, eternally free from the four marks; thus, though there is no delivering, there is delivering.
It is not a matter of transcending. The Buddha further said: "When the Tathāgata speaks of a self, it is the true self of the Buddha;
it is not a 'having-a-self,' for the Buddha has no deluded self. Yet ordinary people think there is a self;
this 'self' of ordinary people is what constitutes their self-clinging. The Buddha spoke again: "Ordinary people are like..."
To speak of them, they are not ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). The *Vyākhyā* states: "Not ordinary persons" means not born [into the state of] birth;
that is to say, they do not give rise to the dharmas of a noble one (*ārya*). The Wei dynasty commentary on the sūtra says: "They are the 'hair-path' (*mārga-roma*) ordinary persons.
This means that the minds of practitioners are unstable, like light feathers drifting east and west with the wind; therefore, they are called "hair-path. Asaṅga... [text ends].

It is said: "An infant" refers to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Because they are deluded, they are like infants. Master Zhiyi of Tiantai composed a verse stating: Sentient beings cultivate cause and effect;
When the fruit ripens, it is naturally perfected. The Dharma-boat naturally ferries them across; Why must one necessarily pull it oneself?
It is just like a fisherman who, having caught a fish, forgets the trap. If you say that the Tathāgata delivers beings, He has been delivering them from the very beginning.
How many ships?
There is no self and no person; sentient beings spontaneously achieve perfect enlightenment, neither arising nor ceasing. The Tathāgata says they are not ordinary beings.
Although this matter is clear and distinct, alas, at the very moment of encounter, one misses it.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s mind is devoid of the four marks of self and person; thus, there is no one who can deliver others.
Since sentient beings spontaneously realize perfect enlightenment and are fundamentally Buddhas, there is nothing to be delivered.

Regarding "neither arising nor ceasing," it means this principle has existed eternally since antiquity and is fundamentally beyond arising and ceasing; therefore, the Tathāgata says they are not ordinary beings, for they are [fundamentally] unarisen.
Because it is the Holy Dharma, it is said that this very mind is the Buddha; because it is primordially complete, it is said that one is not an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Nevertheless, regarding this matter being clear and distinct, the intention of the Master [Zongmi] is as follows:

although the preceding text has explained this principle—that truth and falsehood are distinct, yet the holy and the ordinary are equal, and all possess the one true *dharmadhātu*—what can be done about the masses?
Beings are born deluded regarding the Truth and pursue the false; they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust.

Amidst the movement and stillness of daily life, they miss the opportunity at the very moment it arises—like one who carries a pearl while begging for alms, or one who harbors a treasure yet remains lost in a foreign land.
Long ago, a monk asked Cuiyan, "A single grain of elixir can transform iron into gold; a single word of ultimate truth can transform an ordinary person into a sage.
As a student who has come before you, I ask the Master to apply this 'dot' for me. The Master said, "I will not dot it. The monk asked, "Why do you not dot it?
The Master said, "I fear you would fall into the categories of ordinary and sage. Now tell me, what does a person who does not fall into the categories of ordinary and sage possess?

"Eye. This point of inquiry by the monk was intended to manifest the principle through a concrete phenomenon; it is what is called "if one does not pose this question, there will be no prospect of entering the path based on prior practice.
Therefore, he inquired by borrowing the meaning of the Gate of the Way. Long ago, the True Man said of the Way: [text continues].
Guang said: "The Golden Elixir is the true, singular Qi of the pre-heaven (pre-natal) realm; it is not the dregs of the post-heaven (post-natal) realm.
This single Qi is hazy and profound; it cannot be seen when looked upon, nor heard when listened to, and it cannot be grasped when handled—thus it is called 'the Single Qi.
It is because the original immortals employed the practice of 'nine returns and seven reversals' that they refined it into completion."

The great elixir of the Golden Elixir is what is called the "inner elixir. If a person can ingest even a single grain of it, they will immediately undergo the transformation of the fetus and the replacement of the bones;
their body will fly upward with lightness, and they will ascend to heaven by day, becoming an immortal.

This is used as a metaphor for the words of ultimate truth spoken by the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the Chan school—the subtle and wondrous essence of the mind that practitioners must realize beneath these words.
"It is attained. One can immediately transform from an ordinary person into a sage and attain Buddhahood on the spot, like a goose raised in a bottle that emerges at a single call.
The high monk on the wall who responds at a single call—these are all instances of a single word of ultimate truth;

they are the very model for transforming the ordinary into the sacred. This monk asked again: "I, a student, have come here to request a single point from the Master; I beg you to grant me your guidance."
The teaching is thus revealed and shown. It may be said that, having no place of one's own to rest, one cannot avoid appealing to others.
The Master said: "Not pointing" is an answer given without speaking; it is a clear indication of the path beyond words, which does not permit the opening of a mouth.
The monk asked: "Why did you not point? This monk missed the mark at the very outset, failing to grasp the essential meaning.
"For this reason: Last night the Vermilion Phoenix soared into the Milky Way; at dawn, the woodcutter chased after the flock of geese.
The Master said, "I fear you will fall into the categories of ordinary or sage. These are words for those who have fallen into the weeds; they are repeated instructions.

Now tell me, what kind of eye does one who does not fall into the categories of ordinary or sage possess? This was the master of the *ke* (the ritual director) elucidating the higher meaning and posing an inquiry.
The practitioner should fix their gaze upon this; the following lines provide the answer.
"Even if noble understanding and ordinary sentiment are both exhausted / Opening one's eyes, one remains as before within the dream"—these two lines answer what was stated above.
The intent is that the practitioner must transcend both the ordinary and the holy, establishing a distinct way of life.

It is said: "Even if both noble understanding and ordinary sentiment are exhausted, you remain dreaming within a dream. Generally speaking, one must not allow the person to dwell upon either the ordinary or the holy;
furthermore, even this mind of non-dwelling must be swept away. Only then can one attain liberation and freedom. As it is said:
"At the ultimate end, neither delusion nor awakening should be clung to; even golden dust in the eye is difficult to retain."
Reaching the shore, one has never needed a boat; The level Great Way leads straight through to Chang’an.
Knowing clearly that awakening does not depend on another, Face and form are distinct, yet all are of one kind.
These four lines are a verse upon the meaning of the preceding sutra passage: "In truth, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. This is because sentient beings...
