Originally complete, the principle of true suchness dwells upon the shore of nirvana and enters the realm of the deathless; how could it require the Tathāgata to deliver it? Thus it is said:
"Upon reaching the shore, one has never needed a boat. The second line states that the Great Way is level and straightforward, without cultivation or realization;
it is the lot of every person, and each is perfectly fulfilled. Therefore it is said: "The Great Way penetrates the long [distance]."
Peaceful. It may be said: "Everywhere is the Chang'an Road; every door is the house of an ancient Buddha. Regarding these three lines:

since sentient beings already possess this Way, they understand that it has existed from the beginning, not arising because a Buddha appeared, and thus they awaken to this principle. As for the concluding line:
because the Buddha and sentient beings have been of one essence from the very start, it is said, "The features and face are clearly all the same. Therefore, it is said:
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
The first three threes and the latter three threes— Any deliberation or calculation is utterly inadequate;
When both intellect and emotion are severed, One must investigate again through three lifetimes and nine kalpas.
Regarding the first phrase, "the three before and the three after," this has already been recorded above.
Formerly, when Asaṅga entered Mount Wutai, he encountered an old man leading an ox at Huayan Monastery’s Vajra Cave. The old man invited him into the monastery;
the old man called out for the youth Guṇḍi, who emerged at the sound to welcome him. He released the ox and led Asaṅga up into the hall.
When Wumen saw the hall and its buildings, all of which were radiant with a golden hue, the old man sat upon his couch and pointed to an embroidered cushion, commanding Wuzhuo to sit.
The old man asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Wumen replied, "I come from the South. The old man asked, "How do you maintain the Buddha-dharma in the South?
Wumen said, "In this age of the Dharma’s decline, the bhikṣus rarely uphold the precepts and regulations. The old man asked, "How many followers do you have? Wumen replied, "Sometimes..."
[Daowu] was there for three hundred days, or perhaps five hundred. Wenyi asked, "How is the Dharma maintained here? [The Old Man] replied, "Dragons and snakes are mixed;
ordinary people and sages dwell together. Wenyi asked, "How many followers are there? [The Old Man] replied, "Three times three before, and three times three after.
The Old Man called to his attendant boy to serve tea along with butter and curd. Wenyi partook of the flavors, and his mind became suddenly clear and expansive. The Old Man picked up...
The glass cup asked, "Is there such a thing as this in the South? Wumen said, "No. [The guest] asked, "Then with what do you drink your tea?
Wumen had no reply. Seeing that the sun was setting, he then asked the old man, "May I stay for one night? The old man said:
"You still have a mind of attachment; you shall not stay overnight. Wen said, "I, [Name], am free from a mind of attachment.
The old man asked, "Have you ever received the precepts? Wen replied, "I have received them long ago. The old man said, "If you have no mind of attachment, what use is receiving the precepts?
Wen took his leave. The old man ordered a youth to escort him. On the way, Wen asked the youth, "Three times three before, and three times three after—what does this mean?"
“How much? the Master called out. “Virtuous One,” Wen replied. The Master asked, “How much is it, Wen? Wen then asked, “Where is this place?
He replied, “It is the Vajra Cave Prajñā Monastery. Wen was moved to sorrowful realization that the old man was none other than Mañjuśrī.
"We shall not see you again," he said. He then prostrated himself before the youth and requested, "I pray for a single word as a parting gift.
The youth replied: "No anger on the face is the true offering; No anger in the mouth emits a wondrous fragrance; No anger in the heart is the true treasure."
"Stainless and undefiled, it is the true eternal. Having spoken these words, the youth vanished along with the temple.

Only within five-colored clouds was Mañjuśrī seen riding a golden lion, coming and going amidst the mists. Suddenly, white clouds came from the east and covered them, so that they were no longer visible.
Mingzhao composed this verse: "Vastly encompassing the sands of the world, this supreme monastery fills the eyes."
Mañjuśrī engaged in dialogue; yet, in that very moment, one does not know how the Buddha-eye was opened. Turning one's head, one sees only the verdant mountains and cliffs.
The Master of the *ke* (commentary) cites this exchange to clarify the meaning herein: that it does not fall within the realm of ordinary beings or sages.
Formerly, Mañjuśrī said, "Three by three before, three by three after. Together with Aśvaghoṣa, he clearly pointed out that, within the sphere of one’s own being, there is but one.

This principle requires that people not fall into the realm of thought, mind, or verbal deliberation, but realize it directly. Should one engage in any calculation or conjecture, it will prove inadequate for the truth.

Even if you were to transcend the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and bring both emotion and measurement to an end—attaining the essential meaning before the sound and clarifying the source beyond the phrase—you would still not be permitted to settle upon this as a fixed realization; you must further undergo three births and nine kalpas.
Re-entering [the path], one finally attains resonance.
Your white-haired parents’ teeth are gradually failing; Diligently provide them with sweet delicacies without delay.
Try to emulate the Lord Śākyamuni of old, Serving your honored parents—return home!
The first two lines are the master’s exhortation to others to honor filial conduct and maintain the appearance befitting the elderly.
Regarding the food and clothing used for the elderly therein, whether one is a layperson or a monastic, as a child one should diligently provide sweet and delicious food;
when going out, one should return early and turn back promptly. Thus, the *Lunyu* says: "While one's parents are alive..."
One must not travel far from one’s parents’ home; if one travels, there must be a fixed destination. If you wish to go to a certain place, you must not exceed the appointed time limit.
If you return after the limit has passed, it will be too late; I fear this may cause your parents to fall into sorrow. Therefore, the *Bodhisattva-śikṣāpada-kṣānti-gāthā* says:
"There are two Buddhas within the hall, yet people of the world, in their distress, do not recognize them. They do not use gold or pigments to create [images]."
This is not carved from sandalwood; simply look at your parents of this present life.
If you can make offerings to them, what need is there to perform other meritorious deeds? Without that which was born of your father and mother, tell me, how could you have obtained this body?
For ten months your mother carried you in her womb, enduring how much toil and hardship. And when it came to sitting...
When they were infants, their lives hung by a thread in peril; in an instant, mother and child met, and resentment was dissolved through shame.
Whether male or female, they were cherished like bright pearls and precious jewels.

Yet, who would have expected that upon reaching adulthood, they would be entirely devoid of filial piety, righteousness, and propriety? When questioned, they glare with eyes wide with rage, responding as if in combat.
The parents snap their fingers and sigh in lamentation; in sorrowful pairs, they shed falling tears.
"If you continue to act as a person such as this, do not even ask for news of your future path. I see that for the unfilial, the thunderbolts of the void strike down;
punishment manifests in poverty in this very life, leaving one destitute and unable to pass day or night. I urge you to reflect and settle yourself, exerting all your strength morning and evening."
With a cheerful countenance, if you desire the marrow of the phoenix and the liver of the dragon, you must seek them out for him. You should disclose all your innermost thoughts and feelings;
do not speak with obstruction or opposition. While alive, let there be no lack of delicacies; after death, there is no need for posthumous remembrance.

If you can apply your mind in this way, Heaven and Earth, along with the spiritual deities, will grant you their protection and aid. If you do not thus become wealthy and establish a household, [you shall surely attain your goal].
One must certainly hold a high office and prominent position. The latter two lines instruct the practitioner to emulate the Buddha’s practice of filial piety;
thus, one should test and learn from the ancient Śākyamuni. Formerly, while the Buddha was on the path of cultivation, he was a parrot in the Snowy Mountains whose parents were both blind.
He would constantly gather fine fruits and first offer them to his parents. At that time, there was a landowner who, at first—
When sowing grain, he made a vow, saying: "The grain that is sown shall be shared and eaten together with all sentient beings.
Parrot, you already know that because the field-owner previously possessed this intention to give, you have always taken [the grain] to provide for your parents.
The other birds had scattered the grain and stalks across the ground. When the owner saw this, anger and vexation arose within him, and he set a net to catch them.
The parrot was caught in the net and said to the owner, "Master, you first showed me kindness; therefore, I did not dare take [the grain] before. Why do you now seek to capture me?
The owner replied, "I am taking the grain for someone. The bird said, "I have blind parents; I wish to offer this grain to them. The owner...
Wenlian said, "From this day forward, one should always take [the birds] from here.
If even animals act thus, how much more so should humans practice filial piety toward their parents? The Buddha said, "The bird was my own self; the owner was Śāriputra."
The Brahma King who was his father and mother is Māyā. Because he has practiced filial piety and nurtured his parents since the beginning of kalpas, he has now attained Buddhahood;
thus he knows gratitude and repays that kindness, attaining Great Nirvāṇa. It is not only within the human realm that one repays the debt of gratitude to one's parents;
even among birds and beasts, one likewise repays their kindness. The final phrase, "serving one's venerable parents," constitutes a separate section.
He exhorted his descendants: "If one serves one's parents with the same devotion as a Buddha, one shall likewise attain Buddhahood. Therefore he said: "Return! Come! The Dharma-body is without form;
it does not reside within the mind. It is beyond the intermediate state, transcending both the internal and the external. To perceive me through sound or form is to remain outside [of realization].
Tire. Prince Zhaoming classified this section of the sutra as the twenty-sixth chapter, "The Dharma-body is Without Characteristics," based on the Buddha’s teaching:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person walks upon a deviant path."
"One who cannot see the Tathāgata" means that one cannot see the Dharma-body Tathāgata; therefore, this name is established to show that the Dharma-body is not a mark.
Regarding "it does not reside within the mind," this section has Subhūti address the Buddha, saying:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. This is to realize this Dharma-body.
That which belongs to the seeing of the eye and the hearing of the ear is likewise inconceivable by the mind and beyond deliberation;
therefore, it is said that it does not reside within the heart-mind. Regarding the phrase "severing the intermediate and the internal and external":

having realized the Dharma-body, one severs the six consciousnesses in the intermediate state, and the six internal sense organs as well as the six external objects are all seen to be empty in essence; hence it is said, "severing the intermediate and the internal."

Furthermore, the treatise cites a verse which says: "One who merely sees forms and hears sounds does not know the Buddha, because the *dharmadhātu* of true suchness (*tathatā*) is not an object of consciousness.
Those who see me through sound and form have not yet emerged from the womb of saṃsāra.
If one perceives the Buddha by means of vocal sounds and physical marks, this appearance is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), not the *dharmakāya*, which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Such principles do not exempt one from the cycle of birth and death. Since that which possesses form and is conditioned is the womb of the cycle of birth and death, it is said:
"One has not yet emerged from the wheel-matrix."
If one departs from sound and form, it is difficult to see the Tathāgata; to seek him afar in vain is futile.

Mañjuśrī is on Mount Wutai—this is the "hand-eye" of the master of the lineage (kejiā), revealing what is already seen. Fearing that people might mistake something for the truth by departing from sound and form, [the text] states:
"If one departs from sounds and forms, it is difficult to see the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. This requires one to realize that sound and form *are* themselves the Dharma.
The physical body and its marks and signs likewise flow forth from within the *dharmakāya*. If one sees the marks and signs, one sees the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata.
Changshui said: "This portion [of the teaching] establishes the provisional as real; therefore, it is not separate from the marks and signs."
Thus one beholds the Dharma-body. Those who labor in vain to seek it afar—this reveals that Mañjuśrī’s Great Wisdom is precisely that which hears sound and sees form;
there is no need to seek Mount Wutai from afar, for how could it ever be separated from our daily activities?
In the past, Asanga asked Sudhana, "I wish to see Mañjuśrī; who is he? Sudhana replied, "The moment you..."
To give rise to a single thought of pure mind is itself the attachment to words. [The Master] said: "I have given rise to a single thought of pure mind;
why do I not see Mañjuśrī? Cui said: "Your single thought of pure mind is Mañjuśrī himself.
Why must you seek Mañjuśrī further? Therefore it is said: 'In vain one labors to seek him afar.'"
Having marks is itself marklessness; marklessness is also not the truth. Since neither of these two positions can be established, only the oneness [of reality] is truly intimate.
The first two lines refer to Subhūti’s response to the meaning of the Buddha’s question, saying: "So it is, so it is."
Regarding the thirty-two marks: when contemplating the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the intention is this: if one sees the marks and secondary characteristics, one is seeing the Dharma-body;
therefore it is said that "having marks is itself being markless. As for the next phrase, "being markless is also not the truth," this is because Subhūti subsequently answered the Buddha’s question:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not [rely] on the thirty-two marks."
Contemplating the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, one realizes that the Dharma-body cannot be perceived as having characteristics; hence it is said: "The absence of characteristics is also not the truth.
The latter two lines mean that within the true Dharma-realm, both the presence and absence of characteristics are equally untenable;
only the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) is the point of intimate realization. Therefore it is said: "The single essence is where intimacy lies. This may be understood.
That is to say, neither of the two extremes is established; the Middle Way is vast and level.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Dharma-body is Not a Phenomenon.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, what do you think? [Up to: This person walks upon a deviant path and cannot see the Tathāgata.

The commentary states: The meaning of this section is as follows. Having heard in the seventeenth doubt previously that the Dharma-body should not be perceived by means of the various marks of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), the Buddha, fearing that there might be further doubt, posed this question.
"Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks? The Buddha’s intention was this:
the thirty-two marks refer to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), whereas perceiving the Tathāgata refers to the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata. This clarifies the meaning of the Buddha's question.
[The questioner] asks: "Can one perceive the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata within the marks and signs of the Saṃbhogakāya?
Subhūti, having understood the meaning of the question, replies: "So it is, so it is. One perceives the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
The intention is that seeing the thirty-two marks is itself seeing the Dharmakāya; therefore, he says, "So it is, so it is."
This is so. It may be said that the Dharma-body pervades all places, including all sentient beings and all lands.
The Buddha feared that Subhūti might become attached to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and fail to realize that the essence of the Dharma is empty and profound;

therefore, he again used the wheel-turning king (cakravartin) to dispel his doubts. This was because the marks and signs of the wheel-turning king are identical to those of the Tathāgata. However, by means of...
The marks of a king arise from merit, yet his afflictions have not been severed. The marks of a Buddha manifest from the Dharma-body, for ignorance has been eternally eliminated.
Thus, the ordinary person and the sage differ; their mental natures are distinct. Subhūti, you have profoundly understood the essence of the Dharma.
Thereupon, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks.
His intention was that the Dharma-body cannot be perceived through marks; he realized that the Dharma-body is not seen through marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that Subhūti had deeply realized the essence of the Dharma, spoke a verse to certify this:

"If one sees me by means of form—form being the thirty-two marks, and 'me' being the true self of the Dharmakāya—you cannot see my Dharmakāya with the eyes. Why? Because the Dharmakāya has no marks of form; therefore, it cannot be seen."
To see [the Buddha] through form is to seek me by means of sound; yet the sound of the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is itself the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Therefore, the Dharma-body of the Buddha cannot be heard with the ears. Sound and form are merely the objective realms (dust-objects) perceived by the conscious mind.
If one seeks to see or hear my Dharma-body through sound and form, such a person walks a deviant path and is unable to see the Tathāgata.
As for the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata: it is neither form nor sound, without shape and without characteristics.

It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. It does not diminish among ordinary beings, nor does it increase among sages. When looked upon, it is not seen; when awakened to, it is fully manifest.
Master Fu’s verse says: "Nirvāṇa contains the four virtues; only I am in accord with true permanence. [Equal in fame.]
The eight sovereign powers: I alone am the most spiritual and preeminent. Neither sound nor form, how could mind-consciousness ever measure me?
When looked upon, I cannot be seen; yet when the principle is realized, my form is manifest.
Adorned with wondrous marks, the marks of a sacred wheel-turning monarch are themselves the marks of a Tathāgata. The Dharma-body is all-pervasive;

yet the body of a Tathāgata differs from the body of a sacred wheel-turning monarch. If you can see through this point thoroughly, then the egret rests in its snow nest and the hare dwells in the moon palace.
Should it not be so, however—

This passage cites the meaning of the sūtra and provides a brief explanation of the Tathāgata’s body of retribution and response (*vipākaphala-kāya*), which consists of the thirty-two marks of excellence adorned with myriad virtues.
The Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) possesses an upright and majestic appearance and likewise possesses the thirty-two marks;
thus, his marks are identical to those of the Tathāgata. However, if one discusses the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it is all-pervasive...

He pervades the worlds of the ten directions without leaving this seat; his body fills the atoms and lands, his Buddha-body suffuses the entire Dharma-realm, and he appears universally before all sentient beings.
Thus, he differs from a noble wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), yet he does so by means of being such a wheel-turning monarch.
Not having realized the Buddha-nature, they have not yet emerged from birth and death; they merely enjoy worldly blessings, which eventually come to an end. Thus, Changshui said:

"The marks of a Buddha manifest from the Dharmakāya, whereas the marks of a king arise from causes of merit; the difference between the ordinary and the sage is as vast as that between clouds and mud."
They are identical in essence yet distinct. If one can see through this point thoroughly, then this is the master of the school examining the practitioner.

If one can see clearly and penetrate to the core whether the body of the Tathāgata and the body of the Sage-King are the same or different—like a heron perched in a snow nest or a rabbit dwelling in a moon palace, where from afar they appear to be the same—then one has truly understood.
When viewed closely, they appear distinct; yet when compared to the egret, the snow, and the rabbit, they are the same.

There is a difference in their movement and stillness, which serves as a metaphor for the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) and the Buddha. Although their physical marks and signs are identical, the essence and function of the Universal Monarch and the Buddha differ.

It may be said: "Only when the egret flies up amidst the snow is it seen; only when the parrot speaks among the willows is it known. If this is not yet so, then [the following] classification applies.

The Master’s intention was this: if one cannot yet discern [the truth] within the presence of the Tathāgata, the Holy King, and has not yet attained thorough insight, it is for this reason he said, "If this is not yet so."
"The spark of fire has already vanished beyond the heavens, yet the deluded person still gazes at the stars beside the moon.

These two lines are the Master’s response to the aforementioned meaning of "not yet so. To be deluded regarding principle and pursue phenomena, taking the false for the true, is to lack the eye of discernment.
In reality, this merely highlights that they are unable to distinguish between the physical marks of a Wheel-Turning King and those of a Buddha.
Although they are similar, the wondrous function of the Buddha’s Dharma-body is truly distinct from that of a wheel-turning monarch.
Thus, it is likened to a spark of flint already vanishing into the heavens, yet the deluded person, unaware of this, still looks to the stars beside the moon, mistaking them for fire.

This punishes the error of taking the marks of a holy king to be the marks of a Tathāgata; hence it is said: "The deluded person still looks to the stars beside the moon. This may indeed be called the third [point].
Drawing from the waves, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the deluded person still scoops out the water of the night pond.
The public case is already complete, yet one asks again; with attachment to feelings, one turns over the confession and wrongly assumes responsibility.
If one does not respond to form and sound by practicing the deviant path, there will be no cause for the accumulation of offenses upon meeting the Dharma King.
This verse restates the meaning of the preceding sutra and provides a brief explanation of its first two lines. Regarding the term "gong'an" (public case), National Teacher Puying said:
"What is called a gong'an is a metaphor for the official documents of a government office. Where the Dharma resides, the order or disorder of the royal way truly depends upon that government office.
To speak of "public" (gong) is to mean that the sages and worthies follow the same path throughout the world.
This is the ultimate principle of following the same path. A "case file" (an) is the formal written record of how the sages and worthies established order.
Thus, those who possess the world have never lacked a public office; and where there is a public office, there has never been a lack of case files and official documents.
This is because one wishes to adopt them as models in order to adjudicate what is improper in the world. Public cases are thus put into practice.
Thus, the principle of the Dharma is applied; when the principle of the Dharma is applied, the world is rectified. When the world is rectified, the Way of the King is realized.
Now, the teachings of the Buddhas and the karmic conditions of the Patriarchs are likewise termed "public cases" (gong'an).

These are certainly not the arbitrary views of a single person, but rather the convergence of the spiritual sources of all the Sages, in perfect accord with the wondrous intent across the three periods of time and the ten directions throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds.

Bodhisattvas receive this same ultimate principle; therefore, it is called a "public case" (gong'an). What is now termed a "case of present perfection" refers to the passage in the Sutra where the Buddha asks Subhūti:
"What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti replied: "So it is, so it is. The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks."
This response—that one should contemplate the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata through the marks and signs—is what is called the "Public Case of Manifestation.

Regarding the further inquiry, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, if one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, then a Wheel-turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata. This is what is called the "Further Inquiry. [End of] *Ai*.
Regarding "the one who, in turn, mistakenly accepts [the teaching]": initially, Subhūti was attached to emotional sentiment.

He held that the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) were themselves the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Yet, when the Tathāgata challenged him by using the analogy of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), Subhūti reversed his previous position;
he claimed his own understanding was mistaken and accepted that the physical marks and signs were the Dharma-body, and thus—[he fell into error].
It says: "One does not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. This is because one has invited error through one's own misrecognition;

it refers to the inversion of affectionate attachment and the mistaken assumption of responsibility. Regarding the latter two lines, "one should not practice deviant paths through sound or form," this refers to the verse spoken by the Buddha in the sutra:
"If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person..."
Regarding the phrase "those on a false path cannot see the Tathāgata" and "the offense is incurred because there is no cause for seeing the Dharma-King," the intent of the commentary is as follows:
if one perceives the Buddha’s Dharma-body through physical forms or vocal sounds, this constitutes a wrong view and walking upon a false path.
One summons the causes for the karmic offenses of afflictions; there is no way to behold the Buddha’s Dharma-body. Thus it is said:
"The offenses are bound, and there is no cause to see the Dharma King.
For nine years he faced the wall, realizing his own errors; it would have been better to withdraw from the world and return alone in his single sandal.
"Do not say that the news from Shaolin has been cut off; the white clouds still embrace the thatched gate.
(The first two lines clarify Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall, manifesting the Way beyond words and revealing the principle of the solitary, eternal reality.
Yet he himself knew it was not so, and it would have been wiser for him to withdraw and return to the West. This is just like Subhūti...)
"Ti. This translates as "to acknowledge one's own error in misrecognizing the marks and signs [of the Buddha], thereby taking them to be identical to the Dharma-body. Thus it is said:

"It would be better to withdraw the body and return with but a single shoe. Regarding the latter two lines, "Do not say that the news of Shaolin has been cut off," the commentator exhorts practitioners not to claim that after Bodhidharma returned to the West with his single shoe, the transmission at Shaolin here in this land was severed.
Rest. There is no such path. Simply observe the billowing white clouds and the winding green waters; with the rustic gate closed alone, Bodhidharma sits in meditation—when has he ever departed?

If one discusses this news, from antiquity to the present, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as all things sentient and insentient, are without interruption. This is the subtle and wondrous principle. Thus said Tianning Kai.
The Chan Master’s verse says: "The One Dharma is originally non-existent; the myriad dharmas are empty. Within this, how can there be any realization of perfect penetration?
I thought the news from Shaolin had been cut off, But the peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze."
How many days until the three realms are stilled? When will the six dusts cease their turmoil?
The single path to the West transcends birth and death; recite Amitābha’s name together and reach the destination.
(The first two lines lament this Saha world, where all sentient beings within the three realms and six paths wander therein.)
Coming without ceasing, one wanders through birth and death; on what day will one attain awakening?

Again, one is vexed by the dharmas of the six sense objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena—committing boundless transgressions; when will this ever come to rest? Thus it is said: "Busy in the morning, busy in the evening;
the mind-monkey and will-horse are utterly frantic. The six gates are deeply locked and firmly fastened; the blazing fire..."
Within that light, one immediately attains coolness. The latter two lines praise the Western World as the great path for exiting the three realms and the six destinies of saṃsāra;
thus it is said, "The single path to the West transcends birth and death.
You people, if you are willing to unite your minds and recite this one sound of *Namo Amitābha Buddha*, you shall all reach that land.
The head. It is born together with one in the lotus-womb of the Western Pure Land by transformation.

Without interruption and without cessation, it has existed eternally from of old. It does not perish, nor is it ever born again. While mountains and rivers undergo formation and destruction, this remains tranquil and secure.
Prince Zhaoming classified this section of the sutra as the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Neither Annihilation nor Extinction.
This is because the Buddha taught that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristics of annihilation or extinction regarding phenomena.
The Buddha’s intention was not to regard the Tathāgata by means of physical marks and signs, but rather to cause practitioners to depart from them.
The characteristic of grasping and attachment is not the same as the view of annihilation found in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

It does not mean that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not achieve their form through the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and merit; rather, because they wish to cultivate merit for the sake of manifesting the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is said that there is no cessation.
Because one seeks to realize the true body through wisdom, it is said: "without cessation. Thus, the name is established as "without interruption and without cessation.
That which has existed eternally from antiquity is precisely this principle; since there is no interruption or extinction, it may be called "eternally existing from antiquity.
Regarding the phrase "not ceasing and not being born again": the above clarified that the *bodhi* realized by the Tathāgata does not arise [from conditions].
[This] is brought about by merit. This is precisely the merit cultivated by a bodhisattva;
though it seeks to become the cause for the realization of Bodhi, it is likewise unable to produce the fruit. To sever this doubt, the Buddha said: "Do not harbor such a thought.
The Tathāgata does not attain Bodhi by means of the marks of physical perfection (*lakṣaṇa*). The 'marks of perfection' are merely the marks of merit. Indeed, [it is] great...
Relying on the causes of the merit one has cultivated, one attains the fruits of that merit; it is simply a matter of being free from the mind of grasping and attachment.
The *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "The single reality" refers to the essence of the minds of sentient beings.
From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished, extending even to the minds of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, followers of the Two Vehicles, and ordinary beings.

Now, as for the mind: because it is the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither arising nor ceasing, it is called the "ever-active mind. Therefore, it is said that what does not cease does not arise again.
The following passage provides analogies to substantiate this. Regarding the formation and destruction of mountains and rivers, this reveals the principle of non-ceasing and non-arising.
Although worlds undergo the stages of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, this Bodhi-mind of true reality is fundamentally non-existent [in terms of such change].
It is born without ceasing; it has neither formation nor destruction. Thus it is said: "This is peaceful and secure. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa and are scorched by the great conflagration, my land remains peaceful and secure, ever filled with devas and humans.
It further says: "I am always on Vulture Peak Mountain and in other various abodes. Wēnlíng comments: "Peaceful and secure" refers to the reality (*tattva*).
The Land of Reward Adornment is also called the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*). As for "the Spirit Mountain" (*Liṅshān*), it refers to one's own numinous spirit.
Being neither form nor vessel, it cannot be consumed by the fires at the end of an eon; it spans from antiquity to the present, eternally abiding and indestructible.
When this is clearly realized, the defiled land is itself the pure land.
Without coming and without going, it illuminates the past and soars through the present. It is inherently possessed by every person; even brass cannot be exchanged for gold.
This principle presents the truth of neither arising nor ceasing: not only is there no formation or destruction, but there is also no past, future, or present.
Although the shifting of the three periods does not exist, one has never been apart from them.
It transcends the three periods of time; hence it is said: "It illuminates the past and soars through the present. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"To not give rise to dualistic characteristics within a single dharma is called neither coming nor going nor abiding. Because it does not abide..."
...up to the point that there is no agent and no one who craves; therefore it is said that there is neither coming nor going.
"Each person is inherently endowed with this" concludes the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Although each person is inherently endowed with this Way, from the perspective of the individual, it is no different from that of a Buddha. If one does not cultivate merit through the marks and signs [of a Buddha], then—
If one generates the bodhicitta and immediately brings it to cessation, this is like brass.
If one cultivates merit through the marks and signs of physical perfection while remaining free from attachment, this is true wisdom; it is likened to pure gold.

If one clings to the notion of original possession without cultivating the marks, signs, and merit, one will ultimately fail to realize the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said: "Brass is not exchanged [for gold]."
It is gold.
Neither born nor extinguished, Neither severed nor eternal; Permanence, bliss, self, and purity— Not something unworthy of discussion.

These four phrases reveal the principle of neither arising nor ceasing. Regarding the first two phrases, the Master’s intention is that arising and ceasing, as well as annihilation and permanence, are also termed the "four marks of arising and ceasing.
These belong to the views of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), while annihilation and permanence belong to the views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

All four are fundamentally empty; this is precisely to be free from the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* states: "The non-arising of arising is the profound stillness of true nature;
the arising of non-arising is the manifest presence of karmic fruition. Thus one should know: if one clings to the existence of thought as it arises, this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*);
if one seeks non-arising apart from arising, this is the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Both fail to penetrate the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). There is no... [text ends]
There is the principle of non-arising and non-extinction. If one realizes non-arising, then there is neither arising nor non-arising;
how could one dogmatically cling to the dual views of "arising" and "non-arising"? If one awakens to this principle of non-arising, the four marks are all eliminated.
Regarding the latter two phrases, "permanence, bliss, self, and purity": since one has already departed from the aforementioned four marks, it is precisely appropriate [to realize these].
We shall now discuss the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*. That is to say: ordinary beings are deluded regarding their own nature;

they conceptually construct the five aggregates as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Therefore, the Buddha causes sentient beings to cultivate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity in order to destroy these misconceptions.
Thus, by relying on the Buddha’s teachings, sentient beings cultivate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and so forth, thereby realizing the two [truths].
Because those who ride these vehicles still delude themselves regarding true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity, the Buddha refutes their attachments, stating:
"They reckon the permanent as impermanent, bliss as suffering, the self as non-self, and purity as impurity.
Furthermore, he refutes the four inverted views of the two vehicles and again demonstrates: "Permanence is the meaning of the Dharma-body; bliss is Nirvana."

The meaning of "I" is the Buddha; the meaning of "Pure" is the Dharma. Although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, truly possess immeasurable and boundless virtues, these four virtues alone encompass them all completely.
Chapter Twenty-seven: On Neither Annihilation nor Extinction.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if you should think [as follows], up to: “In the Dharma, I do not teach a mark of annihilation or extinction.”
The commentary states: This section is titled "The Meaning of Neither Being Severed nor Ceasing.
Because Subhūti had previously heard that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not to be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks, he feared this doubt might arise;
therefore, he raised the question, saying: "If you were to think thus: 'The Tathāgata does not attain Arhatship by virtue of being endowed with the marks...'"
"Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi"—this recounts Subhūti’s doubt, namely that one does not attain awakening by means of fully perfected marks;
this refers precisely to the marks that have been refuted. The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying:
"Do not harbor such a thought. It is not because of fully perfected marks that the Tathāgata attained awakening. This is an admonition.
Do not doubt this; it reiterates the characteristics of what has been refuted. The Buddha spoke again to Subhūti, saying:

"If you were to think that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are teaching the annihilation of all phenomena, you would be thinking that since they do not cultivate merit through the perception of marks, the bodhicitta they have generated would thereby become annihilated."
This is the fault of [such] extinction. Therefore, the Buddha again says, "Do not entertain such a thought.

This is a repeated admonition; do not harbor doubts. The Buddha further asks, "For what reason? whereby he himself interrogates the preceding meaning. For what purpose should one not entertain such a thought?
The subsequent text provides the reason, stating: "One who has resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, regarding all dharmas..."

It is not taught that there is a characteristic of annihilation; rather, for a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, the causes of the merit they cultivate and the fruits of the merit they obtain all possess complete characteristics, yet they cultivate merit in order to realize the fruit of Buddhahood without grasping at or becoming attached to these marks and signs. This non-attachment is itself true wisdom. Because there is wisdom, it is the True Body (Dharmakāya).

Possessing merit— [Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The final sentence "Possessing merit—" suggests the continuation might have been "possessing merit, one is the Enjoyment Body (Sambhogakāya)," or similar.]
Because of its virtue, it is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya*. Therefore, regarding the Dharma, it does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation.

A Zen Master, Zhe-zhi, composed a verse: "Each characteristic is not a characteristic; The complete characteristics have no basis. Dharma after dharma gives rise to wondrous dharmas; Emptiness after emptiness, their essences are not the same.
Annihilation or non-annihilation— To know this is to awaken to the profound school. If there is no thought of self or others,"
Only then do we know this to be ultimate impartiality.

It is not something acquired through cultivation, yet it is fundamentally possessed; it is eternally self-adorned. Although the Dharma is transmitted, it is not truly transmitted; how could it ever be severed or extinguished?
In the past, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, before the multitude of humans and devas, the World-Honored One said: "I have the pure Dharma-eye and the wondrous mind of Nirvana;
I entrust them to Kāśyapa, so that you may widely propagate and transform others. Now tell me, what exactly was transmitted at that time?
The first section concerns those for whom the marks are not complete. Because it was previously stated that the marks and signs are not the Dharma-body, Subhūti adhered single-mindedly to this view;
since one does not attain bodhi by means of complete marks, it is said here that "the marks are not complete."

This is precisely what is meant by annihilationism. As for that which is inherently possessed: the Tathāgata possesses the marks of perfection and cultivates merit, yet does not grasp at these marks and signs;
it is through true wisdom that one realizes Bodhi. Therefore, this does not belong to the category of annihilationism.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Although one knows that the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is by nature bodiless, yet..."
The primary marks and secondary signs adorn his physical body (*rūpakāya*). That which is fundamentally possessed is the wisdom true body (*jñāna-dharmakāya*).
The adornments are the merit-corresponding body (*puṇya-nirmāṇakāya*). The *Śāstra* states: "That which is fully endowed with the adornment of merit is the corresponding body;
that which is adorned with wisdom is the true body. Although the Dharma is transmitted, it is not transmitted, for Buddhas transmit it to one another through the patriarchs.
The Patriarchs transmitted this to one another. However, within the reality of the ultimate principle (*tattva*), there is fundamentally not a single dharma that is transmitted.
Although this principle has nothing to be transmitted, because it is equally received by both the holy and the ordinary within their inherent nature (*prakṛti*), it is fully possessed by all;

therefore, it is said: "How could it ever be severed or extinguished? The following passage extends the meaning of "no transmission. Formerly, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One...
Regarding the "Superior" [section]: this clarifies the event of the Buddha holding up a flower at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at the very end of his life.
The text is excerpted from the *Brahmādevapṛcchā-saṃdehavyāvartana-sūtra*. Although this scripture contains many accounts concerning kings, they have been omitted here.
It describes how, when Brahmādeva offered a golden *utpala* lotus, the World-Honored One picked it up and showed it to the assembly; yet among humans and devas, none could comprehend it.
[The Buddha] knew that only Kāśyapa had broken into a smile, deeply awakening to this principle which transcends words.
Therefore, the Buddha entrusted him, saying: "I have the pure Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the true mark which is markless, and the subtle, wonderful, orthodox Dharma.
I now entrust them to you, Kāśyapa. You must skillfully protect and uphold them, and cause them to be widely transmitted and transformed. The masters of the school cite this passage.
This proves that the Dharma mentioned above is without interruption and has existed eternally from antiquity; there is nothing to be transmitted.
Furthermore, when it is asked, "What was transmitted at that time? this is an inquiry into the preceding meaning.
The response provided below—namely, what was transmitted between the Buddha and Kāśyapa—is the answer to this.
"The blue-lotus eyes look upon the assembly of devas and humans; the golden-colored dhūta alone breaks into a smile.
These two lines answer the meaning of the preceding [verse]. They demonstrate that what is not transmitted is yet transmitted; how could there be any annihilation?
Therefore, at the place where the flower was held up and the smile was given, there was silent realization and mental penetration—how could it ever have been annihilated?
A single lamp can continue a hundred thousand lamps; The light of the mind-seal penetrates, and the Dharma is put into practice.
Not transmitted by the thousand sages, it cannot be extinguished by blowing. The linked brilliance and arrayed flames become increasingly distinct.
The first line uses a metaphor to clarify the meaning of the "separate transmission outside the teachings," just as one lamp continues a hundred [thousand].

A thousand lamps, each lamp continuing the flame of the next, burning without end. The second phrase, "the light of the mind-seal penetrates," precisely reveals the Way of the separate transmission outside the teachings.

From the four and seven patriarchs of India to the two and three ancestors of this land, down to the five schools, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have succeeded one another, transmitting mind-to-mind through successive generations. This has spread throughout the lands of the ten directions.

It spreads without end. This Dharma-gate is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. If a single bodhisattva guides hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta, his own progress on the bodhisattva path is not thereby extinguished; rather, it continues according to the Dharma he teaches.
And by this, one increases all wholesome dharmas within oneself; this is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. It means that the Dharma-Command is capable of being enacted.

In the past, Huanglong Nan personally carried out this command; none of the Buddhas of the ten directions dared to contravene it, and none of the ancestral masters of successive generations or all the sages and worthies dared to overstep it.
All immeasurable Dharma-gates and all subtle meanings—[the heavens... (text fragmentary).

The old Master’s tongue has been brought down; from beginning to end, it is a single seal, and none dare differ from it. Setting aside for a moment those who would differ, where does this seal reside?
It is neither monk nor layman; it is without partiality and without faction. The army follows the turning of the seal; the general proceeds according to the talisman.
This is what is meant by the World-Honored One holding up the flower and Kāśyapa smiling, and by Bodhidharma facing the wall and the Second Patriarch finding peace of mind.
Seeing the flower, Lingyun’s doubts were completely purified; striking the bamboo, Xiangyan suddenly forgot all that he knew. Panshan attained sudden enlightenment at the meat market;
Maitreya welcomed people in the fish market. Truly, it is as the saying goes: "In times of distress or haste, one must remain centered on this;
whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one dwells within it. Since there is such marvel as this, there is furthermore such [a state].
This radiance is both so vast and so all-pervasive. Yet, why is it that you people still experience delusion and awakening?
Do you understand? "Fortunately there is no place it does not shine, yet there is still a time when it is not clear.

These latter two lines present the meaning of what precedes them, revealing that this Way is not transmitted by the thousand sages and not spoken of by the patriarchs. It may be illustrated as follows:
One lamp kindles a hundred thousand lamps; its light is inexhaustible. Thus it is said: "It cannot be extinguished by blowing.

Because it is a transmission through non-transmission, it remains undiminished to this day. Consequently, the succession of fragrances and the array of flames become ever more distinct. It may truly be said:
"Since the blossoming of the five petals joined in fragrance at Shaoshi, the flowers have continued to bloom until the present."
A single point of spiritual radiance fills the great void; It is neither Chan, nor Teaching, nor Confucianism.
Who can realize this unified whole? Only one with the true eye is a Great Man worthy of it.
The opening line clarifies that a single point of spiritual radiance fills the great void, shining upon heaven and reflecting the earth. Da'an said: "You..."
All such people as these each possess their own priceless great treasure: a single point of spiritual radiance.
From the gateway of the eyes, it emits light that illuminates the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; from the gateway of the ears, it emits light that perceives and gathers all sounds.
Thus, through these six gateways, it constantly emits radiance day and night; this is also called the Samādhi of Emitting Light. You are not few in number, each of you...
Take care of yourself. Thus it is said: "It fills the great void. This second line clarifies that this single point of numinous light is neither Chan, nor Teaching (Dharma), nor Confucianism;
the three teachings are without distinction, for they all equally receive the One Mind. As Master Fu said:
"The Daoist cap, the Confucian shoes, and the Buddhist *kāṣāya*—unite these three houses into one. If you can recognize the message within them," [you will understand].

The *udumbara* flower is originally a white lotus; it may be said that awakening through many lifetimes does not require a thousand patched robes, and that a single point of numinous clarity does not reside in a lamp.
As for the latter two lines, although they possess the numinous light integrated into a single whole, they do not distinguish between the three teachings.
How many people could truly understand this? It requires those of high caliber who possess the true eye. Only those who can put it into practice will reach the ground where there is no division.
As the ancient masters said: "One must read the sutras and study the books; honor the Sangha, honor the Way, and also honor the Confucians.
Emperor Huizong’s heart was biased toward the Way; Emperor Wu’s nature favored the Sangha; and Qin Shi Huang buried the Confucians.
How could Confucianism ever perish? When Māra slandered the Buddha, how could the Buddha have been removed?
In this world of great illumination, there is a benevolent and compassionate sovereign;
the three teachings return to the same source, all being but one suchness. Thus it is said: "Only one with the true eye can be called a great man."
Celestial music and the *xiāo sháo* flute play as flower-rain falls; Having traveled through other lands, the Sage has returned for the first time.
A multitude like clouds and oceans welcome him with all manner of forms; Beholding his golden countenance, he returns from whence he came.
The first two lines reveal the splendor of the Western Realm: celestial music constantly resounds and heavenly flowers perpetually rain down. Maitreya...
The Sūtra says: "In that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays; the ground is made of gold, and six times throughout the day and night, it rains *māndārava* flowers.

As for those who travel to other regions, because the Bodhisattvas of that land wish to make offerings of the most sublime things to the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, in a single *kṣaṇa*, they universally pay homage to the ten [directions]."
When the Buddhas and sages have spontaneously completed their offerings before the Buddha, they return just as they were at the beginning;
therefore, it is called the "first circuit. As the Sūtra says: "The sentient beings of that land always, at the clear dawn..."
Each person, taking various exquisite flowers in their robes, made offerings to ten trillion Buddhas in other directions;

then, at the time of the meal, they returned to their own lands to eat, walk, and practice. The latter two lines state that those in this land who practice mindfulness of the Buddha give rise to three kinds of minds and cultivate three kinds of practices; when their lives come to an end, they will go straight ahead with right mindfulness to Amitābha.

Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude arrive like clouds to welcome the practitioner.
Seated upon a vajra pedestal, in the time it takes to snap one’s fingers, they are reborn in that land.
Having attained birth in the highest grade, they personally behold Amitābha and receive the prediction of their own buddhahood; thus it is said: "To witness with one's own eyes the Golden One."
May you return in peace.
Explanatory Commentary on the Essential Ritual Manual of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra, Scroll Seven;
Explanatory Commentary on the Essential Ritual Manual of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
compiled by Chan Master Zongjing of Baifu Monastery in Longxing Prefecture;
and recompiled by the Śramaṇa Juelian, a successor to the ancestral patriarchs of the Cao-Dong Orthodox Lineage.
Not receiving and not coveting; contented and ever-satisfied. Without sin and without merit; passing the days according to conditions.
One must strictly avoid making distinctions or complaints. Prince Zhaoming judged this section of the scripture as the Twentieth Chapter: "Non-Receiving and Non-Coveting."
8. Furthermore, when the Buddha says that a bodhisattva does not accept merit, he means that they should not accept the tainted (sāsrava) retributions of the triple world;
therefore, it is said "not accepting. Moreover, regarding the merit they have performed, they should not be greedily attached to it;
this refers to supramundane, untainted (anāsrava) retributions, which they may accept without being greedily attached. Therefore, these [two points] are established.
This is called neither receiving nor craving. As for "contentment and constant sufficiency": since one does not receive tainted merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*), this is contentment;
since one does not crave or cling to untainted retribution (*anāsrava-vipāka*), this is constant sufficiency.
The Buddha told Siṃhavikrīḍita: "One who has few desires does not seek or take. One who is content, when obtaining little, does not [become dissatisfied]..."

Because of regret and remorse, it is said: "One who is content is always satisfied. Regarding the phrase "neither sin nor merit," this clarifies that this bodhisattva knows all dharmas are without self and has attained patience (*kṣānti*).
Thus, regarding the merits they perform, they should not be greedily attached; consequently, there is no merit to be received.
Since there is no merit to be received, there is likewise no sin to be received. This is because they have realized the person (*pudgala*) [is empty].
The two attachments to dharmas are the emptiness of the nature of sin and merit. "Passing the days according to conditions" explains the preceding text: one who is content is always sufficient.
Because this Bodhisattva does not accept blessings and virtues, nor is he greedily attached to them, he simply passes the days according to conditions.
Longtan Xian said: "Roaming freely according to one's nature, being expansive and unconfined according to conditions; simply exhaust all mundane sentiments, and there is nothing else."
The Noble Understanding. Thus it is said: "Drink and feed as circumstances permit, and then rest; know that this body is but a temporary lodging, like a floating bubble.
Since one has recognized the face given by one's mother, the water-buffalo is seen to be nothing other than an ox. One must strictly avoid making such distinctions."

This is also an exposition: there is neither sin nor merit. Since this bodhisattva does not crave or cling to either sin or merit, they possess no mind of discrimination, acceptance, or rejection regarding them; thus, the merit they cultivate becomes the fruit of untainted purity.
Therefore, it is said: "One must by all means avoid making distinctions."
"A single bowl for a thousand households" is the livelihood of the patched-robed monks (*śramaṇa*). Although they possess not a single thing, they increase the merit of all sentient beings.
Regarding "a single bowl for a thousand households," the preceding passage by Śākya [Xing] describes the life of a monk who passes his days according to conditions:
apart from the three robes and a single bowl, he does not store even a fraction of an inch; he wears rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) and eats decomposed food, remaining without fixed abode.
Regarding cooking over a fire and seeking alms according to the Dharma, one may say: "A single bowl for the food of a thousand households; a solitary body wandering ten thousand miles.

This is indeed the living path of the patch-robed monk (nàzǐ). Thus, from the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment until his entry into *nirvāṇa*, he always stayed beneath trees, possessing only the three robes and a single bowl, begging for food as circumstances allowed.
An ancient worthy said: "There is a dharma of peace and happiness, transmitted down through all the sages."
Worthy one, if you can simply rely on the Buddha’s teachings, what need is there for fields and estates? When hungry, rely on the alms bowl to beg;
when weary, stretch out your legs and sleep. If not even a hair’s breadth of discursive thought arises, the merit of your enjoyment will be boundless.

Though you possess not a single thing, you are a monk who passes his days beautifully according to conditions. Although your body is poor and you have nothing at all, you are able to [benefit] sentient beings.
Sentient beings [act as] fields of merit. Thus, the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) said: "The giver has not a single thing to give;

the receiver has not a single thing to receive, yet they act as a field of merit. This refers to this wondrous path of true emptiness, wherein both the giving and the receiving, as well as the object given, are all unobtainable.
Wēnlíng says: "Within the Universal Gate, there is fundamentally no giving or receiving. This is what is meant by the 'Three'..."
The essence of the wheel is emptiness.

Failing to perceive this, one gives rise to worldly conditions; as craving and attachment turn, delusion deepens. If one can attain the light of turning-back illumination, then that which was to arise shall not arise.
The first two phrases reveal the characteristics of the initial arising of ignorance; this pertains to the gate of origination (*utpāda-mukha*).

Because one habituates oneself to obscurity due to ignorance, it is called "non-awakening" (*a-vijñapti*). "Dust" (*rajas*) refers to the six sense objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*) which serve as the objective conditions (*ālambana*). "Condition" (*pratyaya*)...

This refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) which act as the subjective perceivers. Because the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can perceive "solitary shadows" (*pratibimba*) across the three periods of time, it gives rise to the perceiving consciousnesses.

The sensory objects (*viṣaya*) serve as the parents of these perceptions; acting as the domain of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they trigger the six consciousnesses within the six sense organs, whereby their discernment forms seeds.
With ignorance (*avidyā*) as the root, subsequent defiled attachment arises, leading inevitably to craving (*rāga*).
Grasping arises from craving; it moistens karma and leads to rebirth. Therefore, craving is the root of birth and death.
Because this continuity is inexhaustible, it is said that "craving turns and becomes ever deeper. As for the latter two lines:
if one can turn the light back upon itself, this is called non-acceptance and non-craving, which is the gate of cessation and return. This reveals the absence of...
It is clear that these have no substantial reality, like a person in a dream. While dreaming, they are not non-existent; yet upon waking, nothing at all can be found.
Thus, if one is able to refrain from pursuing the external objects of the six sense-pollutions (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the remaining eleven factors are entirely empty and quiescent.
Yet, by turning the light back upon itself to reflect inwardly, one’s original face is found to be neither deficient nor redundant;
thus, in this very life, it is precisely non-arising. Therefore, in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, King Paramārthasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bodhisattvas perceive arising within the dharma of non-arising. The Buddha said: "All dharmas are without cessation; therefore, they are without arising. If one practices the profound...
Prajñā truly knows that ignorance gives rise to the eleven factors of dependent origination. If ignorance is severed, these eleven factors are all exhausted.

It is like a human body: if life is severed, it perishes accordingly. Those of false views and external paths, seeking liberation, sever desire and sever death, yet they do not know how to sever birth.
Birth is precisely the deluded thought of ignorance. If dharmas are without birth, then...
There is no extinction [of death]. It is like a person throwing a clod of earth at a lion; the lion pursues the person, while the clod extinguishes itself.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he merely cuts off birth, and death extinguishes itself. If a clod of earth is thrown at a dog, the dog pursues only the clod.
If one does not know how to chase away the clod of earth, it will never cease; so too it is with the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Not knowing how to sever birth, they can never escape death.
Because the Bodhisattva deeply understands the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, he is free from birth and death.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: On Non-acceptance and Non-attachment.
[Sūtra] If a bodhisattva [fills worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges]... for this reason it is said that they do not accept merit.
The commentary states: This section is titled "Neither Receiving Nor Greed.

Because in the preceding section, although the Bodhisattva practices giving and realizes that the nature of merit is empty, there still remains the sense of something being received; therefore, the Buddha says: "If a Bodhisattva..."
If one were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift, this describes the Bodhisattva in the preceding section.
Specifically, in the eighth section, Subhūti says: "The Bodhisattva realizes that the nature of merit is empty;
yet the Tathāgata says that the merit is great. Furthermore, in the nineteenth section, Subhūti also says: "Because merit is non-existent, the Tathāgata..."
It is said that the merit is great; these two types of giving constitute the virtues of a bodhisattva, for they realize that the nature of conditioned giving is empty.
The Buddha further stated: "If there is another person who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains patience (*kṣānti*), etc.
This reveals that the bodhisattva herein should not, by means of tainted karmic retribution, receive [anything].
Although they experience the retribution of outflows (*āsrava*), they do not grasp at them with attachment.

Furthermore, knowing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty and being devoid of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). For this reason, they surpass the aforementioned bodhisattvas.

This serves as a counter-illustration: if the mind of a bodhisattva has objects of attachment, the merit they induce becomes tainted (*sāsrava*); if the mind is free from attachment, it becomes untainted (*anāsrava*). Therefore...

The Buddha said: "Furthermore, if there is a person who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains *kṣānti* (patience), they will obtain the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas) because, within the Dharma, both the grasping at a self and the grasping at a person are empty.
Therefore, they surpass the merit obtained by the aforementioned bodhisattvas. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti once more, saying: "For what reason is the bodhisattva herein superior?"
The former bodhisattvas, because they do not accept merit, do not accept the outflowing rewards of merit; for this reason, they surpass the former bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how is it that a bodhisattva does not accept merit?
Subhūti raised this doubt because he wondered: since a bodhisattva does not accept merit...
[Subhūti] asked: "How can one attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
The Buddha answered Subhūti: "A bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to the merit they have performed. For this reason, it is said that 'merit is not received. The meaning is as follows:
since there is the retribution of outflowing dharmas (*sāsrava*), one should not receive the retribution of non-outflowing dharmas (*anāsrava*). Although it is received, [it is not clung to]."

Because of grasping and attachment, one attains the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*). Therefore it is said: "The merit and virtue performed by a Bodhisattva should not be greedily attached to.
Master Zhiyi of Tiantai composed a verse stating: "The marks of conditioned giving are swallowed back up after three lifetimes;

Though one practices much wisdom with the seven treasures, how could one know to abandon the six sense faculties? Only by leaving behind all worldly desires can one turn away and cast off the bonds of affection and gratitude. If one attains..."
Free from the characteristics of greed, one should reach the gate of the Dharma King.
Those who possess seeking and suffering are tormented by the eight winds and the five desires; those without attachment or greed attain mastery through the three insights and six supernormal powers.
If you go thus, by the waterside and beneath the forest trees, the moon is cold and the wind is clear. If you do not go thus, the bridge is broken and the road ends;
there must be another way to communicate this message. Do you understand?

"Those who seek existence suffer" refers to the passage in the Sūtra concerning those who take the seven treasures, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and offer them in alms, seeking only the retribution of merit.
Although they obtain this retribution of merit, when it is exhausted, they return once more to the three miserable realms; thus, they suffer.

Furthermore, in the present life, being tormented by the mutual friction of the eight winds and the five desires is also suffering. As for the "eight winds," these are gain and loss... [and so forth].

Defamation, praise, fame, insignificance, suffering, and pleasure—these are the eight winds (*aṣṭau vāyavaḥ*). As for the five desires (*pañca-kāma*), they are wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep; these are called the five objects of craving.
Because one is tormented and oppressed by the intersection of these eight winds and five desires, one is submerged in ignorance through attachment and wanders aimlessly in the pursuit of gain.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are nine ways of stealing with a thieving mind: first, taking while feigning a pitiable appearance; second, manifesting... [text continues].
1. Taking by means of deportment; 2. Taking by feigning illness; 3. Taking by claiming to be a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); 4. Taking by subduing others through the Dharma;
5. Taking by devising clever schemes; 6. Taking by lending money at interest; 7. Taking by gentle speech; 8. Taking by force when not given; 9.
Taking back what was already given—all these constitute the intent of theft and will inevitably lead one into the three miserable realms. Is this not so?
"Suffering. Regarding "being without attachment and without craving," this refers back to the sutra:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who knows that all phenomena are without self and attains patience (*kṣānti*), then even when performing deeds that result in outflow-free (*anāsrava*) retribution, they do not crave or cling to them; therefore, they attain the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*)."
Thus, by not clinging to signs, one attains the three明 (vidyās) and the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), is no longer bound by birth and death, and achieves great sovereignty.
The Buddha told Siṃhavikrīḍita: "Clinging to the characteristics of phenomena gives rise to delusion (moha). Because of delusion, craving (tṛṣṇā) arises. Because of craving, there is bondage.
Because of bondage, there is birth. Because of birth, there is death. Because of death, there is impermanence (anityatā). Not to cling..."
One who is free from signs does not give rise to delusion. Because delusion does not arise, there is no craving.
Because there is no craving, there is no bondage. Because there is no bondage, one does not undergo birth. Because one does not undergo birth, there is no death.
Because there is no death, it is called the true permanence of *nirvāṇa*. Is this not, then, the mastery of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*)?

As for the three knowledges: first is the knowledge of the clarity of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-jñāna-vidyā*). The Buddhas of the Three Vehicles attain that divine eye regarding the superior and wondrous realms of the heavens.
Second is the knowledge of the clarity of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-vidyā*). Regarding the objects of the three periods of time, the Buddha has no...

It is not known. This is not the same as that of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Third is the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-vidyā*). At the time of realizing the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), one is far removed from the four outflows;

this is not the same as what is realized by the two vehicles. Regarding the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first is the power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*), which shakes and vibrates the ten directions.

Transforming one into many and transforming many into one, and so forth—this is the supernormal power of mastery over the body (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*). Second is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*):
surpassing the ears of humans and devas, one is able to hear various sounds as they truly are. Third is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*):

being able to know the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions. Fourth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*): being able to know [the ten... of past existences.
The fifth is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), which can perceive all sentient and non-sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
as well as their physical forms, births, deaths, and the retributions of their good and evil deeds.

The sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), which can know whether the outflows of all sentient beings, both oneself and others, have been exhausted or not.
Therefore it is said: "The three knowledges and six supernormal powers are mastery. To "go thus" means to manifest this aforementioned meaning.
To go thus in a state free from attachment and craving, one then dwells with ease and mastery by the waters and beneath the trees.
When the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages are forgotten, one must not dwell in attachment; this is the realm of the unconditioned and the non-active. It may be said:
one roams at ease while beholding the moonlight, and dwells in spontaneity while listening to the sound of the spring. Therefore, the Buddha’s compassion says:

"The method of Zen meditation has nothing particularly marvelous about it; it simply requires that the life-root be severed, that doubts be suddenly cast off, and that all external conditions be set aside."
It is intensely brilliant; it has been pierced through in every direction, settled with a thousand certainties.

One nurtures the holy embryo by the waterside and beneath the forest trees, and only then emerges into the world to benefit sentient beings—yet this is still merely the matter of establishing the mysterious gate of transformation.
To not proceed in this manner is the hand-eye of the Master of the Teaching; it is a separate path, one that is without attachment and without craving.
This is the locus. To go further than this, it is said: "Do not proceed in such a manner. Do not abide in the realm of non-action;
this is called the "Path Beyond," which not even a thousand sages have traveled. Thus, the bridge is broken and the road ends, allowing no further treading upon it.
A bridge is a means for crossing rivers and streams; a road is a path for entering a royal city.
By analogy, this illustrates the methods for advancing on the Way within the Teachings. There are the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of perfect enlightenment, one begins with the five grades of contemplative practice, the three types of provisions, and the four stages of preparatory application, each of which has its own commonality.
"Path" (tu) refers to the bridges and causeways for crossing over. "Way" (lu) refers to the fifty-five stages; it is the true path of Bodhi.

The intention of the present section is this: if one does not proceed in such a manner, it is because this principle is originally and spontaneously perfected, not something attained through cultivation.

Therefore, one does not employ these practices of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*), nor does one traverse this path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*). Thus, the bridge is broken and the road comes to an end.
As for those who communicate the message through a different way: this principle is not borrowed from the thousand sages, nor is it sought among the myriad activities.
It does not increase in the sage, nor does it decrease in the ordinary person; it simply requires the practitioner, during walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, to emerge [from delusion].
It does not follow accordingly; it enters but does not dwell in emptiness. Outwardly it does not seek branches; inwardly it does not abide in concentration.
It casts off the golden lock and breaks through the profound barrier. Do you understand this? This is the meaning of the master’s inquiry:
"Do you still know what I have said up to now? The following text provides the response.
"The old monk laughs and points to where the monkeys cry; there is yet more of the sacred traces above.
These two lines respond to the previous statement that "the bridge is broken and the road ends," conveying the meaning of communicating a separate message. This refers to this principle.

Since this has been spontaneously perfected from the very beginning, it does not depend upon cultivation or realization. Therefore, when the bridge is broken and the road reaches its end, one transcends all expedient means;
there is another, extraordinary dimension. Now, those who are essential to the school must, at the intersection of person and environment, attain realization at the place where the monkey cries.
If one can, while hearing sounds and seeing forms, remain undeluded in the present moment, one turns back to hear one's own nature.
Nature. When one turns back to perceive the True Principle, the true mind is revealed within sound and form.
Thus it is said: "There is yet another spiritual trace above. Therefore Yongming said: "The solitary monkey’s cry drops the mid-autumn moon;
the wild guest’s chant exhausts the midnight lamp. Who can understand this realm at this moment? The monk sitting in meditation deep within the white clouds."
Countless lines of Brahmi script, wild geese in the clouds; A single melody of non-arising, a zither at the bottom of the stream.
Virtue surpasses the sands of the Ganges, so there is no need for them at all; The pure wind and bright moon are the true connoisseurs.
The first two lines are the Master’s explicit revelation of the True Sutra of the Wordless, which does not fall into ink or paper; therefore, he says "countless."

The characters of the Brahmī script proceed like wild geese in the clouds, arrayed in order across the void without any deliberate effort; this serves as a metaphor for the perfectly interfused realm of the Mahāyāna.
As clouds drift and birds fly, and as dust speaks and lands speak, there is nothing that does not proclaim and expound this sutra.
It may be said that the wind-swept branches and moonlit shores everywhere expound *tathatā*, while the misty clouds and forest groves all proclaim the wondrous Dharma.

Furthermore, a single melody of non-arising is like the sound of mountain stream water, all of which serves as the resonance of the zither; the flowing water and the swaying wind both perform the *Mahā*.
The white clouds form a canopy and the cascading springs act as the zither. Regarding the final two lines, the commentator’s intention is as follows:
