Regarding this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, if there is anyone who receives, upholds, reads, recites, and explains it to others, even by means of the merit of four lines alone, it surpasses the merit of bestowing jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If one uses the True Sutra of No-Letters and the Song of Non-Arising, then clouds and birds soar, waters flow and winds move; both sentient and insentient beings are all [enlightened].
They perform together. Thus, although the merit of upholding [the teachings] may be superior, within the principle of this *dharmadhātu*, it is entirely irrelevant.
Only the pure breeze and the bright moon are those who truly understand; they are the ones who hear the Dharma preached by the insentient.
The lute’s melody of non-arising is finally fit to be heard and received by those who appreciate the true sound.
Spring comes and autumn goes; when will they ever cease? It is a pity that sentient beings have turned white-haired once more.
Among the outskirts of Dongkuo lie many ancient tombs; beneath Mount Beimang lies a skull.
The first two lines lament that time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow or a weaving shuttle; with spring departing and autumn arriving, it hastens people toward old age.
Thus it is said: "Alas, sentient beings have turned white-haired again. Master Ciming said: "Yesterday one was an infant; today one is already old.
This floating life is but a dream-like illusory body; human life is difficult to preserve for long. Heaven and...

Hell is entirely created by the mind. The pines on the northern ridges of the Southern Mountains, and the grasses on the southern slopes of the Northern Ridges— a single rain moistens them boundlessly, yet the roots and sprouts are either robust or withered. Those who travel for study across the Five Lakes merely ask the void for answers.
In death they cast off their summer shirts; in life they don their winter coats. Clearly, those who are without affairs unnecessarily give rise to affliction.
The final two lines lament death. Those who have descendants have new or ancient graves; those without descendants are corpses abandoned in the wild.
Master Qí of the Brahma Heaven said: "Riches are but days without poverty; greed is but years of seeking wealth.
Since antiquity, men have become ghosts, vainly using paper as money. White bones lie deep beneath the mud; green moss covers the ancient tombs."
The void may yet be measured, but the limits of birth and death cannot be known.
Your literary brilliance, White Attendant, is rare in this world; yet you still seek Tuṣita and loathe saṃsāra.
I now exhort you, O scholar of letters: mind the Buddha of the West and return!

The first two lines cite an ancient precedent as an illustration. The Court Gentleman (Shilang) was surnamed Bái and named Jǔyí; he was a man of the Tang dynasty who was ennobled as the Minister of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè).

He was skilled in literary composition and, in his later years, turned toward Buddhism. He donated his residence to establish Xiangshan Temple and styled himself the Layman of Xiangshan (Xiāngshān Jūshì).
For months at a time, he abstained from eating pungent vegetables or meat. He once composed a hymn of praise which says: "In the worlds of the ten directions..."
"Throughout the realms, above and below, I now know them all; there is none like the Buddha. Sublime and majestic, he is the Teacher of Gods and Men;
therefore, I prostrate at his feet, praising him and taking refuge in him. Consequently, in the first year of the Huichang era, a merchant ship encountered a storm and was driven to a great mountain.
There, a Daoist said: "This is one courtyard of Mount Penglai; here are the locks and keys."
[The monk] replied, "It is very firm. This is where Bai Juyi (Bai Letian) once resided; it has simply not yet reached China.
When Bai Juyi heard this, he composed a poem, saying: "I study the True Void, not the path of immortals; I fear these words of yours are but empty rumors.
The seas and mountains are not my place of return; If I must return, I shall return to Tuṣita Heaven. He once made a vow, saying: "I shall exhort one..."
One hundred and eight people shared a single aspiration and formed an assembly for rebirth in the upper realms.

They practiced the recitation of Maitreya’s name and sat in meditation upon his countenance, vowing that they would surely be born in Tuṣita in a future life. In his later years, he suffered from wind-stroke and paralysis;
he then relinquished three hundred thousand in salary and emoluments to commission the artisan Du Zongjing to paint a depiction of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, nine feet in height.
The painting was three feet wide and one zhang long. In the center was Amitābha, with Avalokiteśvara to his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to his right.
Humans and devas gazed up in reverence as they were surrounded by their retinues. Flowers, birds, ponds, and trees were adorned with sandalwood.
The disciple Juyi burned incense, prostrated himself, and knelt before the Buddha, making this vow: "May the merit of these prostrations and recitations be dedicated to all sentient beings. I.
May all sentient beings who are like me—old or sick—be freed from suffering and attain happiness;
may they sever evil and cultivate goodness, and according to their vows, be reborn upon the blue lotus flowers. He spoke again in verse:
"In the Pure Land of the World of Ultimate Bliss, There are no evil realms nor any manifold sufferings. I vow that those like my own self, old and sick, Shall together be born in Amitābha’s land."
He immediately manifested his transformation before the presence of the Buddha of Longevity (Amitāyus). Thus it is said: "He even sought Tuṣita Heaven out of weariness with saṃsāra.

The latter two lines are the commentator’s citation of an example to exhort the literary men of today to all emulate Bai Shilang, wearying of the world and reciting the Buddha’s name, so that they may together return to the Western Pure Land.

Dignified deportment is tranquil. This is the path of the mind within the stupa. There is no need for clever analysis or explanation. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, it is inexhaustible and leaves nothing remaining.
This section was identified by Prince Zhaoming as the "Section on Dignified Deportment and Tranquility. Thus it is said.
Dignified deportment refers to the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; within these four modes of deportment, one is the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Quiescence refers to the Buddha’s dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); for the Tathāgata’s dharma-body comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
Therefore, this name was established. Regarding the phrase "the tower measures the path of the mind," this explains the meaning presented above.
Alternatively, one suspects that the two characters "tǎ zhàng" (塔丈) may be a scribal error; they should instead be read as "hé zhàng" (曷仗). However, there are those who harbor doubts, asking:

if the Tathāgata did not accept karmic rewards while formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, how could he possess the characteristics of coming and going upon reaching the fruit [of Buddhahood], thereby causing sentient beings...
To give offerings upon birth and thereby obtain merit—such doubts are precisely the conceptual discriminations of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, the Buddha told him: "The majestic deportment of the Tathāgata employs manifest activity, yet the essence of the Dharma-body is suchness, unmoving;
hence it is called 'quiescent' (*śānta*). This is because the Tathāgata’s body of Dharma and response manifests and conceals itself to save sentient beings; it is not...
The noble ones of the Three Vehicles cannot fathom it; thus it is said: "How can one rely on the path of the mind?
It may be called a state beyond deliberation, difficult for consciousness and emotion to measure. Within the *tathatā* and *dharmadhātu*, there is neither self nor other.
There is no need for clever analysis or explanation, for the principle of the *dharmakāya* resides within every deportment; how could one rely on the path of the mind to measure it? One need not.

Because one discriminates the characteristics of coming and going, it is said: "There is no need for skillful analysis or argumentation. Regarding "walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—without end and without remainder":
this explains the deportments (īryāpatha) below by means of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. "Without end and without remainder" means...

This explains the aforementioned "quiescence. Since the principle of the Dharmakāya does not rely upon the conceptual paths of the mind, it is neither deficient nor redundant throughout the four modes of deportment.
It may be said: "Sent forth, it is as vast as space and cannot be contained; drawn back, not even a hair’s breadth of trace is seen.
The infinite wondrous functions and supernormal powers are all present within ordinary daily activities."
It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere. If one can realize this, there is no need for any effort at all.
Regarding that which "comes from nowhere and goes nowhere," in this section the Buddha addresses Subhūti:
"If anyone says that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught."
Why is this? One who comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is therefore called a Tathāgata.
This clarifies that the Dharmakāya has no marks of coming or going. If a person can realize this, it summarizes all the preceding discourse.
If one is a practitioner who realizes that the Dharmakāya neither goes nor comes, it is simply present within one's deportment.
It is manifested within both movement and stillness; in truth, it is effortless. One might say: "The mountain named 'Stone' is truly effortless;
to seek water apart from the waves is indeed difficult. For there is no Dharma-body outside the form-body, and no form-body outside the Dharma-body.
Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma."
Therefore it is said: "Not expending any effort at all.
Everyone possesses the four great elements; I see that the myriad dharmas are empty. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, Coming and going are identical with the Real.

The first phrase clarifies that all sentient beings possess individual physical forms composed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and formed through the provisional conjunction of the five aggregates: sensation, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and form.

Because these four great elements are nominally identical to those of the Tathāgata’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which possesses the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, it is said: "Every person is endowed with the four great elements. The second phrase clarifies...
Although the Tathāgata possesses the four great elements and engages in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, his application [of these] differs from that of sentient beings;
therefore it is said: "I see that all phenomena are empty. Here, "I see" carries the sense of attachment, for that which is able to see is taken to be the self.
That which is seen consists of the myriad dharmas. Since the "self" that sees them does not exist, the myriad dharmas seen are themselves empty.

When both person and dharmas are empty, the Dharma-body is quiescent. The final two lines clarify that since the Tathāgata has realized that all dharmas are empty and has realized the principle of the Dharma-body, although he possesses the marks and signs of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), these appear solely for the sake of delivering sentient beings; therefore, regarding...
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—amidst these four modes of deportment—and whether coming or going, there is nothing that does not accord with the Real.

If one clarifies this principle and penetrates its source, one will then know that in movement and stillness, in all actions, and in walking, pacing, sitting, and reclining, every single instance accords with the Way and every thought returns to the Source.
Where, then, is there anything that is not the equal, singular Dharma-realm of True Reality? Thus it is said: "Coming..."
Going is identical with reality.
○ Chapter Twenty-nine: The Stillness of Dignified Bearing.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if someone were to say... (up to) ...he is called the Tathāgata because there is nowhere to go.
The commentary states: In this section, the Buddha summons and addresses Subhūti. The three instances where he is called "Tathāgata" all manifest the Buddha who is the true nature of the Dharmakāya.

When the Buddha says, "If anyone speaks of a Tathāgata as coming or going, sitting or reclining, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught," the intent is to say that if one regards [the Buddha] in terms of coming, going, sitting, or...
To say that walking and sitting constitute the Dharma-body is to remain within the realm of signs; therefore, one does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.

For the true Buddha is signless, eternally abiding in quiescent extinction, fundamentally devoid of coming and going or movement and stillness, such that he cannot be characterized by walking or sitting.
That the Buddha currently appears to come, go, sit, and lie down is the Nirmāṇakāya (Rūpakāya) of the Tathāgata; it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Therefore, Maitreya said: "This is the retribution of merit; for the sake of transforming all sentient beings, such karma manifests spontaneously.
Thus do the Buddhas appear throughout the ten directions. Why is this so? The Buddha asks himself this question: why is it not... [as before]...?
"Do you understand the meaning of what I have said? He then answered himself: "What I call the Tathāgata is the true Buddha of the *dharmatā*.
Since the true Buddha is without marks, it neither comes nor goes; the *dharmakāya* is omnipresent and remains eternally unmoving. As a verse says:
'The *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas come and go, yet the *tathatā* is always unmoving. Therefore, there is nowhere from which it comes."
There is nowhere from which he comes; therefore, he is named Tathāgata. The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Tathatā" means that there is one and no second, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty. "Tathāgata" is the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena. Because phenomena are empty, there is neither coming nor going.
The Zen Master Zhiyi composed a verse: "From where does the Tathāgata come? [The text continues with the practice of cultivation.]

Through the merit of many kalpas, one severs the view of self and person; only then does one penetrate the True Doctrine. Seeing forms yet not seeking after them, the body is empty and phenomena are likewise empty.
Coming and going without attachment, all arrivals and departures are entirely unimpeded.
Whether sitting, reclining, or walking, [the body] is fundamentally without coming or going; its majestic deportment is unmoving, tranquil, neither still nor wavering.

This first section of the text restates the meaning of the sutra. Although the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) of the Tathāgata manifests the appearance of coming and going for the sake of transforming sentient beings, his *dharmakāya* (dharma-body) is unconditioned and fundamentally has no coming or going. Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "The understanding is ultimate."

The "meeting" (hui) is such that its substance has no fixed location; this clarity is the response (ying) of the Real (zhen). Arising from the realm of reality, the moon in the water suddenly appears; this clarity is the response of the Real.
The subsequent section of the text likewise restates the meaning of the scripture. "Dignified demeanor" (wei-yi) reveals the Response Body (yingshen);
whether coming or going, sitting or reclining, these belong to the conventional truth (sudi). "Immovable" reveals the Dharma [Body].
The body comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which is quiescent, neither moving nor shaking, simultaneously negates the two extremes and reveals the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
"Do you understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught?

This single phrase is the point where the master exerts his effort for the sake of others; he carefully questions the practitioner to ascertain whether they understand the profound meaning of the Buddha's teachings.
The following passage provides the answer:
"Responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings without exception, yet ever remaining upon this seat of Bodhi.
These two lines answer the meaning of the preceding question. This text is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, specifically the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata’s Signs."
The Bodhisattva Sarvarutasāgaravatī spoke in verse: “The Buddha’s body fills the entire Dharma-realm, Appearing universally before all Tathāgatas.
Responding to conditions and meeting with those who seek him, there is nowhere he does not reach, Yet he ever remains upon this seat of enlightenment.”
The Master [Zongmi] borrows the latter two lines to reveal that the Tathāgata’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with conditions and responds to stimuli, reaching everywhere without exception;
yet his dharma-body remains quiescent, never leaving its original seat. This may be described as "occupying a single seat while manifesting throughout the ten directions."
He manifests a single sound that is heard simultaneously throughout all lands of the dust motes.
Majestic and immovable, King of the Dharma— how could there be a monkey leaping through six windows?
Laughing, he points to the true void which has no face; pushing the clouds away, he lets the moon descend upon a thousand rivers.
The first two lines summarize the meaning of the sutra. To clarify that the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere is to manifest that the Dharmakāya is immovable;
it does not follow after the sense organs and their objects, and thus it is likened to a monkey that does not leap through the six windows.
Now, regarding the "King within the Dharma," the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The Dharmakāya is the essence itself, possessing the great light of wisdom."
Luminosity. It universally illumines the Dharma-realm; it is true and authentic cognition, the intrinsically pure mind.
It is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is cool, unchanging, sovereign, and immovable. This luminosity is the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, which attains great mastery among all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the King of Dharmas. If a practitioner awakens to this principle, light will radiate from the gates of the six sense faculties.
The earth shakes, yet the monkey remains at ease; the six windows are silent and still. The latter two lines directly point out:
the Dharma-body is formless, and the ultimate principle is shapeless. What face or features could there be? An ancient worthy said: "Throughout the entire body, there is no front or back."
Pervading the entire realm, it leaves no trace of form. At the very end of the *Kejia* (Kegong), he exerted all his strength to uphold [the truth];

thus, like pushing the moon through the clouds, it descends simultaneously upon a thousand rivers. Object and wisdom are undivided; person and dharma are one body. It may be said: "The primordial chaos has neither interior nor exterior."
Harmony blends above and below in tranquility.
Amidst the shadows of reeds lies a single skull, half-reclining on yellow sand and half-buried in a mound of earth.
The skull alone possesses the breath of the heart; when will the struggle for fame and profit ever cease?
The first two lines lament that when people die, their corpses are sent to the outskirts;

their skulls lie scattered across the ground, scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind, left in a state of chaotic filth and loathsomeness, so hideous as to be unfit for sight. All people throughout the great earth are exactly like this.
It is said: "In the past, that which was required to be laughed at—the red countenance—has turned into ashes; today, the white bones in this desolate garden have become mere mounds of mud.

The final two lines lament this skull: "Today it is thus scattered and decayed; yet in years past, when those three inches of breath remained, one relied on one's own arrogance and strength, contending for fame and seizing profit without rest.
Danxia [first... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "丹霞先" (Danxia first...), leaving the full context of the master's teaching incomplete.)
A poem on birth says: Seeking the realm beyond smoke and clouds for oneself— Why need one pridefully dwell in a small boat at the Valley’s Mouth?
Where now lie the altars of the Three Sovereigns? The mountains and rivers of the Five Emperors are all but exhausted. Countless heroes and geniuses are buried in earthen tombs.
How many men of letters and arms lie now in desolate mounds! During their lives they did nothing but struggle for fame and profit, never once turning back to practice the Way in their youth.
How bitter it was during the end of the Han and the remnants of the Tang! The hearts of men, high and low, were utterly at odds.
"Greed and hypocrisy are beyond description; this chaotic age is like tangled hemp—return, return!

These four lines constitute the Master’s lament for the degeneracy of the times and the perversity of human hearts. When he speaks of "the end of the Han," he refers to the three kingdoms of Wu, Wei, and Shu.
Subsequently, there were the Five Barbarians and the Sixteen Kingdoms, each ruling as a sovereign king. [The text ends with] "remnants..."
As for the Tang dynasty, there were ten states and ten kings, all of whom were usurpers and pretenders. To say now, "How bitter it is!"—alas!
The times are a world of decadence, and the people are a breed of the frivolous and shallow; they are what is called greedy and hypocritical.
It is beyond description; these are the words of the Patriarch’s poignant lament, and thus he deeply sighs over them.

The final phrase, "The world in chaos is like hemp," means that when those who lead are numerous, disorder ensues. Weapons and strife cover the earth; men cease their plowing and hoeing, and women cease their weaving at the looms.
Of the people throughout the land, eight or nine out of ten perish. An ancient poem says: "In an age of chaos and military desolation, slaughter..."
The atmosphere was turbulent. A beautiful woman entered the palace gate carrying her child. It would not have troubled the hand of a warrior brandishing his halberd;

it was simply that she did not betray the bond of a man’s sworn oath. Where are those jade-like features and flower-bright faces now? Only their physical remains and traces of blood remain to this day.
I have come moved by the events of a former dynasty, to mourn the spirit of this heroine of Hechuan. Return, O returner! (End of) Kejia.

The intention is this: since the world is as chaotic as tangled hemp, it is better to recite the Buddha’s name and return home. Depart early from this defiled land and proceed directly to the Pure Land.
Even for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds, one should exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name at the time of their death.
Relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, one is born in the lower grade; within the lotus flower, one experiences bliss as if in a celestial palace. Therefore, we urge one another:
in this age of chaos, which is like hemp in abundance, come, let us return!

The principle of the "unified mark" (yīhéxiàng) does not reside in conceptual discrimination; it may be proclaimed freely in every place. For nine years he faced the wall, cutting through all obstacles like driving a nail or severing iron.
This section was designated by Prince Zhaoming as the "Section on the Principle of the Unified Mark," based upon this passage of the sutra.

Subhūti replied to the Buddha: "If these atoms were truly existent, and if the world were truly existent"—these two sections of the text reveal that both the elements and the atoms lack intrinsic nature.

By using this as an analogy for the Dharma, it shows that there is no nature of either identity or difference, thereby manifesting the principle of the perfect fusion of the single integrated mark. Therefore, this name is established. It does not reside in discrimination.
As stated above, regarding the principle of the "unified aggregate" (*piṇḍagraha*), the identity or difference between atoms and the world cannot be distinguished.
Therefore, Subhūti replied: "It is not atoms, it is not the world, and that which is not an unified aggregate is called an 'unified aggregate.

This is because the principle of the unified aggregate is to be eliminated; thus, he said, "it does not reside in conceptual discrimination. Regarding the phrase "expounding freely in all places," it is because...

The principle of the unified totality (yīhéxiàng) is beyond verbal expression. Within the realm of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), however, there are differentiated verbal explanations for the sake of transforming sentient beings;
therefore, it is proclaimed freely in various places. As for the passage concerning "facing the wall for nine years," this is one section [of that teaching].

The commentary concludes the preceding text. It does not dwell on conceptual discrimination. It states that Bodhidharma’s nine years of facing the wall were profoundly unconventional and did not conform to worldly sentiments;
they did not involve verbal explanations, but solely clarified true nature and directly manifested the primary truth (paramārtha-satya).

Truly possessing the means to cut through nails and sever iron, he revealed it clearly at the moment the flower blossomed after the three prostrations before the divine light: "The scale-weight was originally iron."
This section presents the meaning of non-discrimination mentioned previously. Long ago, the First Patriarch Bodhidharma sat facing a wall at Shaolin.
One day he said to his disciples, "The time has come; I wish to return to India. Each of you should speak of what you have attained.
At that time, Dao Fu said, "As I see it, I do not cling to the marks of words, nor am I separate from them."
The nun Zixiang said, "I take these written characters as the function of the Way. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my skin.
The nun Zongchi said, "As I see it, it is like Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; having seen it once, there is no further need for seeing. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist; yet, in my place of vision—"
"There is not a single dharma that can be attained. The Patriarch said, "You have attained my bones. Huike prostrated and stood in his place.
The Patriarch said, "You have attained my marrow. He spoke again: "In the past, the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the Wondrous Mind of Nirvāṇa were entrusted to Kāśyapa.
It was passed down in succession until it reached me; now I entrust it to you. He recited this verse: "I have come from the West..."
In this land, the Dharma was transmitted to deliver those of deluded minds. One flower blooms and five petals unfold; the fruiting occurs spontaneously.
Now, regarding the words of the patriarch: when Shen Guang made three prostrations, he grasped the meaning beyond words.

This was precisely the seasonal cause and condition, identical and no different from the principle of the "single unified mark. To clearly point this out: at this juncture, [the text] presents the previous case of Bodhidharma.
Facing the wall, Shen Guang performed three prostrations; the unspeakable Way was clearly revealed. It is just like a scale-weight:
it turns out to be iron after all.
The motes of dust throughout the three thousandfold world system all come together within a single thought-moment—the Tathāgata’s mark of total integration.

The first two phrases, "toppling the great void," recapitulate the meaning of the sutra. The phrase "with the atoms of the three thousandfold world-system" cites the atoms of the world-system as the illustrative analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), while simultaneously indicating the phenomena to which they correspond (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Changshui states that both the atoms of the world-system and the corresponding phenomena are all my own.
The objects of the Dharma are the spheres of perception; these spheres do not exist apart from the single thought-moment of the perceiving mind.
Therefore, the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only; thus it is said that they both arise within the single thought-moment of the mind.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s “single unified mark,” these two phrases also restate the meaning of the sutra to conclude by returning to the principle of perfect interfusion and non-duality. Since it has been said:
The principle of the unified totality (*ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa*) is precisely this: not seeing empty space, but seeing only True Suchness (*tathatā*).
That is to say, apart from the true mind, not a single thing can be found; therefore, it is said that one "pushes over the vast void."
Chapter Thirty: The Principle of the Unified Mark.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family... [as above] ...Subhūti said: "It is very much so, World-Honored One."

The commentary states: Regarding the meaning of this section, because within the preceding twenty-nine sections it was shown that the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has coming and going—which is "different"—while the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) has no coming or going—which is "one"—the Buddha feared that Subhūti might hold a view of difference and identity.
Therefore, within this section, a metaphor is established to pose a question. First, the identity and difference of the world’s subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are raised to sever doubts;
next, the self and dharmas as expressed in speech are raised to demonstrate their freedom from [dualistic] views. Now, to explain the text of the first [section], there are three general divisions:

first, the identity and difference of the atoms of the constituent realms (*dhātu*) are treated to reveal the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); second, the subtle atom is explained as a metaphor for the fact that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has no distinct nature; third...
This explains the world-system (*loka-dhātu*). By means of this metaphor, it is shown that the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) possesses no single inherent nature (*eka-svabhāva*).
First, the realm of dust is presented as a metaphor; thus the Buddha asked: "If the three thousandfold world-system were ground into atoms, would this multitude of atoms be considered many?

This metaphor regarding the identity and difference between the world and its constituent dust serves to reveal the absence of intrinsic nature. Here, the term "world-system" is used as a metaphor for the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, "dust particles" (paramāṇu) are a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). The world is unity; the dust particles are multiplicity.

To crush the world into dust is to show that the world has no single nature; this is used as a metaphor for how the *nirmāṇakāya* arises from the *dharmakāya*, wherein the *dharmakāya* has no single nature—thus, multiplicity breaks through unity.

To aggregate dust particles into a world is to show that the dust particles have no distinct nature; this is used as a metaphor for the emptiness of the *nirmāṇakāya*, wherein both the *dharmakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* are non-existent.
"Different" refers precisely to the refutation of difference. This mutual refutation serves to negate both extremes and reveal the Middle Way; that is, it is neither one nor different.
Thus the verse says: "The Transformation Buddhas come and go, while the Dharma-body is eternally unmoving.
Within this Dharmadhātu, they are neither one nor different."
[Sūtra]: "For what reason? If this multitude of atoms... [as far as] ...it is not a multitude of atoms; it is called a 'multitude of atoms'.

This section of the sūtra constitutes the second chapter, which explains the atom (*paramāṇu*) as a metaphor for the fact that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) has no distinct nature. Regarding the phrase "For what reason":
it interrogates the meaning of the previously mentioned "vast multitude of atoms. If this multitude of atoms were substantially existent, [it would follow that they are not truly atoms].
The Buddha does not speak of this multitude of atoms. This statement that "the Buddha does not speak" intends to reveal that the substance of the atoms is fundamentally empty;

thus, they are used as a metaphor for the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body) of the Tathāgata. Although it is fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), its substance is in reality not the ultimate truth.
Therefore, the verse says: "The transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the one who preaches the Dharma. Why is this so?

This explains the preceding passage concerning the "dust of the realms. When the Buddha speaks of a "multitude of subtle dust particles," he is reiterating his previous statement that [the world] is broken down into subtle dust particles.
If one knows that the world is broken to form subtle dust particles, yet those subtle dust particles are entirely the world, then the dust has no real nature;
therefore, it is said, "it is not subtle dust. This is because one speaks of "subtle dust" only by departing from the attachment to intrinsic nature.
He said: "This is called a minute particle.
[Sūtra] World-Honored One, that which the Tathāgata has spoken of as a trichiliocosm—up to—"is not a world; it is merely named a world."
Regarding the meaning of this section of the sutra: the phrase "the trichiliocosm spoken of by the Tathāgata" refers back to the previously mentioned trichiliocosm.
If one understands that the combination of particles constitutes the world, and that the world is entirely composed of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), then the world has no substantial nature.
Therefore, it is said: "it is not a world. This is because the world is spoken of only by way of departing from the attachment to its inherent nature. Thus it is said.
It is said: This is called the "world" (*dhātu*). Thus, there are no separate dust-motes; the entire world constitutes a dust-mote.
By this analogy, there should be no separate "response" (*nirmāṇa*); the entirety of phenomena arises as the response. There is no separate world; the accumulation of dust-motes forms the world.
By this analogy, there are no separate phenomena; the entire response is itself the phenomenon. This is the simultaneous illumination that reveals the Middle Way.
[Sūtra] For what reason? If the world were a real entity... [up to] ...it is not a unified whole; it is called a unified whole.
The meaning of this section of the sūtra constitutes the third topic: explaining the world by means of the metaphor of the Dharma-body, which possesses no single nature.
The phrase "For what reason? interrogates the preceding world. If the world were truly existent, it would be a "unified totality" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*).

By using this principle of unified totality to conversely reveal that the world is not truly existent, we know that the principle of unified totality is precisely the principle of the harmonious interpenetration and non-obstruction of the dharmas of the realms and sense-fields. Thus, the verse says:

"The world is reduced to atoms"—this metaphor illustrates that meaning. When the Tathāgata speaks of a "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the fact that all phenomena, such as the elements and atoms, are fully endowed with names and characteristics;
this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). That which is not a unified whole is [the ultimate truth].
By means of the dharmas of the realms and sense-objects, although names and characteristics are fully present, their nature is fundamentally empty; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which is called the "unified whole" (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) is the Dharmakāya, which is able to be both one and different, yet neither one nor different—a perfect fusion without obstruction.
This is precisely the Middle Truth.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, that which is a "unified whole" (ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa)—up to—"is merely the object of attachment for ordinary persons. The meaning of this passage of the Sūtra is as follows:
regarding the principle of the unified whole, it is said to be "inexpressible. The intended sense is that if one speaks of the Dharmakāya—
It is one; yet fearing that the listener might definitively cling to it as being one, it cannot be so described.
If one were to say the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is different, the listener would then cling to it as being different, and thus it cannot be so described.

If one were to say the dharma-body (dharmakāya) is not one, the listener would again cling to it as being not one, and thus it cannot be so described. If one were to say the response-body is not different, yet the listener...
Furthermore, if one insists that they are not different, then it cannot be said [that they are identical]. This principle of a unified characteristic (*ekakalpa-lakṣaṇa*) is likewise inconceivable;
it is simply that ordinary beings do not understand it and thus give rise to craving and attachment themselves. Master Fu’s verse says: "What difference is there between the elements and the dust?
Retribution and response are likewise so. Neither cause nor effect—what comes after and what comes before? Within phenomena, they penetrate through."
In the ultimate principle, both are abandoned. To reach the path of non-arising, one must recognize the original source.
Even if the world were shattered into atoms as fine as dust, the Compassionate Honored One—skillful in the profound essentials—established provisional names to discourse upon the true nature.
Thus, the minds of ordinary beings are brought to an end of their greedy seeking.
The first section cites the meaning of the sutra to clarify that the Tathāgata established his teachings by expounding various dharmas for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
Fearing that these sentient beings might not yet fully comprehend the path of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), he employed various parables to make them easy to understand.
In this present sutra, the elements (*dhātu*) and sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are used as metaphors for the Dharma and its response; therefore, it is said to be "skillful. As for...

To form a realm (*dhātu*) by aggregating atoms (*paramāṇu*), and to reduce a realm back into atoms, serves as a metaphor for how the whole phenomenon (*dharma*) arises as the response (*yìng*), and how the whole response is itself the phenomenon.

This is most subtle and ingenious. Regarding the "profound essentials": this refers to the profound and wondrous comprehensive essentials. Indeed, this single metaphor encompasses eight meanings pertaining to both the mundane and the supramundane.
The metaphors of the realm and the atoms possess the qualities of being neither one nor different, yet capable of being one and capable of being different.

The four meanings—the dharmas themselves must likewise be neither identical nor different from the four meanings of being able to be identical and able to be different—these eight meanings are clarified by a single analogy.

Is this not indeed the profound and essential summary? The subsequent section also restates the meaning of the sūtra to clarify that among the teachings spoken by the Buddha over forty-nine years, there are the three vehicles and five teachings; when viewed through the lens of the True Eye, [it is as follows].
All of these are expedient means (*upāya*). They merely discuss the one vehicle’s true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the true limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhūtakoṭi*);

within this, to speak of "being able to be one" and "able to be different," or "neither one nor different," is entirely a matter of worldly conventions. Within true emptiness, [such distinctions do not exist].
None of these [scriptures] contain such a statement. Vimalakīrti said: "The Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories.
Even the Tathāgata’s body of dharma and response, which he causes all ordinary beings to know, is but a provisional designation established by skillful means;
in reality, it cannot be apprehended. How much less so my own ordinary physical body, consciousness, mind, and all other phenomena—how could these possibly be real? Therefore...
This causes the ordinary person’s mind of greedy attachment to naturally subside.

If you understand it in this way, you will return to the root and revert to the source, turning away from dust and uniting with awakening. If you do not understand it in this way, your compassion will be equal to that of all Buddhas.
"Pitiable are those who conjoin with sentient beings; none at all are like this.
This is the Master’s admonition and exhortation to practitioners. It constitutes the first section of the text, meaning that those who can understand it in this way—
The commentary says: Since the body of the Dharmakāya belongs to the realm of names and numbers, it is already unattainable;
how much more so my physical body, consciousness, mind, and all conditioned phenomena that are perceived? All these are immediately empty and false, and truly unattainable.

Therefore, they cause the minds of ordinary beings to cease their greedy seeking, so that they naturally return to the root and revert to the source, turning away from defilement and uniting with awakening. The next section of the text states:

Those who do not understand it in this way merely apply their intellectual emotions to the patriarchs’ words. One who would truly practice must not set foot in the realm of returning to the source, reverting to the origin, turning one's back on defilement, or merging with awakening.
Rather, one must enter the entanglements and extend a helping hand, blending with the light and sharing in the dust.
This is precisely like the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, who, upon first attaining perfect penetration, obtained two kinds of excellence: the first is that, above, he [unites] with all...
The Buddha. First, through the power of identical compassion, he descends to share the same sorrowful longing as sentient beings;
second, by entering the ten dharma realms and manifesting the thirty-two transformations, he preaches the Dharma to benefit living beings.
"If it is not at all like this"—this passage is the Master’s way of sweeping away both of the aforementioned methods simultaneously. He takes up both "like this" and "not like this" together.
Turning aside, he directly reveals the path of the sudden school (Tonjong) in which mind itself is the Way.
Therein, one sees no Buddhas above to be realized, nor sentient beings below to be saved; yet, he extends his response downward toward them.
"The Great Spirit raises his hand but a little, and he splits apart the ten million layers of Mount Hua.
These two lines answer the meaning of the previous statement, "Not at all like this," which refers to not abiding within the single true dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*).
The Buddhas and sentient beings are utterly non-existent. It is like the Great Spirit of Gigantic Power (Jùlíng) manifesting his great function to cleave apart Mount Huá and Mount È with an axe.
As for the term "Gigantic Power," he is the deity of Mount Tàihuá; "Gigantic Power" is his name.
Because his mother once possessed karmic conditions of defilement, she suffered punishment at the foot of this mountain. Gigantic Power desired to rescue her.
"My mother's transgressions are too great for my power to overcome. I have come from afar to the west of Mount Hua to pay respectful homage at the abode of Chan Master Guangzhao of Jingyue Peak.
I prostrate and inform you: My mother is currently suffering punishment on this mountain and has not yet emerged. I now wish to request the Master’s aid to save her.
The Master then wrote the character "Oṃ" and placed it upon the divine axe. Thereupon, he took the axe to the summit of the mountain and applied it.
With a single stroke of his axe, the mountain split asunder. Through the power of this *dhāraṇī* mantra, his mother was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After practicing the Way for three years, Juling attained transformation at the summit of Mount Hua, later becoming the Great Deity Vajrapāṇi.
Thus it is said: "He split open Mount Hua, which reaches to the color of the heavens, releasing forth the Yellow..."
The sound of the river reaching the sea;
a single lifetime’s existence gathered by none of the six sense bases. All phenomena of the past are beyond compare;
with a light stroke, the three thousand worlds are rent asunder, until even the waters of the Ganges flow backward.
The first two lines refer to a single lifetime; they speak of the *prajñā* of true emptiness.

"Not contained within the six" means that this principle cannot be subsumed by the six sense organs, the six sense objects, or the six consciousnesses—this is the meaning of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the phrase "from the myriad dharmas mentioned before," the commentator’s intention is that this *prajñā* of true emptiness is precisely what was previously...
In the second section, up to this thirtieth point, although immeasurable and profound dharmas have been explained through the *dhāraṇī* of letters, they cannot emerge from this sphere of practice;
they cannot be compared to it and thus fall short. Hence it is said they are "not its peers," which refers to the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The final two lines restate the meaning of the sūtra, lightly cleaving open [the truth] through the wondrous function of the *dharmakāya*.

[The text] breaks [the barriers]. When the trichiliocosm is shattered into fine dust, every particle of dust becomes the realm of Vairocana, and every phenomenon (*dharma*) is endowed with the eternally abiding true mind.
Therefore, phenomena and their responses are undivided, and the realms and particles are without obstruction; they all return to the principle of perfect interfusion and vastness.
As for the Yellow River’s waters flowing backward: since this involves shattering the world [into dust], it is already... [as above].
Dust. When dust accumulates, it forms a realm; this serves as a metaphor for the fact that the Dharma-body is itself the response-body, and the entire response-body is itself the Dharma-body.

Directly, one attains the state where the great earth sinks flat and empty space shatters to pieces. There is no dharma outside the mind, and only the true emptiness is revealed. Therefore, it is said: "The water flows backward."

He said, "The Yellow River has nine bends; its waters emerge from Kunlun. The monk asked again, "What is it like to be a person within that realm?
Shuang said, "The flowing water passes by without anyone looking back; one claps one's hands and gazes toward Fusang.
This is a case of citing an ancient master to point directly at you with the nine-bend Yellow River, clearly explaining the source of the water as it emerges from Kunlun.

"Lun. This metaphor represents the Great Compassion of the World-Honored One. Although he establishes various verbal teachings, skillful means, and parables—much like the nine bends of the Yellow River—the general intent points directly to the true source of Prajñā. It moistens the faculties and nourishes all things;
therefore, it does not involve a gradual journey, but reveals itself at the very center. The final two phrases are the Master’s lament: "Those who miss it are many," clarifying the world.
"Venerable One, although this is a clear and direct pointing to the true source of Prajñā and the Great Road of Chang'an, alas, sentient beings are unable to tread upon it;
it is as if they were losing their way with eyes wide open under the bright sun and blue sky."
"During the Eastern Jin, Master Huiyuan once formed a society; among the 'Retired Subjects' were Fang Zhu and other men of extraordinary talent.
Yuanming (Tao Qian) joined the assembly and was often addicted to wine; tonight, let us set aside our cups and return home.
These four lines are the master’s admonition for people to discern the illusory nature of the phenomenal world and together return to the Pure Land. (Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin...)
As for the Master: his name was Huìyuǎn. He was a native of Lóufán in Yànmén, which is present-day Dàizhōu in Héduōng. His surname was Jiǎ.
He was born during the Shízhào period. At the age of twenty-four, he listened to Dharma Master Dà'ān lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Having attained great enlightenment, in the ninth year of the Dàyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ, he arrived at Mount Lú. He struck the ground with his staff and said, "If there is a spring here, I shall stay.
As he raised the staff, water gushed forth following it. He subsequently took up residence there. At the place where he lived, there was a pond;

one day the water suddenly receded until it became level ground. Not long after, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain broke out, and heaven and earth were suddenly plunged into darkness. The mountain...
The river shook and trembled. After a long time, the darkness cleared. The ground on all four sides was level, plain, and pure, with no grass or trees at all.
On another day, as before, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain arose together. On the following day, they suddenly saw that the beams, rafters, and pillars had been completely hewn by axe and chisel;
they were already formed into their proper shapes and piled up in heaps. The Master and the Governor of Jiangdong submitted a memorial regarding this.

When the construction of the temple was completed, he requested the title "Donglin Temple" (East Forest Temple). The main hall was named "Divine Operation" (Shenyun), in which he enshrined an image of Amitābha.
He established the White Lotus Society and gathered eighteen great worthies together to jointly cultivate the Pure Land practices for thirty years.
Daoci did not descend from the mountain for the first eleven years. During this time, he beheld the sacred image three times, yet he did not let anyone know.
Later, on the evening of the last day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year, he arose from meditative concentration and suddenly saw Amitābha Buddha filling the void of space.
Within his circular halo were various transformation Buddhas, with Guanyin and Shizhi standing in attendance at his left and right. The Buddha said:
"By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you; seven days from now, you shall be born in my land.
Furthermore, he saw Buddhasena, Huichi, and Tanshun standing by the Buddha's side. He bowed forward to them and said, "The masters' aspirations were directed toward me;
why have you arrived so late? Once he knew the time had come, he said to his disciples, "When I first resided here..."
"Thirdly, I beheld the holy image; now I behold it once more. It is certain that I shall be born in the Pure Land.
On the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Leave my remains beneath the pine forest," and having finished speaking, he passed away.
During the Jin dynasty, there was Liu Chengzhi, styled Zhongsi and known as Yimin. A native of Pengcheng, he was a descendant of King Zhuang of Chu and was a man of profound [wisdom].

He was well-versed in the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi and had mastered the teachings of the hundred schools of thought. Orphaned at a young age, he served his mother with such filial piety that it became renowned.
Confident in his own aspirations, he did not seek to conform to the ways of the secular world. When he first donned the scholar’s robe, he served as a military aide (*cānjūn*).

Both Xiān Ān and Liú Yù admired his virtue and recommended him to higher office, yet he declined both offers with great resolve. By nature, he was fond of Buddhist principles; thus, he associated with Lèi Cìzōng, Zhōu Xùzhī, Zōng Bǐng, Zhāng Juàn, and Bì...
These individuals all came to Mount Lu together. Master Huiyuan said to them, "Now that you have come here, how could you not intend to journey to the Pure Land?
Chengzhi then carved the text of a vow into stone to record this event.

Subsequently, he established a separate meditation hall north of the West Grove Stream, where he cultivated the Way in tranquility and poverty, diligently studying profound principles while concurrently upholding the prohibitive precepts. This was the foundation of his school.
Zhang and the others all looked up to him with admiration and sighed in praise. He once sent a letter to Guanzhong to discuss the principles of the scriptures with Kumārajīva, Sengzhao, and Daoyang.
He composed the "Verses on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha" (*Nianfo Sanmei Shi*) to express his intent regarding exclusive recitation and seated meditation.

Less than half a year had passed when, while in a state of meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha’s light illuminating the earth, all turning the color of gold. Fifteen years later, while in the midst of mindfulness of the Buddha...
In the midst [of his meditation], he saw Amitābha Buddha. The light from his jade-like brow shone forth as he lowered his hand to comfort and welcome him.
Cheng said, "May the Tathāgata stroke my head and cover me with his robe. Instantly, the Buddha stroked his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him.
On another day, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he again saw people entering a pool of seven treasures, where lotuses were blue and white. His...
The water was deep and clear. A man appeared with a halo around his neck and the *svastika* symbol emerging from his chest. Pointing to the pond water, he said, "This is water of eight virtues;
you may drink it. Cheng drank the water, which was sweet and delicious. Upon waking, a wondrous fragrance emanated from his pores.
He then said to himself, "My karmic affinity for the Pure Land has reached its fulfillment. He further invited monks to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He recited it nearly several hundred times. Later, at Mount Lu, he invited the assembly of monks to gather and measured their number.
Facing the images, he burned incense, prostrated himself twice, and made this vow: "By means of the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that there is Amitābha Buddha.
This incense shall first be offered to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, next to Amitābha Buddha, and furthermore, with the wondrous Dharma..."
Because he had attained rebirth in the Pure Land through the merit of this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he made a vow that all sentient beings might likewise be born in the Pure Land.
Then, parting from the assembly, he lay upon his bed facing west, joined his palms, and passed away into parinirvāṇa.
During the Jin dynasty, Fang Zhu died suddenly and entered the underworld to see the King of Hell. The King said, "According to your records, you once exhorted one person to recite the Buddha's name;
they have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land. By virtue of this merit, you too shall be enabled to attain rebirth in the Pure Land."

Chuzhu said, "I have already recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* ten thousand times and am also making pilgrimages to Mount Wutai; therefore, I do not yet wish to be reborn in the Pure Land.
The King said, "Reciting sutras and performing prostrations are indeed virtuous deeds, yet they are not as good as being reborn in the Pure Land.

After Chuzhu had remained silent for a long while, the King realized that his resolve could not be swayed, so he released him to return to the human world. This is what is meant by the saying: "The commander-in-chief of the three armies may be taken away."
...so it is. "The will of a common man cannot be taken away from him.
During the Jin dynasty, there was Tao Qian, styled Yuanming. His life story has already been cited previously. When the Layman lived in Chaisang, he was near Mount Lu;
together with Lu Xiujing, he frequently came to visit Master Huiyuan. Huiyuan, admiring his expansive and untrammeled spirit, invited him [to stay].
Regarding his entry into the monastic community: Huiqian was by nature fond of wine. He said that if he were permitted to drink, he would remain; Huiyuan granted him this permission.

Qian entered the mountains, but after some time, having run out of wine, he knit his brows in dissatisfaction and departed. He once composed the *Sou Shen Ji* (Inquiries into the Divine), which recorded many accounts of the miraculous efficacy of the Buddha.
Cognition and vision do not arise; one reflects back to return to the source. The fundamental nature is beyond words and explanations.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are neither correct nor biased, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete.
This section was annotated by Prince Zhaoming, who judged this passage of the sutra to be the "Section on the Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
This is because Subhūti below states that one must see the Buddha through the four marks before being permitted to know all dharmas in such a manner.
Seeing thus and resolving with faith thus, one does not give rise to the marks of dharmas; for this reason, this name is established—to signify that knowing and seeing do not arise.
"Reflecting back to return to the source" clarifies *śamatha*, which is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

By the power of concentration, one is able to eliminate the two attachments to persons and dharmas, simultaneously manifesting the principle of the emptiness of both person and dharma; hence it is said, "reflecting back to return to the source."
That "the fundamental nature is beyond verbal expression" clarifies *vipaśyanā*, which is wisdom (*prajñā*).

By the power of this wisdom, one is able to expound the *piṭaka* and *yāna*, proclaiming various *dharmaparyāyas* to guide and benefit all sentient beings. Although one expounds all phenomena, one realizes that their essential nature is empty and attains true liberation;
therefore, it is said that "the fundamental nature is beyond verbal expression. [This applies to] seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing.
The term "and so forth" clarifies samāpatti, which is the contemplation of the Middle Way. In the preceding text, concentration and wisdom were explained individually;
here, concentration and wisdom are fused as a pair. "Seeing and hearing" refers to seeing thus, which is wisdom. "Perceiving and knowing" refers to knowing thus, which is concentration.
To speak of them collectively as "seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing" signifies the simultaneous illumination that reveals the Middle Way.

Regarding the phrase "neither correct nor biased," this simultaneously negates both extremes to reveal the Middle Way. Now, the Master instructs that practitioners must not be partial or narrow-minded.
In the midst of ordinary daily life, within the spheres of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one must not cling to the sense organs, their objects, or the sensory realms;
yet, one must not depart from these organs and objects to seek a separate, inherent nature. Therefore, it is said to be "neither correct."
Thus, not abiding within quiescence is non-bias; not abiding upon alertness is non-defilement; not following agitation is non-purity;

and not sinking into the indeterminate is neither deficient nor complete. To be "neither deficient nor complete" means to transcend the three truths while the three contemplations are perfectly integrated.
"Non-deficient" means that the three contemplations are one mind and the three truths are one realm.
There is no "roundness" [as a separate entity]; rather, it is the single essence, perfectly interfused and unimpeded, wherein the three truths are distinct and clear.
This is the dharma-gate of the profound entry into the One Vehicle.
The numinous light is vast and boundless; the bright sun stands precisely in the center of the sky.
These two lines clarify both the Dharma and the metaphor; they are the locus where the three truths are perfectly interfused.

From the appearance of Śākyamuni in the world to the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, all have revealed this single segment of numinous light. It is like the bright sun adorning the heavens, shining everywhere without exception.
Thus, Xuansha said: "The entire earth, with its sentient and insentient beings, and the myriad phenomena of the forest and the peaks—all are one."
All phenomena are entirely within this light of mine; they are freely enjoyed therein. Thus it is said: "The numinous light is vast and surging;
the bright sun stands precisely in the heavens."
"Knowing and seeing, they deliver sentient beings, yet sentient beings are likewise blind"—
these two lines above cite the meaning of the sūtra.
This refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi), who, within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), possess the capacity...

Regarding what is discriminated: if one knows and perceives while delivering sentient beings, it is not only the bodhisattva who clings to marks; rather, the sentient beings being delivered would likewise cling to the four marks.
As it is said: "If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
This statement implies that if the bodhisattva who is able to deliver others already possesses the four marks, then the sentient beings being delivered [would likewise do so].

There are also four characteristics; therefore, it is said that sentient beings are likewise blind. The following two lines also cite the meaning of the sutra to clarify that the Tathāgata has severed discriminatory views and does not cling to the marks of dharmas. "That which is not the mark of dharmas" means that the mark of dharmas does not arise.
This non-dharma-mark is, within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), incapable of admitting any other entity; it is devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of marks. It is not...
It belongs to the realm of causes and conditions; it is the essence of quiescent extinction and ultimate reality. Therefore, it is said that one has finally reached the city of Nirvana.
Chapter Thirty-one: The Non-arising of Knowledge and Vision.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Buddha has taught [the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span].
[Commentary] This section of the sūtra clarifies the departure from the two views of self and dharmas (*ātma-dharma-dṛṣṭi*).

Because within the preceding thirty sections, the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-objects (*viṣaya*) were shown to be the objective spheres (*ālambana*) of the self and dharmas, it was made known that they are not real. Now, the subjective grasper (*ālambaka*) is refuted.
The mind that perceives a self within my Dharma is precisely the deluded conceptualization arising from ordinary beings.
Now, by casting this aside and causing such conceptualization to be forgotten, one immediately enters the stage of the sages.

Furthermore, regarding the initial departure from the view of self, there is both the view of a true self and the view of a deluded self. The view of a deluded self is merely false conceptualization; it is what sentient beings [possess].
It is seeing. That which is the seeing of the true self is free from attachment; it is the seeing of the Tathāgata.

Since one is already free from attachment, to speak of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span is to demonstrate that within this state of non-seeing, there is seeing.
Sentient beings who are deluded believe that the Tathāgata truly possesses these four views; therefore, it is said: "No."
[He] understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. For this reason, the Buddha questioned Subhūti with four views:
"Does this person understand the meaning of what I have taught? Subhūti, understanding the meaning of the Buddha's question, replied:
"This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? Subhūti himself inquires into the preceding meaning: "For what reason is this person [so]?"

They do not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Subhūti, because he understands the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught, he knows that all four views are not false conceptualizations; they are the view of the true self. Therefore it is said:
"These are called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span. Changshui said: "The Buddha’s teaching on the view of self and so forth is not..."

The views of a self, persons, and so forth that take them to be real are merely conventional designations for a self, persons, and so forth. Sentient beings do not understand this and claim they truly exist.
[Sūtra] Subhūti, from the arousal of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*... [up to] ...that which is the non-characteristic of dharmas is called the characteristic of dharmas.
The preceding passage has already eliminated the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); this present passage, however, eliminates the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*).
It is also a summary that concludes the subduing [of the mind] and abiding in right practice. In the second section above, Subhūti first asked: "How should one who has generated the bodhicitta abide?
How should they subdue their mind? The Tathāgata replied: "One should abide in this way; one should subdue [the mind] in this way."
Having subdued their minds, he now concludes by saying: "Those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta should, regarding all phenomena, know, see, believe, and understand them in this way.
This concludes the previous point concerning how one should abide in the Mahayana view.
"Not giving rise to the marks of phenomena" means not grasping at or becoming attached to any phenomena; this concludes the previous point concerning the subduing of the deluded mind. This...
The Tathāgata has explained that he intends to cause sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta and to practice in accordance with the truth.
Therefore, Subhūti, upon hearing the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, you immediately understood its meaning. Thus, the Buddha earnestly exhorted those who have given rise to the bodhicitta:
regarding all phenomena, you should know, see, and resolve them in this way, so that no conceptual signs of phenomena arise. Subhūti...
Regarding what was said about the "characteristics of dharmas" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): the Buddha then called out to Subhūti to re-examine the meaning of the preceding point.

He stated that what are called the characteristics of dharmas—namely, knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding—are all characteristics of dharmas. Since they possess names associated with the numerical categories of dharmas, they belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
As for the Tathāgata’s statement that these are "not characteristics of dharmas," this is because, among the three skillful means (*upāya*), [the ultimate nature is devoid of such designations].

Because it is a mind free from conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa-citta*), it is said: "This is not the characteristic of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*); it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

As for what is called "the characteristic of phenomena," because within the three skillful means the discriminating mind is empty and one enters the principle of non-discrimination—being neither mundane nor ultimate, and being free from both nature and characteristics—it is said:
"This is called the characteristic of phenomena. This is precisely the middle way truth (*madhyamā-pratipad-satya*).
If one is attached to knowledge, views, and intellectual understanding, it will be difficult to accord with the wondrous meaning of the Tathāgata.

To realize that there is no self, person, or life-span is itself like a mirage or a flower in the sky. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To establish knowledge within knowledge and views is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and views are devoid of seeing, this is nirvāṇa.
Now, when the characteristics of phenomena do not arise, do you still maintain such intellectual understanding?

Regarding the passage "If one is attached to knowledge, views, faith, and understanding," this section means that for one who has generated the bodhicitta, if they grasp at knowledge, views, faith, and understanding regarding all phenomena, there will be conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*). Once there is conceptual differentiation, the view of dharmas (*dharmadṛṣṭi*) is established.
Once the view of dharmas exists, one cannot realize the principle of non-conceptualization. Therefore, it is difficult to accord with Suchness (*tathatā*).
This refers to the "wondrous meaning" [of the title]. In the main text it is said: "If one is attached to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, there is a fear that the transcriber has erred.
Regarding the passage on "awakening to the absence of self, person, life-span, and so forth," this section clarifies how Subhūti understood the meaning of the Buddha’s question.
Although the World-Honored One spoke of the four views of self, person, and so forth, these are the true self of the Tathāgata;

they are not like the deluded selves that ordinary beings falsely believe to be real. Since this is not the self-view of ordinary beings, we know that the Buddha’s manifestation of a "provisional name-self" is like a mirage or a flower in the sky—neither of which can be apprehended. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says regarding knowledge and vision: [and so forth].

This citation of the scriptural text serves to explain and present the meaning established above. If one is attached to knowledge, views, faith, or understanding, it is difficult to accord with the subtle meaning of the Tathāgata;
this clarifies that while the view of dharmas persists, one remains deluded regarding the principle. As for "knowledge and views being without view," etc., this likewise presents the preceding point:
realizing that there is no self, person, or life-span, which are like a mirage or flowers in the sky; this clarifies that the view of self is empty.
Yet it is not unreal. As for the phrase "the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) do not arise," this is the master’s pedagogical method;
he interrogates the practitioner to clarify that the person who previously resolved upon bodhicitta does not give rise to discriminative thoughts regarding any phenomena.
The Buddha’s seal states: "To know, see, and have faith-and-understanding in this way is precisely the non-arising of the characteristics of phenomena right now. One must believe this.

Do you understand? This master of the *ke* (classification) requires people to realize that these three—knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), and non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—are all empty.
But tell me, do you yet have faith and understanding? The reason for this will be revealed in the following text.
"The great trichiliocosm is a bubble in the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.

These two lines clarify the principle that dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) do not arise. Both the conditioned environment (*pariṇata-niśraya*) and the primary retribution (*upapatti-deha*) are utterly unattainable.
This clarifies that the person and the environment are like bubbles and like lightning; who could give rise to knowledge, views, or discrimination?

That which is called the hundreds of thousands of worlds arises and perishes in disorder, like flowers in the sky. Therefore it is said: "The sands of the trichiliocosm are but bubbles upon the ocean."
Regarding "all sages and worthies": the former clarifies that the vision of dharmas is already empty; this clarifies that the vision of persons does not exist.
Within the true mark (dharmatā), it is not only the three grades of worthies and ten stages of sages that are empty; even the realm of the Buddhas is empty. Therefore, it is said:
"All sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning."
The Dharma is empty and non-self; the Way is not kin. When the tree falls and the vines wither, laughter turns ever new.
As the wind sweeps away all the "yellow leaves" that stop the crying, Throughout the thousand forests, the whole body reveals its true nature.
The first line cites the meaning of the Sūtra, specifically the passage concerning "being free from the view of dharmas. Furthermore, there are three ways of generating bodhicitta.
"Seizing the mind" means not engaging in conceptual discrimination. Second, one likewise does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena (*dharma*).

Third, because one possesses knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding regarding the gateways of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*), one is free from the view of phenomena; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). "Not-self" means...
This is precisely the primary truth (*paramārtha*), which is free from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
This view of self is the cognitive mind that perceives a self and dharmas. This cognitive mind is itself a conceptualization that arises; this conceptualization, too, is empty. Therefore, it is said:
"It is not I. That "the Way is not a relative" means that within the Sūtra there is no arising of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
This non-arising of dharmas is the principle of non-discrimination; yet even this principle is discarded, hence it is said to be "not a relative.
This is to shatter clinging attachments. The next phrase cites the fundamental tenet as proof: "This Way of the World-Honored One should be known thus, seen thus, and believed thus."
[The Master] said, "Understand! Do not give rise to the mark of dharmas. When the tree falls and the vine withers, there is a new turn that is truly marvelous.
Formerly, Shushan went to Guishan and asked, "I have heard your teacher’s words: 'There is the phrase and there is no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree.
Suddenly the tree falls and the vine withers; where does the phrase return? Guishan laughed heartily. Shushan said, 'I..."
"Four thousand *li* away, he came to pay his respects to the Master carrying a bolt of cloth for sale. How could you have deceived him?

Guishan called to his attendant, "Bring back the money and return it to this venerable monk. He then instructed him, saying, "In the future, there will be the 'One-Eyed Dragon' who will come to pierce through [his delusions] for you.
Later, when he arrived at Mingzhao and recounted the previous conversation, Mingzhao said, "Guishan may truly be said to be straight from head to tail; however—"
This was not meeting with one who understands. Shu asked, "When the tree falls and the vines wither, where do the words return?
Zhao said, "It would make Moshan’s laughter even fresher. At these words, Shu had an awakening and said, "Moshan originally had a blade within his smile.
The final two lines clarify that the Buddha spoke the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon, and the patriarchs [spoke] the seventeen hundred [verses].
The hundred koans are all but yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying; they are employed temporarily to quell the deluded thoughts of sentient beings for the sake of their transformation.
Yet, when one reaches the ultimate, most profound, and subtle realm of principle, none of them are of any further use. This is why the World-Honored One could do nothing but hold up a flower.
Kāśyapa could only smile. Now, within this sutra, it is said that those who have resolved for bodhicitta should know, see, and believe in all phenomena in this way:
not giving rise to the marks of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This is precisely the point where the wind sweeps away the yellow leaves used to stop a child’s crying;
when the thousand forests are revealed in their entirety, the true nature (*tianzhen*) alone is manifest. It may be said: "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, there is only..."
There is one truth:
people are busy in the morning and busy at evening; why do sentient beings not contemplate this early?
Human life is like a spring dream that must inevitably end; life is like a wind-blown lamp—how could it last long?
The first two lines lament that worldly affairs are endless and restless, urging people to achieve awakening and practice diligently without delay.
The latter two lines illustrate that human life cannot endure long; though one may be at ease today, there is no guarantee for tomorrow.
It is as brief as a spring dream and as impermanent as a wind-blown lamp. Thus, Shiwu’s poem says: "The wind-tossed mast..."
Coming and going through the official ferry-crossing, station horses fly like the wind, busy day and night. Risking favor and craving glory, they scheme for office;
vying for fame and seizing profit, they engage in commerce. Human wealth and honor bring joy for a fleeting moment; the bitterness of hell lasts for ten thousand kalpas.
From antiquity to the present, there is no medicine to cure this; why not go forth to practice cultivation sooner? A brief dream within a spring.
This is like the dream of the yellow millet. An ancient saying goes: "In a mere moment upon a coral pillow, one has traveled thousands of miles throughout Jiangnan.
When the conditions for the Pure Land arise, one’s original aspiration is fulfilled; the single spiritual essence shall never again fall into a womb.
The Dharma-body and liberation are both equal and complete; with a fleeting glance, one turns the head and goes forth or returns.
The first phrase refers to the conditions for birth in the Pure Land. According to one's desires, one may be born at will within the ponds of the nine grades.
Once born, if one wishes to go to the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas, one goes there immediately according to one's wish. Or...
