Necklaces appear according to thought to suit the body; vessels of *sudhā* arrive following every念 (thought). The golden halls possess a radiance that swallows sun and moon; the jade towers have no..."
The dust settles upon the ground. The Dharma King speaks the ultimate truth for me, until even empty space breaks into a broad smile.
The second line states that for the sentient beings of this land, there are three conditions that must converge to give rise to life: ten months spent in the womb.
Amidst various sufferings, one cannot have one's own way. Therefore, the Master exhorts practitioners:
may your single, spiritual, true nature go directly to the lotus womb to take up its substance, and never again enter a mother’s womb.
The final two lines mean that if practitioners of this land can indeed be born in the Pure Land, they will immediately attain the three virtues in full; hence it says, "Dharmakāya."
Liberation is equal and uniform; it is no different from that of the Buddhas.

Since this is such a wondrous state, why do the sentient beings of this land not suddenly and urgently turn their heads now? Why not cast down all worldly conditions at once and, day and night, single-mindedly recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" to return to the Pure Land?
Manifestations through transformation are not real; they are like dew or lightning. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are not firm or stable.
Giving with a mind fixed on signs results in rebirth among humans or devas. This section is the "Part on Manifestations that are Not Real," as determined by Prince Zhaoming. Indeed...

One does not grasp at signs. Furthermore, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are like dreams and illusions, this name is established to indicate that they are manifested emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*) and not real.
As for "like dew and like lightning," this clarifies that the Buddha manifests an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to demonstrate identity with birth and cessation;
it likewise belongs to the category of conditioned and impermanent phenomena, being hollow, false, and unreal. Therefore, six metaphors are used as analogies.

That which is like dew is used as a metaphor for the delusory body, which shifts and changes from moment to moment; its arising and ceasing are impermanent, resembling dew upon the grass that dries up when the sun rises.
That which is like lightning is used as a metaphor for the dharmas currently being contemplated; they do not abide for even a single kṣaṇa, just like a flash of lightning.
Since these belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how could they possess any solidity? One should realize this lack of solidity.

This refers to realizing the true and eternal. As for "those who practice giving while dwelling on signs," this clarifies that even if one were to fill immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift, it is merely a conditioned fruit and retribution,
resulting only in the enjoyment of blessings within the human and celestial realms.
By upholding even four lines of this sutra, one enters the ranks of the sages and transcends the mundane. By reciting these repeatedly, the adamantine essence becomes most firm.
The first two lines clarify the upholding of the sutra; through unconditioned merit, one attains Buddhahood. As for the "four lines," they refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*):
they are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way.
Contemplation: This sutra is spoken by a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha. For when a *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha preaches the Dharma, he is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and without attachment;
likewise, the practitioner who propagates this sutra is also able to remain free from attachment. Therefore, their merit is immeasurable.
Because they thus enter the state of the sages and transcend the mundane, the merit of expounding it surpasses that of giving alms for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

The latter two lines are the master’s admonition and exhortation for later students: whenever one recites [the scriptures], one must employ the wondrous contemplation of perfect interfusion, dwelling single-mindedly to contemplate the principle of the Three Truths.
One must not merely follow the lines of the text or count the characters, thereby only increasing one's intellectual views and knowledge;
this would be like the spring birds crying by day or the autumn insects chirping at night—driven by the seasonal winds, they ultimately have no intentionality.
This is what is meant. When it is said here that one must "frequently turn the thought," it requires a person to be diligent and earnest, maintaining right mindfulness without forgetting.
One thought lasts ten thousand years; ten thousand years are but one thought. This single thought cannot be explained or annotated by means of paper, ink, or written characters;
it is the True Sutra without words, the wondrous essence of the *Vajra*, indestructible by water or fire, and therefore called "most firm."
Formerly, the King of East India invited the twenty-seventh patriarch, Prajñātāra, for a meal. The King asked, "Why do you not read the sutras?
The Patriarch replied, "This poor monk, when inhaling, does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates; when exhaling, does not engage with external conditions.
I am constantly turning this very sutra, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of scrolls. This refers to the meaning of repeatedly turning the dharma in one's thoughts.
Xuansha also said: "Virtuous one, where are you? If you now wish to emerge from the field of the five aggregates, you must simply recognize your secret adamantine essence.
An ancient said: "Perfectly complete and all-pervasive, it extends throughout the realms of the sands;
even the great earth, mountains, rivers, the lands of the ten directions, and all things such as light and darkness, form and emptiness—none are not [it]."
This is your vajra-body.
Expound the four-line verse, with the six perfections as its beginning; whether horizontal or vertical, there is no obstruction—prajñā is suchness itself.
The first line refers to proclaiming and explaining for others the four-line verse concerning all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and so forth.

The second line mentions the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*): namely, generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Through generosity, one transcends stinginess and greed; through ethical discipline, one transcends the violation of precepts; through patience, one transcends...

Through diligence one transcends indolence; through meditative concentration one transcends distraction; through wisdom one transcends ignorance. Thus they are called the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Regarding the phrase "already as the first": taking generosity (*dāna*) as the head of the five perfections, there are two kinds of generosity:
first, the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣa-dāna*); second, the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). Now, the master of this treatise says: for the sake of others, he expounds the four...

Verses and gāthās such as these constitute the gift of Dharma; therefore, it is said that they are the beginning of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*). Regarding the final two lines, the intention of the commentator is that one should expound even a four-line verse for others as a gift of Dharma.
This is intended to cause practitioners to cultivate the myriad practices (*sādhana*) equally, thereby perfecting the four minds.
Through the harmonious integration of the six perfections, which are unimpeded whether practiced vertically or horizontally, one realizes the essential nature of all phenomena.
"Emptiness. That which "cannot be apprehended" uniquely reveals the *tathatā* (suchness) of *prajñā*.
**Chapter Thirty-two: The Manifestation of Response is Not the Real.** [Sūtra] Subhūti, if there be anyone...
[as far as] ...it is like dew and like lightning; one should contemplate it in this way.

The commentary states: The meaning of this section is as follows. From the seventeenth section onward, the Buddha told Subhūti that one who has resolved upon bodhicitta possesses no notion of a "crosser" or a "crossed-over.

Because they delight in cultivating merit and virtue, they do not grasp at or cling to it, thereby realizing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Up to Section Thirty: The Tathāgata uses the analogy of crushing the elements into dust to illustrate the two bodies, the Dharma-body and the response-body. He is able to...

"O virtuous woman, for one who has resolved upon bodhicitta, even their merit surpasses that [of the former].

The teachings spoken by the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) serve as the primary authority for the sūtras. Those who receive, uphold, and expound them are the ones who propagate the sūtras.

therefore, their merit is immeasurable. The propagators of the sūtras are likewise able to transcend the characteristics of verbal expression, and for this reason, their blessings surpass those of others.
Regarding "how to expound the teaching for others," the Buddha asks himself: "How does one expound the teaching for others? He then answers himself:

The meaning is this: when expounding the teaching for others, if one can do so without the mental activities of arising and ceasing, speaking the Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*), then one accords with ultimate truth by not grasping at marks, manifesting only...
Because it is *tathatā* (suchness). This means that the mind is such as its object; hence it is called "Suchness-Suchness" (*tathā-tathatā*).
This is because both mind and object are true, and thus the *dharmakāya* is immovable. As for the question "Why?", the Buddha himself raises this to connect with the preceding text:
"For what reason do you preach to people, not grasping at marks, being such as suchness and immovable? The Buddha fears that some might doubt, saying: "If..."

For what reason, then, is it said that the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa? Because "nirvāṇa" carries the meaning of immovability and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Now, nirvāṇa is quiescent, whereas preaching the Dharma is bustling and active; since movement and stillness are opposites, how can these two coexist?
[The Master] preserved [this text]. Fearing that such doubts might arise, he therefore spoke this verse to resolve them.

This verse refers to "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), which are all things in the world—both the environment and its inhabitants, the defiled and the pure, and the phenomena of arising and ceasing.

Since the Buddha was born among humans, he manifested himself as subject to arising and ceasing; thus, he too belongs to the category of conditioned and impermanent phenomena. Impermanent phenomena are empty...
Because they are provisional and unreal, they are illustrated by the six metaphors of a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, and a flash of lightning.
Once one knows that all things are impermanent, provisional, and unreal, there is nothing that is not the Way of True Permanence. One should practice contemplation in this manner;

such contemplation is precisely the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*. For *prajñā* encompasses the three contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*upāya*), and the middle (*madhyama*). By means of this wondrous wisdom—
To contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—their various distinctions such as the environment and its inhabitants, defilement and purity—is the contemplation of the provisional;

this is the contemplation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). With this wondrous wisdom, to contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being subject to arising and ceasing, impermanent, and like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, a dewdrop, or a flash of lightning, is the contemplation of emptiness; this is the contemplation of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). With this wondrous...

Wisdom contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as being both the ultimate and the conventional, neither empty nor existent; this is precisely the Middle Way, contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

One who can contemplate all conditioned phenomena in this manner, fully possessing the threefold contemplation and the three truths in perfect fusion, does so because the contemplating subject is itself wondrous wisdom—the single mind’s threefold contemplation. As for the object...
Contemplating non-existence is the wondrous realm; it is the three truths within a single realm.

One who can penetrate this meaning will realize that the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is ever-present in the world—how could it ever undergo extinction? What is called "entering extinction" refers only to the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

Regarding the first section, "bestowing the seven treasures and so forth," this cites a metaphor from the sutra regarding the giving of the seven treasures. Such acts result only in the reception of blessings within the realms of humans and devas;
thus they belong to the category of seeking existence and are therefore delusive. Since one has not yet transcended the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), these must be discarded.
Section Two. Regarding the phrase "upholding this sutra and so forth," this is the Master’s [the Patriarch’s] skillful employment of conventional expression (*upāya*).

Although the merit of receiving, upholding, and expounding even a four-line verse is superior, such merit is not ultimate; for since it involves attachment to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it too must be discarded.
Therefore it is said: "The Real is not established; the false is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are discarded, yet not even emptiness remains. This is it.
Furthermore, regarding the passage "sitting in meditation in the water-moon *bodhimaṇḍa*," this text presents the aforementioned meaning that [phenomena] are not real.
It instructs the practitioner that within the *prajñā* of true emptiness, both receiving and holding the sutra and its exposition are all unreal.

Therefore, sitting in meditation at the *bodhimaṇḍa* is identical to the moon in the water; and while upholding the sutra and expounding it to accomplish the Buddha-work, it remains likewise [unreal].
It is like a flower in the sky; this expresses the general meaning of unreality. Yongming Shou said:

"To establish a moon-in-water *bodhimaṇḍa*, to adorn the world of the emptiness of nature, to array illusory offerings, to prostrate before a reflected assembly of the Dharma, to perform acts as the gate of resonance in an echo, and to cultivate the myriad practices of sky-flowers. This refers to crossing over the illusory.
Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings," this passage also demonstrates the aforementioned meaning that [beings] are not real.
It is taught for the sake of people solely for the purpose of liberating sentient beings. Since they are illusory transformations and lack substantial reality, how can they be liberated?
Furthermore, since the *bodhi* realized is quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*), and within the principle of quiescent extinction there is no taking up of realization, the Buddha told Viśuddhamati:
Within the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there are in fact no bodhisattvas nor sentient beings. Why is this? Because both bodhisattvas and sentient beings are illusory transformations;
since these illusory transformations cease, there is no one who attains realization. Yongming Shou said:

"Constantly roam within the dharma-gate of illusion, entering and exiting the gate of contemplation without obstruction, subduing the demonic armies that are like reflected images, and performing great deeds within the dream."
The Buddha’s work consists of extensively delivering sentient beings—who are like illusions—so that they may together realize the bodhi of quiescent extinction.
As for the phrase "ordinary emotions and sagely understanding are both empty," this is the hand-eye of the Master of the School; he seizes upon people's clinging emotions.
When I previously spoke in such a manner, I intended to seize away both ordinary emotions and sagely understanding, for birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream.
Regarding this matter, Fenghui addressed the assembly, saying: "Before I have even ascended the seat, all people throughout the great earth have already attained Buddhahood.
What further Dharma is there to be preached? What further beings are there to benefit? Moreover, enlightenment and affliction are fundamentally quiescent from the start;

Without abandoning the gateway of causes, they guide ordinary beings toward rebirth, whereby those beings immediately hear the Dharma and gaze upon the golden countenance [of the Buddha].
They may truly be called practitioners who achieve both perfect cultivation and perfect realization.

The Diamond Prajñā-pāramitā is the root and source of the six perfections; it is the most firm and solid both internally and externally. Throughout the three thousand great chiliocosms, it has been transmitted for ten thousand ages.
This section [concerns] the postscript to the Diamond Prajñā-pāramitā Sūtra, which takes the wisdom of the Diamond Prajñā as the [foundation of] the six perfections.
The source of these [virtues], and even all myriad practices, are established through the true wisdom of *prajñā*.
Therefore, the five perfections are like the blind, while *prajñā* is like a guide. Thus, giving without *prajñā* yields only the glory of a single lifetime.
In future lives, one will suffer remaining retribution. If one upholds the precepts without Prajñā, though one may briefly be born in the higher desire realm, one will fall back into the hells.
If one practices patience without Prajñā, one may obtain a handsome form as a karmic reward, yet fail to realize the patience of cessation.

If one exerts diligence without Prajñā, one merely performs the labor of arising and ceasing, failing to advance toward the fruit of true permanence. If one practices meditative concentration without Prajñā, one merely...
The meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the desire realm are not equal to the Vajra-like Samādhi.
If the myriad virtues lack Prajñā, emptiness becomes a cause for outflows and fails to accord with the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding "inner and outer being firm and solid":

because this Prajñā is the root-source of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the six internal sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the six external objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are none other than the functioning of Prajñā-wisdom; hence it is said, "Inner..."
The external is the most solid. Regarding the phrase "the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system" and so forth:

because this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was not intended for circulation in this land alone, but rather circulated throughout billions of four-continent worlds, it is said that it has been transmitted for ten thousand ages.

The silent discourse at the twin śāla trees has been proclaimed again and again by each successive patriarch. It opens up six ways of awakening and entry; sentient beings possess great affinity for it.
Regarding the "silent discourse at the twin śāla trees" and so forth: this Way can only be transmitted mind-to-mind and is not established in written words.
Therefore, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa; this is called the silent resonance with the true mind.
From Kāśyapa onwards, the patriarchs have transmitted it from one to another, reiterating this Way until the "one flower and five petals" and the "thousand flowers vying for beauty" flourished.
It secretly reached later generations and directly connected with those of superior capacity; thus there arose the raising of an eyebrow, the twinkling of an eye, and the lifting of a fist.
Pointing a finger; or administering blows and shouts; brandishing a whisk or striking with a mallet; or holding a trident and drawing a bow, rolling up a robe and dancing with a ceremonial tablet;
or dragging stones and carrying earth, beating drums and blowing a hair-whistle;

or remaining silent or speaking a single word, calling out or laughing—a laugh—these and all such various skillful means are intimate acts for the sake of others, manifesting the wordless within movement and stillness.

This is the Way. Regarding the phrases "opening, showing, awakening, and entering," although the religious teachings differ in their hidden or manifest aspects, they are one and the same in opening up and showing that principle;
thus, the points at which practitioners each awaken and enter are not different. Wénlíng says:

"Opening" means breaking through the shroud of ignorance. "Showing" means pointing out the true essence that was previously lost in delusion. "Awakening" means seeing clearly and with sudden clarity. "Entering" means reaching profound realization and attaining it for oneself.
Furthermore, it is said: "Opening" is the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*); "showing" is the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*);
"awakening" is all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); and "entering" is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Once sentient beings have awakened, [they realize this].
Is this wisdom not indeed a great cause and condition?
To speak the "Story of Shattering Non-arising": One will certainly go to the West, to Amitābha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one constantly hears the fragrance of Prajñā.

Regarding the first two lines, the Master’s intention is as follows: "I have used the ritual protocols of this sutra to reveal and explain them with such clarity that it may be called 'breaking open the discourse on non-arising. If there are practitioners who believe, understand, accept, and uphold them..."
By reading, reciting, expounding, and seeing or hearing with sympathetic joy, one will forever eliminate the four marks (*catur-nimitta*) and manifest the single reality (*eka-tattva*).
One will certainly attain rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). The latter two lines describe the realm of experience within Amitābha’s land:
having seen Amitābha, one constantly hears the subtle and wondrous Dharma of Prajñā; therefore, Prajñā is [the mother] of all Buddhas.
Mother, one is born from the very nature of Amitābha; thus, those born in the Pure Land perceive only the fragrance of the Buddha’s virtues and not the fragrance of the two vehicles.
Just as upon entering a campaka grove, one perceives only the fragrance of the campaka and no other fragrance.
Thus, Wutand said: "A single phrase of Amitābha is my own assertion; There is not another dharma to be pondered.
Clearly and directly pointing to the path home, The Utpala flower blooms with its fragrance pervading the world."
The term "contemplation" (guan) refers to internal mental awareness and illumination. As it appears at the beginning of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*:
"When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty. This is found in this sutra.

Thus, one should ultimately contemplate in this manner. Just as those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta verify the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena, students should not seek to understand it through the vision of the physical eye;
rather, by doing so, they will be as if personally attending upon the Yellow-Faced One (the Buddha). May all who hear this [attain] such realization.
There was none who did not suddenly attain awakening and experience immeasurable joy; they believed and accepted it, and reverently put it into practice.
But tell me, what is it that they believe, accept, and put into practice?
In this section of the sutra, one should contemplate the meaning in this manner. Thus, the term "contemplate" (*guan*) is an etymological explanation.
The single character "contemplate" is defined as the sense of internal mental awakening and illumination.

This awakening and illumination is precisely what the end of the present sutra refers to when it says, "one should contemplate in this way"—that is, the threefold contemplation of perfect interfusion. Its...
Regarding the term "Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra": the word "that" (其) is a term used to point to the Dharma;
it points specifically to this single character "contemplation" (觀), which is found in detail within the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. As for what is called "the heart" (心), Master Xuanzang said:

"If one were to recount all matters exhaustively, the words would exceed two hundred thousand stanzas; yet if one extracts the essential pivot, the principle is fully contained within these fourteen lines."
Regarding "The mind is that which manifests the essential and wondrous destination": it is the core of the six hundred fascicles; therefore, it is called the "destination" (*gui*).
Taking this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as an analogy for that *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*, it too is the core of the six hundred fascicles. Thus, it begins by saying:
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara refers to the practitioner who is capable of contemplation. "Contemplation" (guan) refers to the wisdom of illuminating observation.
"Sovereign" (zizai) means being without restriction or impediment; thus, he is called "Sovereign.
By means of the unimpeded wisdom of provisional and ultimate truth, the Bodhisattva illuminates the realm where emptiness and form are interfused, merging his spiritual mind with true emptiness.
It cannot be obstructed; nor can the ears and eyes be hindered by sounds and forms. Therefore, it is said: "The Bodhisattva who dwells in mastery.
The phrase "when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*" clarifies the object of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation.
It is the practice that is undertaken. "Profound" (*gambhīra*) has the meaning of being distinctively differentiated;

it is not the shallow practice of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), but rather the extremely profound *prajñā* of the bodhisattva—the wisdom of contemplation capable of observing. "Time" refers to the moment when the bodhisattva transcends contemplation.
"To contemplate and see that the five aggregates are all empty" means that this bodhisattva, by means of profound *prajñā*, utilizes the wisdom capable of observation.

"To clearly perceive the five aggregates" refers to the objects of observation. As for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it consists of the five sense faculties and the six sense objects, and is the most coarse.

The three aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are the mental factors (*caitta*). The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*). These four aggregates [together with the aggregate of form] constitute the basis of existence.
It is most extremely subtle, difficult to sever, and difficult to empty. What is now called the emptiness of the five aggregates is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

However, when a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva first contemplates the emptiness of phenomena and is able to rely upon it, the self spontaneously becomes empty of its own accord; this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
The phrase "in this sutra and others" clarifies the contemplative wisdom that is cultivated; by means of this [wisdom] within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*...
This wondrous contemplation is analogous to the "awakening illumination" found within the *Heart Sūtra*.
For instance, the phrase "one who has generated the bodhicitta" clarifies the great mind generated by a Bodhisattva.

This "one who has generated the bodhicitta" in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is none other than Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in that *Heart Sūtra*, even as it says: "By relying on prajñā, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
This is *bodhi*. That which certifies the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena clarifies the phenomena that are empty.
It is said that these two sutras are both portions subsumed within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. By comparing these two sutras with one another:
Since their parts are identical, their contemplative illumination is likewise identical; their arousal of the great mind (*mahācitta*) is likewise identical;

and the dharmas that are realized as empty are likewise identical. For this reason, they certify that all dharmas are identical. Regarding the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the *Zongjing* states:

"First, the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence; this is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Second, the nature of transgression is fundamentally empty; this is the [perfection of] ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)."
The first is the true mark of *dānapāramitā*. The third is the patient endurance of the three types of mental states; it is the true mark of *kṣāntipāramitā*.
The fourth is the diligent cultivation of wholesome dharmas; it is the true mark of *vīryapāramitā*. The fifth is the non-distraction and non-savoring of the mind;
it is the true mark of *dhyānapāramitā*. The sixth is that which is neither object nor wisdom; it is the true mark of *prajñāpāramitā*.
By expanding and fulfilling this, one realizes that all phenomena are nothing other than the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is said:

"This is the seal that certifies the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena. As for the instruction, "The student must not view this with the physical eye," this is the admonition of the master to the practitioner.
One cannot perceive this with the physical eye; it must be understood through the mind.

This means that just as one cannot see external objects when separated by paper or film, nor see the five viscera when separated by skin, so too, given such obstructions, how could one perceive that all phenomena are empty?
As in the two preceding sutras, the Bodhisattva takes the wisdom of *prajñā* as his eye.
It is also called the "Śakara-vajra Firm and Correct Eye. It illuminates all phenomena to their ultimate limit, revealing that there is nothing that is not true emptiness.
If a student can contemplate in this manner, they will be as if personally attending upon the Yellow-Faced World-Honored One;
for the emptiness of dharmas is itself the vision of the Buddha. As for the statement, "All who hear this do not fail to attain sudden enlightenment," etc., it refers to every single...
All practitioners: if you observe the emptiness of all phenomena with the eye of wisdom, you will suddenly and clearly realize your own nature;

you will then be able to believe, accept, and practice it. Only then can it be said that you have personally seen the Tathāgata, personally heard the essentials of the Dharma, and personally propagated it.

"Benefiting all living beings in heaven and among humans. Furthermore, when it asks, "What is it that you believe, accept, and practice?"—this is the master's hand and eye, interrogating the practitioner.
It is as previously stated: he requires the person to believe, accept, and practice.
What principle is it that one truly practices? The following lines provide the answer:
"Wherever the eye turns, the true Prajñā is proclaimed; The mountains and rivers fully manifest the Body of the Dharma King.
These two lines respond to the preceding statement. If one understands, accepts with faith, and practices accordingly, this is precisely the true mind of Prajñā.
Believe this. Therefore, when one encounters color and form with the eyes, one proclaims Prajñāpāramitā.

Thus, the verdant green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (Tathatā), and the lush yellow flowers are none other than Prajñāpāramitā. The great earth, mountains, and rivers fully reveal the body of the Dharma King.
This clarifies that all phenomena arise in dependence upon the Truth, and that every phenomenon is entirely the true mind. It may be said: "The sound of the stream..."
Constantly recite the Verses of the King of Emptiness; the mountain scenery fully reveals the heart-mind of the ancient Buddha.
These five thousand words are wondrous beyond measure; the over eight hundred commentaries are but detailed digressions.
Cherish this, O people: do not seek it outwardly, but turn the light back and directly realize it within yourself.
The first two sentences clarify the title of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from beginning to end, its division into thirty-two sections,
and its total word count of five thousand one hundred and seventy-five characters, as well as the two hundred and fifty-seven characters of the topical outline (mukō) by Prince Zhaoming.
In total, it comprises five thousand four hundred and thirty-two characters. Thus it is said: "Five thousand characters or more; its subtlety is difficult to measure.
This is because this Golden Sutra contains profound and subtle principles that are difficult for people to fathom. As for the "more than eight hundred families":
At that time, although there were eight hundred people engaged in translating and polishing the scriptures, they never provided detailed explanations or pointed out the meaning for others;
hence it is said, "the explanation is superficial. The latter two lines point to the meaning of the wondrousness that is difficult to measure.
Therefore, I urge you all to bring this back to yourself; do not seek it elsewhere.
You must cause the light to turn inward and reflect back to see your own original mind, accepting it directly without departing from movement or stillness.
To be clear and free of doubt within every instance of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—this is what is meant by "accepting it directly."
Ghosts and spirits bow their heads to listen to the sound of the sutra; Through wondrous awakening, they attain perfect penetration and all phenomena become clear.
If people from this assembly can understand it thus, From now on, they shall no longer inquire about their future paths.
Regarding the first two lines: because this sutra uniquely reveals true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and instantly eliminates all forms and appearances, ghosts and spirits bow their heads.
Listen to it; there is no one who does not derive benefit. All shall attain wondrous awakening and perfect penetration, such that the myriad dharmas are all clarified.
The latter two lines are the master’s instruction to the practitioner: if you can, at this very moment, realize the true wisdom of prajñā within this sutra.
Surpassing ghosts, spirits, and other heterodox beings, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood directly; thus it is said: "This time, there is no need to inquire about the future.
To obtain a human body is the most difficult thing; do not pass this fleeting life in vain.
One must rely on the power of the Vajra Samādhi to directly break through the barrier of birth and death.
(The first two lines praise the difficulty of obtaining a human body; it is as rare as rolling a mustard seed onto the peak of Mount Sumeru or tossing a needle into a hole.
Therefore, it is the most difficult thing to attain. Now that one has already obtained this human body which is so difficult to find, one must give rise to the sense of its being a rare encounter.
Contemplate this: one must not let time pass in vain, nor allow the years and months to drift away empty-handed. The latter two lines of the verse are the master’s instruction to the practitioner:
you must rely on the power of the *vajrasamādhi* concentration to sever the innate ignorance and all afflictions that have existed since beginningless time;
only then can you achieve liberation from birth and death. As the ancient masters said: "A hundred years last but a brief moment."
Time. Do not treat these fleeting moments with indifference. Diligent cultivation makes Buddhahood easy to attain;
if you miss this life, it will be difficult to emerge. When impermanence suddenly arrives, who can take your place? Debts must always be repaid by oneself.
If you wish to avoid the judgment seat of King Yama, you need only penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs.
Thirty-two sections; in each section, there is complete truth. Under these words, one should be well-awakened. The four currents flow peacefully and the six realms are at peace.
These are the words of the thirty-two sections of this treatise. This entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* [is extracted] from the orthodox teaching.
In the second section, Subhūti asks: "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha replies that those who have generated the bodhicitta should dwell in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner. In the third section...
Abiding in the middle, one subdues. Within the fourth direction, one cultivates middling subdual.

From the fifth stage to the end, there is only singular subdual, whereby twenty-seven doubts are severed. Through this comprehensive abiding and cultivation, the twenty-seven kinds of delusive doubt are emptied.
Thus, the wondrous path of true emptiness is clarified herein; therefore, every stage is entirely the truth.
Just as with the wondrous principle, every single word is itself True Suchness (Tathatā). Throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm, every form is true.
Therefore it is said: "Every part is entirely the Real. The Master of the Text (Kojia), fearing that people might miss the point here, points this out, saying:
Although each part is entirely the True Reality, the practitioner must awaken to this beneath a single word and know their home before a single phrase;

thus, they may attain the ceasing of the four torrents and the peace of the six kingdoms. As for the "four torrents," these are the torrent of desire, the torrent of existence, the torrent of ignorance, and the torrent of views.
As for the "six kingdoms," when deluded, there is a distinct category within each of the six sense-faculties and their objects.
The mind and its mental factors—the consciousness—have not ceased their grasping and rejecting within their respective objects, just as a kingdom cannot find peace when there are bandits.
Now, by using this sutra to verify the principle, one realizes that delusion is entirely truth;
thus, the stream of birth and death comes to rest, and the bandits of the six sense organs are extinguished. Therefore, the mind attains tranquility and security.
"Looking in the morning and turning in the evening; pulling out the wedges and extracting the nails. When the spring thunder resounds, the Wangzhou Pavilion is toppled.

This section clarifies this sutra: although every part is entirely true, the practitioner must, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, strive with earnest diligence to remain constantly within this state.
Only by forgetting the words upon grasping the meaning—looking in the morning and turning in the evening—can one truly attain it.

It is clear. Having thoroughly realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one naturally casts off the two attachments and severs the two obstacles;
furthermore, one even forgets the two kinds of emptiness. Thus, True Suchness (*tathatā*) becomes manifest herein. Therefore, it is likened to pulling out a wedge or extracting a nail.
Regarding the phrase "the spring thunder resounds," it was previously stated that through awakening in an instant, the four torrents of defilement are stilled and the six realms are brought to peace.
This is further illustrated by the metaphor of the thundering spring peals that topple the roadside pavilions.

According to ancient records, there was a pavilion every ten *li* and a rest station (*dié*) every hundred *li*; today, even at intervals of seventy or eighty *li*, one is still considered a rest station.
Thus, those traveling on the road advance by looking toward the next stage and the next rest station. It is for this reason [that the analogy is drawn].
Yet, compared to the practitioner, it represents the stages of progress on the Way.

What is called "pushing over" is intended to cause the practitioner to forget these stages, so that they do not pass through cultivation and realization, nor traverse the journey, but instead return home to sit in peace. As it is said:
All golden dust is swept away from within the eyes; wherever one traverses, the avian path is profound and mysterious.
Seeing forms does not involve form; hearing sounds is not the hearing of sound. In the state where form and sound do not obstruct, one has personally reached the City of the Dharma King.
The first two lines require the practitioner to turn back the hearing toward its own nature and turn back the seeing toward the True Principle.
Although the eyes see forms, the mind does not interfere with forms; although the ears hear sounds, the consciousness does not cling to sounds. As an ancient master said:
This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing; there is no further sound or form to present to you. If one understands this point, there is nothing at all;
how could the essence and its function be hindered by being either divided or undivided? As for the latter two lines:

if one can truly allow sounds and forms to be no hindrance, one will immediately attain personal arrival at the City of the Dharma King and penetrate deeply into the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), moving freely and expansively through the gates of the six sense faculties.
Mastery. That is to say: when one turns the light back upon itself to reflect inwardly, one returns to the source; the vast and penetrating numinous light has no front or back.
*The Mantra of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Prajñā*.
[Sūtra] Homage to the Bhagavat, the Pratyekabuddha, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Svāhā. The Buddha said:
"This mantra is the Mother of all Buddhas. Those who can recite and uphold it shall have all their sins extinguished;

they shall constantly behold all Buddhas, attain the knowledge of past lives, maintain the true Dharma they hear through dhāraṇī without forgetting, and swiftly realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]."

Regarding this Perfectly Equal Enlightenment, we now join with the assembly of virtuous ones to read this Sūtra of the Supreme Vehicle. We rejoice in the Buddha-work of this auspicious day as it approaches its conclusion;
may all excellent causes be gathered together to adorn the field of merit of the presiding master of this assembly, thereby accomplishing infinite fruits of goodness. As for this matter:
Let us pause for a moment. I ask you all: how would you resolve this public case? Do you understand it? If you pick it up, even the Buddhas cannot see through it;
if you unfold it, the entire dharma-realm finds it difficult to conceal. If you can directly accept and take responsibility for it, [you have understood].
It is certainly possessed by nature from the very beginning. Even so, it still involves traversing a journey. But tell me:
when it is now handed over with both hands, what then?

The first section is the presiding master’s address to the assembly of virtuous practitioners gathered there, who have come together to witness and hear with their own eyes and ears as they read the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the supreme Mahāyāna teaching spoken by the Tathāgata for those who aspire to the Great Vehicle.
In the subsequent section, regarding the expression of joy at this day’s Buddhist service, the intention of the presiding master is as follows: "This golden..."
The Diamond Sutra is rarely encountered in a thousand lifetimes and difficult to meet in ten thousand kalpas.
That we have now established this *dharmapūjā* site to collectively read and study it—analyzing its sections and expounding upon it—is surely a source of great fortune.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddhist services for this day are at the time of the concluding distribution," this refers to the moment when the analysis of this sutra is complete and the assembly is about to disperse; therefore, one universally gathers excellent causes and...
May those who see, hear, rejoice in, uphold, recite, lecture upon, and explain this [text] all obtain excellent causes and inexhaustible merit.

Regarding the "heads of the assembly" and so forth: since the aforementioned analysis and lectures have yielded inexhaustible merit, it should first be dedicated to the field of merit that is the head of the assembly.
As for the term "head of the assembly," the Tathāgata’s threefold [teaching of] the Dharma...
There are over one hundred assemblies, each with its own presiding leader (*parṣad-adhipati*). In the *Avataṃsaka*, there are seven locations and nine assemblies, each with its own presiding leader.

In the present sutra, Subhūti serves as the presiding leader; yet, while the Prajñāpāramitā is taught through him to the bodhisattvas, each of them receives a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood.
Subhūti himself, however, receives a prediction from the Buddha that he shall be named Tathāgata Nāmanimitta. Thus, both self and others achieve *bodhi*.
There is no benefit greater than this. Therefore it is said: "One achieves infinite wholesome fruits. The same applies to cause and effect for the assembly leader today.
As for the phrase "let this matter rest for now," the Master’s intention is as follows: let the preceding analysis of the dedication of merit and other matters rest for now;
hereafter, he will personally manifest his own skillful means (*hanyan*) by rigorously interrogating the great assembly regarding these two cases.
How should one practice? Let us inquire: how is this principle established? Do you understand? You must urgently fix your eyes upon it. The following text elucidates this principle:
that which, when held up, cannot be pierced even by a Buddha, is because this principle leaves no trace and severs all communication;
even the three lights have not yet shone upon it, and even the five eyes find it difficult to peer into. It is fully unfolded.
Regarding the statement that "the Dharma-realm is difficult to conceal": by this principle, it pervades heaven and earth and fills the entire Dharma-realm;
that is to say, every phenomenon is not hidden, but is eternally manifest throughout past and present. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all fully revealed as the body of the Dharma King.
When it says, "If one can directly accept and take responsibility for this," the Master of the Text (Kojia) is exhorting practitioners; I now bring this forward [for discussion].
The Kōan: Pointing directly before your faces, I say: you all, if you can directly accept this principle right now, you will surely find that it is primordially complete.
It is inherent in every person; it is not lacking in anyone. It does not increase in sages, nor does it decrease in ordinary beings.
It is not borrowed from the thousand sages, nor is it sought through the myriad functions. This is the Way that is originally yours.

"Although it is thus," and so forth, is merely the Master of the School (Kejia) picking up at the level of intellectual emotion (*qing*). I now take up this public case (*gong'an*), yet I am still traversing the path.
Therefore, Dongshan Shouchu said: "If one discusses this matter, if one lets go, the moon is bright and the wind is clear on the road to Caoxi;
if one holds fast, the clouds are gathered and the mist is dissipated before the peak of Shaoshi. Such is the talk.
Indeed. Once one has already entered the realm of verbal expression, the Sixth Patriarch said: "The mere two characters 'not established' are already literary elaborations.
To speak of 'direct transmission' and 'pointing directly' has already fallen into a secondary concession. As the Sūtra says: "All spoken words belong to skillful means."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "Now tell me, how is it that he hands it over with both hands?"—it is precisely at this moment that he hands it over with both hands.
I fear that the transcribers have erred; it should rather be the phrase "a single line that does not involve the journey. Moreover, what of it?
This is the master’s inquiry, and what follows is the response.
"Every word reveals the Truth; words are not existent. "Every phrase transcends the school; phrases are fundamentally non-existent.
These two lines answer the meaning of "not traversing the path" mentioned above. This clarifies that the Way is fundamentally without words; one borrows words to manifest the Way.
If a practitioner can, with every word, perceive the Truth, then they will not see the existence of words, but will see only the Real.

In principle, this may be called "attaining the meaning while forgetting the words," or "attaining the fish while forgetting the trap. As for the subsequent phrase, the principle is elucidated by means of the textual expressions.
If a practitioner can transcend the source with every sentence and remain non-abiding in principle, they will perceive neither the existence nor the non-existence of phrases.
Yet one perceives only the Way of Central Harmony. The River Elder’s eulogy says: "Where there are forms and seeking, all is delusion;
where there is no shape and no seeing, one falls into partiality and desiccation. How could the majestic and the subtle ever be separated? A single cold radiance illuminates the Great Void.
The character *chao* (超) likely resulted from a scribal error by the recorder; it should be *zhao* (朝). Let the wise examine this further.
The adamantine essence is profoundly still and empty; The secure barrier is firmly held—there is not a single thing.
If you wish for this mountain monk to provide a guiding thread, All of you, take up this talisman for protecting the body.
The first two lines of the above verse are a commentary on the postscript to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. They state that the principle elucidated within this sutra is...
The fundamental substance of True Suchness (tathatā) is the pure, wondrous nature, profoundly still and empty.

Since it is profoundly still and empty, there is not a single thing upon the substance of True Suchness; therefore, the secure barrier is firmly held, allowing no passage for either ordinary beings or sages.
Therefore, Prajñā is like the sword Taie; to touch it is to lose one's body and life. It is like a great mass of fire;
to be scorched by it is to have one's face burned away. In the ten directions there are no walls, and on the four sides there are no gates.
From the five aggregates at the beginning to unsurpassed bodhi at the end, there is not a single dharma in between that is not empty. Thus it is said: "A single thing..."
"There is none. Regarding the latter two lines, the Master’s intention is as follows: "If someone were to ask me, who has thus composed this verse—'The firm barrier is held fast;
there is not a single thing to be found'—and say, 'Please, Master, provide a single thread of passage,' I would say to him:
'If you want this mountain monk to provide a single thread of passage, you all must first withdraw the talisman that guards your own bodies. This refers to [the state of self-attachment].

The ultimate truth expounded within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇīta Sūtra*, if one can comprehend it, is the very dharma for liberation from birth and death—the excellent remedy for transcending the world.
King Yama is originally an impartial sovereign; he does not covet the wealth of the people, but takes only their [lives].

"If the Underworld Offices were to use money for transactions, the poor would die first while the wealthy would remain"—these four lines clarify that the Ten Kings of the Earthly Realm are actually Bodhisattvas manifesting in transformation. Therefore, they are supremely impartial and free from partiality;
externally they manifest a stern and formidable appearance, yet internally they harbor a heart of compassion. Since they are Bodhisattvas, how could they possibly harbor attachment?

Because he dispenses wealth and justice impartially, he is called the Equal Sovereign (*Samavartin*). The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states: "The transformed King Yama commands the ignorant beings within the hells:
'In the past, you committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds; at the end of your lives, you were born here in this Avīci hell.
You should now resolve to attain Bodhicitta and take refuge in the Triple Gem. Then, leading all the ghosts and spirits, he recites 'Namo...'"

There was no Buddha. Relying on the power of the Buddha’s grace, he immediately passed away and was reborn among the Four Heavenly Kings. Having been born in that heaven, he gave rise to the bodhicitta;
therefore, one should know that Yama and the other kings are all great bodhisattvas who teach and transform those in the hells.

Since you are a bodhisattva, how could you cherish wealth? Now, regarding those who commit transgressions, after their lives have ended, the ox-headed jailers will seize their spirits and bring them before King Yama to investigate right and wrong.
At that time, all karmic creditors will come to testify against them; it is impossible to bribe or seek favor by means of money, wealth, or treasures.
"Delivered! Vast and profound darkness; there is no hope for amnesty. Thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and consigns them to hell.
They shall pass through endless kalpas, with no way to seek escape. This matter is not far off, nor does it concern others."
This is precisely what I have done myself and must now experience myself. Though father and son are close, once they stand face-to-face, there is no one who can take one’s place.
As it is said: "The clear and manifest path of justice is ultimately difficult to conceal; the dark and hidden private sentiments will surely be known.
An ancient worthy said: "It is said that cultivation does not depend on being late; this life may still have a future life ahead. Yet, the retribution of the three miserable realms—"
Five thousand kalpas have passed; how much time has it been since you emerged from the realm of clarity?
In the West, the scenery of Sukhāvatī is profound and serene; jeweled nets radiate light for hundreds of thousands of fathoms.
Bodhisattvas dwell as neighbors, discussing the wondrous meaning, while Śrāvakas act as companions, chanting the perfect sound.
The first two lines state that the scenery of the western land is profound and serene.

The Buddha said that within the buddha-field of Amitābha Buddha, there are further immeasurable jeweled nets covering that land, all made of gold, silver, pearls, and hundreds of thousands of various precious gems.

It was wondrously adorned. On all four sides, jeweled bells hung down, their radiant colors flashing with a brilliance extending for a million *yojanas*, reaching the height of ultimate magnificence and beauty.
There was also a natural breeze of virtue that moved gently; it was neither cold nor hot, soft and mild, flowing neither too fast nor too slow.
It blew upon the various jewel trees and the various jewel bells, producing immeasurable subtle sounds.
The sublime sound of the Dharma spreads the fragrance of ten thousand kinds of refined and pure virtues.
Those who hear it find that the dust of afflictions and habitual tendencies naturally do not arise; when the wind touches their bodies, they all attain bliss.
The final two lines refer to the world of the West, where the great Bodhisattvas and the assembly of Śrāvakas, having finished bathing, either stand upon the ground or [proceed to] preach the Dharma.

There were those who recited the sutras, those who expounded the sutras, and those who transmitted the sutras; or else, in the midst of the void, there were those who lectured on the sutras, recited the sutras, expounded the sutras, and transmitted the sutras.
Among them were those who had attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, up to those who had attained the stage of *arhat*, as well as Bodhisattvas who had reached the stage of non-retrogression.
All of them were joyful, contented, and delighted, having been able to associate with these superior beings.
Virtuous people gather together in one place; they dwell as neighbors to Bodhisattvas and act as companions to Śrāvakas. They discuss the sublime meaning and jointly manifest the perfect sound.
You virtuous ones, listen briefly to this: the Great Mahāprajñā is never absent from walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
This section [of the title] of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Liang" means "good. "Yuan" (conditions) refers to the conditions for lecturing and listening to the teaching.
"Zhong" (assembly) refers to the practitioners of the fourfold assembly present in the congregation. Listen briefly.
The word "this" (ge) is the master’s exhortation to the assembly: listen with earnest sincerity. This Great Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the very essence of true emptiness and great wisdom;
it is the authentic scripture inherently present within the nature of all things. Hitherto, it has been buried in the dust of ignorance, and people have remained deluded, unaware of it.
I now urge you to listen and believe with earnest sincerity. Regarding "walking, standing, sitting, and lying down," this Great...
The wondrous nature of Prajñā-tathatā resides solely within each person; it is never absent from the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—whether in motion or stillness.
A great man said: "Within every mind dwells the Dharma King; walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, he is manifest and majestic.
To seek him through sound or see him through form is but empty turmoil. It would make Meng Bala of East Village laugh until he fell over."
It is inherently possessed by every person; it belongs neither to self nor to others. May all people realize this, lest you let this present life slip away.
This section demonstrates the aforementioned great wisdom of *prajñā*. Since it is never absent whether sitting or reclining, is it not inherently possessed by every person?
Because the self-nature is perfectly luminous, it belongs neither to self nor to others. As an ancient master said: "The house-style of the signless."
It is inherently manifest; the ground of every person’s mind radiates light, suddenly opening up the treasury of one's own spiritual powers.
This is for those who transcend the world and enjoy inexhaustible benefit. Those among you who can realize this are the essential people of this school; you must not miss this principle.
Since it is inherently possessed by each person, you ought to realize it directly and immediately. Therefore, it is said: "In this life, do not let it slip away."
It is said: "If this body does not attain liberation in this present life, when else shall it be delivered?
The Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*) is supreme; the supreme is the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Letting go of all, one beholds Amitābha."
This section clarifies the title of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. The first two phrases clarify that "Mahā" signifies the greatest.

This "Mahā" refers to the fact that True Emptiness is the greatest; it indicates the essence of Mahāyāna within the gate of the suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*), which is the "greatness of essence" (*tattva-mahattva*). This is precisely the mind of all Buddhas and sentient beings. Thus, this "greatest" is Mahā.
The term "Great" (*mahā*) reiterates the supreme meaning mentioned above. It indicates the characteristics of the Mahāyāna within the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind;
specifically, it refers to the "greatness of essence" (*tattva-mahat*) among the [three aspects of] essence, characteristics, and function.

Now, regarding the single dharma of the One Mind, the reason for stating its greatness of essence twice is that the greatness of Prajñā-wisdom pervades the entire Dharma-realm, penetrating as subtly as a minute speck of dust, while remaining free from all constraints.
In all those who realize the state of sagehood, the wondrous essence is concentrated and eternal; though they enter death and emerge in birth, their true mind remains unchanging.
It encompasses the vast without exterior and penetrates the minute without interior; thus it is said: "Emptiness is the greatest. The following two lines clarify the supreme function of *prajñā*.
For this Great *Prajñā* is the great wisdom capable of emptying [all phenomena] throughout both the mundane and supramundane realms.
This is the dharma of the characteristic of that which is empty. Therefore, the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) are boundless, and Prajñā is limitless.
Why is it that within this context one speaks only of *prajñā* and not of "characteristics"? It is because by citing the subject that empties, one reveals the object that is emptied.

This is precisely the characteristic of "Extensiveness" (*lakṣaṇa*) among the Three Greats within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing. If there is a practitioner who possesses this great wisdom of *prajñā*, regarding the four...
Within the midst of majestic deportment, it suddenly appears before one’s eyes; one immediately attains transcendence from the river of birth-and-death craving and reaches the other shore of Bodhi.
Letting go of the hand, one beholds the Self-Nature Amitābha; taking a step, one wanders through the Pure Land of Quiescent Light.
This is the "Greatness of Function" among the Three Greatnesses within the gate of arising and ceasing. What is now called Amitābha is precisely the purity of Original Enlightenment.
Suchness is the Buddha of intrinsic nature. A *udumbara* verse says: Transcending the Pure Land, it excels Saha;
A single step back home brings such great joy. Within the Constantly Quiescent Light, all is decisively severed; In every atom and every land, one beholds Amitābha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
This sūtra is a portion included within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; therefore, Xuanzang once said: "If one were to recount its contents in full detail..."
It is said that this exceeds two hundred thousand verses; yet if one extracts its essential pivot, the principle is exhausted in these fourteen lines.
As for the Heart Sūtra, which reveals the sublime essence to which all returns, it is the very core of the six hundred fascicles. Therefore, it is called the "Heart Sūtra."
Now, one who wishes to realize the supreme Mahāyāna must possess the adamantine right eye. Observe how Śākyamuni and Subhūti manifest great capacity and exercise great function:
they gather the seven treasures equal in size to Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and grind the sands of a trichiliocosm into atoms;
even if one were to practice such giving throughout an entire *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, within the Sole Vehicle of the Supreme Vehicle, not a single dharma can be obtained. Directly...

It causes the courage of gods and humans to fail and the hearts of demons and heretics to grow cold; all are able to risk their lives to take up this task, yet it remains as ever—a ten-thousand-mile expanse of white clouds.
This is the master of the lineage’s instruction for practitioners. Now, those who wish to realize the supreme Mahāyāna, the Diamond Sūtra:
This sutra is the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna; it is none other than the Great Wisdom of Prajñā.

One must possess the adamantine, firm, and indestructible (*akṣaya*) eye of correct vision to illuminate and exhaustively penetrate the emptiness of the essence of all phenomena, reaching their very depths until nothing remains unclear.
Only then will one truly realize this Mahāyāna path. Observe how Śākyamuni and Subhūti—

Regarding the passage beginning with "Ji-ti" (Subhūti) and so forth: it clarifies that there are nine layers of questions posed by Subhūti, to which the Tathāgata responds with thirty layers of answers, thereby severing twenty-seven doubts; all of these manifest the great capacity and great function [of the Buddha].
As for the phrase "gathering the seven treasures, such as Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains," this refers back to the twenty-fourth section [of the preceding text], concerning the trichiliocosm.

If someone were to take all the Sumeru Kings of Mountains and such heaps of the seven treasures as described above and offer them as alms, their merit would not surpass that of one who, from this sutra, recites even a single four-line verse for others and explains it to them; the latter’s merit is superior to the former.
Even if one were to grind the trichiliocosm into atoms as numerous as those previously mentioned in the thirty divisions, if there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family...
If one were to grind a trichiliocosm into fine dust, would that multitude of dust particles not be numerous?
Suppose someone were to practice giving throughout the entirety of asaṃkhyeya kalpas; this refers back to the thirty-second section mentioned previously.
If there were someone who took the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and used them for giving, it would not be as good as [the following].

The merit of a person’s exposition of even a four-line verse is supreme; as for the "Dharma that cannot be attained" in the Ultimate Vehicle (Agrayāna), this reiterates the preceding dialogue between the Tathāgata and Subhūti to reveal the great capacity and great function [of this teaching].

While giving the seven treasures of the world as an offering yields only conditioned merit and does not transcend birth and death, the Dharma that cannot be attained in the Ultimate Vehicle alone is supreme.

This refers back to the aforementioned Bodhisattva who has resolved upon Bodhicitta. For the sake of others, they expound the four-line verse, not grasping at signs, remaining as suchness and unmoving;
this is precisely the non-attainment of any dharma, and because the mind is unstained, it surpasses the previous merit immeasurably.
As for the phrase "directly causing the gods and humans to lose heart," this clarifies the non-attainment of any dharma.

This principle surpasses the merit of previous acts of giving; it is the most supreme path of the Mahāyāna, not for those of inferior capacity such as humans or devas, nor is it within the reach of celestial māras or external paths. Thus it is said: "The gallbladder fails and the heart grows cold.

As for those who can both sacrifice their lives and take up this responsibility, the teachings of the various schools instruct people to take up the most supreme vehicle by sacrificing their lives. Formerly, Deng...
When Yinfeng was pushing a cart, Mazu sat on the road with both legs stretched out. Yinfeng said, "I beg the Master to withdraw your feet.

Mazu replied, "They are already stretched out; I will not retract them. Yinfeng said, "Once you have advanced, you shall not retreat. Yinfeng then pushed the cart, which rolled over and injured Mazu's feet.
Upon returning to the Dharma Hall, Mazu held an axe in his hand and said, "The monk who just now rolled over and injured the soles of this old monk's feet—"
"Come forth! Feng then stepped out before the Patriarch and extended his neck to receive the blade. The Patriarch threw down the axe.

To thus sacrifice one's life in such a manner of commitment is truly the mark of a Great Man. "As before, ten thousand miles of white clouds" refers to the master first granting and then taking back [the student's realization].
If one can thus sacrifice one's life to commit oneself to this Mahayana Way, there is yet another...
The mind that takes responsibility remains present; therefore, the Master of the Section said, "White clouds ten thousand miles away.
By this principle, as long as there is attachment, one will remain distant by a vast margin. An ancient said: "Baizhang has three secrets: 'Drink tea, take care, and rest.
To directly take responsibility [upon hearing these words]—I dare say you have not yet reached the bottom."
Those who have commented upon this sutra number more than eight hundred families, while those who have versified it do not even fill the fingers of one hand when counted.
Indeed, if an ancient master fell into the state of a wild fox for erring by a single character, then one who misrecites this sutra ought to enter hell.

I, Zongjing, reflect that if I were to enter hell, by what means could I rescue and deliver all sentient beings? Since I am already able to forget my own body for the sake of the Dharma, how could I avoid even the Avīci Hell?
The Celestial One committed a transgression against his father. He brandished a precious sword with reckless force and spoke these verses again:

"To destroy the aspiration for Nirvāṇa, to extinguish the Eye of the True Dharma, to sweep away wisdom and insight, and to sever the life-roots—this is how one may repay the unrepayable kindness and requite the debt that is difficult to discharge."
The reason for this is as follows: this phrase introduces what follows from what precedes it. The Master’s intention is this:
even to directly accept and take responsibility for the Supreme Vehicle is still to be far removed from the ultimate principle; how much more so for those who now interpret this sutra?

There are over eight hundred schools of translators, all of whom merely follow the lines and count the characters, chasing after every phrase and seeking out every word. Is this not indeed far removed? Thus he praises this sutra.
Regarding the phrase "those who did not fill [the fingers when] counting on the fingers": this refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At that time, although there were eight hundred people in the translation hall who understood its meaning, those who were able to compose it into written verses were few;
thus, they did not fill the fingers when counted. There were five who filled the fingers, while only three remained who did not.
This refers to Master Fu, the Elder of Chu, the Head of the Monastic Regulations (Ke-zhu).

As for the statement that "the ancients were wrong by a single word," this is the rhetorical device used by the Head of the Regulations to pose a difficult question. "The ancients" here refers to the former Baizhang.

His "wrong answer" regarding the student's single word resulted in his falling into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes; this was because his insight into the Way was not yet clear and his realization of the nature was not yet perfect.
Their perspectives are biased and one-sided; they rely on the literal text to explain the meaning, yet erroneously cling to false interpretations and perversely expound the Sage’s intent.

Therefore, at the time of their questions and answers, they cannot avoid making mistakes. Regarding those who "erroneously versify this sutra and so forth," the phrase "and so forth" refers to such individuals.
Relying on his own natural intelligence and his proficiency in literary meaning, he gathered the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs;
adding his own literary embellishments as a mere imitation, he compiled them into volumes, assigned them titles, and circulated them throughout the world.
If one lacks moral virtue and precepts, yet claims to have realized the stage of seeing the Truth, all such statements are erroneous and cause the subversion of the True Dharma.
This is called deceptive talk regarding Prajñā; it blinds the eyes of sentient beings, leading them into the Avīci Hell where they must swallow iron balls.
There will be no time of escape. I now provide a structural analysis (*ko-p'an*) of this sutra;

I only fear that those with ordinary sentiments and shallow understanding might use their conceptualizing minds to measure the inconceivable wisdom of the Tathāgata, thereby committing errors and incurring sin for themselves.
Therefore, I cite the "Erroneous Answer" and "Mistaken Verses" to pose my questions. As for the *Zongjing* [Record]’s own reflection on not entering hell and so forth, this—
This is the primary point of the treatise, answering the objection in person: "If I do not enter hell, by what means shall I rescue and deliver all sentient beings?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, "I shall re-enter the three miserable realms to uproot their suffering and distress;
among all destinies, I shall liberate those not yet liberated and deliver those not yet delivered. Since he was thus able to sacrifice his own body for the sake of the Dharma and so forth...
The Master’s intention was this: "Since I am now propagating the Great Dharma, I must certainly disregard my physical form; how could I avoid the five heinous crimes that would fill the heavens?

In the past, Devadatta pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha, drew blood from the Buddha's body, struck the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā in the eye with his fist until her eyes were gouged out, and caused a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha—having committed these three grave offenses of the five heinous crimes, he entered [hell].
[Regarding] the Avīci Hell, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "Devadatta and you are of equal nature as brothers by blood; you should inquire after his well-being.
Ānanda, having received this command, went toward the Avīci Hell and inquired, saying: "Are you at ease? He replied: "Although I am in hell, it is like the bliss of the third dhyāna heaven.
The Buddha further commanded him to ask: "Will you return from this hell? He replied: [He did not reply.]
He said, "I shall wait for the World-Honored One to come to this hell; once he has arrived, I will leave the prison. Ānanda said, "The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the three realms;
how could he have any portion [of karma] that leads him into hell? Devadatta replied, "If the Buddha has no portion that leads him into hell, how can I have any time to leave hell?
This was because Devadatta was a manifestation of great spiritual authority (*mahā-upāya*) for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "Horizontally grasping the precious sword and again reciting the verse": this refers to the Master holding the scales of judgment in his hand to manifest great capacity and great function.
He uses the precious sword as a metaphor for the great wisdom of *prajñā*, which is able to empty away attachment to holy understandings and emotional clinging; thus, he once again recites the verse.

The following passage is in verse form: "To destroy the mind of *nirvāṇa* and extinguish the Eye of the True Dharma" means that the commentator [uses] the Vajra-jewel sword to utterly crush and annihilate the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* and the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma transmitted by the Tathāgata.
It further states that the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, faith, and understanding are likewise swept away entirely, leaving nothing but the severing of the life-root.

There is no abiding distinction between ordinary and sage. The Sixth Patriarch spoke in verse to Zhichang: "To see not a single dharma while maintaining a view of non-existence is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun.
To be unaware of a single dharma while guarding a knowledge of emptiness is like lightning flashing in the great void.
This seeing-knowledge arises in an instant; to mistake it is to never have understood the skillful means. You should, in a single thought..."
"Suddenly realizing what is not [the truth], one's own spiritual radiance is constantly manifest; thus one is able to repay the unrepaid kindness"—this is the intent of the commentator (*kejiā*).

It means that by employing the wisdom of urgent application, I sweep away the sentiments of sacred understanding (*shèngjiě*) to repay the unrepaid kindness of our Buddha and to requite the debt of virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs that is so difficult to repay. This is why I preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
Fulfilling the Buddha’s vows and repaying the Buddha’s kindness;

forty-nine years of proclamations, five thousand scrolls of verbal explanations—all exhausted in the wondrous clarity of a single phrase beyond the limit of Vītarāga. The horn-bent mud ox sleeps in the snow.
The first two lines clarify that from the Buddha’s appearance in the world until his passing forty-nine years later, he preached the Dharma in over three hundred assemblies.
These teachings comprise the Three Vehicles and Five Doctrines, all of which were spoken according to the capacities of sentient beings;

thus, they constitute a public proclamation, like an unsealed letter from a Son of Heaven. Together they comprise more than five thousand fascicles, all of which consist of verbal explanations expressed through literary form.
Characters (*akṣara*) are the substance of the teaching that expresses; True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the rational nature that is expressed. Therefore it is said: "words express.
The latter two phrases clarify the phrase "the wondrously luminous true mind": it cannot be fully contained within palm-leaf manuscripts and transcends the era of Bhīṣmagarjitasvara.
With this mind, it is just like the hornless earthen ox sleeping in the snow—this is the Honored One’s clarity.
"Noble one, you dwell entirely on the other shore; the position of correctness is of a single color.
These four lines of verse were spoken when a monk asked Baoyan, "What is the Teaching? Baoyan replied, "The palm leaves cannot contain it all. This is why Danxia composed these four lines as a verse.
The physical radiance of Amitābha Buddha Is like five Mount Sumerus;
The white tuft between his brows curls gracefully, And the blue-black hair atop his head spirals upward.
These four lines praise the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and his brilliance, intending to cause the practitioner to give rise to contemplative visualization. If one can...
If one visualizes each [aspect] clearly and distinctly, one will immediately attain birth in the highest of the high grades and personally behold the Buddha.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The body of Amitāyus Buddha possesses a golden radiance like that of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of *yama-devas*.
He is sixty million billion *yojanas* tall. His white tuft of hair curls to the right, as high as five Mount Sumerus. Thus it is said.
The Buddha’s eyes are like blue lotuses; his pores emit light like the four great oceans; his halo is as vast as a hundred billion trichiliocosms, like Mount Sumeru;
and he is fully endowed with the eighty-four thousand marks and signs, surpassing the marks and signs of all other Buddhas.
Therefore, it is said: "His various marks are majestic and lofty."
The occasion for the completion and distribution of the chanting of the Golden Sutra:

may the merit of this day be boundlessly bestowed upon all those gathered here, so that they may together cultivate and realize [enlightenment], and the seeds of perfuming through seeing and hearing may become fully perfected.

Regarding the first two lines, the commentator’s intent is as follows: "I now provide an exegesis, perform the chanting, and establish the structural divisions of this single fascicle of the Golden [Sutra]."
The Diamond Sūtra: On the Causes and Conditions for the Merit of the Impending Dissolution.
