Even by means of a single four-line verse, dedicating it to the assembly on this day yields merit hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions of times greater than the gift of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
How much more so the merit of this entire sūtra—how could it ever be exhausted? Therefore, it is said: "Blessings are boundless. This refers to the latter two lines.
The Master universally exhorts the assembled multitude to cultivate and advance, intending to say:

if there are practitioners who wish to cultivate and realize [the Way], although this single sutra contains thirty-two sections and twenty-seven doubts, therein, the practice of abiding in cultivation and subduing [the mind] is the essential core of cultivation and realization.
If one can truly do so—whether by reciting the Buddha’s name or by investigating [the nature of mind]—...
Chan. It primarily requires first subduing the deluded mind and subsequently cultivating the practice of non-abiding, thereby dwelling securely in the Mahāyāna bodhicitta.

Therefore, by means of these Mahāyāna Vajra seeds, may all who now see or hear them be perfumed by these seeds, so that they are stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses as the seed for attaining Buddhahood. Thus it is said: "Pervasive."
It is complete.
The site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is perfect and inconceivable. May everyone apply their minds and faculties to recite and chant the Golden Sūtra. The Buddhas and sages know all;
may they offer their supreme blessings.
May the Emperor’s sacred life last ten thousand years. May all sentient beings of the dharma realm be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Having completed the sequential proclamation of this scripture in thirty-two sections and finished the analytical exposition and chanting, [the assembly] concludes.
Therefore it is said: "Perfectly complete. This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is a discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); hence it is called "inconceivable.
It also exhorts one to practice, for every person ought to apply their mind toward this inconceivable Dharma. As for "capacity" (*ki*):...
The "bow trigger" (nǔyá) is the subtle function of the mind; thus it is called the "mental mechanism" (xīnjī).
The phrase "I shall expound and chant this Golden Sūtra, O All-Knowing Buddha and Sage" is the commentator’s appeal for the Buddha’s witness and certification. The intent is:

"As I now explain and proclaim this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I look to the All-Knowing Buddha and Sage for secret empowerment and protection, for by means of this sūtra, all [phenomena]..."
The Buddha and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharmas of all Buddhas all emerge from this sutra;
for it is a sutra protected by all Buddhas, and thus when it is recited, the Buddha’s holy and universal wisdom is invoked.
Regarding the prayer for the Emperor’s holy longevity of ten thousand years: this sutra possesses inexhaustible merit, and through it, one prays for the prolongation of the Emperor’s holy life.
Boundless! May the capital domain be eternally secure. It may truly be said that the four seas sing in praise, sharing the era of King Tang of Yin;
the eight directions drum their bellies with joy, rejoicing together in the age of Yao and Shun.

As for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, by means of the inexhaustible merit of this sutra, I vow that all sentient beings within the ten Dharma-realms shall be reborn together in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Homage to the One Vehicle School (*Ekayāna-nikāya*). To the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* (*Anantārtha-sūtra*), the *Sūtra of True Emptiness and Wondrous Existence*, and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
"Homage" (*namas*) is a term of reverent devotion. Regarding the "One Vehicle School": as stated previously, it was taught for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle;
thus, one knows that this scripture is subsumed within the One Vehicle. As the master’s analytical exposition is nearing its conclusion, he takes refuge.
This is the Great Way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This One Vehicle encompasses immeasurable subtle meanings and *Gaṅgā*-sands of inherent virtues.
As the preceding passage states: "All Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharmas of all Buddhas..."

All emerge from this sutra; hence it is called the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*. Regarding "wondrous existence within true emptiness," the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states that within the manifestation of a single phenomenon and a single principle, and amidst every movement and stillness, there is nothing that does not embody immeasurable meanings.
The five aggregates are themselves nirvana; wondrous existence is itself true emptiness, and nirvana is itself the true emptiness of the five aggregates.
This is precisely the wondrous existence (*wuyou*). One may understand this by analogy with the four great elements, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and even unsurpassed *bodhi*.
To realize the path of the One Vehicle, to possess immeasurable meanings, and for the two truths to be harmoniously integrated—all these are the power of the wisdom of *prajñā*.
Therefore, one knows that the principles and patterns of the words of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* are all the wondrous existence of true emptiness.

I prostrate and pray that the sound of the sutras may ring out clearly, ascending to reach the vault of heaven; that the *brahmā*-language may chime with precision, descending to penetrate the netherworld.

"I prostrate and pray" (*fùyuàn*) means to remain hidden or concealed; it refers to the matters contained within one's heart. "Pray" (*yuàn*) is a term expressing longing, aspiration, and upward-looking hope.
Regarding "the sound of the sutras rings out clearly" (*jīngshēng lángláng*): the *Xúnzǐ* states that on Mount Kunlun there is the *lánggān* tree, which resembles *liúlí* (lapis lazuli).
Crystal is five-colored and its sound is beautiful when struck; now I pray that this sound of reciting the sutras shall ascend to the highest heavens.
"Spring" (chun) refers to the azure sky; its color being a deep azure, it is the very appearance of heaven.
"Ling-ling" is a term from the language of Brahmā, referring to the sound of the sutras. Regarding "ling-ling," the *Da-xuan-jing* states: [text follows].
It is resonant and clear. May the beautiful sound of this recitation reach down to the netherworlds, where there are many sentient beings suffering from their transgressions.

May they all receive these excellent conditions for the dissolution of their sins. I universally pray that wherever the sound of the sutra reaches, all may together cease their suffering, depart from pain to attain joy, and transcend to the other shore. The following text extends this prayer for the cessation of suffering.
For these reasons:
first, may the blades fall from the mountain of knives; second, may the points of the sword-trees be blunted; third, may the flames of the furnace coals be withdrawn;
fourth, may the waves of the rivers be stilled.

These four vows are prayers that the four sufferings within the realm of the hells may forever cease. Regarding the first two vows concerning those who fall upon blades and are crushed on mountain peaks of knives, the *Huìdēng* (Lamp of Wisdom) states:
"Who could have forged these blades and mountains of knives? The flowers contain the water of virtue; they do not bloom for such [sinners].
Good causes must ultimately meet with good conditions, yet evil deeds make it difficult to escape evil realms. One knows the cause by discerning the fruit. Thus one perceives [the truth].
Not yet having recognized the root, one bestows *prajñā* to escape the suffering of the Mountain of Knives; by transcribing the Golden Sūtra, one heals the wounds of the Sword-Tree Hell.

Regarding the latter two lines, which speak of "gathering the flames and calming the waves," an ancient worthy said: "Yin and yang have their ultimate limits, yet water and fire are devoid of sentience.
If one practices goodness, the flames will vanish and the furnace grow cold; if one cultivates virtue, the seas will be tranquil and the rivers clear. This is due to the mind of anger and resentment.
Thus, one encounters the burning of glowing coals due to a deceitful mind, and sinks into the drowning of turbulent waves because of that same intent.

By relying on the power of the Buddha, one is rescued from being boiled in the cauldrons of boiling brine; by depending on the merit of the sutra, one leaves behind the drifting and submerging of the billows.
May the hungry ghosts with needles in their throats be forever freed from hunger and emptiness; may those with scales, shells, feathers, or fur no longer devour one another.
May malevolent stars and portents be swept away from the gates of heaven, and may strange beasts and spectral *chi* demons hide away in the crevices of the earth.
Regarding the "Needle-Necked Hungry Ghosts": among these hungry ghosts in the realm of the departed, there are nine types who, by receiving this grace, shall be freed from suffering.

This clarifies that those who were stingy and greedy have constantly suffered from hunger and emptiness for a thousand lifetimes; those who obstructed the giving of others have perpetually encountered flames for ten thousand kalpas.
As the *Huìdēng lùn* (Treatise on the Lamp of Wisdom) says: "To tread upon clouds and mists and drink the nectar of immortality is not bestowed by another; to lie amidst smoke..."
They burn and devour pus and blood; all this is what they have summoned for themselves. Whether one ascends or sinks through merit or sin, there is not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.

By being stingy with precious coins and exchanging them for coarse food to provide for the Sangha, one incurs the retribution of constantly eating excrement and being obstructed from the benefits of giving.

[The case of] the one whose needle fell into his throat who, through the power of the Buddha, was able to be reborn in heaven: those with scales, shells, feathers, or fur—this refers to the vow regarding the realm of animals.
Having received this grace, one is freed from the suffering of mutual devouring. Thus, the Buddha’s seal says:

"The various classes of beings with scales, shells, or feathers—their minds are no different from the Buddha's; it is only because they initially applied their minds wrongly that their heads and horns have become distinct in this life.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When a person dies, they become a sheep; when a sheep dies, they become a person. The *Zhuan* (Tradition) says:

When a dog dies, it becomes a human; when a human dies, it becomes a dog. In the past, Zhao Wenruo recited the name of the Buddha but once, which caused all those he had killed to attain transcendence.
As for having five nails driven into one’s body, one should contemplate the suffering and harbor fear because of it.
Regarding "malevolent stars and strange portents," this vow seeks to pacify all such extraordinary anomalies in the heavens. *Leng* (The Lankavatara Sutra).
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In this Sahā world, there are eighty-four thousand strange and malevolent stars.
When they appear in the world in various forms, they can bring about all manner of calamities and epidemics for sentient beings.

By receiving the Buddha’s majestic power and relying on the efficacy of this sūtra, these baleful omens shall be extinguished. Regarding "strange beasts and numinous *chī* spirits," this refers to the demons and monsters that plague the human realm.
This is eternal rest. Formerly, on Mount Baiwei in the region of Shu during the Tang dynasty, there were many tigers and leopards.
During the Guanghua era, there was a scholar named Wei who was selected for appointment as the Magistrate of Bannan. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

On his way to his post, he reached Nixi and encountered a woman leading two children; he accompanied the scholar up the mountain. As the travelers cried out in alarm upon seeing the woman, they realized she was actually a large, crimson tiger.
Two small tigers followed behind, hesitating for a while before parting ways with Wei and departing. Wei was ultimately unaware of this, which was due to the power of his upholding the sutra.
Furthermore, there was the Sui monk Fachong, who was devoted to the sutras and treatises and was especially proficient in the Lotus Sutra.
When he reached Lushan in Xiangzhou, a mountain spirit transformed into a lady and went to the temple to request the precepts; she subsequently donated the mountain where she resided.

He established a temple and withdrew to a separate mountain. This, too, was due to the power of upholding the sutra; thus, extraordinary beasts and numinous *chī* spirits were moved to hide within the earth’s caves.

It may be said that by recollecting the *Vajracchedikā*, he was protected by a red tiger and guided along his path, and by chanting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he caused the mountain sprites to abandon their site and move elsewhere.
May those imprisoned and bound receive the descent of heavenly grace; may those whose bodies are entangled by illness soon encounter effective medicine;
may the blind and the deaf see and hear; may the lame and the mute be able to walk and speak; and may pregnant women have their children and themselves reunited in harmony.

May those who have traveled afar witness their early return to their home and country; may the poor, the lowly, and sentient beings of evil karma—those who have mistakenly killed or intentionally harmed all manner of enemies and grievances—have them all entirely dissolved and released.
May the vajra power cleanse and purify body and mind, and may the light of prajñā descend upon this precious throne.
With every step raised and every step taken, may all places be the ground of the Buddha.

This is the preface. It is my universal wish that all manner of sufferings and hardships for those among humanity may, by relying on the majestic power and merit of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, be entirely extinguished.
First, regarding the prisoner: formerly, during the Tang dynasty, there was the monk Shenyan.
He was accused by others of robbery and banditry, and was bound in prison. For over a month, he recited the sutras with singular sincerity;

suddenly, during the night, a golden light filled the entire prison, his shackles and fetters fell away of their own accord, and he was subsequently granted pardon. Thus it is said: "I pray that heavenly grace may descend.
Second, regarding those afflicted by disease: Formerly, during the Tang dynasty, Qiang Bodai suffered from a hereditary foul illness for two hundred generations.
He had reached adulthood. When Bo-da was just beginning to wear the cap of manhood, he fell ill with wind-leprosy (feng-lai).
His parents, believing it incurable, sent him into the mountains. His father packed provisions and left Bo-da beneath a cliff before departing. Suddenly, a monk passed by;

seeing his injuries, he said to him, "If you recite four lines of verse from within the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you may perhaps be freed from this suffering. Bo-da accepted [the instruction].

After he had been instructed in this recitation for several days, his sores gradually dried up. A former monk arrived again and gave him a handful of green grass, saying, "You may use this to wash the sores.
He then boiled the grass in water to bathe with, and his body became completely clean; all the sores and ailments vanished. Thus it is said.
This was truly meeting excellent medicine early on. It may be said that he shone light upon the hells; by receiving imperial grace, he was spared from punishment.
By reciting gāthās, he eliminated calamities, encountering a virtuous elder who administered the medicine. As for the "Three Blind Men," they lived during the Tang dynasty in Jiangling.

There was a man named Senghu, the son of a powerful official. Because his father had accidentally injured a divine python while listening to a sutra, the creature lodged a grievance in the underworld and appeared in a dream to [the father].
The wife transcribed scriptures to deliver a divine python to rebirth. Having no money to pay for the transcription, she sold her son to a merchant from Shu.

The mother obtained the money to transcribe the scriptures and dedicate the merit toward his liberation. She kept one scroll for herself and recited it for nearly thirty years, vowing that mother and son might meet again.
The mother, due to longing for her son, lost the sight of both eyes. She wandered from place to place begging for food.
Later, when Saṃgharakṣita returned to Jiangling and performed a vegetarian feast to offer posthumous prayers for his parents, the mother happened to be begging for food there.

When son and mother met, he immediately burned incense and said, "If there is indeed filial piety, let my tongue lick my eyes and they shall both become clear. He rinsed his mouth with water and licked his mother's eyes with his tongue; her eyes both became clear.
He was restored to his former state; thus it is said: "The blind gained sight. Fourth, regarding the mute:
Once there was a man who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* inside his room. A wicked man outside the wall, harboring hatred, slandered him.
Later, he received the retribution of becoming mute. The man repented, saying: "Because I slandered the sutra, I have incurred this evil retribution. From now on, I shall repent my transgressions."
He recited the *Sūtra on Praising the Good*. At night, he was visited by Subhūti, who told him: "Because you slandered the *Prajñāpāramitā*, you have received such retribution.
He caused the man's tongue to protrude and cut it with a knife; immediately, the man was able to speak.
Subsequently, he left the household life to enter the mountains and practice the Way. Thus it is said: "The mute were able to speak. This may be called unwearied perseverance in one’s resolve, which—
The blind regained their clear vision; through sincere and tireless devotion, those who had lost the power of speech were restored to speech.
As for the "Five Sons and Their Mother in a Circle," in the past during the Song dynasty, there was a laywoman of the Wang clan who was pregnant with her sixth child.

For twenty-eight months she had been unable to give birth; fearing that neither mother nor child might survive, she commissioned monks to print and distribute one thousand copies of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and provided a meal for one thousand monks. That night, she dreamed of a Vajrapāṇi who pointed his mallet at her abdomen.
Upon waking, she suddenly gave birth to two sons. Lady Wang, having achieved the blessing of both mother and children being safe and sound, could not contain her joy and celebration.
When she reached the age of sixty-one, she passed away without illness. Thus it is said: "Mother and child were reunited;
this may be called the power of the Vajra, which caused mother and child to be whole once more, and the merit of Prajñā, which enabled the mother and son to meet again."

Sixth, regarding soldiers returning home: In the past, during the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Chu Xilun who, due to the chaos, was captured by the Qiang and conscripted into a military garrison in the north of the Yellow River.
He served there for nine years, and his family had no news of him. His wife, out of devotion to her husband, spent money to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
for every single character she wrote, she joined her palms and recited the name of the Buddha once. That night...
While he was engaged in battle on the front lines, he was suddenly caught in a wind and rainstorm and did not know where to go;
he saw only a great beam of light, like a leading torch. Following the light with measured steps, he traversed a vast plain and immediately arrived home, where husband and wife met again.
He then opened his scripture case and found that the scriptures were still damp. Thus it is said: "Returning early to one's home and kingdom. (7. During the Tang Dynasty)
There was a wealthy merchant who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and always carried the scripture with him.

While traveling abroad for trade, he stayed overnight on a sea island. A group of merchants seized his wealth and murdered him, binding him with ropes, placing him in a large wicker cage, and weighing it down with a massive stone.
Along with the scripture, they sank them into the sea and departed by ship at dawn. That sea...
There was an island where a monastery stood. That evening, the monks heard the sound of someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from beneath the seabed.
Finding this strange, they ordered a skilled swimmer to enter the water and investigate. There, he saw an old man reading the sūtra inside a cage;
the swimmer hauled him up to the surface. When the monk asked him why he was there, the old man replied, "I was killed and cast into the water."
Realizing he was within a cage, he suddenly found himself in a palace, where food was constantly brought to him and he lived in peace and freedom;

this was surely due to the spiritual efficacy of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He subsequently entered a temple to leave the household life. It may be said that his nine years as a soldier [were spent in vain].
Having obtained the light of the sutra, they were led back home. A single act of sincerity by a merchant moved the power of the monk, who pulled his basket out of the water.
Regarding those who are poor and lowly, this refers to the previous section on "Purifying Karmic Obstacles":

"If one is despised by others, it is because of the karmic offenses of that person's past lives which should have caused them to fall into the evil realms; because people of the present age now despise them, [the retribution of their] past lives..."
Their sinful karma is immediately extinguished, and they shall also attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Therefore, it may be said that those who were killed or accidentally injured receive the extraordinary merit of Prajñā-pāramitā, whereby their souls are restored and their life spans are further increased;
furthermore, by relying on the wondrous power of Vajra, their karmic enmities are unraveled and they achieve rebirth. That all such [karmas] are dissolved and released is the summary.
This is the meaning of the preceding passage. "The vajra power washes away body and mind; the majestic light of prajñā shines upon the precious throne.

These four lines clarify that the majestic light of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā bestows its grace upon the assembly gathered here, such that their bodies and minds become pure, they are free from all illness and suffering, and no calamities arise. Furthermore, it is a prayer for the Dharma hall, the assembly, and the precious throne.

Do not allow external māras to cause disturbance. As for the statement that "every lifting and placing of the feet is the ground of the Buddha," this is because the power of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* causes all those in the assembly to experience every lifting and placing of their feet as the ground of the Buddha.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "When a son of the Buddha dwells on this ground, it is the enjoyment of the Buddha. Constantly...
While remaining therein, whether walking, sitting, or lying down,
I further pray that my seven generations of deceased ancestors may leave suffering behind and be reborn in heaven, and that they may be completely liberated from the karmic pains of the hells.

This is the section on families. By the power of this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, it is universally prayed that the seven generations of deceased ancestors of each person may all receive its benefit.
The first section concerns those who leave suffering behind to be reborn in heaven;

it refers to the time of the Song dynasty when Ren Guan-cha transcribed the Great Teaching of the expressive words (*neng-quan*), thereby avoiding the arrival of the punishment of money and staff upon his person, and [saw] his parents in his dreams.
He was reborn in the celestial palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Regarding the next section, "Liberation from the Suffering of Sin": This refers to Wang of Mingzhou during the Song dynasty.
When Yama granted him a seat, he recited the Golden Sūtra; the anguish of hell ceased at once. By imperial decree, he was commanded to return to life.
He applied himself with diligence to the recitation of the Buddha’s name and, at the end of his life, attained the Pure Land in person.

By means of these inexhaustible merits, may I repay the four debts of gratitude above and provide sustenance for those in the three realms of existence below, so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together ascend to perfect enlightenment.
The intention of the commentator is this: "I now, by means of this, have categorized, judged, and expounded upon the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*; may its merit never be exhausted."
Virtue is that which repays, above, the grace of Heaven and Earth for providing shelter and sustenance; the grace of the sun and moon for their illuminating presence;
the grace of sovereigns and kings for providing land and water; and the grace of parents for giving birth and nurturing. Thus, they are called the "Four Graces.

Furthermore, by means of the inexhaustible merit of Prajñā, one provides support below for the three realms of existence (trayaḥ-bhava), desiring to [liberate] those within the realms of form, desire, and formlessness—the very causes of the triple world (traidhātuka).

Because the fruit has not yet been forgotten, it belongs to the realm of existence (*bhava*). As for the phrase "sentient beings of the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-sattva*), this is the general dedication;
the Master of the Section intends for sentient beings of the ten dharma-realms to receive the majestic radiance of this *prajñā* and together ascend to perfect enlightenment.

The *Gāthā of the Old Man of the River* says: Like a hungry man finding food, a thirsty man finding drink; A sick man finding recovery, one oppressed by heat finding coolness; A poor man finding treasure, an infant seeing his mother;
A drifting boat reaching the shore, a solitary traveler returning home; Encountering sweet rain during a drought, a land possessing loyal and virtuous men;
The four barbarian tribes folding their hands in submission, the eight directions coming to surrender. In every instance it is thus; in every thing it is fully revealed. Throughout all time...

The sacred hells and heavens—east, west, south, and north—require no deliberation. All beings throughout the realms as numerous as the atoms and sands of lands enter entirely into the great adamantine site of enlightenment.

This is the verse of the Old Man of Yefu Creek. It consists of twenty lines in total and elucidates the great wisdom of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, which pervades all mundane and supramundane phenomena without exception. This verse is an expression of joy and praise.
I have now encountered this Golden Sutra of Prajñā. It is like a hungry person eating the exquisite rice of the Gandhavyūha, or like a thirsty person drinking the jade nectar of ambrosia;
it is like a sick person meeting the King of Medicine, Sudarśana, and being instantly cured, or like one encountering the moonlight of the Moon-Loving One and suddenly becoming cool and refreshed;
it is like a pauper obtaining the divine wish-fulfilling jewel, or like an infant beholding Prajñā.
Their biological mother [is like] a compassionate boat that carries the four classes of beings directly to the other shore;

the Guiding Teacher receives those of the nine grades and leads them straight to the Lotus Land. It is like encountering sweet rain after a long drought, or meeting by chance in a foreign land. Thus we know:

when a state possesses loyal and virtuous subjects, the myriad kingdoms offer their congratulations. As for the "Four Barbarians," these are the barbarian peoples from beyond the borders. By means of the Central...

The state maintains the orthodox tradition of robes and caps, handed down from generation to generation; this is called the "Middle Kingdom. The four directions beyond the extreme frontiers of this Middle Kingdom are called the "Four Barbarians.
As the sovereign state holds the orthodox lineage, the Four Barbarians come to offer tribute; thus it is said that [the ruler] merely folds his hands while the eight regions [of the world] submit.
The bordering states of the eight directions, upon reaching the end of each year, all submit their memorial tablets to the Central Kingdom; this is called "coming to offer allegiance.
It may be said that when Yao and Shun possessed virtue, the four seas came as guests; when Tang and Wu practiced benevolence, the eight directions folded their hands in submission.
This metaphor refers to sentient beings. Once they obtain this Dharma of Prajñā, there is nothing among the Four Great Vows or the Eightfold Noble Path that is not fully proclaimed.

Furthermore, every single thing is entirely True Suchness-wisdom; every object completely manifests the mind of the ancient Buddhas. Ordinary beings and sages of past and present share the same essence;
hell and heaven are both one True Reality. East, west, south, and north are simply the Road to Chang’an.
"Without using deliberation, see the person themselves. The Master of the Ritual (ke-ka) further made this vow:
"May all sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms of this Buddha-field and the sands of the Ganges, together clarify the essence of Prajñā-vajra-wisdom. Therefore, it is said:
"Together realizing the Great Vajra Maṇḍala."
The sufferings of the three miserable realms are forever stilled; The six destinies cease following the causes of drowning.
Sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges awaken to True Suchness; All living beings ascend to the other shore.
These four lines are universally dedicated by the Master of the Text. I now dedicate the merit of this analysis of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
I vow that those in the hells—those in the three realms of the sword-path, the fire-path, and the blood-path—may be moistened by this grace and forever find the cessation of their suffering.
Furthermore, I vow for all sentient beings across the realm of gods, the realm of humans, the realm of asuras, the realm of hell-beings, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of animals:
that the initial transition toward these destinies constitutes the cause, while reaching the subsequent destinies constitutes the fruit. May [all beings]...
Entering the six realms of existence, one receives various bodies; now I vow that these six realms shall cease their turbulent submergence. The final two lines concern dedication:
may all sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, fully awaken to the wondrous fruit of True Suchness (tathatā) and together enter the ultimate reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi);
hence it is said they "ascend to the other shore."
"Until the void of space is exhausted, And sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are all exhausted— Since these four dharmas are vast and boundless, May this dedication likewise be so.
This is the master’s summary of the vast dedication, which is like the conduct of Samantabhadra; it uses that which is beyond analogy.

This is an analogy for the meaning of vast and inexhaustible dedication. As long as the realm of space is not exhausted, the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, the karma of sentient beings is not exhausted, and the afflictions of sentient beings are not exhausted, may this dedication of mine never come to an end.
May it continue from moment to moment without interruption, and may my actions of body, speech, and mind never grow weary or exhausted. If these four dharmas are absent...
Exhausted. May all the merit within this present site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), through its dedication, likewise be inexhaustible.
*The Commentary on the Essential Rituals of the Vajra [Ritual]*, Scroll Nine (End).
Postscript to the Commentary on the Essential Points of the Ritual Procedures for the Vajra (*Vajra-vidhi-krama*) Alas!
These ritual procedures for the Vajra of our school were composed by the Chan Master Zongjing. This is because Prajñāpāramitā is the teaching of the Mahāyāna.
It is taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas, revealing the profound essence of the One Vehicle and serving as the source of all phenomena.

It expounds the true emptiness of non-emptiness and reveals the true mark of formlessness. By clearly understanding that all things are illusory, one realizes they are like dreams, phantoms, bubbles, and shadows.
If one traces its root and source, it can be seen within the concepts of self, person, multitude, and life-span.

Truly, this is the secret essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs’ transmission of the mind; it is indeed the true doctrine of the Bodhisattvas’ turning of the teaching. Now, as for this "Mirror of the School" (Zongjing):

He was a man of the Song dynasty. His wisdom and insight were bold and far-reaching; his practice and realization were perfectly integrated. His characters encompassed the texts of the Tripiṭaka, while his principles realized the subtlety of the One True Reality.
Based on the full text of the thirty-two divisions of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he categorized and judged the great meaning of the entire scripture.
He extracted the essential framework and clarified the source of *prajñā*. Through the proclamation of verses and hymns, he demonstrated the nature of *tathatā*.

This wondrous principle is like a finger pointing at the moon: once the moon is seen, one forgets the finger. When one realizes that the moon of the mind is solitary and perfect, only then can one believe that its light encompasses the myriad phenomena.
Thus, the true words are made transparently clear and the secret meanings are rendered luminous and harmonious, so that both the wise and the ignorant may all attain Bodhi.
The "Dust and Purity" (Goujing) [text] is universally regarded as Prajñā. From the Song dynasty until the present day, it has been seen, heard, received, and upheld by every household, known to all.

The masters Da and Gui of the Tai [edition] have already published their commentaries; however, their wording and meaning are so profound and abstruse that they truly give rise to a chronic ailment among later students.
Furthermore, as the textual explanations are neither too expansive nor too concise, they fail to achieve a balanced middle ground—a point for which I have long lamented.
If you, sir, wish not to forget the intent of your former teacher, how could you possibly compose this in haste? You must instead request those with discerning eyes to collate and revise it.
Only when it is fully compiled will it be truly perfect. He immediately commissioned Mr.

Zhang Dànzhāi to carry offerings to the capital to join me in respectfully inviting the Master of the Great Dharma, Master Lián of Shàoshì Mountain, for a grand re-assembly. Furthermore, he requested Mr. Wú of Bīngshān to oversee the compilation and bring it to completion.
It was intended to be carved into printing blocks to be transmitted for eternity, so as to fulfill the vow entrusted by our late Master. Constantly...

In the Land of Tranquil Light, may they be made to give rise to joy. Should those from all quarters who study the Way suddenly devote their whole hearts to reading and contemplating these annotated texts, their deluded emotions will be eliminated, and the light of wisdom will arise, illuminating the vision of their originally inherent countenance.
By means of this extraordinary cause, I pray—
The sun of Shun shines with the same radiance as the sun of the Buddha;
may the Golden Wheel and the Dharma Wheel turn together.
At this time...

the junior monk Ying’ān Dàodēng, who received imperial edict at Zhìhuà Temple, respectfully records this colophon.
